chapters.title: A Trial Is a Decision
chapters.summary: This chapter asks what a clinical trial is for. It opens with SELECT, the semaglutide cardiovascular outcomes trial, and a ledger of what such a trial costs in patients, money and time, then argues that trialists should want a Bayesian approach because of the price of a trial, of being wrong and of waiting, and reviews evidence on how much efficiency real adaptive and Bayesian trials achieved and whether the approach is spreading. A counterweight section states the strongest objections. The chapter states the traditional trial fairly: a fixed sample size from a power calculation, randomization, alpha spending for interim looks, a multiplicity correction and a p-value in the clinical study report, together with what that apparatus costs. It then recasts the same choice as a decision, where a prior, a utility and a rule say when acting beats waiting, and shows that with a flat prior and one look the Bayesian rule is the one sided test. It previews the thesis and four mechanisms (the deviation scale, a single calibrated threshold with shrinkage, informative priors and optimal stopping), says what the regulator needs and does not need, gives a short history and maps the book. It proves nothing new; it fixes the vocabulary and the claim that the saving comes from monitoring, multiplicity and prior information and not from a lower bar.
chapters.literature: The probability that one treatment is better and allocation by it (Thompson 1933); sequential analysis (Wald 1947); the economics of experimentation (Grundy, Healy and Rees 1956); preposterior analysis and decision theory (Raiffa and Schlaifer 1961); trials as decisions for future patients (Anscombe 1963, Colton 1963); sequential boundaries (O'Brien and Fleming 1979, Lan and DeMets 1983); Bayesian interim monitoring (Berry 1985, Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar 1994); the SELECT trial (Lincoff and colleagues 2023, Ryan and colleagues 2020); trial costs (Sertkaya and colleagues 2016, Moore and colleagues 2018, 2020); adaptive efficiencies (Saville and Berry 2016); BNT162b2 (Polack and colleagues 2020); REMAP-CAP (Gordon and colleagues 2021); RECOVERY; substantial evidence of effectiveness (FD&C Act section 505(d), 21 CFR 314.126); ICH E8(R1), E9 and E9(R1); the FDA draft on Bayesian methodology (January 2026) and the EMA concept paper (2025).

chapters.title: The Life of a Drug: Phases I to IV
chapters.summary: This chapter walks through the life of a drug, Phase I to IV, and asks at each phase which decision is made and with what evidence. Phase I looks for safety and a dose, Phase II for signs of activity and the dose to carry forward, Phase III for confirmation and the regulatory decision, and Phase IV for what appears after approval. The chapter treats the phases as a sequence of options, where each phase buys information that is worth having only if it can change the next decision. It covers bioequivalence by two one sided tests (TOST) and a posterior summary, and then reads the phases in Bayesian terms: what a prior from one phase becomes in the next, and where the traditional separation of phases hides information. The rofecoxib story (VIGOR, APPROVe) appears as a Phase IV lesson on safety that a trial too small for harm cannot see. It proves nothing new.

chapters.title: The Regulatory Framework
chapters.summary: This chapter explains the legal and regulatory frame in which a trial is designed. It begins with the statutory standard of substantial evidence in section 505(d) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the 1997 amendment that allows one trial with confirmatory evidence, the regulation 21 CFR 314.126 on what adequate and well controlled means, and the 2026 draft on substantial evidence. It describes what a traditional submission looks like and what changes with a Bayesian adaptive design. It then goes through the ICH principles (E3, E6(R3), E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E11A, E20, M4, M15), the FDA design guidances (adaptive designs, master protocols, multiple endpoints, optimizing dosage, external controls, AI credibility), the history of Bayesian methods at the regulators before 2026 and the January 2026 FDA draft on Bayesian methodology with the response to it. It separates what the documents require, recommend and permit, describes how to interact with FDA (PDUFA meetings, the Complex Innovative Trial Design and MIDD paired meeting programs, CPIM, drug development tool qualification), and gives the EMA and MHRA counterparts. Case studies include REBYOTA, BNT162b2, pediatric belimumab, and the devices Superion and OPTIMIZER Smart.
chapters.literature: The standard of substantial evidence (FD&C Act 505(d), FDAMA 1997, 21 CFR 314.126); FDA guidance on adaptive designs (2019), master protocols (2022, revised 2026), multiple endpoints (2022), external controls (2023), expedited programs (2014), the Bayesian draft (2026) and the single trial draft (2026); the 2010 FDA guidance on Bayesian statistics in medical device trials (Campbell and colleagues 2011, 2023, Pennello and Thompson 2008); the Complex Innovative Trial Design program (FDA 2020); the 21st Century Cures Act (2016); ICH E9, E9(R1), E8(R1), E11A, E20 and M15; EMA reflection papers on adaptive designs and platform trials and the Bayesian concept paper; Ruberg and colleagues (2023) on Bayesian approaches in drug development; Evans and colleagues, Gelman and colleagues, and Lee and colleagues (all 2026) on the FDA draft.

chapters.title: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up
chapters.part: Basics: Comparing Groups, Randomizing, and Updating Beliefs
chapters.summary: This chapter builds the comparison of two treatments from the ground up with simulated and real trial data. It starts with one trial and two endpoints, reruns it many times, and derives the randomization test, the normal approximation and the z test. It defines the p-value carefully, explains confidence intervals and their duality with tests, and defines type I error, type II error and power. It explains why a one sided level of 0.025 is used, and covers noninferiority and equivalence against a margin, with the SURPASS CVOT noninferiority margin as an example. It closes with where the traditional trial stands and what changes next. Examples are RECOVERY (a rate ratio and an interval) and ANDROMEDA SHOCK (what not significant does and does not mean). The chapter proves nothing new; it sets down the traditional machinery that later chapters compare against.
chapters.literature: Randomization and the logic of the test (Fisher 1935, 1946); the Neyman and Pearson framework for errors and power (1933); the design of experiments (Cox 1958); p-value misreadings (Goodman 2008) and the ASA statement (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016); interval methods for proportions (Newcombe 1998); noninferiority testing (Blackwelder 1982, Dunnett and Gent 1977, Rothmann and colleagues 2003); FDA noninferiority guidance (2016); ICH E9 and E10; SURPASS CVOT (Nicholls and colleagues 2025); dulaglutide REWIND (Gerstein and colleagues 2019); RECOVERY (dexamethasone, 2021); ANDROMEDA SHOCK (Hernandez and colleagues 2019).

chapters.title: Randomization From the Ground Up
chapters.part: Basics: Comparing Groups, Randomizing, and Updating Beliefs
chapters.summary: This chapter asks why trials randomize and what randomization buys. It sets out the counterfactual problem and confounding by indication, what goes wrong without randomization, and the methods: simple, permuted block, stratified randomization and minimization, with how a schedule is actually generated and why allocation must be concealed. It develops randomization inference, discusses what randomness is (incompressibility and Kolmogorov complexity, and Arnold's measure), blinding, and intention to treat with the estimands framework and intercurrent events. It then asks why a Bayesian still randomizes, through ignorability of the assignment mechanism and the Bayesian arguments for randomizing. A long section covers covariate adjustment: ANCOVA, change from baseline, analyzing as you randomized, not testing baseline balance, binary and time to event outcomes, estimators robust to model misspecification, what FDA and EMA say, and the Bayesian version. It ends with what the protocol should state. Case studies are the MRC streptomycin trial, RECOVERY and the Women's Health Initiative.

chapters.title: Prior, Likelihood, Posterior
chapters.part: Basics: Comparing Groups, Randomizing, and Updating Beliefs
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces Bayesian inference through the same kinds of trials as before. It starts with Bayes' rule on a diagnostic test, exchangeability and de Finetti informally, and the coin with the Beta family. It shows the posterior mean as a weighted average and the prior's effective sample size, then redoes the two group comparison in traditional and Bayesian form, side by side, and explains why the two nearly agree. It compares credible and confidence intervals, introduces the posterior predictive distribution, and works the normal normal model on the log hazard ratio. It shows sequential updating, where the posterior today is the prior tomorrow, and that looking at the data does not change the posterior. It closes with what a protocol must say. Two trials that stated their success rule as a posterior probability are discussed: Pfizer and BioNTech BNT162b2 and REMAP-CAP. The chapter proves nothing new.
chapters.literature: Bayes' rule and the likelihood principle (Savage 1954, Edwards, Lindman and Savage 1963, Berger and Wolpert 1988, Berger 1985, Lindley 1985); Bayesian data analysis (Gelman and colleagues 2013); the BNT162b2 phase 3 trial (Polack and colleagues 2020, Pfizer statistical analysis plan 2020, FDA EUA review 2021); REMAP-CAP (Gordon and colleagues 2021); Morita, Thall and Muller (2008) on effective sample size; ICH E9 and E20; the FDA draft guidance on Bayesian methodology (2026).

chapters.title: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities
chapters.part: Basics: Comparing Groups, Randomizing, and Updating Beliefs
chapters.summary: This chapter asks how much evidence a result carries. It defines the p-value, reviews the ASA statement and the dirty dozen of misinterpretations, and develops the false positive risk. It compares the exact p-value with the Bayes factor, with a Gaussian example in closed form and Lindley's paradox, and asks how small a Bayes factor can be, which gives calibrations of the p-value. It then asks how much evidence is enough on three scales, shows that a test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss, and gives the Bayes risk of a test, what a fixed level implies as information grows, the type I error of the Bayes rule, and the Jeffreys table in terms of a threshold. It moves from p-values to posterior probabilities of benefit, including the FDA success criterion, the flat prior case where Bayes and the p-value agree, and how an informative prior changes the mapping. It compares four quantities side by side. Examples: EOLIA, ANDROMEDA SHOCK and false positive risk in practice (Zia and colleagues).

chapters.title: Choosing and Defending Priors
chapters.part: Basics: Comparing Groups, Randomizing, and Updating Beliefs
chapters.summary: This chapter treats the prior. It begins with the fact that the traditional design has no stated prior but does carry an implicit one, describes where priors come from in a sponsor's program (including the phase 2 selection problem), and gives skeptical, enthusiastic and noninformative priors. It shows why default flat priors fail on the scale that matters, through independent beta priors on the risk difference and flat priors on logistic coefficients, and introduces the conditional means prior. It measures how much a prior weighs by effective sample size, treats prior data conflict and robust priors, and gives sensitivity analysis over the prior scale, including the tipping point prior. It then reads what the FDA draft says, including the device precedent, compares the protocol side by side with the traditional one, shows how to write the prior into the protocol and what can go wrong. Cases are pediatric belimumab in lupus, REMAP-CAP and the multiplatform heparin trials, EOLIA and BNT162b2.

chapters.title: Error Rates, Power, and Sample Size
chapters.summary: This chapter turns to power and sample size. It gives the textbook calculation for binary, continuous and time to event endpoints, its sensitivity to the design alternative and the power curve, and what the regulator sees. It then shows that a conventional power calculation is assurance under a point mass prior, derives a closed form, states what assurance is not, and reviews Bayesian sample size criteria. A long section develops the moderate deviation sample size: the fixed n test has no memory of n, the power function and sample size equation, a surprising result about the saving, the role of prior odds in the constant, many parameters and endpoints, and a reading of SELECT against the formulas, with a candid statement of where the saving is and is not. It continues with sizing for the population in the sense of Anscombe and Colton. Cases: what a sample size costs, SELECT, why the phase 2 design alternative is too large, and platform arithmetic.
chapters.literature: Sample size for survival (Freedman 1982, Schoenfeld 1981, 1983) and the SampleSizeProportions package (Joseph and colleagues 2023); trial size as a decision for the future population (Anscombe 1963, Colton 1963); assurance and Bayesian power (O'Hagan, Stevens and Campbell 2005, Spiegelhalter and Freedman 1986, Crisp and colleagues 2018, Kunzmann and colleagues 2021); Bayesian sample size (Adcock 1988, 1997, Joseph and colleagues 1995, 1997, Lindley 1997, Chaloner and Verdinelli 1995, Pezeshk 2003, Sahu and Smith 2006, Brutti and De Santis 2008, Joseph and colleagues 2019 consensus); the cost of trials (Moore and colleagues 2018, 2020, Saville and Berry 2016); SELECT (Ryan and colleagues 2020, Lincoff and colleagues 2023); the FDA Bayesian draft and ICH E9, E9(R1).

chapters.title: Multiplicity and Shrinkage
chapters.summary: This chapter asks what multiplicity is and how to pay for it. It starts with many chances for luck and what counts as the family, then the traditional toolbox: Bonferroni, Holm, Hochberg, closed testing, fixed sequence and graphical procedures, and what the FDA multiple endpoints guidance asks for. It discusses subgroups and forking paths, and why a Bayesian must also ask how the result was chosen. The Bayesian alternative is shrinkage instead of threshold inflation: the idea, Stein, Efron and Morris and the batting averages, a numerical illustration of the winner's curse, and what shrinkage does not do. It treats false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg) and prior probabilities, where familywise control is not the target, and the Bayesian view of multiplicity, then a large trial with many subgroups (RECOVERY). It works through the four operation ulcer trial, compares the two ways to pay for looking, and extends to platforms across arms and drugs. Cases: I-SPY 2, REMAP-CAP and the FDA master protocol position.

chapters.title: Interim Looks and the Three Deviation Scales
chapters.summary: This chapter asks how to look at accumulating data without losing control of the error. It shows why repeated testing at a fixed level fails, develops the Armitage recursion, and compares O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock and the families between them, plus other boundary families (Armitage plans, the triangular test and designs with futility boundaries). It covers spending functions and the information fraction, futility boundaries (binding and non binding), and what a data monitoring committee does. The Bayesian sequential problem follows: the posterior does not depend on the stopping rule, a short history of Bayesian monitoring, the Bayes sequential decision problem, and Wald's test with its large deviation ledger. The chapter then develops the three deviation scales and their tolls, where the surcharge comes from, the seventy percent result, four boundaries compared and a sequential power calculation. It compares traditional and Bayesian monitoring side by side, runs one outcomes trial under three rulebooks, and gives a reporting template for the monitoring committee. Cases: truncated trials overestimate (Bassler and colleagues), heparin in Covid 19, the EOLIA futility stop and the Women's Health Initiative stop for harm.

chapters.title: Anytime-Valid Inference and E-values
chapters.summary: This chapter asks what validity at every stopping time requires, and what it costs. It begins with what a group sequential design does not cover (unplanned looks and continuous monitoring), then defines e-values as bets, test martingales and Ville's inequality, a betting martingale for a binary endpoint, the growth rate (how big a bet), and the odds of Cornfield in 1966. It covers likelihood ratio, mixture and process e-values (sequences of e-values indexed by time), passes from e-values to p-values and confidence sequences, and states the surcharge that validity at every stopping time costs. It relates e-values to Bayes factors, compares the power and stopping time of e-value, Bayesian and group sequential designs on a two arm binary design and a time to event design reconstructed from SELECT, and explains why the orderings differ. It adds a Bayes risk comparison, asks when a sponsor should pay the surcharge, shows a negative result for the mixture e-value with many subgroups at once, and gives what the regulator will ask. The case is BNT162b2, which had several interim looks on a schedule fixed in the statistical analysis plan.

chapters.title: Safety Signals and Safety Monitoring
chapters.summary: This chapter treats safety, where the question is whether harm is present and what to do about it. It starts with the rofecoxib cumulative signal: what the traditional analysis said, what a Bayesian reading adds, a move from inference to decision, and the naproxen hypothesis as a model comparison. It treats continuous monitoring with a posterior probability and an e-value, signals in spontaneous reports (the traditional proportional reporting measure and the gamma Poisson shrinker), toxicity monitoring inside a trial (the traditional counterpart, the Bayesian rule and operating characteristics), and aggregate safety assessment, which joins blinded pooled review, unblinded committee review, hierarchical models across adverse event terms and surveillance by a maximized sequential probability ratio test. It connects the two views and says what the regulator will ask.

chapters.title: Operating Characteristics by Simulation
chapters.summary: This chapter asks how a Bayesian design earns an error rate. It first describes what a traditional design computes and what goes in the SAP (the fixed sample design and the group sequential design), then the Bayesian success rule and why it has no error rate until calibrated, and why the uncalibrated rule inflates the error. It gives the calibration of the threshold and the interim boundary by simulation, with the algorithm and how to choose them, and a worked two arm binary trial with four looks: type I error across the null space, the null boundary, power, expected sample size, early stopping and bias, and the sources of calibration noise. It covers scenario grids and the worst case, the Goldilocks design, what the simulation report must contain, and software, reproducibility and what to submit. Cases: BNT162b2, REBYOTA, DAWN and Superion.
chapters.literature: Bayesian designs calibrated to frequentist operating characteristics (Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar 1994, Lewis and Berry 1994, Thall and Simon 1994, Rubin 1984, Little 2006); simulation for design (Muller and colleagues 2007, Berry and colleagues 2010, Morris, White and Crowther 2019, Mayer and colleagues 2019); group sequential theory (Jennison and Turnbull 2000, Wassmer and Brannath 2016, O'Brien and Fleming 1979); the Goldilocks design (Broglio and colleagues 2014); adaptive design reporting (Dimairo and colleagues 2020); FDA guidance on adaptive designs (2019), Bayesian statistics in device trials (2010) and the Bayesian draft (2026); ICH E20; BNT162b2 (Polack and colleagues 2020, Pfizer statistical analysis plan); REBYOTA (FDA briefing 2022); DAWN (Nogueira and colleagues 2018, Stryker statistical analysis plan); Superion (FDA summary of safety and effectiveness 2015, Pennello and Thompson).

chapters.title: Predictive Probability, Interim Monitoring, and Stopping
chapters.summary: This chapter asks when to stop for futility or success, and what the best rule is. It begins with the traditional interim: conditional power, futility rules, and sample size reestimation with the promising zone. It introduces predictive probability of success, from conditional power to the normal case, the exact beta binomial computation and a time to event example. It reviews the traditional phase 2 design (Simon's two stage design) where Bayesian monitoring started, predictive probability monitoring for phase 2, what that design is and is not, and the economic threshold. It describes the Goldilocks design with two predictive probabilities, then the Bayes optimal rule by backward induction: the decision problem, the sufficient statistic reduction, what backward induction does and does not do, and a single arm example. It compares designs, shows the protocol side by side and gives the regulatory reading. Cases: CALGB 49907, I-SPY 2, DAWN, BNT162b2 and GBM AGILE.

chapters.title: Response-Adaptive Randomization and Bandits
chapters.summary: This chapter asks when allocation should change as data accrue. It starts with the traditional default of fixed allocation (why one to one, and when unequal allocation is justified), then frames allocation as a bandit problem: exploring and exploiting, Thompson sampling, the Bellman equation, the Gittins index, regret and the Lai and Robbins bound, and why the analogy does not transfer as design advice. It tells the ECMO story (the Harvard two stage trial, the UK collaborative trial, how much the prior matters, what the rule did to information). It sets out the critiques of response adaptive randomization, the case against and the case for with the replies, and reproduces the critique. It explains time trends, the failure that matters most, with simulation and fixes, and when randomization helps with many arms, and gives what the regulators say and practical guidance. Cases: I-SPY 2, REMAP-CAP, BATTLE and SHINE with its Bayesian reanalysis.
chapters.literature: Allocation by the probability of being better (Thompson 1933); sequential design of experiments (Robbins 1952); the Gittins index (Gittins 1974, Gittins and Jones, Whittle 1980); regret (Lai and Robbins 1985, Auer and colleagues 2002, Agrawal and Goyal 2013, Kaufmann and colleagues 2012, Russo and colleagues 2016); bandits in trials (Berry 1978, Berry and Fristedt 1985); play the winner (Zelen 1969, Wei 1978, Rosenberger 1993, Rosenberger and colleagues 2001, Hu and Zhang 2004, Hu and Rosenberger 2006); ECMO (Bartlett and colleagues 1985, O'Rourke and colleagues 1989, Ware 1989, Kass and Greenhouse 1989, Royall 1991, UK Collaborative ECMO Trial 1996); critiques and replies (Korn and Freidlin 2011, Thall, Fox and Wathen 2015, Proschan and Evans 2020, Villar, Bowden and Wason 2015, Villar and colleagues 2018, Hey and Kimmelman 2015, Robertson and colleagues 2023); I-SPY 2 (Park and colleagues 2016, Barker and colleagues 2009); REMAP-CAP (Angus and colleagues 2020, Gordon and colleagues 2021); BATTLE (Kim and colleagues 2011); SHINE (Johnston and colleagues 2019, with a Bayesian reanalysis); Trippa and colleagues (2012).

chapters.title: Dose Finding and Dose Optimization
chapters.summary: This chapter asks which dose to carry forward. It starts with the traditional 3+3 design, its operating characteristics by simulation and what six patients can tell you. It then gives model based and model assisted designs: the continual reassessment method, the Bayesian optimal interval design (BOIN), mTPI, mTPI 2 and Keyboard, a comparison, escalation with overdose control, a worked logistic model decision and protocol language. It goes beyond the maximum tolerated dose to efficacy, toxicity and dose optimization: why the MTD is a poor target for modern agents, what the FDA guidance asks, a utility formulation, EffTox and phase 1/2 designs, late onset toxicity and time to event interval designs, and randomized dose comparison. It covers dose response estimation outside oncology by MCP Mod, adaptive enrichment, and seamless phase 2/3 designs. Cases: use of model based designs, BOIN and FDA's fit for purpose determination, sotorasib, dulaglutide AWARD 5, lecanemab phase 2b and ASTIN.

chapters.title: Time-to-Event Endpoints
chapters.summary: This chapter treats time to event endpoints. It starts with the traditional analysis (Kaplan and Meier, the log rank test and the Cox model), then shows that events are the information, derives the gamma posterior for a hazard, and gives predictive probability in an event driven trial. A section on non proportional hazards covers why the hazard ratio misdescribes a delayed or cure type effect, power loss under a delayed effect, and tests built for such effects (weighted log rank, restricted mean survival time and modestly weighted tests). It ends with regulation and practice, key points and exercises.
chapters.literature: The product limit estimator (Kaplan and Meier 1958); the log rank test (Mantel 1966, Peto and Peto 1972); the proportional hazards model and partial likelihood (Cox 1972, 1975, Breslow 1974, Kalbfleisch and Prentice 1978); event driven sample size (Schoenfeld 1981, 1983, Freedman 1982); early life table and survival models (Berkson and Gage 1952, Boag 1949, Irwin 1949, Holford 1976); weighted log rank and the Fleming and Harrington class (Harrington and Fleming 1982, Fleming and Harrington 1991); modestly weighted tests (Magirr and Burman 2019); restricted mean survival time (Karrison 1987, Royston and Parmar 2011, 2013, Uno and colleagues 2014, Trinquart and colleagues 2016); the hazard ratio as an estimand (Hernan 2010, Struthers and Kalbfleisch 1986, Alexander and colleagues 2018); Bayesian survival models (Ibrahim, Chen and Sinha 2001, Chen, Ibrahim and Sinha 1999, Murray and colleagues 2014, Roychoudhury and colleagues 2021); FDA guidance on oncology endpoints (2018), adaptive designs (2019), ICH E9 and E9(R1), and the Bayesian draft (2026).

chapters.title: Borrowing Information
chapters.summary: This chapter asks how external information can enter a trial without bias. It starts from what the traditional design does with prior data and the traditional objections to external and historical controls, then gives the Bayesian idea: exchangeability and hierarchical models, power priors and the normalized power prior (with a rare disease example that chooses the discount by marginal likelihood), commensurate priors, and meta analytic predictive priors with robust mixtures. It measures borrowing by effective sample size and conflict, and the cost of borrowing in type I error and power under drift. It covers pediatric extrapolation and ICH E11A, noninferiority with borrowed information and margin synthesis, indirect comparison through a common comparator (the tirzepatide chain), borrowing across subgroups in basket trials, and a case where borrowing failed (an NSCLC external control). It also covers prognostic covariate adjustment and digital twins, and gives a decision guide. Cases: REBYOTA, pediatric belimumab and OPTIMIZER Smart.

chapters.title: Master Protocols and Platform Trials
chapters.summary: This chapter asks how one trial infrastructure can answer many questions. It starts with the cost of separate trials, defines master protocol, basket, umbrella and platform, and describes frequentist multi arm multi stage designs. It does the shared control arithmetic (including the number of false positives), then concurrent and non concurrent controls: the regulatory position, a simulation of the bias, and the Bayesian time machine. It treats multiplicity across arms (FDA, EMA and Bayesian error control) and Bayesian platforms: I-SPY 2 graduation by predictive probability, GBM AGILE as a registration platform, REMAP-CAP domains and response adaptive randomization, the COVID anticoagulation multiplatform and the pragmatic pandemic platforms RECOVERY and PANORAMIC. It compares traditional and Bayesian platforms, covers governance, firewalls and the monitoring board, EPAD (a platform that never opened an arm), and what changes in the protocol.

chapters.title: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials
chapters.summary: This chapter reconstructs landmark trials to show what a Bayesian design would have changed and what it would have cost. SELECT (semaglutide and cardiovascular events) is the main case: the trial as conducted, three monitoring schemes and SELECT's own design with one error rate, the saving in calendar time and exposure, what the monitoring committee would have seen, and what a committee and a regulator would have had to accept. REWIND (dulaglutide) is the case where the scheduled design wins, with a Bayesian reconstruction and the final data under skeptical priors. SURPASS CVOT is an active comparator with a noninferiority margin, TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 a prespecified biomarker strategy with baseline tau strata, and BNT162b2 a Bayesian confirmatory trial that led to an authorization. The chapter values the saving (events and quality adjusted life years, trial cost, timeline and the acceleration bound), compares the protocol side by side and states the limits of reconstruction.
chapters.literature: SELECT (Lincoff and colleagues 2023, Ryan and colleagues 2020); REWIND (Gerstein and colleagues 2019); SURPASS CVOT (Nicholls and colleagues 2025) and the imputed MACE analysis of tirzepatide (Sattar and colleagues 2026); TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (Sims and colleagues 2023); BNT162b2 (Polack and colleagues 2020, Pfizer statistical analysis plan, FDA emergency use review 2021 and the licensure 2021); FDA guidance on cardiovascular risk in diabetes drugs (2008); the cost of pivotal trials (Moore and colleagues 2018); the FDA single trial draft (2026) and the Bayesian draft (2026); the FDA adaptive design guidance (2019); ICH E9.

chapters.title: Bayesian Reanalyses of Landmark Trials
chapters.summary: This chapter reanalyzes published trials in Bayesian terms from their reported estimates. It starts with the normal approximation and its posterior, then GUSTO (when prior trials disagree with the new one), EOLIA (probable benefit after a nonsignificant primary analysis), ANDROMEDA SHOCK (the same pattern with a hazard ratio) and RECOVERY (subgroups and shrinkage). It states what the four reanalyses share and what a reanalysis can and cannot claim: prespecification, prior choice, the regulator's view, and why a reanalysis is not a new trial. A section on what critics say places the cases in the literature on reanalysis and sets the critique of de Grooth and Cremer (that many priors do not contribute to consensus) beside the skeptical prior as an adversary. It ends with exercises.
chapters.literature: GUSTO (GUSTO Investigators 1993) and its Bayesian reanalysis (Brophy and Joseph 1995); EOLIA (Combes and colleagues 2018) and its reanalysis (Goligher and colleagues 2018, with the editorial of Lewis and colleagues 2018); ANDROMEDA SHOCK (Hernandez and colleagues 2019, Zampieri and colleagues 2020); RECOVERY (2021); the ECMO debate (Ware 1989, Kass and Greenhouse 1989); EXCEL (Stone and colleagues 2016, Brophy 2020); systematic reanalysis programs (Wijeysundera and colleagues 2009, Quintana and colleagues 2017, Ryan and colleagues 2019, Albuquerque and colleagues 2021); prior convictions (Diamond and Kaul 2004); skeptical and enthusiastic priors (Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar 1994, Freedman and Spiegelhalter 1983, Parmar and colleagues 1994); beyond subjective and objective (Gelman and Hennig 2017); the critique by de Grooth and Cremer (2024); the FDA Bayesian draft (2026).

chapters.title: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators
chapters.summary: This chapter asks what a Bayesian protocol must say and how to work with regulators. It goes through the protocol section by section, traditional first and then what changes: the prior, the success criterion and its calibration, the interim schedule and decision rules, adaptive randomization, safety rules and the estimand. It covers the statistical analysis plan and the simulation report, structured protocols (ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025), reporting guidelines (SPIRIT, CONSORT 2025, the adaptive designs extension, guidance on statistical analysis plans and the Bayesian checklists ROBUST and BARG), the data monitoring committee and firewalls, and the interaction timeline with FDA (including Special Protocol Assessment). It covers EMA and other regulators and the substantial evidence question of two trials, one trial, and where Bayesian evidence fits. Cases: BNT162b2, DAWN, REBYOTA, pediatric belimumab and the named examples in the January 2026 draft. It states what the Bayesian design does not buy, gives checklists and open questions.

chapters.title: Notation
chapters.summary: This appendix gathers the notation of the book and its link to the code. It lists the symbols used in the chapters (effects, priors, posteriors, thresholds, error rates, information and sample sizes), the correspondence between the notation and the arguments of the functions in the bayestrials package (such as the one sided type I error alpha, an effect theta, response rates p0 and p1, the number of patients or events n, and the number of simulated trials nsim), a list of abbreviations (for example FDA, EMA, ICH, DMC, SAP, MID, ESS, PP, FWER, FDR and MCP Mod), and a list of key terms from the whole book. It is a reference for readers who meet a symbol out of its chapter and want its meaning, its usual scale and the name of the matching function argument. It is also a place to look up an abbreviation before reading the chapter that defines it. The list of key terms at the end collects the vocabulary a reader would search for. Readers who meet a symbol out of its chapter can start here. It contains no results.
chapters.literature: None. The symbols follow the usual statistical conventions of the cited literature on Bayesian trials, group sequential designs and e-values.

chapters.summary: This appendix gives the regulatory documents cited in the book with their status as of November 2026, the products and trials named in FDA's January 2026 Bayesian draft guidance, and the FDA programs a sponsor can use. The documents include the FDA draft on Bayesian methodology, ICH E20 on adaptive designs, the FDA guidances on adaptive designs, master protocols, substantial evidence, multiple endpoints, optimizing dosage, data monitoring committees, externally controlled trials and device statistics, ICH E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E10, E11A, E4, M11 and M15, FDA guidances on artificial intelligence and new approach methodologies, formal meetings and special protocol assessment, the diabetes cardiovascular risk guidance, the EMA and HMA question and answer document on complex trials, the EMA reflection paper on platform trials and the MHRA draft on external control arms. The programs are the Complex Innovative Trial Design and MIDD paired meeting programs, Critical Path Innovation Meetings and Drug Development Tool qualification. It contains no results.
chapters.literature: FDA, EMA, MHRA and ICH documents as cited in chapter 3 (the regulatory framework), including the FDA review of REBYOTA (2022) and the FDA leader memo on belimumab (2025).

chapters.title: Software and Code
chapters.summary: This appendix describes the software that accompanies the book. It covers installation (R and the bayestrials package, with its tests), how the package is organized (functions in snake case whose prefix names the part of the book, with one argument convention throughout), a worked example, reproducibility (seeds visible beside every simulation, Monte Carlo error reported with results), the companion lab (an interactive tutorial with modules matching the chapters and a Bayesian trial simulator), and established trial design software in wide use: rpact, gsDesign, RBesT, SampleSizeProportions and SampleSizeMeans, BOIN, trialr, adaptr, bcrm, Stan and brms, FACTS and East Horizon, with a brief statement of the purpose of each. The descriptions cover only the purpose of each tool, so the reader should consult the tool's documentation for current features and versions. It contains no results.

results.name: The three deviation scales (evidence tolls)
results.summary: A fixed level test, a Bayes rule and an anytime valid rule act at three different sizes of the squared standardized score; for the normal mixture the anytime valid bar exceeds the Bayes bar by a surcharge that is about 2 log(1/alpha) at large information.
results.statement: Let $Z_n$ be the standardized score at information $I_n$, $q = I_n\tau^2$ for a normal prior of scale $\tau$, and $L_n = \log(1+q)$ the Ockham penalty. The one sided fixed level test at level $\alpha$ acts when $Z_n \ge z_\alpha$. For the symmetric normal mixture, the exact Bayes factor rule with threshold $b$ acts when $Z_n^2 \ge (1 + 1/q)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log b\}$ with $Z_n > 0$ for a one sided claim, and the anytime valid rule at level $\alpha$ is the same with $b = 1/\alpha$. In the large information approximation these bars are $Z_n^2 \ge L_n + 2\log b$ and $Z_n^2 \ge L_n + 2\log(1/\alpha)$, so that the anytime valid rule requires about $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ more, in squared standardized units, than the Bayes rule at $b = 1$ (exactly $7.38(1 + 1/q)$). This is a property of the normal mixture construction and not a universal cost of anytime validity: other e processes, such as iterated logarithm confidence sequences, behave differently.

results.name: The surcharge for validity at every stopping time is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement, as a comparison of boundary terms
results.summary: For the normal mixture e value rule, against the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar (posterior odds of one), the large information surcharge 7.38 is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial standardized requirement 10.51; this compares boundary terms and is not an exact sample size identity.
results.statement: With per observation standardized effect $\theta$, the information needed to act satisfies, in the large information approximation, $n_{\mathrm{MD}}\theta^2 = \log n_{\mathrm{MD}} + C$ for the Bayes rule and $n_{\mathrm{LD}}\theta^2 = \log n_{\mathrm{LD}} + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)$ for the anytime valid rule. Subtracting gives $(n_{\mathrm{LD}} - n_{\mathrm{MD}})\theta^2 = 2\log(1/\alpha) + \log(n_{\mathrm{LD}}/n_{\mathrm{MD}})$, and the last term is positive. On the standardized scale the surcharge $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ at $\alpha = 0.025$ is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement $(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2 = 10.51$ at 90 per cent power ($7.38/10.51 \approx 0.70$). This compares boundary terms asymptotically. It is not an exact sample size identity (at $\theta = 0.20$ and $C = 0$ the larger roots differ by about 80 per cent of the fixed requirement), and the exact surcharge is $7.38(1 + 1/q)$. The baseline is the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar; a calibrated Bayesian rule has already paid part of the surcharge, so calibration narrows the realized gap.

results.name: The Bayes factor bar exceeds the fixed level bar once information times prior variance passes about 46
results.summary: Against a single unadjusted look, the Bayes rule with a point null asks for more evidence than the fixed level test once the data carry about 46 times the information in the prior.
results.statement: At one sided $\alpha = 0.025$ the fixed level test acts when $Z_n \ge z_\alpha = 1.96$ (that is, $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge 3.84$), and the Bayes rule with equal prior odds acts, asymptotically, when $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge L_n$ with $L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2) \approx \log n$. They cross at $n^\ast = e^{3.84} \approx 46$, that is at $I_n\tau^2 \approx 46$ (the exact Gaussian expression gives 41.6), which is $n > 46$ for a unit information prior. At $\tau = 0.25$ on the log hazard ratio scale this needs $I_n > 730$, about 2,900 events (exact crossing 41.6: 666 and about 2,660 events). Beyond the crossing the Bayesian bar against a single unadjusted look is the higher one.

results.name: Moderate deviation sample size equation
results.summary: A Bayes rule whose bar grows like the logarithm of the sample size has an implicit sample size equation, the textbook formula with the critical value replaced by the square root of log n plus a constant.
results.statement: For the moderate deviation rule, which acts when $Z_n^2 \ge \log n + C$ (with $Z_n > 0$ for a one sided claim), the power against an effect $\theta$ with information $I$ per unit of $n$ is $\Phi\big(\sqrt{nI}\,|\theta| - \sqrt{\log n + C}\big) + o(1)$. Setting this equal to $1-\beta$ gives the sample size equation $n I \theta^2 = \big(\sqrt{\log n + C} + z_\beta\big)^2$, which is the textbook equation with $z_\alpha$ replaced by $\sqrt{\log n + C}$. The formula is an asymptotic approximation; it is not claimed to predict the size of any particular trial, including SELECT, whose planned size (1,225 events for a design hazard ratio of 0.83; the textbook formula gives about 1,211) is close to the textbook calculation at its own design alternative.

results.name: Moderate deviation and textbook sizes at the SELECT hazard ratio of 0.80 (not a prediction of SELECT's size)
results.summary: At a hazard ratio of 0.80 and 90 per cent power the textbook formula gives 844 events and the moderate deviation formula more; SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83, where the textbook formula gives about 1,211 events against the planned 1,225, so the formula does not predict SELECT's size.
results.statement: For a hazard ratio of 0.80 ($|\log\mathrm{HR}| = 0.2231$, $Z = |\log\mathrm{HR}|\sqrt{d}/2$ in terms of $d$ events) and 90 per cent power, the textbook calculation at one sided 0.025 calls for 844 events, and the moderate deviation calculation calls for 1,067 events at equal prior odds and 1,255 at prior odds of two to one against. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 per cent power, one sided 0.025 and 1,225 planned events, with one interim at two thirds of them (Ryan et al. 2020), and the observed hazard ratio was 0.80 on 1,270 events (Lincoff et al. 2023). The textbook calculation at the design hazard ratio gives about 1,211 events, close to the plan, so the comparison at 0.80 changes the design alternative and does not show that the moderate deviation formula predicts or explains SELECT\'s size.

results.name: Calibration of a posterior probability rule by the null maximum
results.summary: The smallest threshold that holds a monitored posterior probability rule to level alpha is the (1 minus alpha) quantile of the largest posterior probability reached over the looks in null simulations, so one simulation serves every threshold.
results.statement: Let $M$ be, for one simulated null trial, the largest posterior probability $\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > a \mid \text{data})$ that the trial reaches at any look it attends. The rule "success if the probability exceeds $c$ at any look" rejects exactly when $M > c$, so its type I error is $\Pr(M > c)$, and the smallest $c$ with type I error at most $\alpha$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$. The $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$ over the null simulations is a Monte Carlo estimate of it: it fixes the rejection proportion in the calibration sample and not the population error (the binomial standard error near 0.025 is about 0.0008 at 40,000 runs), so the threshold should be validated on independent null simulations. A single simulation serves every candidate $c$ (common random numbers). If futility stopping is part of the design, $M$ is the maximum over the looks the trial actually reaches.

results.name: Exact backward induction for binary endpoints on a cubic lattice
results.summary: For a two arm binary trial the Bayes optimal stopping rule depends only on the success counts and the stage, so backward induction is exact on a lattice of order T cubed states.
results.statement: For fixed prior parameters and horizon $T$ pairs, in a two arm trial with binary outcomes and independent beta priors, the optimal policy at stage $k$ is a function of $(s_1, s_0, k)$ only, where $s_1$ and $s_0$ are the success counts in the two arms, and the Bellman recursion evaluates $\sum_{k=0}^{T}(k+1)^2 = (T+1)(T+2)(2T+3)/6 = O(T^3)$ states, each in constant time.

results.name: A utility only backward induction rule declares treatment better half the time under the null
results.summary: A stopping loss that does not penalize false positives gives a good treatment choice rule and a useless confirmatory rule, because it declares treatment better in about half of null trials.
results.statement: In the calculation of Polson and Sokolov with $\kappa = 0.0005$ and a maximum of 100 pairs, utility only backward induction declares treatment better with probability 0.513 under the null (Monte Carlo standard error 0.005) and 0.98 at the large effect, with an expected sample size of 14.4 per arm. The classification loss version with $\gamma = 0.975$ has a null declaration probability of 0.026, power 0.903 and an expected sample size of 54.3 per arm at the large effect. This is a simulation result for the stated loss, prior and horizon.

results.name: SELECT reconstruction, median events at decision with conditioning
results.summary: In our reconstruction of SELECT at hazard ratio 0.80, a calibrated Bayesian rule stops at a median of 464 events among trials that declare efficacy and 486 over all trials, against 817 for SELECT's planned design (one interim analysis with Lan-DeMets spending, then the final); the e value rule and a four look design are slower or less powerful.
results.statement: In the SELECT reconstruction (true hazard ratio 0.80, normal prior of scale 0.25 on the log hazard ratio, at most 1,270 events, rules evaluated at every second event, 40,000 simulated paths, SELECT designed for hazard ratio 0.83 with 90 per cent power, 1,225 planned events and one interim at two thirds, Ryan et al. 2020), the median number of events at decision among simulated trials that declare efficacy is 464 for the Bayesian rule calibrated to 2.5 per cent one sided, 612 for the e value rule and 952 for a hypothetical four look O\'Brien-Fleming design. Over all trials, counting a trial that never crosses at its maximum, the medians are 486, 714 and 952. Power is 0.947, 0.831 and 0.977, and the realized one sided type I errors are 0.025, 0.0058 and 0.0255 (the Bayesian rule is calibrated to 2.5 per cent, the e value rule is bounded by it). SELECT\'s planned design (interim at 817 of 1,225 events with Lan-DeMets O\'Brien-Fleming type spending, then final) has median 817 in both senses, power 0.974 and type I error 0.0254. A single unadjusted look would cross at 309 events on the mean path, a mean path approximation and not a stopping time. The reconstruction is ours and not the sponsor\'s, and it is a counterfactual, not a power calculation made before the trial.

results.name: Four operation ulcer example, adjusted p value against posterior probability
results.summary: In the four operation ulcer example the Bonferroni adjusted p value for best against worst is 0.0855, while the hierarchical posterior probability that drainage is worse than 75 per cent resection is 0.952 on a contrast shrunk from 1.053 to 0.464.
results.statement: In the four operation ulcer example (counts illustrative, at the scale of the 1965 trial of Novick and Grizzle), the Bonferroni adjusted $p$-value for best against worst is $0.0855$, while the hierarchical posterior probability that drainage and vagotomy is worse than 75 per cent resection is $0.952$, on a contrast shrunk from $1.053$ to $0.464$. A posterior probability of $0.952$ is not a claim of statistical significance under strong familywise error control.

results.name: Reproduction of the BNT162b2 beta binomial analysis
results.summary: The statistical analysis plan's beta binomial model with a Beta(0.700102, 1) prior, applied to 8 versus 162 cases, gives a posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent of 1 minus 2e-28 and a point estimate of 95 per cent, matching the published interval within a tenth of a point.
results.statement: With the plan's prior $p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)$ and $s_1 = 8$ cases in the vaccine arm out of $s = 170$, the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(0.700102 + 8, 1 + 162)$. The posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent is $1 - 2\times 10^{-28}$, which clears the final analysis threshold 0.986. The 95 per cent credible interval for vaccine efficacy is about $(90.4\%, 97.6\%)$ and the point estimate is 95.1 per cent (plug in) or 94.9 per cent (posterior median), against the published 95.0 per cent with interval 90.3 to 97.6, without modeling the small difference in surveillance time between the arms.

results.name: Shared control false positive counts for four arms
results.summary: With a shared control, the chance of at least one false positive among four null arms falls from 9.6 to 7.8 per cent and the chance of two or more rises from 0.4 to 1.7 per cent, while the mean count stays at 0.10.
results.statement: For four null arms each tested at one sided level 0.025, four independent trials give at least one false positive with probability 9.6 per cent and two or more with probability 0.4 per cent. With a shared control and equal allocation these are 7.8 and 1.7 per cent, and with square root allocation (control $\sqrt{k}$ times an experimental arm) they are 8.6 and 1.2 per cent. The mean count is 0.10 in every case. The shared control values are Monte Carlo (400,000 draws).

acceleration-bound.name: Acceleration bound
acceleration-bound.summary: An upper bound on events averted if approval had moved earlier by the Bayesian saving for a whole treated population, which the book says is a bound and not a forecast.
acceleration-bound.body:
## What it is
The calculation supposes approval moved earlier by the all-trial median saving and that N patients received the treatment during that window, at the trial's placebo event rate of about 2.4 percent a year and its relative reduction of 20 percent. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]
The events averted are N times that rate times that reduction times the years saved. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]

## Why it matters
Two orders of magnitude separate it from the in-trial figures. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]
That asymmetry is the real economics of trial design: the value of a trial is overwhelmingly in the decision it enables for the population outside it. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]

## In the book
The post-trial population size is the $M$ of the loss function in the working paper. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]
For REWIND the all-trial median decision is the end of the trial, so there is no median calendar saving. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]
The summary table ranks the population QALYs row last and defends it only as a bound. [21/summary-of-the-accounting]

## Pitfalls
The calculation assumes approval, reimbursement, manufacturing and clinical uptake would all move forward by the full years, and none of those would. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]
Manufacturing capacity for these agents was the binding constraint on access, so the realistic acceleration is a fraction of the statistical one. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is the acceleration bound a forecast? A: No, it is an upper bound under assumptions that did not hold. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]
- Q: Which assumption would you relax first? A: The book names approval, reimbursement, manufacturing and uptake as all moving forward by the full time. [21/timeline-and-the-acceleration-bound]

ace-reporting-guideline.name: ACE reporting guideline
ace-reporting-guideline.summary: The CONSORT 2010 extension for reporting adaptive trials, which adds items on the prespecified adaptations.
ace-reporting-guideline.body:
## What it is
The CONSORT 2010 adaptive-designs extension (ACE) is the reporting counterpart for adaptive trials. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
It extends CONSORT 2010, predates CONSORT 2025, and adds items on the prespecified adaptations. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Why it matters
A Bayesian adaptive design is reported in two layers: the generic randomized-trial items and the adaptation items ACE supplies. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The guideline is not a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## In the book
The book lists ACE beside SPIRIT 2013, CONSORT 2025, a guideline on the content of statistical analysis plans, and the Bayesian checklists. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The Bayesian items that these lists do not name are the prior, calibrated success criterion, interim schedule, simulation report, software with seeds, and prior sensitivity. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
Placing each where the generic checklist asks for its traditional counterpart satisfies the intent of all the lists. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Pitfalls
None of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does ACE add to CONSORT 2010? A: Items on the prespecified adaptations. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
- Q: Is ACE required by regulators for a Bayesian trial? A: No. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spir.t: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025

adaptive-enrichment.name: Adaptive enrichment
adaptive-enrichment.summary: A design that starts with broad enrollment and restricts to responsive biomarker subgroups as interim data accumulate.
adaptive-enrichment.body:
## What it is
When benefit or the best dose differs by a biomarker-defined subgroup, broad enrollment can dilute estimates, and one dose may be wrong for part of the population. [sec-dose-enrich] An enrichment design starts broad and restricts to responsive subgroups as data accumulate. [sec-dose-enrich] At each interim, the subgroup posterior probability of benefit $\Pr(\theta_g > 0 \mid \text{data})$ maps to one of three actions: continue broadly, restrict enrollment to promising subgroups, or stop. [sec-dose-enrich]

## Why it matters
The thresholds are calibrated by simulation, which is what the FDA draft Bayesian guidance asks for. [sec-dose-enrich]

## Pitfalls
The multiplicity cost is real: subgroup-by-interim looks multiply chances of a chance finding. [sec-dose-enrich] Hierarchical models that borrow across subgroups are the Bayesian answer. [sec-dose-enrich] For dose-finding, dose-selection and enrichment decisions are usually treated separately unless the trial is built for both. [sec-dose-enrich]

## Check yourself
- Q: Name the three interim actions. A: Continue broadly, restrict to promising subgroups, or stop. [sec-dose-enrich]

adaptr.name: adaptr
adaptr.summary: An R package that simulates Bayesian adaptive multi-arm trials with response-adaptive randomization, early stopping and calibrated stopping rules.
adaptr.body:
## What it is
adaptr is an R package for simulating Bayesian adaptive multi-arm trials. [sec-software-tools] It handles response-adaptive randomization, early stopping and calibration of the stopping rules, summarized as operating characteristics. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
The book calls it the closest open R counterpart to the simulation part of `bayestrials` for multi-arm designs. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
The book lists it among the R packages on CRAN. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does adaptr summarize its simulations as? A: Operating characteristics. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Which part of bayestrials is it closest to? A: The simulation part, for multi-arm designs. [sec-software-tools]

adequate-and-well-controlled-investigati.name: Adequate and well-controlled investigation
adequate-and-well-controlled-investigati.summary: The study type defined in 21 CFR 314.126 that the statute requires: a clear objective, a valid control comparison, bias minimized, and an adequate analysis.
adequate-and-well-controlled-investigati.body:
## What it is
The statute leaves the phrase undefined, and FDA's regulation at 21 CFR 314.126 defines it. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means] Its purpose is to distinguish the effect of the drug from other influences, such as spontaneous change in the disease course, placebo effect, or biased observation. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]

The book paraphrases seven characteristics. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- A clear statement of objectives and of the method of analysis. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- A design that permits a valid comparison with a control. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- Subjects selected by an adequate method. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- Assignment that minimizes bias and assures comparability at baseline, usually by randomization. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- Measures against bias by subjects, observers and analysts, usually blinding. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- Well-defined and reliable methods of assessing response. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- An adequate analysis of the results. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]

## Why it matters
The book calls this the most useful list for a trialist to carry. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means] The regulation expects the protocol to state the proposed analysis methods, which is the regulatory root of pre-specification, for Bayesian analyses as for frequentist ones. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]

## In the book
The regulation names placebo concurrent control, dose-comparison, no treatment, active treatment and historical control as recognized control types. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means] The 2026 draft cautions that external controls differ from the treated group "because of the lack of randomized treatment assignment". [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which item of the list is the root of pre-specification? A: Item 1, a clear statement of objectives and of the proposed methods of analysis in the protocol, together with item 7, an adequate analysis. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]
- Q: Is historical control an admitted control type? A: Yes, but the 2026 draft warns about its weakness. [3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-controlled-means]

3/the-regulation-what-adequate-and-well-.t: The regulation: what "adequate and well-controlled" means

adverse-event-hierarchy.name: Adverse event hierarchy
adverse-event-hierarchy.summary: A hierarchical model across adverse event terms that shrinks many rare events toward a common distribution before flagging.
adverse-event-hierarchy.body:
## What it is

A hierarchical model across adverse event terms, as in Xia, Ma and Carlin, shrinks the many rare events toward a common distribution before flagging. [sec-safety-aggregate] It works in the same way as the gamma-Poisson shrinker does for spontaneous reports. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Why it matters

A trial reports many adverse event terms, so unadjusted flags multiply by chance. Berry and Berry borrow strength across adverse event categories within a trial, the within-trial version of the same remedy for multiplicity. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## In the book

After shrinkage a false discovery rate flag, such as the double FDR of Mehrotra and Adewale, limits the expected false-discovery proportion among flagged terms. Their procedure groups adverse events by body system. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Pitfalls

- Shrinkage protects against noise in rare cells, not against bias. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the hierarchy borrow across? A: Adverse event terms, shrinking rare ones toward a common distribution. [sec-safety-aggregate]

aggregate-safety-assessment.name: Aggregate safety assessment
aggregate-safety-assessment.summary: A sponsor safety review built from four layers: blinded pooled review, unblinded committee review, hierarchical models across terms, and a false discovery rate flag.
aggregate-safety-assessment.body:
## What it is

A trial's safety review is not one statistic. Four layers sit side by side; the sponsor runs three, and the unblinded comparison of arms belongs to the independent DMC, whose comparative results the sponsor does not see. [sec-safety-aggregate]

- [[blinded-pooled-review]] asks whether the overall event rate is higher than expected, without revealing the arms. [sec-safety-aggregate]
- The independent DMC's unblinded review compares arms, with the boundaries and posterior rules of the monitoring and toxicity sections. [sec-safety-aggregate]
- A hierarchical model across adverse event terms shrinks many rare events toward a common distribution before flagging. [sec-safety-aggregate] See [[adverse-event-hierarchy]].
- A false discovery rate flag, such as the double FDR of Mehrotra and Adewale, limits the expected false-discovery proportion among flagged terms. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Why it matters

Which layer is a trigger for action and which only a hypothesis for review is a decision for the safety plan to state, and the regulator will ask for it. [sec-safety-aggregate] The FDA guidance recommends reviewing accumulating events in aggregate and not one report at a time. [sec-safety]

## In the book

Outside the trial, surveillance of marketed products uses [[maxsprt]]. [sec-safety-aggregate] 21 CFR 312.32 lists an aggregate analysis showing more frequent events on drug than on control among the evidence that triggers an [[ind-safety-report]]. [sec-safety]

## Pitfalls

- No monitoring rule shortens or lengthens the reporting clocks. [sec-safety-reg]

## Check yourself

- Q: How many layers does the book list, and which one reveals no arm labels? A: Four. The blinded pooled review. [sec-safety-aggregate]

allocation-concealment.name: Allocation concealment
allocation-concealment.summary: Keeping the randomization list hidden from those who decide whether a patient enters, until the patient is irreversibly enrolled.
allocation-concealment.body:
## What it is
Sequence generation produces the unpredictable list. Allocation concealment keeps that list hidden from the people who decide whether, and when, a patient enters the trial, until the patient is irreversibly enrolled. [sec-randomization-concealment]

## Why it matters
Concealment is about the time before the assignment. [[blinding]] is about the time after it. A trial can be concealed and open label, which prevents selection bias but not bias in treatment and assessment. A trial cannot be properly blinded without concealment. [sec-randomization-concealment]

## In the book
The practical means are central randomization by an interactive response system, sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes and pharmacy-controlled coded packs. Central telephone or web randomization is the strongest and the usual choice in pivotal trials. [sec-randomization-concealment]

Schulz and colleagues examined 250 controlled trials. Inadequately concealed allocation went with odds ratios exaggerated by about 41 percent, and unclear concealment by about 30 percent. These are averages over one body of trials, an association and not a randomized comparison. [sec-randomization-failures] Another paper describes clinicians holding envelopes up to bright lights and opening several at once. [sec-randomization-failures]

The site sees only the kit number, returned after the patient is irreversibly enrolled. [5/how-the-schedule-is-actually-made] The protocol should say how concealment was done, and the book gives a model paragraph. [sec-randomization-concealment]

## Pitfalls
Even a perfectly random list is useless if the enrolling clinician can read it. [sec-randomization-failures]

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a trial be concealed but open label? A: Yes. Investigator selection bias is prevented, but bias in treatment and assessment is not. [sec-randomization-concealment]
- Q: Which method is strongest? A: Central telephone or web randomization, because it cannot be opened in advance. [sec-randomization-concealment]

ancova.name: ANCOVA
ancova.summary: Regress the follow-up outcome on treatment and the baseline value, which multiplies the variance of the effect by about one minus R squared.
ancova.body:
## What it is
For a continuous outcome with a prognostic baseline covariate, the standard adjusted analysis is analysis of covariance: regress the outcome on treatment and the covariate, and read the treatment coefficient. [5/continuous-outcomes-ancova]

If the covariate explains a fraction $R^2$ of the outcome variance within arms, the variance of the effect and the sample size for a given power are multiplied by about $1 - R^2$. [5/continuous-outcomes-ancova]

## Why it matters
With a baseline-to-follow-up correlation $\rho$, the variance relative to the final-value analysis is 1 for the final value, $2(1 - \rho)$ for the change score and $1 - \rho^2$ for ANCOVA. The change score beats the final value only when $\rho > 0.5$, and ANCOVA is better than both at every $\rho$. [5/change-from-baseline-or-ancova]

## In the book
For 90 percent power at a two-sided 5 percent level and a difference of 0.4 standard deviations, the example has the baseline explaining 30 percent of the variance. The book uses `covadj_ancova_gain` for this calculation. [5/continuous-outcomes-ancova]

FDA says power and sample size can be based on adjusted or unadjusted methods, and that the unadjusted choice is often more conservative. [5/continuous-outcomes-ancova]

In ANCOVA, with baseline as a covariate in a linear model, the treatment effect is identical whether the outcome is the raw follow-up value or the change, so reporting on the change scale is a separate question from estimation. [5/change-from-baseline-or-ancova]

## Pitfalls
The gain applies to a planned adjusted analysis: the covariate must be committed to in the protocol. [5/continuous-outcomes-ancova] The change-score analysis is unbiased in a randomized trial, but it spends precision. [5/change-from-baseline-or-ancova]

## Check yourself
- Q: When does the change score beat the final value? A: Only when the baseline correlation exceeds 0.5. [5/change-from-baseline-or-ancova]
- Q: By what factor does ANCOVA scale the variance? A: About $1 - R^2$. [5/continuous-outcomes-ancova]

andromeda-shock-trial.name: ANDROMEDA-SHOCK
andromeda-shock-trial.summary: A septic shock trial comparing capillary refill and lactate targeting, reanalyzed on the hazard ratio scale under five priors to show the EOLIA pattern again.
andromeda-shock-trial.body:
## What it is
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK randomized 424 adults with septic shock in 28 intensive care units to an 8-hour resuscitation targeting capillary refill time or serum lactate. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
Twenty-eight-day mortality was 34.9 percent (74 of 212) in the capillary refill arm and 43.4 percent (92 of 212) in the lactate arm, hazard ratio 0.75 with 95 percent interval 0.55 to 1.02 and $p = 0.06$. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]

## Why it matters
It shows the same pattern as EOLIA: the primary test did not reject the null, yet sizeable benefits stayed compatible with the data. [sec-reanalyses-share]
A cheaper, faster strategy that is probably better need not clear $p < 0.05$ to be adopted. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]

## In the book
Zampieri and colleagues used four priors on the odds ratio and found a posterior probability of benefit above 90 percent under all of them. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
The book works on the hazard ratio scale with five normal priors: flat, neutral (standard deviation 0.35), skeptical (0.15), pessimistic (mean log 1.1, standard deviation 0.15) and optimistic (mean log 0.8, standard deviation 0.20). [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
Its pessimistic row gives a lower probability of benefit than Zampieri's, which is not a contradiction because priors, scale and model differ. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
Capillary refill needs a finger and a stopwatch, and lactate needs a laboratory. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]

## Pitfalls
Our hazard ratio rows are not a replication of Zampieri's odds-ratio table. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
A hazard ratio of 1.1 is a ten percent higher instantaneous hazard, not a ten percent higher probability of death. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
Whether to adopt the strategy needs a utility function, a measured cost difference and a mapping to absolute mortality, which the posterior probabilities do not supply. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]

## Check yourself
- Q: How much prior skepticism does the result tolerate? A: The table of five priors shows it; a sufficiently concentrated prior at no effect also lowers the probability of benefit. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
- Q: Why is the choice of strategy not settled by the posterior alone? A: It also needs costs and utilities. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]

anytime-valid-inference.name: Anytime-valid inference
anytime-valid-inference.summary: Inference whose error guarantee holds at every stopping time, however the looks were chosen, built from e-values and test martingales.
anytime-valid-inference.body:
## What it is

A group sequential design is a promise made in advance: the number of looks, their timing and the boundary at each are fixed in the protocol. [sec-evalues] Anytime-valid methods give a guarantee that does not depend on the schedule. [sec-evalues] The central object is the [[e-value]]. [sec-evalues]

## Why it matters

Four situations leave the plan behind: an unplanned look, an external publication, continuous review, and extending the trial. [sec-evalues-gap] A guarantee that is a property of the data path covers all of them. [sec-evalues-gap] If the schedule is known and will be kept, a group sequential design is the more powerful choice. [sec-evalues-gap]

## In the book

A naive z test at the 0.025 level applied at every look inflates the false positive rate as looks increase. [sec-evalues-gap] The e-value rule, monitored after every observation, stays within its bound by [[villes-inequality]]. [sec-evalues-gap]

The always-valid p-value is $p_n = \min(1, 1/\max_{m\le n} E_m)$. [sec-evalues-p] It is nonincreasing in $n$. [sec-evalues-p] The validity costs the [[surcharge]]. [sec-evalues-surcharge]

No FDA or ICH guidance names e-values, test martingales or anytime-valid inference as of November 2026. [sec-evalues] A sponsor proposing one is proposing a method and should expect to justify it in a CID paired meeting. [sec-evalues] The book knows of no confirmatory drug trial that has used an e-process as its primary analysis. [sec-evalues-practice]

## Pitfalls

- The protection is against optional stopping only. It does not repair bias from unblinding, selective data collection or invalid model changes. [sec-evalues-reg]
- A posterior is coherent under any stopping rule, but a decision rule calibrated to type I error under a stated monitoring scheme is not. [sec-evalues-pay]

## Check yourself

- Q: A DMC adds a fifth, unscheduled look after the trial's own interim signal. Does a classical boundary schedule cover it? A: No. A look triggered by an interim signal in the trial's own data is outside the guarantee. [sec-evalues-gap]
- Q: When should a sponsor not pay for anytime validity? A: When the monitoring schedule is under its control and will be kept. [sec-evalues-pay]

armitage-recursion.name: Armitage recursion
armitage-recursion.summary: An exact numerical recursion for the density of the accumulated score at each look, which gives crossing probabilities for any boundary.
armitage-recursion.body:
## What it is

Armitage, McPherson and Rowe observed that the accumulated score is a Markov process. Given the score at look $k$ the next score is a normal increment, so the density of the score at look $k+1$ among trials that have not stopped is an integral of the density at look $k$ against a normal kernel, truncated at the boundary. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

With $S(t)$ Brownian motion with drift $\xi$ and $f_k(s)$ the density on the event of no stop through look $k$, the recursion is as follows. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_1(s) &= \phi_{t_1}(s - \xi t_1)\,\mathbf 1\{s < b_1\sqrt{t_1}\}, \\
f_{k+1}(s) &= \int_{-\infty}^{b_k\sqrt{t_k}} f_k(u)\,\phi_{\Delta_{k+1}}\bigl(s - u - \xi \Delta_{k+1}\bigr)\,du, \qquad s < b_{k+1}\sqrt{t_{k+1}},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\Delta_{k+1} = t_{k+1} - t_k$. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

## Why it matters

The type I error of the design is $\sum_k p_k$ at $\xi = 0$, and power is the same sum at the alternative's $\xi$. A futility boundary enters by truncating the integral in the other direction. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

## In the book

The package computes it with `gs_crossing_prob`, using Gauss-Legendre nodes, accurate to many digits. [11/the-armitage-recursion] Four equally spaced unadjusted looks at 1.96 give a one-sided type I error of 0.0631, more than two and a half times the nominal 0.025. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

The recursion is exact except for numerical integration, because it uses only independent normal increments and the fact that the standardized statistic is a function of the score. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

## Pitfalls

- Real trials depart from the Brownian model. Jennison and Turnbull show the canonical joint distribution holds asymptotically for a wide class of endpoints, and the simulation report is where departures are checked. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

## Check yourself

- Q: What makes (look index, score) a Markov chain? A: Independent normal increments and a standardized statistic that is a function of the score. [11/the-armitage-recursion]
- Q: How do you get power from the recursion? A: Sum the crossing probabilities at the drift of the alternative. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

arnold-randomness-measure.name: Arnold's measure of randomness
arnold-randomness-measure.summary: A geometric diagnostic that sums squared gaps between points on a circle to flag sequences that are too regular or too clumped to be random.
arnold-randomness-measure.body:
## What it is
V. I. Arnold proposed a geometric way to judge how random a set of points on a circle looks. His measure asks whether the points are spread the way independent draws would be: evenly spaced points are too regular, and clumped points are too attracted to one another. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]

Take $T$ points on a circle of length $L$. Let $x_1,\dots,x_T$ be the gaps between neighbors, so $\sum x_i = L$. The stochasticity parameter is the normalized sum of squared gaps: [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]

$$
s \;=\; T \sum_{i=1}^{T} \left(\frac{x_i}{L}\right)^{2}, \qquad 1 \le s \le T .
$$

## Why it matters
Evenly spaced points give $s = 1$, strong repulsion. All points in one place give $s = T$, strong attraction. For independent uniform points the expected value is $s_1 = 2T/(T+1)$, close to 2 for large $T$. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]

A schedule from a linear congruential generator with a short period or poor lattice structure fails such tests. That is a reason to use a modern generator such as the Mersenne Twister, the R default, or PCG64, and not to write one's own. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]

## In the book
With $T = 15$ points modulo 100, the sequence $37i$ sits at about 1.19, near the floor of 1, and is unmistakably too regular. The sequence $3^i$ is at about 1.55, inside the central 95% interval of random sets, so the measure does not reject it. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]

## Pitfalls
The measure is a diagnostic and not a theorem. With $T = 15$ the random distribution is wide, and a single sequence inside the interval proves nothing. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness] Such diagnostics detect pattern but do not certify an allocation mechanism. [5/key-points]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does $s = 1$ mean? A: The points are evenly spaced, strong repulsion, too regular to be random. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]
- Q: What is the expected $s$ for independent uniform points? A: $2T/(T+1)$, close to 2 for large $T$. [5/arnolds-measure-of-randomness]
