asa-statement.name: ASA statement on p-values
asa-statement.summary: The American Statistical Association's 2016 consensus on what a p-value can and cannot show, read together with Goodman's list of twelve common misreadings.
asa-statement.body:
## What it is

The ASA statement (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016) is the consensus statement of the profession on what a p-value can bear, and regulators and journals cite it [sec-evidence]. Goodman's "dirty dozen" lists twelve misreadings of the p-value [sec-evidence-asa]. A p-value is the probability of a test statistic at least as large as the observed one if the null hypothesis were true [sec-evidence-pvalue].

## Why it matters

Three misreadings recur in every trial team [sec-evidence-asa]. The fix the statement suggests is to surround the p-value, not to abolish it: a pre-specified primary analysis, an effect estimate with an interval, and an account of everything that was looked at [sec-evidence-asa].

## In the book

- "p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null is true" is false. The p-value is a probability of data given the null, and the probability of the null needs a prior [sec-evidence-asa].
- "A non-significant result means there is no effect" is false. EOLIA reported p = 0.09, and a later Bayesian reanalysis put the probability that ECMO lowers mortality between 88% and 99%, depending on the prior [sec-evidence-asa].
- "p = 0.05 in one trial and p = 0.001 in another means the second effect is bigger" is false, because the p-value mixes effect size with trial size [sec-evidence-asa].

## Pitfalls

The p-value is not a bad tool. It underlies the type I error control that regulators require [sec-evidence-pvalue]. Trouble starts when it is asked a question it was not built for [sec-evidence-pvalue].

## Check yourself

- Q: A trial reports p = 0.03. Is there a 3% chance the drug does nothing? A: No. The p-value is about the data given the null, not the null given the data [sec-evidence-asa].
- Q: A trial has p = 0.09. Does the drug do nothing? A: Not necessarily. The trial only failed to clear the bar [sec-evidence-asa].

sec-evidence.t: Weighing Evidence: p-values, Bayes Factors, and Posterior Probabilities

sec-evidence-asa.t: The ASA statement and the dirty dozen

assurance.name: Assurance
assurance.summary: The average of the power curve over a prior on the effect, the unconditional chance that the trial succeeds given what the sponsor believes.
assurance.body:
## What it is

With a prior $\pi(\theta)$ on the effect, the probability that the trial succeeds is the average of the power curve [9/power-is-conditional]:

$$
\text{Assurance} = \int \text{Power}(\theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta .
$$

This is eq-assurance. O'Hagan, Stevens and Campbell named it; earlier versions are predictive power and expected power [9/power-is-conditional]. For a normal prior $N(m, s^2)$ and a z test with standard error se,

$$
\text{Assurance} = \Phi\!\left(\frac{m - z_\alpha\,\mathrm{se}}{\sqrt{s^2 + \mathrm{se}^2}}\right).
$$

This is eq-assurance-normal [9/a-closed-form].

## Why it matters

A conventional power calculation is assurance under a point-mass prior [sec-power-assurance]. Uncertainty lowers assurance even when symmetric, because the power curve flattens near one [9/a-closed-form].

## In the book

For a trial sized for 0.20 at 90% power, a prior mean of 0.20 with standard deviation 0.10 gives assurance 0.75, and standard deviation 0.20 gives 0.65. Near a point-mass prior it is about 0.89 [9/a-closed-form]. For phase 3 sized on a phase 2 estimate, assurance is often 50% to 70% [9/a-comparison].

## Pitfalls

Assurance is a forecast, not a measure of evidence and not an error rate. It does not replace the scenario table of operating characteristics [9/what-assurance-is-not]. Type I error is computed under the null, whatever the sponsor believes [9/what-assurance-is-not]. Keep the design prior (to forecast) apart from the analysis prior (to be defended) [9/what-assurance-is-not].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does more uncertainty about the effect raise or lower assurance? A: It lowers it, for a prior centered on the design value [9/a-closed-form].
- Q: Is assurance the Type I error under the design prior? A: No, type I error is computed under the null [9/what-assurance-is-not].

sec-power-assurance.t: A conventional power calculation is assurance under a point-mass prior

astin-trial.name: ASTIN
astin-trial.summary: A Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial of a neutrophil inhibitor in acute ischemic stroke that stopped for futility at an interim.
astin-trial.body:
## What it is
The Acute Stroke Therapy by Inhibition of Neutrophils (ASTIN) trial was a Bayesian adaptive dose-response study of a neutrophil inhibitor in acute ischemic stroke. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke]

## In the book
Rather than a few fixed doses, it modeled the dose-response curve over a wide range with a smoothing model, so each dose borrowed strength from its neighbors. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke] The accumulating posterior chose later patients' doses, targeted the dose near maximum effect, and drove early stopping for efficacy or futility under prespecified rules. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke] The trial stopped for futility at an interim analysis. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke]

## Why it matters
The dose-finding model, allocation rule and stopping rule were all specified in advance and evaluated by simulation, as the 2026 FDA draft expects for a Bayesian design. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke]

## Pitfalls
The book keeps the description general. The exact dynamic linear model and allocation criterion should be taken from the original papers. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke]

## Check yourself
- Q: How did ASTIN share information across doses? A: A smoothing model of the dose-response curve. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke]
- Q: How did it end? A: Stopped for futility at an interim. [17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-response-trial-in-stroke]

17/astin-a-bayesian-adaptive-dose-respon.t: ASTIN: a Bayesian adaptive dose-response trial in stroke

award-5-trial.name: AWARD-5
award-5-trial.summary: A Bayesian seamless dose-finding trial of dulaglutide in type 2 diabetes, the best-documented precedent for the design.
award-5-trial.body:
## What it is
AWARD-5 tested dulaglutide in type 2 diabetes. It started in 2008 with seven doses and two controls. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding]

## In the book
Stage 1 used response-adaptive randomization with interim analyses every two weeks, scored by a composite clinical utility index of HbA1c, weight, heart rate and blood pressure. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding] Longitudinal modeling predicted the 12-month outcome from early data. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding] The algorithm selected two non-adjacent doses, 0.75 and 1.50 mg, at the earliest permitted time, and stage 2 used fixed randomization against controls. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding] In April 2009 randomization to 3.0 mg was stopped on the monitoring board's recommendation after heart rate increases and pancreatic safety concerns. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding] Both doses were approved by FDA in 2014. By Berry's estimate the design saved at least a year. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding]

## Why it matters
It needs a prespecified algorithm, an agreed role for the data monitoring committee, which could depart from the algorithm only on safety, and a simulated operating-characteristics report. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which two doses advanced to stage 2? A: 0.75 and 1.50 mg. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding]
- Q: Why was the 3.0 mg dose stopped? A: Increases in heart rate and pancreatic safety concerns. [17/dulaglutide-award-5-seamless-dose-finding]

backward-induction.name: Backward induction
backward-induction.summary: Finding the Bayes-optimal stopping rule for a stated loss and cost by working backward from the end of the trial over the sufficient-statistic lattice.
backward-induction.body:
## What it is

For a sequential decision problem with a finite horizon, a best rule exists for a stated loss and can be found by working backward from the end [sec-bi]. After $k$ pairs the trial stops and declares a winner, or pays a cost $\kappa$ for one more pair [15/the-decision-problem]. With $V_k(s_1,s_0)$ the minimum expected loss, the Bellman equation is

$$
V_k(s_1,s_0) = \min\Big\{ h_k(s_1,s_0),\ \kappa + \sum_{y_1,y_0\in\{0,1\}} \Pr(y_1,y_0 \mid s_1,s_0,k)\, V_{k+1}(s_1+y_1,\, s_0+y_0) \Big\},
$$

with $V_T = h_T$ at the horizon [15/the-sufficient-statistic-reduction].

## Why it matters

The sufficient-statistic reduction collapses the exponential decision tree to a lattice with $(k+1)^2$ states at stage $k$, so the recursion is exact and costs $O(T^3)$ states [15/the-sufficient-statistic-reduction]. It prices stopping explicitly through the cost per patient and the loss per error [sec-compare].

## In the book

A loss ratio of 39:1 gives $\gamma = 0.975$, which matches one-sided 0.025 only for a flat prior at a single analysis [15/the-decision-problem]. In the book's example a classification-loss policy gives power 0.903 with an expected sample size of 54.3 pairs against 100 for the fixed design [15/the-sufficient-statistic-reduction]. A utility-only rule declares treatment better with probability 0.513 under the null, so it is no confirmatory rule [15/what-backward-induction-does-and-does-not-do].

## Pitfalls

The rule is optimal only for the stated loss and prior, and the loss function is the design [15/what-backward-induction-does-and-does-not-do]. The lattice assumes outcomes are seen before the next decision and balanced allocation; delays and response-adaptive allocation make it harder [15/what-backward-induction-does-and-does-not-do]. No guidance mentions backward induction, so submit it as a pre-specified table [sec-reg13].

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a 39:1 loss ratio correspond to? A: $\gamma = 0.975$, which matches one-sided 0.025 only for a flat prior at a single analysis [15/the-decision-problem].
- Q: Why can the policy be computed exactly? A: The posterior depends on the history only through $(s_1, s_0, k)$ [15/the-sufficient-statistic-reduction].

15/what-backward-induction-does-and-does.t: What backward induction does and does not do

V(\pi_t, m) = \max\Bigl\{ \underbrace{m \max_k \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k]}_{\text{stop and treat}},\; \max_k \Bigl( \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k] + \mathrm{E}\bigl[ V(\pi_{t+1}, m-1) \mid \pi_t, \text{arm } k \bigr] \Bigr) \Bigr\},

results.name: Exact backward induction for binary endpoints on a cubic lattice
results.summary: For a two arm binary trial the Bayes optimal stopping rule depends only on the success counts and the stage, so backward induction is exact on a lattice of order T cubed states.
results.statement: For fixed prior parameters and horizon $T$ pairs, in a two arm trial with binary outcomes and independent beta priors, the optimal policy at stage $k$ is a function of $(s_1, s_0, k)$ only, where $s_1$ and $s_0$ are the success counts in the two arms, and the Bellman recursion evaluates $\sum_{k=0}^{T}(k+1)^2 = (T+1)(T+2)(2T+3)/6 = O(T^3)$ states, each in constant time.

results.name: A utility only backward induction rule declares treatment better half the time under the null
results.summary: A stopping loss that does not penalize false positives gives a good treatment choice rule and a useless confirmatory rule, because it declares treatment better in about half of null trials.
results.statement: In the calculation of Polson and Sokolov with $\kappa = 0.0005$ and a maximum of 100 pairs, utility only backward induction declares treatment better with probability 0.513 under the null (Monte Carlo standard error 0.005) and 0.98 at the large effect, with an expected sample size of 14.4 per arm. The classification loss version with $\gamma = 0.975$ has a null declaration probability of 0.026, power 0.903 and an expected sample size of 54.3 per arm at the large effect. This is a simulation result for the stated loss, prior and horizon.

barg.name: Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines
barg.summary: Author guidelines for reporting Bayesian analyses, one of the few reporting checklists written for Bayesian work and not a regulatory requirement.
barg.body:
## What it is
The Bayesian Analysis Reporting Guidelines (BARG) are one of the few guidelines written for Bayesian analyses, and they are author guidelines. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The other Bayesian lists are the seven-item ROBUST checklist and a consensus checklist for clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Why it matters
Generic protocol and reporting checklists have no named place for a prior, a calibrated threshold or a simulation report. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
BARG helps an author report them. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## In the book
A report that gives the prior and its source, the success criterion with its threshold and calibration, the interim schedule and the simulation report, the software and seeds, and the prior sensitivity analyses, each where the generic checklist asks for its counterpart, satisfies the intent of all these lists. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The sponsor checklist turns the same content into numbered items. [23/checklists]

## Pitfalls
None of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The reviewer checklist asks more than a reporting guideline does, for example whether the simulated design is the design that was run. [23/checklists]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is BARG a regulatory requirement? A: No. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
- Q: Who is the clinicians' consensus checklist for? A: Clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spir.t: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025

basket-trial.name: Basket trial
basket-trial.summary: A trial of one therapy in several tumor types or biomarker subgroups, where a hierarchical model lets small baskets borrow from one another.
basket-trial.body:
## What it is

A basket trial tests one therapy in several tumor types or biomarker-defined subgroups that share a molecular target. Each basket is small, and the question is which baskets respond. [sec-borrowing-basket] The traditional design runs a separate single-arm test in each basket with a multiplicity adjustment. The Bayesian design puts the baskets in a hierarchical model, for $K$ baskets with response rates $p_1,\ldots,p_K$: [sec-borrowing-basket]

$$
y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b).
$$
This is eq-hier. [sec-borrowing-basket]

## Why it matters

Berry and colleagues applied the hierarchical model to oncology subpopulations and reported designs needing fewer patients per subgroup than independent analyses at the same type I error, under their own scenarios. The quoted figure is 4 to 7 fewer patients per group, and shows what the method can achieve, not what it will. [sec-borrowing-basket]

## In the book

In a mechanism example with ten baskets of 30 patients, nine baskets have 12 responders (40%) and one has 3 (10%). The outlier raises $\tau_b$, the nine typical baskets are pulled down from 40%, and the outlier is pulled up from 10%. [sec-borrowing-basket] If all ten have 12, the estimate stays at 40% and intervals narrow. [sec-borrowing-basket] Variants include the calibrated hierarchical model (CBHM), BLAST and EXNEX. [sec-borrowing-basket] FDA lists basket trials under borrowing and asks for justified exchangeability and explicit effect modifiers. [sec-borrowing-basket]

## Pitfalls

A basket that does not respond has its response overestimated, by almost three-fold in the example, and its null hypothesis of no response may be rejected more often than under independent analyses, a false positive. The remedy is calibration by simulation with some baskets not responding. [sec-borrowing-basket]

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to a 10% outlier among nine 40% baskets? A: It is pulled up toward the others, a response overstatement. [sec-borrowing-basket]
- Q: Which error should be reported? A: The false positive rate for non-responding baskets. [sec-borrowing-basket]

All likelihoods, quadrature sums and grid weights are computed on the log scale (log-sum-exp), so well-defined posteriors never produce NaN, even when some grid points have a vanishing integrated likelihood.

battle-trial.name: BATTLE
battle-trial.summary: A biopsy-mandated trial in pretreated advanced non-small cell lung cancer that moved allocation toward treatments performing better within biomarker groups.
battle-trial.body:
## What it is

BATTLE was a biopsy-mandated trial of pretreated advanced non-small cell lung cancer with about 255 patients and four treatments: erlotinib, vandetanib, erlotinib plus bexarotene, and sorafenib [16/battle]. After an initial period of equal randomization, a Bayesian probit model moved allocation toward the treatments performing better within biomarker groups [16/battle].

## Why it matters

It is described as the first completed biomarker-based, adaptively randomized trial in this disease [16/battle]. It shows RAR used among several arms within biomarker strata [16/battle].

## In the book

The book also cites an earlier Bayesian adaptive randomization design for recurrent glioblastoma, evaluated retrospectively on four phase 2 trials [16/battle]. The lesson drawn is the caution of the multi-arm and time-trend sections: allocation inside small biomarker strata moves on little data [16/battle].

## Pitfalls

Because allocation moves on little data in small strata, the burn-in, the cap and an analysis that respects calendar time matter more, not less [16/battle]. The book's guidance for such designs is a fixed control share, a burn-in, capped probabilities and concurrent controls [sec-rar-practice].

## Check yourself

- Q: What preceded the adaptive allocation in BATTLE? A: An initial period of equal randomization [16/battle].
- Q: Why is RAR in small biomarker strata risky? A: Allocation moves on little data [16/battle].

bayes-factor.name: Bayes factor
bayes-factor.summary: The ratio of the probabilities that the alternative and the null assigned to the observed data, which turns prior odds into posterior odds.
bayes-factor.body:
## What it is

The Bayes factor measures the evidence in the data for one hypothesis against another. For a null $H_0:\theta = 0$ and an alternative with prior $\pi(\theta)$ [sec-evidence-bf]:

$$
\mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; \frac{p(y \mid H_1)}{p(y \mid H_0)} \;=\; \frac{\int p(y \mid \theta)\,\pi(\theta)\,d\theta}{p(y \mid \theta = 0)},
$$

$$
\underbrace{\frac{\Pr(H_1 \mid y)}{\Pr(H_0 \mid y)}}_{\text{posterior odds}} \;=\; \mathrm{BF}_{10} \times \underbrace{\frac{\pi_a}{\pi_0}}_{\text{prior odds}},
$$

the second being eq-bf-odds [sec-evidence-bf]. It weighs the data against both hypotheses and averages the likelihood over the prior, which is where its penalty for vague alternatives comes from [sec-evidence-bf].

## Why it matters

The p-value says nothing about how well an alternative explains the data. The Bayes factor does, but it needs a prior under the alternative [sec-evidence-together]. With a normal alternative $N(0,\tau^2)$ and $k = I_n\tau^2$ the integral is closed form:

$$
\mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; (1 + k)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left\{\tfrac12 Z_n^2 \,\frac{k}{1+k}\right\}, \qquad 2 \log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;=\; Z_n^2 \,\frac{k}{1+k} \;-\; \log(1+k).
$$

This is eq-bf-gauss, the finite-sample version of the Schwarz criterion [sec-evidence-gaussian].

## In the book

With $\tau = 0.25$ and $I_n = 400$ the penalty is 3.26, so the Bayes factor reaches 1 only near $|Z_n| \approx 1.8$, where the one-sided p-value is 0.036 [sec-evidence-gaussian]. See [[ockham-penalty]] and [[lindleys-paradox]].

## Pitfalls

The answer depends on the prior scale $\tau$. Choosing $\tau$ after seeing the data is as open to abuse as choosing the test statistic afterward, so pre-specify it [sec-evidence-lindley]. Sources sometimes write the ratio the other way up as $\mathrm{BF}_{01}$, its reciprocal [sec-evidence-bf].

## Check yourself

- Q: What turns prior odds into posterior odds? A: Multiplication by the Bayes factor [sec-evidence-bf].
- Q: Why does a vague alternative lower the Bayes factor? A: It spends prior mass on effects the data rule out [sec-evidence-gaussian].

bayes-risk.name: Bayes risk
bayes-risk.summary: The expected loss of a test over both the parameter and the data, weighing each error by its prior probability and cost.
bayes-risk.body:
## What it is

Let $D(y) = 1$ declare the treatment effective, $\pi_0 = \Pr(H_0)$, and let the loss be $\ell_1$ for declaring a useless drug effective (a false positive) and $\ell_0$ for withholding a useful one. The Bayes risk is [sec-evidence-bayesrisk]:

$$
r(D) \;=\; \pi_0\,\ell_1\,\alpha(D) \;+\; (1-\pi_0)\,\ell_0 \int \beta_\theta(D)\, g(\theta)\, d\theta .
$$

This is eq-bayes-risk. A frequentist who reports $\alpha$ and $\beta$ reports its ingredients, but not the weights [sec-evidence-bayesrisk].

## Why it matters

The rule that minimizes $r(D)$ is found one data set at a time:

$$
D^{B}(y) = \mathbf 1\{\mathrm{BF}_{10}(y) > b\}, \qquad b = \frac{\pi_0}{1-\pi_0}\cdot\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_0},
$$

which is eq-bayes-rule [sec-evidence-bayesrisk].

## In the book

With equal odds and loss, the exact bar on $|Z_n|$ is $\sqrt{(1 + 1/q)\log(1+q)}$. The type I error of the Bayes rule exceeds 5% for small trials, passes 5% at the crossing, and then falls roughly like $(q \log q)^{-1/2}$ [sec-evidence-bayestype1]. The fixed-level test has Bayes risk at least $\pi_0\ell_1\alpha$ at every $n$. For the Bayes rule both error rates tend to zero [sec-evidence-bayestype1]. A fixed bar spends a constant error forever [sec-evidence-bayestype1].

## Pitfalls

The alternative $N(0,\tau^2)$ puts mass on harmful effects, so $\Pr(H_1\mid y)$ is not the benefit probability $\Pr(\theta>a\mid y)$. Restricting the rule to $Z_n>0$ does not preserve optimality [sec-evidence-bayesrisk].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the fixed 5% test have Bayes risk that goes to zero as n grows? A: No, because its type I error stays at alpha [sec-evidence-bayestype1].
- Q: What does the Bayes rule threshold b contain? A: The prior odds times the loss ratio [sec-evidence-bayesrisk].

bayes-rule.name: Bayes' rule
bayes-rule.summary: The rule that reverses a conditional probability: the posterior is proportional to the prior times the likelihood.
bayes-rule.body:
## What it is
Bayes' rule reverses a conditional probability. A screening test has sensitivity 90%, specificity 95% and the disease has prevalence 2%. Sensitivity is a probability about the test given the disease, but the patient wants the probability of disease given a positive test. [sec-bayes-rule]

Writing the joint probability of disease and positive in two ways gives the answer. The prior $\mathbb{P}(D)$ is the belief before the result, the likelihood is $\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D)$ viewed as a function of the unknown state, and the posterior $\mathbb{P}(D \mid +)$ is the belief after. [sec-bayes-rule]

For a parameter $\theta$ and data $y$: [sec-bayes-rule]

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

## Why it matters
In a trial the unknown is no longer disease or not but a continuous quantity such as the response rate or the log hazard ratio, and the prior is a distribution over its values. [sec-bayes-rule] The Bayesian adds the prior and the multiplication. What is given up is practical: the answer depends on a prior that must be chosen, defended and written into the protocol. [sec-bayes-rule]

## In the book
A patient with a positive test has a 27% chance of having the disease, not 90%, because the disease is rare and most positives come from the large healthy group. [6/key-points]

ICH E9 permits Bayesian approaches when the reasons are clear and the conclusions sufficiently robust. It does not forbid them. [sec-bayes]

## Pitfalls
The denominator does not depend on $\theta$. It only rescales the product to integrate to one. [sec-bayes-rule]

## Check yourself
- Q: A test is 90% sensitive and 95% specific, prevalence 2%. Is a positive result 90% likely to mean disease? A: No, about 27%. [6/key-points]
- Q: What is the shape of the posterior? A: The prior times the likelihood. [sec-bayes-rule]

bayes-sequential-decision-problem.name: Bayes sequential decision problem
bayes-sequential-decision-problem.summary: Choosing a stopping time and terminal decision to minimize expected loss plus sampling cost, solved by backward induction on a sufficient statistic.
bayes-sequential-decision-problem.body:
## What it is

A design is a pair $(T, d)$: a stopping time $T \le N_{\max}$ adapted to the data and a terminal decision $d$. Let $\ell(\theta, d)$ be the terminal loss and $\kappa(\theta)$ the cost per enrolled patient. The Bayes rule minimizes expected total loss $\ell(\theta, d) + \kappa(\theta)\,T$ under the prior. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

With $V(n,S)$ the minimal expected future loss in state $(n, S)$:

$$
V(n,S) = \min\Bigl\{\min_d \mathbb{E}[\ell(\theta,d) \mid n, S],\;\; \mathbb{E}[\kappa(\theta) \mid n, S] + \mathbb{E}_{\text{pred}}\bigl[V(n+1, S+X_{n+1})\bigr]\Bigr\}.
$$

[11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

## Why it matters

The traditional design chooses the boundary to control a type I error and then asks what it costs. The Bayes design chooses the boundary to minimize expected loss and then asks what error rates it has. For error-calibrated use the second must be turned into the first by simulation. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

## In the book

A decision tree over $N_{\max}$ steps has exponentially many branches. Indexed by the sufficient statistic it becomes a table over states, filled by backward induction. For a single-arm binary endpoint the lattice has order $N_{\max}^2$ entries. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

The set of states where stopping is optimal is the stopping region, and its boundary is the Bayes boundary. The continuation region narrows toward the horizon because the option value of another observation shrinks. Early in the trial the boundary is wide, since a premature decision is expensive. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

## Pitfalls

- The exact shape of the continuation region depends on the loss and sampling cost, and it need not be triangular. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

## Check yourself

- Q: What makes the problem computable? A: The posterior depends on the data only through a sufficient statistic, so the state is $(n, S_n)$. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]
- Q: Why does the continuation region narrow near the horizon? A: The option value of another observation shrinks with fewer remaining observations. [11/the-bayes-sequential-decision-problem]

bayesian-adaptive-design.name: Bayesian adaptive design
bayesian-adaptive-design.summary: A trial design that can meet the legal standard of evidence sooner and with fewer patients on inferior arms, through monitoring, joint handling of arms and prior information.
bayesian-adaptive-design.body:
## What it is
The book's thesis has two sentences. A regulator approves a drug on evidence that meets a legal standard, and a Bayesian adaptive design can meet it sooner and with fewer patients exposed to inferior arms. [sec-decision-thesis] The saving comes from monitoring, from handling multiple arms jointly and from prior information, not from a lower bar. [sec-decision-thesis]

## Why it matters
Four mechanisms are usually run together and the book keeps them apart. M1 is the deviation scale. M2 is one calibrated threshold for monitoring plus shrinkage for estimation. M3 is informative priors. M4 is optimal stopping under a sampling cost. [sec-decision-thesis] M2 and M4 rest on structure a regulator can verify by simulation, M3 on a judgment that must be defended, and M1 is a mathematical fact with a trade-off. [sec-decision-thesis]

## In the book
Saville and Berry simulated 5,000 programs in which one in ten treatments works. A traditional sequence needed 1,966 patients and 12.0 years; an adaptive platform needed 640 patients and 3.2 years. This is a simulation, not an empirical result. [1/what-efficiency-looks-like-in-real-trials] REMAP-CAP reported tocilizumab meeting its efficacy criterion with posterior probability 99.75 percent. [1/what-efficiency-looks-like-in-real-trials]

## Pitfalls
The book does not claim that a Bayesian design dominates. [1/what-we-claim-and-what-we-do-not] In the REWIND reconstruction the scheduled design acts more often, though the Bayes rule decides earlier when it decides. [1/the-counterweight] Every gain has a price: a prior to defend, simulations to run and a design that is more work to specify. [1/what-we-claim-and-what-we-do-not]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the saving come from a lower bar? A: No, it does not. [sec-decision-thesis]
- Q: Where is a Bayesian design judged by the regulator? A: In simulated operating characteristics under a pre-specified design. [1/what-we-claim-and-what-we-do-not]

bayesian-borrowing.name: Bayesian borrowing
bayesian-borrowing.summary: Using external or earlier data in the analysis of a trial through a prior, with the amount of borrowing fixed in advance or adjusted by the data.
bayesian-borrowing.body:
## What it is

Bayesian borrowing puts earlier data into the prior for the current trial's parameter. Borrowing a whole historical control arm of $n_h$ patients is a prior with effective sample size $n_h$ [[effective-sample-size|(effective sample size)]]. [sec-borrowing-idea]

The methods differ in what they assume about the current control rate $p_c$ and the historical rate $p_h$: they are equal (full pooling), close with a fixed discount (power prior), draws from a common distribution (hierarchical model, MAP prior), either like $p_h$ or unrelated (mixture priors), or tied by a parameter the data update (commensurate priors, normalized power priors). [sec-borrowing-idea] The first two are static and the last three are dynamic, and FDA uses the same split. [sec-borrowing-idea]

## Why it matters

Every patient who need not be randomized to control can be treated, or the trial can finish sooner. [sec-borrowing] Done well, borrowing recovers precision a small trial cannot supply, and done badly it can introduce substantial bias that the small trial cannot reveal. [sec-borrowing]

## In the book

A traditional trial uses prior data only before it starts, to choose the alternative, the control rate and the sample size, and then ignores it in the analysis. [sec-borrowing-traditional] The Bayesian design lets prior data enter the analysis through a prior on the control parameter. [sec-borrowing-sidebyside] REBYOTA and OPTIMIZER Smart are the two regulatory cases of dynamic and static borrowing. [sec-borrowing-idea]
In the book's simulation, 60 treated and 30 control patients borrow a historical arm of 100 patients with 30 responders: full pooling raises power from 0.43 to 0.79, and matching that without borrowing would take roughly 170 control patients instead of 30. [sec-borrowing-drift]

## Pitfalls

Borrowing is not free: the price is measurable by simulation, and the regulator will ask to see it before agreeing to the design. [sec-borrowing] The methods decide how much to rely on external data once it is admissible, and do not make inadmissible data admissible. [sec-borrowing-external]

## Check yourself

- Q: Which of the five relationships between $p_c$ and $p_h$ are static? A: Full pooling and a power prior with a fixed discount. [sec-borrowing-idea]
- Q: What is the effective sample size of borrowing a whole historical arm of $n_h$ patients? A: $n_h$. [sec-borrowing-idea]

bayesian-logistic-regression-model.name: Bayesian logistic regression model
bayesian-logistic-regression-model.summary: A two-parameter logistic dose-toxicity model with informative priors, used with interval probabilities and an overdose bound.
bayesian-logistic-regression-model.body:
## What it is
The BLRM of Neuenschwander and colleagues uses a two-parameter logistic model with informative priors. It estimates the slope too, and needs informative priors to behave. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] It applies the overdose-control idea to interval probabilities of the DLT rate. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control]

## Why it matters
It shows what the posterior looks like at a decision point and how one early DLT is weighed against all the other data, which the 3+3 rule forgoes. [sec-dose-blrm]

## In the book
Doses are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 mg with reference dose 8 mg, and $\mathrm{logit}\,p(d) = \log\alpha + \beta \log(d/8)$. The priors are $\log\alpha \sim N(\mathrm{logit}\,0.25, 2^2)$ and $\log\beta \sim N(0, 1)$. [sec-dose-blrm] Four cohorts: 0 of 3 at 1 mg, 0 of 3 at 2 mg, 1 of 3 at 4 mg and 1 of 6 at 8 mg. [sec-dose-blrm] Underdosing is below 0.16, target 0.16 to 0.33, overdosing 0.33 or above. [sec-dose-blrm] The 16 mg dose is excluded because its overdose probability exceeds 0.25, and the next cohort gets 8 mg. [sec-dose-blrm]

## Pitfalls
The result depends on the prior. Rerun the table with a different `prior_sd` before trusting it. [sec-dose-blrm]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why was 16 mg excluded? A: Its probability of overdosing was above the bound of 0.25. [sec-dose-blrm]
- Q: Did the single DLT at 4 mg stop escalation? A: No, the model weighed it against the other data. [sec-dose-blrm]

bayesian-monitoring-history.name: History of Bayesian monitoring
bayesian-monitoring-history.summary: The lineage of Bayesian stopping rules from Freedman and Spiegelhalter in the 1980s and 1990s to the calibrated posterior rules of this book.
bayesian-monitoring-history.body:
## What it is

The Bayesian monitoring rule of the chapter has a lineage. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]

## Why it matters

The rule of the chapter keeps the posterior of these earlier proposals and adds the calibration of operating characteristics by simulation that a regulator asks for. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]

## In the book

- Freedman, Lowe and Macaskill proposed stopping rules that incorporate clinical opinion as a prior. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]
- Freedman and Spiegelhalter compared Bayesian monitoring with group sequential methods. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]
- Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar proposed skeptical and enthusiastic reference priors and a range of equivalence, with a rule that stops when the posterior probability of benefit, or of exceeding that range, passes a threshold. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]
- Grossman and colleagues gave a unified method for monitoring and analyzing controlled trials, and Fayers, Ashby and Parmar wrote the tutorial. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]
- Berry argued from the likelihood principle that interim analyses should not be penalized, and Rosner and Berry gave a Bayesian group sequential design for a multiple-arm trial. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]

The wider history of Bayesian trial design is in the book's decision chapter. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]

## Pitfalls

- Armitage held the other view: the logic of repeated significance tests applies to the trial, and a conclusion must account for how often the data were examined. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does this book add to the earlier Bayesian monitoring rules? A: Calibration of operating characteristics by simulation. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]
- Q: Which argument did Berry make? A: From the likelihood principle, that interim analyses should not be penalized. [sec-ch10-bayeshistory]

bayesian-protocol.name: Bayesian protocol
bayesian-protocol.summary: A confirmatory protocol that keeps the traditional skeleton and changes the sections that depend on how evidence is summarized: prior, success criterion, interim rules and operating characteristics.
bayesian-protocol.body:
## What it is
A Bayesian protocol shares most sections with a group sequential protocol and differs in a handful, and the handful is where reviewers will spend their time. [sec-protocol]
A traditional protocol states a null hypothesis, a one-sided type I error of 0.025, a fixed sample size or event count, scheduled interim looks and a stated multiplicity procedure. [23/traditional-first]

## Why it matters
Four things stay the same: the estimand, the default randomization, the calibration bar of one-sided familywise error 0.025, and the need to prespecify. [23/what-changes]
The sponsor owes the reviewer a simulation rather than a formula in each moved row. [23/what-changes]

## In the book
The prior is stated in full, with its effective sample size, the source of any informative component and a prespecified sensitivity analysis. [23/what-changes]
The success criterion is $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$, where $a$ is the minimum benefit and $c$ the minimum probability, both to be justified. [23/the-success-criterion-and-its-calibration]
The sample size becomes a maximum, and the looks are prescheduled with decision rules at each one. [23/what-changes]
Adaptive randomization, if used, belongs in the protocol with its limits: burn-in, floors, caps and analysis stratified by allocation period. [23/adaptive-randomization]
Safety can be stated as a posterior probability whose false-stop rate is simulated, and it sits outside the efficacy error budget. [23/safety-rules]
Nothing about the estimand is different, and the common error is to describe a convenient model in estimand language afterwards. [23/the-estimand]
Three rows carry most of the difference: interim looks, multiple arms and operating characteristics. [23/what-changes]

## Pitfalls
The protocol should not say "continuous monitoring": operating characteristics depend on when and how often the rule is evaluated. [23/interim-schedule-and-decision-rules]
Calibration is this book's default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing, not FDA's universal requirement. [23/what-changes]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which section has no traditional counterpart? A: The prior. [23/the-prior]
- Q: What replaces the closed-form power calculation? A: The simulation report. [23/what-changes]

bayesian-reading-of-phases.name: Bayesian reading of the phases
bayesian-reading-of-phases.summary: Each phase updates a posterior and hands it to the next, so one probability model spans the whole development program.
bayesian-reading-of-phases.body:
## What it is
Each phase updates a posterior and hands it to the next. Phase I produces a posterior over the dose-toxicity curve that becomes the prior for dose selection in Phase II. Phase II produces a posterior over the dose-response curve, and its predictive distribution gives the probability that Phase III will succeed. Phase III produces the evidence for approval, and Phase IV keeps updating. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

## Why it matters
The distinction is not that the traditional path passes verdicts and the Bayesian path passes distributions. A Bayesian program specifies one probability model across the phases, so what one phase learns propagates into the predictive probabilities of the next, whereas the traditional path links phases through estimates and judgment. [sec-lifecycle-reading] The rest of the book is about the conditions (calibration, pre-specification, simulation) under which a regulator will accept the alternative. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

## In the book
The phase map pairs each phase with its question, traditional design and Bayesian method. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

- Phase I asks safe or not and which dose. The traditional design is 3+3 and the Bayesian method is model-based escalation. [sec-lifecycle-reading]
- Phase II asks whether it works and at which dose. Traditional designs are fixed-dose arms or a single-arm response test; Bayesian methods are dose-response models, predictive probability and adaptive allocation. [sec-lifecycle-reading]
- Phase III asks whether it is confirmed. The traditional design is fixed or group sequential at type I error 0.025; the Bayesian method is a posterior success criterion calibrated to error control, or borrowing. [sec-lifecycle-reading]
- Phase IV asks about harm after approval. Traditional tools are spontaneous reports and observational studies; Bayesian methods are empirical Bayes shrinkage and sequential monitoring. [sec-lifecycle-reading]


## Check yourself
- Q: What becomes the Phase II prior for dose selection? A: The Phase I posterior over the dose-toxicity curve. [sec-lifecycle-reading]
- Q: Do traditional programs pass information forward? A: Yes, through estimates, models and safety findings. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

sec-lifecycle-reading.t: A Bayesian reading of the phases

bayesian-reanalysis.name: Bayesian reanalysis
bayesian-reanalysis.summary: Rereading a published trial from its reported estimates under a family of stated priors, to ask what we should now believe, not whether the trial crossed its threshold.
bayesian-reanalysis.body:
## What it is
A published trial gives a likelihood, not a conclusion. [sec-reanalyses]
The same three steps recur: reduce the report to an approximately normal likelihood for a log relative risk, a log hazard ratio or a risk difference; combine it with a small family of priors that represent defensible positions; and report posterior probabilities of effects large enough to matter. [sec-reanalyses]
The chapter applies this to GUSTO, EOLIA, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK and RECOVERY. [sec-reanalyses]

## Why it matters
Existence and magnitude of an effect are separate questions, and a posterior adds direct probability statements at chosen thresholds. [sec-reanalyses-share]
Each prior stands for a position someone held or could defend, so showing the posterior under each shows readers where they stand. [sec-reanalyses-share]
Decisions need utilities: the reanalyses supply probabilities and a utility turns them into choices. [sec-reanalyses-share]

## In the book
Each trial did its job: it answered the question its protocol asked. [sec-reanalyses]
In EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK the primary test did not reject the null, and the intervals (0.55 to 1.04 and 0.55 to 1.02) already showed that sizeable benefits were compatible with the data. [sec-reanalyses-share] EOLIA stopped for futility at its fourth analysis, after 240 patients. [sec-reanalyses-share]
The book's numbers differ from published reanalyses because it uses normal approximations on the stated effect scale and simple stand-in priors. [sec-reanalyses]

## Pitfalls
A reanalysis is done after the results are known, so the choice of priors, thresholds and scale is made in the light of the answer; it is exploratory in ICH E9's sense and should list every prior tried. [22/prespecification]
The FDA Bayesian draft is written for a trial designed to be Bayesian and says nothing that turns a post hoc reanalysis into evidence of effectiveness. [22/the-regulators-view]
A reanalysis uses the data once more: it cannot add patients, repair a design flaw or change the probability that the trial would have rejected a null effect. [22/a-reanalysis-is-not-a-new-trial]
A strongly positive posterior after a negative trial is a reason to run a confirmatory trial with priors written in the protocol. [22/a-reanalysis-is-not-a-new-trial]

## Check yourself
- Q: A trial misses $p < 0.05$ and a reanalysis gives a high probability of benefit. Is the trial now positive? A: No, the primary analysis missed its threshold and a reanalysis cannot change that. [sec-reanalyses-eolia]
- Q: What should an honest report list? A: Every prior tried, not only the favorable ones. [22/prespecification]

22/a-reanalysis-is-not-a-new-trial.t: A reanalysis is not a new trial

sec-reanalyses-eolia.t: EOLIA: probable benefit after a nonsignificant primary analysis

sec-reanalyses-limits.t: What a reanalysis can and cannot claim

bayesian-sample-size-criteria.name: Bayesian sample size criteria
bayesian-sample-size-criteria.summary: Rules that turn a design prior and an analysis prior into a sample size: average length, average coverage, worst outcome and posterior probability criteria.
bayesian-sample-size-criteria.body:
## What it is

Inoue, Berry and Parmigiani separate the Bayesian rules into families. Most involve two priors: the design prior that predicts the data and the analysis prior that turns data into a posterior [sec-power-criteria]. The criteria are the average length criterion (ALC), the average coverage criterion (ACC), the worst outcome criterion (WOC) and the posterior probability criterion [sec-power-criteria].

## Why it matters

Read by the question each answers, the length and coverage criteria size an estimate, the posterior probability criterion and assurance size a decision, and expected-utility criteria size a decision together with its cost [sec-power-criteria]. The power calculation is the posterior probability criterion with a point-mass design prior and a flat analysis prior [sec-power-criteria].

## In the book

At $\theta = 0.3$ (a point-mass design prior) and a flat analysis prior, 90% power needs 234 per arm [sec-power-criteria]. Under the design prior $N(0.3, 0.1^2)$ the assurance at 234 per arm is only 0.81 [sec-power-criteria]. With a flat analysis prior the ALC reduces to $n \ge 2(3.92\sigma/\ell)^2$ [sec-power-criteria]. If the informative prior is also the analysis prior, the prior alone gives $\Pr(\theta > 0) = \Phi(3) = 0.9987$, so the trial is unnecessary for an analyst holding it [sec-power-criteria]. In the lupus example, 50% on control and a hoped-for 25% on treatment needs 77 per arm by power. An estimation-based width of 0.3 gives 75 per arm [sec-power-lupus].

## Pitfalls

The criteria take their inputs from the design prior, so a sensitivity analysis applies. A smaller trial buys feasibility and costs the guarantee of a decision [sec-power-lupus]. For a confirmatory trial the regulator still asks for the operating characteristics of the final analysis [sec-power-criteria].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which criterion needs no design prior when the variance is known? A: The average length criterion [sec-power-criteria].
- Q: How does a power calculation appear among these criteria? A: As the posterior probability criterion with a point-mass design prior and a flat analysis prior [sec-power-criteria].

functions.name: decide_ss_acc_woc
functions.title: Average coverage (ACC) and worst outcome (WOC) criteria for a fixed-length interval
functions.usage:
decide_ss_acc_woc(
  n,
  l,
  sigma = 1,
  design_mean = 0.3,
  design_sd = 0.1,
  analysis_mean = 0,
  analysis_sd = Inf,
  gamma = 0.9
)
functions.description: The interval has fixed length l and is centred at the analysis-posterior mean. Coverage is computed under the design prior N(m_d, s_d^2). ACC averages the coverage over the marginal distribution of the data; WOC is the minimum coverage over the central gamma region of the data (the worst outcome in a set of probability gamma). With matched design and analysis priors and known variance the coverage is constant in the data and ACC = WOC.

bayesian-time-machine.name: Bayesian time machine
bayesian-time-machine.summary: A model that lets the control rate drift across calendar periods and borrows from neighboring periods with a smoothing parameter to use non-concurrent controls.
bayesian-time-machine.body:
## What it is

The time machine lets the control rate drift as a random walk across calendar periods and estimates the current control rate by borrowing from neighboring periods, with a smoothing parameter $\sigma_s$ controlling how fast the rate may change. Small $\sigma_s$ pools almost everything and large $\sigma_s$ is nearly the concurrent-only estimate. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine] It is the idea of Saville and colleagues, used in I-SPY 2, proposed for GBM AGILE and Precision Promise, and cited in FDA's Bayesian draft. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]

## Why it matters

When nothing changes, borrowing is nearly free. Under a step of 8 points in the last period, pooling is worse than the current period alone. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]

## In the book

The book's code is an illustrative first-order Gaussian smoother over four periods of 100 control patients, not the published second-order model. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine] Three histories were simulated: constant, linear drift of 2 points per period, and an 8 point step in the last period. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine] The learned smoother, which must infer a break from four periods, is worse than the current period alone under the step. Only the loosest fixed smoothing improved on concurrent-only data, and that value was fixed with knowledge of the scenarios. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]

## Pitfalls

Borrowing gains precision when history is stable and gives it back when history breaks. Three scenarios do not establish that it is better for other histories. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine] The simulation report must include a step change. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does large $\sigma_s$ approximate? A: The concurrent-only estimate. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]
- Q: Which history hurts pooling most? A: The step change in the last period. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]

20/how-big-is-the-bias-a-simulation.t: How big is the bias? A simulation

functions.name: platform_time_machine
functions.title: Time machine: estimating the current control rate under period drift
functions.usage:
platform_time_machine(
  shift,
  nsim = 4000,
  seed = NULL,
  p0 = 0.3,
  n_per = 100,
  taus = c(0.01, 0.03, 0.1)
)
functions.description: Simulation study of estimators of the control rate in the current (last) period when the true control rate drifts across periods. The true rate in period j is p0 + shift[j] and is used only to generate the binomial counts and to score the estimators. Every estimator is computed from the simulated counts and n_per alone, so identical observed counts give identical estimates whatever the scenario that produced them.

bcrm.body:
## What it is
bcrm is an R package for the Bayesian continual reassessment method for dose finding. [sec-software-tools] CRAN archived it on 8 May 2026. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
The book marks it as relevant to the dose-finding chapter. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
Because it is archived, it no longer installs from CRAN by default. [sec-software-tools]

## Pitfalls
Do not expect a default CRAN install to work. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does bcrm not install by default? A: CRAN archived it on 8 May 2026. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Which method does it implement? A: The continual reassessment method. [sec-software-tools]

belimumab-pediatric-lupus.name: Pediatric belimumab in lupus
belimumab-pediatric-lupus.summary: A pediatric lupus trial whose wide interval was supported by a post hoc Bayesian robust mixture analysis borrowing from two adult trials, with a tipping point at weight 0.55.
belimumab-pediatric-lupus.body:
## What it is

The pediatric trial of intravenous belimumab in systemic lupus erythematosus (C1109, PLUTO) randomized 93 children, 92 in the analysis below. At week 52 the SRI-4 response was 28 of 53 (52.8%) on belimumab and 17 of 39 (43.6%) on placebo, a difference of 9.2 points with an odds ratio of 1.5 (95% CI 0.6 to 3.5). [sec-borrowing-belimumab]

## Why it matters

That interval is far too wide to stand alone. FDA recommended a post hoc Bayesian analysis borrowing from two adult trials (C1056 and C1057) with the same SRI-4 endpoint and the same 10 mg/kg dose. [sec-borrowing-belimumab]

## In the book

The prior was a robust mixture with an informative component built from the adult placebo and 10 mg/kg arms and a minimally informative component, with borrowing weight $w$. [sec-borrowing-belimumab] The analysis was a tipping-point analysis over $w$. The posterior probability of efficacy reached at least 97.5% whenever $w$ was 0.55 or more, and the review division judged such a weight reasonable given a similar disease course, similar pharmacokinetics and similar baseline characteristics. [sec-borrowing-belimumab] The tipping point reports the smallest borrowing that supports the conclusion and leaves its plausibility to the clinical and pharmacological evidence. [sec-borrowing-belimumab]

## Pitfalls

The analysis was post hoc. The case study stresses that future programs should pre-specify it, with the discussion starting before the IND. [sec-borrowing-belimumab]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why was borrowing needed? A: The pediatric odds ratio of 1.5 had a 95% CI of 0.6 to 3.5. [sec-borrowing-belimumab]
- Q: What did the tipping point show? A: Posterior probability of efficacy of at least 97.5% for $w$ of 0.55 or more. [sec-borrowing-belimumab]

sec-borrowing-belimumab.t: Belimumab in pediatric lupus: a robust mixture and a tipping point

beta-prior.name: Beta prior
beta-prior.summary: The convenient family of priors for a probability, Beta(a, b), with mean a/(a+b); Beta(1,1) is flat.
beta-prior.body:
## What it is
The convenient family of priors for a probability is the Beta distribution, $\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)$, with density proportional to $\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}$ on $[0,1]$ and mean $a/(a+b)$. [sec-beta]

Beta(1,1) is flat: every value of $\theta$ is equally believable. Beta(2,2) is a gentle bell centered at one half. Larger $a$ and $b$ give narrower bells. [sec-beta]

## Why it matters
The binomial likelihood has the same algebraic form as the Beta density, so the update is addition: [sec-beta]

$$
\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b), \quad h \text{ heads}, \; t \text{ tails} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + h,\; b + t).
$$

The prior is worth $a + b$ patients, so the flat Beta(1,1) is worth two and Beta(30,70) is worth one hundred. [sec-ess]

## In the book
With 7 heads in 10 tosses, the Beta(2,2) prior gives Beta(9,5) with mean $9/14 = 0.643$. The flat prior gives Beta(8,4) with mean $0.667$. The traditional estimate is 0.70. [sec-beta]

In Bartlett's 1985 ECMO trial all 11 newborns assigned to ECMO survived. With a flat prior the posterior is Beta(12, 1). [sec-beta]

The BNT162b2 trial used the prior Beta(0.700102, 1), a prior of real shape and almost no weight. [sec-ess]

## Pitfalls
Two descriptions are in use: Beta(a,b) as $a-1$ prior responders, or as $a+b$ pseudo-observations. They differ by the two pseudo-observations of the flat prior. [sec-beta]

## Check yourself
- Q: Prior Beta(2,2), then 7 heads and 3 tails. What is the posterior? A: Beta(9,5). [sec-beta]
- Q: What is the mean of Beta(a,b)? A: $a/(a+b)$. [sec-beta]

sec-beta.t: The coin and the Beta family

sec-ess.t: Posterior mean as a weighted average, and the prior's effective sample size

bioequivalence.name: Bioequivalence
bioequivalence.summary: The finding that a generic or reformulated drug delivers the same exposure as the reference, declared when the 90 percent confidence interval for the geometric mean ratio lies within (0.80, 1.25).
bioequivalence.body:
## What it is
A generic or reformulated drug must deliver the same exposure as the reference product, measured by the area under the concentration-time curve and the peak concentration (Cmax), each of which must meet the criterion. The parameter is the ratio $\rho = \mu_T/\mu_R$ of geometric means. Bioequivalence is concluded when the evidence places $\rho$ within $(0.80, 1.25)$, classically when the 90 percent confidence interval for $\rho$ lies inside it. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## Why it matters
The classical analysis is the [[two-one-sided-tests|TOST]] procedure, equivalent to checking that the 90 percent confidence interval lies inside $(\log 0.80, \log 1.25)$. [sec-lifecycle-be] A Bayesian version asks directly for the posterior probability of equivalence. In a simplified normal model with a reference prior,

$$
\Pr\bigl(\log 0.80 < \eta < \log 1.25 \mid d\bigr) = F_{t_{n-1}}\!\left(\frac{\log 1.25 - \bar d}{s/\sqrt n}\right) - F_{t_{n-1}}\!\left(\frac{\log 0.80 - \bar d}{s/\sqrt n}\right).
$$

This is equation eq-lifecycle-be. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## In the book
Under the reference prior each one-sided posterior tail probability equals the corresponding one-sided TOST p-value, so the posterior probability of equivalence is $1 - p_L - p_U$. [sec-lifecycle-be] TOST at 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, but not the reverse. In an illustrative scenario a data set passes the 0.90 posterior rule with probability 0.9291 and fails TOST with p-value 0.0709. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## Pitfalls
TOST is the standard in FDA's final guidance of May 2026, so a posterior-probability rule would need agreement with the regulator and an evaluation of its operating characteristics. [sec-lifecycle-be] The model is a simplification, not the regulatory crossover analysis, and some highly variable drugs use reference-scaled approaches. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which implication holds, TOST success to posterior above 0.90, or the reverse? A: TOST success at 0.05 implies a posterior probability above 0.90, not the reverse. [sec-lifecycle-be]

sec-lifecycle-be.t: Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary

blinded-pooled-review.name: Blinded pooled review
blinded-pooled-review.summary: Review of the pooled event rate of the whole trial, without revealing arms, to see whether it exceeds the background rate expected in comparable patients not receiving the investigational drug.
blinded-pooled-review.body:
## What it is

Blinded pooled review of the whole trial asks whether the overall event rate is higher than expected, without revealing the arms. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Why it matters

It lets a sponsor watch safety while the trial stays blinded. The FDA guidance recommends keeping individual treatment assignments blinded where the trial is blinded, with unblinded aggregate review by a group independent of the sponsor's study team. [sec-safety]

## In the book

Given credible external information about adverse event rates in comparable patients not receiving the investigational drug, Gould and Wang describe Bayesian monitoring for potential excess risk using pooled blinded data. Their title calls it the canary in the coal mine. [sec-safety-aggregate] It sits beside the unblinded DMC review, which compares arms. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Pitfalls

- It needs credible external rates for the comparison to mean anything. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the pooled blinded review compare the overall rate with? A: The expected rate from external information on comparable patients not receiving the investigational drug. [sec-safety-aggregate]

blinding.name: Blinding
blinding.summary: Keeping participants, investigators or analysts unaware of the assigned treatment after allocation, to protect against bias in reporting, care and judging outcomes.
blinding.body:
## What it is
Randomization protects the comparison against bias in who receives each treatment. Blinding, also called masking, protects it against bias in what happens afterward: how patients report symptoms, how investigators care for them and how outcomes are judged. [sec-randomization-blinding]

ICH E9 defines a double-blind trial as one in which neither the subject nor any of the investigator or sponsor staff involved in treatment or evaluation are aware of the treatment received. [sec-randomization-blinding]

## Why it matters
The book lists open label, single blind, double blind, triple blind (also the data analysts) and blinded outcome assessment. Blinding matters most when outcomes are subjective, such as pain, depression or symptom scores. [sec-randomization-blinding]

## In the book
RECOVERY compared dexamethasone with usual care without blinding. The primary outcome was death within 28 days, an objective endpoint that limits assessment bias. [sec-randomization-blinding] When masking is impossible, as with surgery or devices, the protocol should use blinded outcome assessment and objective endpoints. [sec-randomization-blinding]

Maintaining the blind takes work: matching placebos, a double-dummy design when comparators differ in form, independent unblinded staff and a prespecified emergency unblinding procedure. [sec-randomization-blinding]

## Pitfalls
Side effects can unblind, such as nausea, a rash or a visible lab change. [sec-randomization-blinding] The DMC and its statistician see unblinded data and the sponsor does not, so the charter should state who sees what and when. [sec-randomization-blinding]

## Check yourself
- Q: When is an open-label trial still informative? A: When the outcome is objective, as with death within 28 days in RECOVERY. [sec-randomization-blinding]
- Q: Can a trial be properly blinded without concealment? A: No. An investigator who knows the next assignment already knows the arm. [sec-randomization-concealment]

bnt162b2-trial.name: BNT162b2 trial
bnt162b2-trial.summary: The phase 2/3 vaccine trial whose success rule was a posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 percent, with a weak Beta prior.
bnt162b2-trial.body:
## What it is
The phase 2/3 trial of the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine is the book's cleanest large example of a Bayesian success rule. Its statistical analysis plan used a beta-binomial model, conditional on the total number of first COVID-19 cases $s$, of whom $s_1$ occur in the vaccine arm. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]

## Why it matters
With equal allocation and follow-up, a case falls in the vaccine arm with probability $p = (1 - \mathrm{VE})/(2 - \mathrm{VE})$. The prior is $p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)$, with mean 0.4118, the value of $p$ at VE $= 30\%$. The plan calls it minimally informative. Its effective sample size is 1.7 cases. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]

## In the book
- Design feature: efficacy was declared if $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.986$ at the final analysis, and above 0.995 at an interim. The thresholds were calibrated to a one-sided type I error of 2.5%. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]
- Plan: final analysis at 164 cases, with interim looks at 62, 92 and 120 cases. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]
- Result: 8 cases in the vaccine group against 162 in the placebo group, so $s = 170$ and $s_1 = 8$. The posterior is Beta(0.700102 + 8, 1 + 162). [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]
- The posterior probability that VE exceeds 30% is $1 - 2 \times 10^{-28}$. The 95% credible interval for VE is about (90.4%, 97.6%), with a point estimate of 95.1% (plug-in) or 94.9% (posterior median). The paper reports 95.0% with interval 90.3 to 97.6. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]
- FDA authorized the vaccine for individuals 16 years and older on 11 December 2020, and approved the biologics license on 23 August 2021. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]

## Pitfalls
With ESS 1.7 and 170 cases the prior is irrelevant to the conclusion, and a flat prior would shift the interval by well under a point. The statistical analysis plan cited is version 10 dated 7 October 2022, not an archived 2020 version. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]

## Check yourself
- Q: What posterior probability did the final analysis need? A: $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} > 30\% \mid \text{data}) > 0.986$. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]
- Q: Does the prior carry the result? A: No. It was chosen to be defensible, not to carry the result. [6/pfizer-biontech-bnt162b2-phase-3-c4591001]

results.name: Reproduction of the BNT162b2 beta binomial analysis
results.summary: The statistical analysis plan's beta binomial model with a Beta(0.700102, 1) prior, applied to 8 versus 162 cases, gives a posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent of 1 minus 2e-28 and a point estimate of 95 per cent, matching the published interval within a tenth of a point.
results.statement: With the plan's prior $p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(0.700102, 1)$ and $s_1 = 8$ cases in the vaccine arm out of $s = 170$, the posterior is $\mathrm{Beta}(0.700102 + 8, 1 + 162)$. The posterior probability that vaccine efficacy exceeds 30 per cent is $1 - 2\times 10^{-28}$, which clears the final analysis threshold 0.986. The 95 per cent credible interval for vaccine efficacy is about $(90.4\%, 97.6\%)$ and the point estimate is 95.1 per cent (plug in) or 94.9 per cent (posterior median), against the published 95.0 per cent with interval 90.3 to 97.6, without modeling the small difference in surveillance time between the arms.

boin-design.name: Bayesian optimal interval design
boin-design.summary: A model-assisted phase 1 design whose escalate, stay or de-escalate decisions come from fixed boundaries on the observed DLT rate.
boin-design.body:
## What it is
BOIN of Liu and Yuan is derived from a Bayesian argument, but at the bedside it is a table. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design] The observed DLT rate at a dose is compared with two fixed boundaries: escalate if it is at most $\lambda_e$, de-escalate if at least $\lambda_d$, otherwise stay. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design] The boundaries minimize the chance of a wrong decision between three simple hypotheses, at the target, at $0.6\,\Gamma$ and at $1.4\,\Gamma$. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design] They do not depend on the dose or the number treated. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design]

## Why it matters
The protocol carries a grid of DLT counts and patient numbers, like the 3+3, so no software is needed on the day. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design]

## In the book
With cohorts of three and the book's target DLT rate, the rule is to escalate on zero DLTs and de-escalate on one or more (at a target of 0.30, one DLT in three means stay). [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design] A dose is eliminated with all higher ones if the posterior probability that its DLT rate exceeds the target is above 0.95. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design] With 30 patients BOIN selects the true MTD more often than the 3+3. [17/comparing-the-designs] At 15 patients it is about level with the 3+3 in scenario B. [17/comparing-the-designs]

## Pitfalls
FDA's determination concerns a context of use and does not exempt a sponsor from simulations for its own trial. [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design]

## Check yourself
- Q: With cohorts of three, what does BOIN do after one DLT? A: De-escalate at the book's target (at a target of 0.30, one DLT in three means stay). [17/the-bayesian-optimal-interval-design]
- Q: What must the protocol attach for BOIN? A: The boundaries, the elimination rule and a simulation report. [17/protocol-language]

bonferroni-correction.name: Bonferroni correction
bonferroni-correction.summary: Test each of k hypotheses at alpha divided by k, which controls the familywise error rate whatever the dependence, at a cost in power.
bonferroni-correction.body:
## What it is

With $k$ hypotheses and a familywise level $\alpha$, test each at $\alpha/k$. Equivalently, multiply each $p$-value by $k$ and compare to $\alpha$. [10/bonferroni]

The union bound guarantees the probability of any false rejection is at most $\alpha$, whatever the dependence between the tests. [10/bonferroni]

## Why it matters

The guarantee needs no assumption and can be explained to a clinician in one sentence. That is why Bonferroni is in every guidance and every statistical analysis plan. [10/bonferroni]

## In the book

For $k=6$ the per-test level is $0.025/6 = 0.00417$, and the critical value moves from $z=1.96$ to $z=2.64$. [10/bonferroni] In the six-endpoint example all three adjusted procedures reject only E1, whose $p$-value 0.004 is just under 0.025/6. [10/hochberg]

Dunn made the inequality a multiple-comparison method. Dunnett gave an exact procedure based on the multivariate $t$ distribution for several treatments against one control, which is less conservative because it uses the correlation induced by the shared control. [10/bonferroni]

## Pitfalls

- The cost is power. A trial sized for 90% power at the unadjusted level has noticeably less after adjustment. [10/bonferroni]
- When one or two hypotheses are truly effects, Bonferroni pays to guard against errors that cannot occur. [10/bonferroni]
- There is no good reason to use plain Bonferroni when Holm is available, other than protocol simplicity. [10/holm]

## Check yourself

- Q: What is the per-test level for six hypotheses at 0.025? A: 0.00417. [10/bonferroni]
- Q: Does Bonferroni need independence? A: No, the union bound holds whatever the dependence. [10/bonferroni]

borrowing-under-drift.name: Borrowing under drift
borrowing-under-drift.summary: The type I error inflation and power change that borrowing causes when the true current control rate differs from the historical rate.
borrowing-under-drift.body:
## What it is

Drift is the gap between the true current control rate and the historical rate. The central calculation takes 60 treated and 30 control patients, a historical arm of 30 responders in 100, and the rule $\Pr(\delta>0 \mid \text{data}) > 0.975$. It compares no borrowing, full pooling, a power prior with $a_0=0.3$ and a robust mixture, for drift from $-0.15$ to $+0.20$. The enumeration is exact. [sec-borrowing-drift]

## Why it matters

Without drift, borrowing buys power: matching the power of full pooling without borrowing would need roughly 170 control patients rather than 30. [sec-borrowing-drift] With upward drift it inflates type I error, and with downward drift it costs power. Neither is controlled by the trial. [sec-borrowing-drift]

## In the book

The type I error without borrowing barely moves, which is what the traditional design buys by discarding prior data. [sec-borrowing-drift] The robust prior is not a cure at a ten point drift. [sec-borrowing-drift] Kopp-Schneider and colleagues show that borrowing cannot improve power over an optimal current-data test while preserving strict conditional type I error control. [sec-borrowing-regulator] FDA asks for the prior effective sample size, conflict simulations including a no-effect scenario and sensitivity analyses, and does not recommend measuring borrowing by type I error inflation. [sec-borrowing-regulator] If the true control rate is 40% instead of 30%, the type I error is 14.6% under full pooling, 5.4% under the power prior and 8.9% under the robust prior, and at a 20 point drift full pooling rejects 52% of the time. [sec-borrowing-drift] A sponsor should report the type I error at the edge of the drift range it considers plausible. [sec-borrowing-regulator]

## Pitfalls

A cap on borrowing, such as 30% to 50%, and a recalibrated threshold are two protective devices, each of which gives up part of the gain. [sec-borrowing-regulator] Reporting only the no-drift column hides the price. [sec-borrowing-regulator]

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict the direction: a true control rate above history, does a borrowing rule reject a true null more or less often? A: More often. [sec-borrowing-drift]
- Q: What does drift below history cost? A: Power. [sec-borrowing-drift]

calgb-49907.name: CALGB 49907
calgb-49907.summary: A trial of capecitabine against standard adjuvant chemotherapy in older women with early breast cancer, stopped for futility on a Bayesian monitoring rule.
calgb-49907.body:
## What it is

CALGB 49907 compared capecitabine with standard adjuvant chemotherapy in women aged 65 or older with early-stage breast cancer [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice]. The design planned up to 1,800 patients, with a Bayesian monitoring rule on the noninferiority comparison and noninformative priors [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice].

## Why it matters

It shows the value of futility stopping where the new drug is worse, not just no better [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice]. The criterion was a probability statement with a pre-specified boundary, crossed by the data and not chosen after the fact [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice].

## In the book

At the first interim, after 600 patients, the posterior probability that capecitabine would fail the noninferiority criterion was 96 percent, over the pre-specified 80 percent futility boundary [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice]. Enrollment stopped at 633 patients, 65 percent fewer than the planned maximum [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice]. After further follow-up the hazard ratio was 2.09 (95% CI 1.38 to 3.17), confirming the superiority of standard chemotherapy [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice]. Berry describes it as, to his knowledge, the first fully Bayesian randomized trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice].

## Pitfalls

The quantity reported at the interim is a posterior probability of failing noninferiority; the design as described in the primary report did not stop on a [[conditional-power]] value [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice].

## Check yourself

- Q: How many patients were enrolled against the planned maximum? A: 633 against 1,800, 65 percent fewer [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice].
- Q: Which quantity crossed the boundary? A: The posterior probability of failing noninferiority, 96 percent against 80 percent [15/calgb-49907-futility-stopping-in-practice].

calibration.name: Calibration of the success threshold
calibration.summary: Choosing the posterior threshold c, for a given effect threshold a, as the 1 minus alpha quantile of the largest null posterior probability, so the type I error is controlled.
calibration.body:
## What it is

Let $M$ be the largest posterior probability $\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > a \mid \text{data})$ that a simulated null trial reaches at any look it attends [14/the-algorithm]. The rule "success if the probability exceeds $c$ at any look" rejects exactly when $M > c$ [14/the-algorithm]. So the smallest $c$ with type I error at most $\alpha$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$ over the null simulations, which `oc_calibrate` computes [14/the-algorithm].

## Why it matters

Without calibration the rule inflates the error, because each look is a new chance for noise to cross the bar [sec-sim-inflation]. Calibration is this book's default for confirmatory adaptive designs without borrowing [sec-simulation].

## In the book

The four-call workflow simulates the null, calibrates $c$ to 2.5 percent, simulates the alternative and reports the operating characteristics [14/the-algorithm]. A threshold of $c = 0.975$ is a 2.5 percent test at one look, and $c = 0.991$ is a 2.5 percent test at four looks [sec-sim-inflation]. Raising $a$ lowers the calibrated $c$ and lowers the power at $p_1 = 0.45$ [14/choosing-a-and-c]. If futility is binding, it is simulated inside the null run and the calibration takes credit for it; if it is non-binding (the usual regulatory assumption), calibrate on the maximum over all looks ignoring futility [14/the-algorithm].

## Pitfalls

A design with non-binding futility should calibrate on the maximum over all looks, the more conservative choice [14/the-algorithm]. The calibrated $c$ is itself an estimate, so use at least $10^5$ trials and validate on a fresh seed [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does one simulation serve every candidate $c$? A: Common random numbers: the type I error is $\Pr(M > c)$ for the same simulated $M$ [14/the-algorithm].
- Q: Does raising $a$ raise or lower the calibrated $c$? A: It lowers it, because exceeding a larger effect is harder to do by chance [14/choosing-a-and-c].

functions.name: oc_calibrate
functions.title: Calibrate the success threshold c to a one-sided type I error
functions.description: Returns a threshold c at which the empirical type I error in the supplied null simulation (the fraction of simulated trials whose posterior probability exceeds c at any attended look) is at most alpha: the 1 - alpha quantile ("higher" rule) of oc_max_pp(). Because the rule is pp > c, the empirical error is at most alpha, with equality up to Monte Carlo ties.

  fut = NULL,

)
functions.description: Equal allocation, looks at cumulative per-arm sample sizes looks. Success is declared when Pr(p1 - p0 > a | data) > c at any look; optionally the trial stops for futility at the first look where that probability falls below fut.
