results.name: Calibration of a posterior probability rule by the null maximum
results.summary: The smallest threshold that holds a monitored posterior probability rule to level alpha is the (1 minus alpha) quantile of the largest posterior probability reached over the looks in null simulations, so one simulation serves every threshold.
results.statement: Let $M$ be, for one simulated null trial, the largest posterior probability $\Pr(p_1 - p_0 > a \mid \text{data})$ that the trial reaches at any look it attends. The rule "success if the probability exceeds $c$ at any look" rejects exactly when $M > c$, so its type I error is $\Pr(M > c)$, and the smallest $c$ with type I error at most $\alpha$ is the $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$. The $(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $M$ over the null simulations is a Monte Carlo estimate of it: it fixes the rejection proportion in the calibration sample and not the population error (the binomial standard error near 0.025 is about 0.0008 at 40,000 runs), so the threshold should be validated on independent null simulations. A single simulation serves every candidate $c$ (common random numbers). If futility stopping is part of the design, $M$ is the maximum over the looks the trial actually reaches.

cardiovascular-outcomes-trial.name: Cardiovascular outcomes trial
cardiovascular-outcomes-trial.summary: A large event-driven trial whose primary endpoint is a composite of cardiovascular events, the setting for the book's SELECT, REWIND and SURPASS-CVOT cases.
cardiovascular-outcomes-trial.body:
## What it is
The chapter tests Bayesian monitoring on cardiovascular trials that were actually run, chosen to differ: SELECT, REWIND and SURPASS-CVOT. [sec-cases]
Their primary endpoints are composites of cardiovascular events analyzed as time to first event. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
For new type 2 diabetes drugs, the 2008 FDA guidance asked for cardiovascular evidence, in practice comparing the upper bound of the 95 percent interval for the cardiovascular risk ratio against margins of 1.8 and 1.3. [sec-cases]

## Why it matters
A cardiovascular outcomes trial is usually the only trial behind the cardiovascular claim, which makes the one-trial-plus-confirmatory-evidence standard the one in play. [sec-cases]
They are event driven, so the question is how many events a monitoring rule needs. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]

## In the book
SELECT is the favorable case and REWIND the case where the scheduled design wins. [sec-cases]
Each case closes with what a data monitoring committee and a regulator would have had to accept. [sec-cases]
The side-by-side table says the traditional design wins for marginal effects and fixed looks, as in REWIND, and the Bayesian reconstruction wins for large effects with a committee that can commit to a plan, as in SELECT. [sec-cases-side]
Randomization, blinding, endpoint, firewall and the intention-to-treat estimand do not change. [sec-cases-side]
Several such trials are running now, among them PREVAIL with 9,541 participants. [sec-cases-current]

## Pitfalls
SELECT enrolled people without diabetes and is not governed by the 2008 diabetes guidance, which is REWIND's setting. [sec-cases]

## Check yourself
- Q: Where does the book say the scheduled design wins? A: Marginal effects and fixed looks, as in REWIND. [sec-cases-side]
- Q: Why is the substantial-evidence standard in play? A: A cardiovascular outcomes trial is usually the only trial behind the cardiovascular claim. [sec-cases]

cid-program.name: Complex innovative trial design program
cid-program.summary: An FDA program giving selected sponsors a pair of meetings on a novel design, such as a Bayesian one, with simulation work in hand.
cid-program.body:
## What it is
The 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 directed FDA to promote novel trial designs, including complex adaptive and Bayesian designs. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program] FDA's response was the CID paired meeting program, described by the final guidance of December 2020. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program] A sponsor applies with a description of the design, and accepted sponsors receive a pair of meetings, the second after the simulation work discussed in the first. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program]

## Why it matters
It is the main route for a sponsor proposing a Bayesian or otherwise complex adaptive design. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program] Admission is selective, and the meetings do not replace the ordinary milestones. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program] Use the CID program for the trial's decision rules and the MIDD program for the models that feed them. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program]

## In the book
A CID package normally includes the proposed design, the scenarios, the operating characteristics and a comparison with a simpler alternative. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program] Two case studies come through the program: a pediatric multiple sclerosis non-inferiority study and an EMAS epilepsy study. [sec-regulatory-practice] The program is active, a PDUFA commitment. [sec-documents-named]

## Check yourself
- Q: What do accepted sponsors receive? A: A pair of meetings. [3/the-complex-innovative-trial-design-cid-paired-meeting-program]
- Q: Which program fits a design that is Bayesian or simulation-driven? A: The CID paired meeting program, or Type C otherwise. [3/how-to-choose-the-meeting]

clinical-trial-simulation.name: Clinical trial simulation
clinical-trial-simulation.summary: Running a trial design many times on a computer against assumed true effects to estimate its operating characteristics when no formula exists.
clinical-trial-simulation.body:
## What it is

For designs without a closed formula, the answer usually has to be computed by running the design many times against assumed truths [sec-simulation]. ICH E20 defines a simulation as "the repeated execution of a large number of hypothetical clinical trials" [sec-sim-report].

## Why it matters

FDA's 2019 guidance says that when analytic methods are not available, operating characteristics should be evaluated by simulation (Section VI.A) [14/what-goes-in-the-traditional-sap].

## In the book

The function `oc_post_table` stores the posterior probability for every possible pair of success counts at each look [sec-sim-rule]. A simulated trial then costs two binomial draws and a lookup, so a hundred thousand four-look trials take a fraction of a second [sec-sim-rule]. Every simulation in the book passes `seed =` to `oc_simulate` [sec-sim-software].

Industrial practice calls this flight-simulating a trial: specify a structure, simulate many assumed truths, and judge the design by how it behaves across all of them [sec-sim-goldilocks].

## Pitfalls

Verification is the sponsor's job. Three cheap tests are to reproduce a known analytic result, to check invariances, and to rerun with a different seed and compare [sec-sim-software]. Never leave debug settings in a final run [sec-sim-software]. A simulation done after the data are in is not a prespecified operating characteristic [sec-sim-software].

## Check yourself

- Q: What should a one-look simulation with $c = 0.975$ reproduce? A: Approximately the exact type I error of the fixed design, 0.0252 in the book [sec-sim-software].
- Q: Why must parallel runs use independent random streams? A: Using the same seed on every worker is wrong; the book suggests L'Ecuyer-CMRG streams [sec-sim-software].

functions.name: oc_post_table
functions.title: Posterior probability table for a two-arm binary trial
functions.usage: oc_post_table(n, a = 0, prior = c(1, 1), G = NULL)
functions.description: Returns the matrix T[x0 + 1, x1 + 1] = Pr(p1 - p0 > a | x0, x1) for x0, x1 successes out of n per arm with independent Beta(prior) priors on each arm. Each entry is the exact rank-scale integral of prob_superior() (relative tolerance 1e-10), so exchangeable states give exactly 0.5 and concentrated or U-shaped posteriors are not truncated. When a = 0 the table is exchangeable and only half of it is integrated. It is computed once per look, so that a simulated trial reads its posterior probability by table lookup. Tables are cached within the session under a key that records n, a and prior exactly (to full double precision), so distinct arguments never share a table.

clinical-trial.name: Clinical trial
clinical-trial.summary: A trial is a measurement of a treatment effect and, at the same time, the basis for a decision to approve, continue or stop.
clinical-trial.body:
## What it is
A clinical trial assigns patients to treatments and follows them to compare outcomes, and the book frames it as a measurement and a decision at once. [sec-decision-setting] The traditional trial compares a new treatment with control, randomizing patients one to one and testing a null hypothesis that the treatment is no better than control. [sec-decision-traditional] Patient outcomes swing with the natural history of the disease, the environment, the psychological response to being treated and supportive care. D. R. Cox called this "large uncontrolled variations". [sec-decision-setting] Because the variation between patients is large and cannot be removed, a trial gives evidence, not certainty. A single trial can establish an effect beyond reasonable doubt, and the law allows approval on one adequate and well-controlled trial when it is persuasive enough, but even a decisive result leaves some probability that the effect is smaller than estimated or absent. What a trial does is change what we believe, and then someone has to act: approve or not, continue or stop, give the next patient drug A or drug B. [sec-decision-setting]

## Why it matters
The traditional apparatus was built to make the measurement honest and to put a fixed ceiling on one kind of wrong decision. [sec-decision-setting] The book asks what changes when the decision is put in the foreground. [sec-decision-setting] A pivotal trial is also costly: the median estimated cost was $19.0 million per trial for 138 pivotal trials behind 59 novel agents. [1/the-price-of-a-trial-of-being-wrong-and-of-waiting]

## In the book
SELECT randomized 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes, to weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, at 804 sites in 41 countries. [sec-decision-select] The primary composite endpoint occurred in 569 of 8,803 patients on semaglutide and 701 of 8,801 on placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.80 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.72 to 0.90. [sec-decision-select] The trial was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 percent power at one-sided 0.025 and 1,225 planned events. [sec-decision-select]

## Pitfalls
A trial is not a proof. The traditional design is coherent, and its central strength is that the type I error rate is a promise about the procedure, made before any data exist. [sec-decision-traditional]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does a trial give evidence rather than certainty? A: Variation between patients is large and cannot be removed, so even a decisive trial leaves some probability that the effect is smaller than estimated or absent; one trial can still be enough for approval when it is persuasive. [sec-decision-setting]
- Q: What two roles does a trial play? A: It is a measurement and a decision. [sec-decision-setting]

closed-testing.name: Closed testing
closed-testing.summary: The principle behind Holm, fixed-sequence and graphical procedures: reject a hypothesis only if every intersection containing it is rejected at level alpha.
closed-testing.body:
## What it is

The procedures above are special cases of one principle due to Marcus, Peritz and Gabriel. A closed test starts from hypotheses $H_1,\dots,H_k$ and forms all intersection hypotheses, such as "$H_1$ and $H_3$ are both true". Each intersection is tested with any valid level-$\alpha$ test. [10/closed-testing]

An individual hypothesis $H_i$ is rejected if every intersection that contains $H_i$ is rejected at level $\alpha$. [10/closed-testing]

## Why it matters

This controls the familywise error rate strongly. A true intersection of nulls is wrongly rejected with probability at most $\alpha$, and any false rejection of an individual hypothesis requires rejecting the intersection of all true nulls. [10/closed-testing]

For a clinician the lesson is that "the multiplicity adjustment" is not one formula. It is a rule for how a result about one hypothesis may depend on results about others, chosen at the protocol stage. [10/closed-testing]

## In the book

Holm's procedure is the closed test that uses Bonferroni for each intersection. A more powerful intersection test, such as one using the correlation between endpoints, gives a more powerful closed procedure. [10/closed-testing]

The same logic yields the gatekeeping and fixed-sequence procedures that dominate practice. [10/closed-testing] Graphical procedures control the familywise error rate because each step is a closed-test shortcut. [10/graphical-procedures]

## Pitfalls

- The choice of intersection test is where the power is won or lost, and it must be fixed in the protocol. [10/closed-testing]

## Check yourself

- Q: When is H1 rejected in a closed test? A: When every intersection hypothesis containing H1 is rejected at level alpha. [10/closed-testing]
- Q: Which classic procedure is closed testing with Bonferroni for each intersection? A: Holm's. [10/closed-testing]

commensurate-prior.name: Commensurate prior
commensurate-prior.summary: A prior that centers the current parameter on the historical one with a precision parameter that the data update, so agreement between sources is itself learned.
commensurate-prior.body:
## What it is

Hobbs, Carlin, Mandrekar and Sargent (2011) put agreement between sources into a parameter of its own [sec-borrowing-commensurate]. With $\eta_c$ the current and $\eta_h$ the historical parameter (logits for binary data), the commensurate prior says

$$
\eta_c \mid \eta_h, \tau_c \sim N(\eta_h,\; 1/\tau_c),
$$

where $\tau_c$ is the commensurability precision with its own prior (eq-commensurate). [sec-borrowing-commensurate] The prior is typically a spike-and-slab or a discrete mixture that allows a large and a small value. [sec-borrowing-commensurate]

## Why it matters

A large posterior $\tau_c$ means the current data support closeness and the historical data count heavily. A small one down-weights them. [sec-borrowing-commensurate] This makes borrowing dynamic.

## In the book

In the two-stage version the historical posterior is held fixed and borrowing runs one way, as a regulator thinks of an already reported trial. In the fully Bayesian joint model information flows both ways. [sec-borrowing-commensurate] A version places the commensurate model on a power prior, combining discounting and agreement. [sec-borrowing-commensurate] The paper treats Gaussian data, and the extension to generalized linear models is in Hobbs and colleagues (2012). [sec-borrowing-commensurate]

## Pitfalls

A method that learns agreement from a small current control arm has little to learn from. In a small trial the commensurate prior behaves much like a static one with weights fixed by the prior on $\tau_c$. [sec-borrowing-commensurate]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a small posterior $\tau_c$ say? A: The current data do not support closeness, so the historical data are down-weighted. [sec-borrowing-commensurate]
- Q: Why is it weak in a small trial? A: A small control arm has little information about agreement. [sec-borrowing-commensurate]

concurrent-control.name: Concurrent control
concurrent-control.summary: Control patients randomized while an arm was open, and eligible for it, as opposed to non-concurrent controls randomized earlier.
concurrent-control.body:
## What it is

Concurrent controls are those randomized while the arm was open. Non-concurrent controls were randomized before it opened. They are tempting because they are free patients and dangerous because of drift in standard of care, patient mix, sites and conduct. [20/concurrent-and-non-concurrent-controls]

## Why it matters

FDA's June 2026 draft asks that the primary comparison use only concurrently eligible controls, who met the drug's eligibility criteria and could have been randomized to it. The shared control keeps most of its efficiency gain with only concurrent controls. [20/regulatory-position] The EMA draft defines concurrent controls as having a positive probability of randomization to the arm and says non-concurrent controls are usually not acceptable for the primary analysis of the primary endpoint. [20/regulatory-position]

## In the book

In a simulation with success on standard care rising 2 points a year, the concurrent comparison is unbiased and rejects at about the nominal 2.5%, while pooling all controls gives a type I error more than three times nominal. [20/how-big-is-the-bias-a-simulation] A linear calendar-time term removes the bias under smooth linear drift, but depends on the model being right. [20/how-big-is-the-bias-a-simulation] The Bayesian time machine is a less rigid alternative. [20/the-bayesian-time-machine]

## Pitfalls

Pooling improves power partly spuriously when drift is present. [20/how-big-is-the-bias-a-simulation] A sponsor using non-concurrent data should justify it in advance, pre-specify the method and run sensitivity analyses giving it less weight or none. [20/regulatory-position]

## Check yourself

- Q: Does pooling all controls under upward drift inflate or deflate type I error? A: It inflates it. [20/how-big-is-the-bias-a-simulation]
- Q: What does the EMA draft allow for non-concurrent data? A: Supplementary analyses or rarely observed secondary endpoints. [20/regulatory-position]

conditional-means-prior.name: Conditional means prior
conditional-means-prior.summary: A prior built from beta statements about response probabilities at chosen covariate values, so a clinician specifies beliefs on the scale she can think on.
conditional-means-prior.body:
## What it is

Bedrick, Christensen and Johnson moved elicitation from the coefficient scale to the scale where beliefs exist. The investigator states priors for the response probability at several covariate values, and the prior on the coefficients is what those statements induce through the link [sec-priors-cmp]. For $p$ coefficients take $p$ independent beta priors $\tilde m_i \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a_{1i}, a_{2i})$; the induced prior is

$$
\pi(\beta) \propto \prod_{i=1}^{p} F(\tilde x_i' \beta)^{a_{1i} - 1}\,\bigl[1 - F(\tilde x_i' \beta)\bigr]^{a_{2i} - 1}\, f(\tilde x_i' \beta),
$$

which is eq-cmp [sec-priors-cmp].

## Why it matters

A clinician cannot say what the log-odds slope is, but can say what she expects at 10 mg and at 50 mg [sec-priors-cmp]. For the logistic link the prior is literally $a_{1i} + a_{2i}$ pseudo-patients, so its weight is countable [sec-priors-cmp].

## In the book

Expecting about 30 percent response at 10 mg and 70 percent at 50 mg, with the confidence of 10 patients each, gives Beta(3, 7) and Beta(7, 3), with $a_{1i} = \nu_i m_i$ and $a_{2i} = \nu_i(1 - m_i)$ [sec-priors-cmp]. The default $N(0, 10^2)$ puts nearly all its mass at the extremes [sec-priors-cmp]. The ESS is $\nu_i$ at each design point, here 10 at each of two doses [sec-priors-ess].

## Pitfalls

Independent beta statements at two doses do not enforce a monotone dose-response. If monotonicity is required, constrain the ordered probabilities or the slope [sec-priors-cmp]. The same belief gives different coefficient priors under logit and probit links [sec-priors-cmp].

## Check yourself

- Q: With 30 percent expected response and prior sample size 10 at a dose, what beta prior results? A: Beta(3, 7) [sec-priors-cmp].
- Q: Why can the ESS of this prior be counted exactly under a logistic link? A: It equals $a_{1i} + a_{2i}$ pseudo-patients [sec-priors-cmp].

conditional-power.name: Conditional power
conditional-power.summary: The probability that the final statistic exceeds the critical value, given the interim data and an assumed value of the treatment effect.
conditional-power.body:
## What it is

Conditional power is the probability that the final statistic $Z_1$ exceeds the critical value $z_\alpha$, given the interim data and an assumed value of the effect [15/conditional-power]. With the B-value $B_t = Z_t\sqrt{t}$ and drift $\xi$, the future increment is normal whatever the past was, so

$$
\mathrm{CP}(\xi) = \Pr(Z_1 > z_\alpha \mid Z_t) = 1 - \Phi\!\left(\frac{z_\alpha - Z_t\sqrt{t} - \xi(1-t)}{\sqrt{1-t}}\right).
$$

[15/conditional-power]

## Why it matters

It answers "could this trial still win?" and is the basis of stochastic curtailment: stop when the outcome is nearly decided [15/conditional-power]. A futility rule may stop if $\mathrm{CP}(\xi_a) < 0.10$ or $0.20$ [15/futility-rules].

## In the book

Three choices of $\xi$ are in use: the design alternative $\xi = z_\alpha + z_\beta$, the current trend $\xi = Z_t/\sqrt{t}$, and the null $\xi = 0$ [15/conditional-power]. At half the information of a trial designed with 90 percent power at one-sided 0.025, a trial exactly on the null path still has positive conditional power under the design alternative [15/conditional-power].

## Pitfalls

It treats $\xi$ as fixed and known, so it gives no credit for uncertainty about the effect [15/conditional-power]. A DMC that reports only one of the numbers has made a modeling choice without saying so [15/conditional-power]. It is a decision tool, not an inferential one, and futility stopping can only reduce the chance of rejecting, so it never inflates type I error [15/futility-rules]. The Bayesian remedy is [[predictive-probability-of-success]] [15/from-conditional-power-to-predictive-probability].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which choice of drift is optimistic after a poor interim? A: The design alternative [15/conditional-power].
- Q: Does a non-binding futility rule protect the type I error if the DMC ignores it? A: Yes, the final test is at the full $\alpha$ whether or not the rule is followed [15/futility-rules].

confidence-interval.name: Confidence interval
confidence-interval.summary: The range of effect sizes the data do not rule out; the 95 percent describes the long-run record of the method, not one interval.
confidence-interval.body:
## What it is
For an approximately normal estimator the 95% interval is the estimate plus and minus 1.96 standard errors: [sec-testing-ci]

$$
\hat\theta \;\pm\; 1.96 \times \mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) .
$$

This is equation eq-testing-ci. [sec-testing-ci] The 95% is about the procedure: if the trial were rerun many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true effect. [4/what-the-95-refers-to]

## Why it matters
A p-value says whether the data are compatible with no effect, not what effect is likely. [sec-testing-ci] ICH E9 section 5.5 asks that estimates "should be accompanied by confidence intervals, whenever possible". [sec-testing-ci] Test and interval are one calculation: the 95% two-sided interval holds exactly the values a two-sided 5% test would not reject. [4/tests-and-intervals-are-the-same-thing]

## In the book
For the binary trial the interval for the risk difference is $0.15 \pm 0.132$, that is 0.017 to 0.283, so a gain of 2 points and one of 28 are both compatible. For the continuous trial it is 1.10 to 8.28 mmHg. [sec-testing-ci] Newcombe compared the score-based interval with ten other methods. [4/what-the-95-refers-to]

## Pitfalls
It is not a 95% chance that the true difference lies in 0.017 to 0.283. A statement of that form is a credible interval and needs a prior. [4/what-the-95-refers-to] The test and interval agree exactly only with the same standard error. [4/tests-and-intervals-are-the-same-thing] The analysis plan should name the interval method. [4/what-the-95-refers-to]

## Check yourself
- Q: In 50 reruns, how many intervals should miss the truth? A: About 2 or 3 (5 percent of 50 is 2.5), though in 50 trials the count is itself random. [4/what-the-95-refers-to]
- Q: What does a one-sided 0.025 test amount to? A: Rejecting essentially when the lower limit of the two-sided 95% interval is above zero. [4/tests-and-intervals-are-the-same-thing]

confidence-sequence.name: Confidence sequence
confidence-sequence.summary: A sequence of intervals that covers the true parameter at all sample sizes at once with probability at least 1 minus alpha, so it can be read at any stopping time.
confidence-sequence.body:
## What it is

A confidence sequence is a sequence of intervals $C_n$ such that $\mathbb{P}(\theta \in C_n \text{ for all } n) \ge 1-\alpha$. It is built by inverting the e-process over null values. [sec-evalues-p]

## Why it matters

It can be read at any time, including the time the data monitoring committee stopped the trial. [sec-evalues-p] The estimation principle in the Adaptive Designs guidance, that estimates be "sufficiently reliable", is what the confidence sequence is for. [sec-evalues-p]

## In the book

The idea goes back to Darling and Robbins, was studied by Lai, and has a group sequential counterpart in the repeated confidence interval of Jennison and Turnbull. [sec-evalues-p] A confidence sequence is wider than a fixed-sample interval at the same $n$. [sec-evalues-p]

The protocol wording in the chapter reports always-valid p-values and a 95 percent confidence sequence in the clinical study report at the final analysis. [sec-evalues-reg] The book suggests running an e-process beside a Bayesian rule and reporting the e-value, its always-valid p-value and a confidence sequence as a frequentist evidential record. [sec-evalues-pay]

## Pitfalls

- The extra width is the price of validity at every stopping time. [sec-evalues-p]

## Check yourself

- Q: Is a confidence sequence narrower or wider than a fixed-sample interval at the same $n$? A: Wider. [sec-evalues-p]
- Q: What can it be read at that a fixed interval cannot? A: Any time, including the time the DMC stopped the trial. [sec-evalues-p]

confounding-by-indication.name: Confounding by indication
confounding-by-indication.summary: When the reasons a doctor chooses a treatment are related to the outcome, the comparison of treated and untreated patients is biased.
confounding-by-indication.body:
## What it is
The commonest way for the selection term (the bias term of Equation 5.1 that randomization sets to zero) to be nonzero in medicine is confounding by indication: the reasons a doctor chooses a treatment are themselves related to the outcome. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

A physician who thinks a new drug is promising may offer it to patients who seem strong enough to benefit and keep the old treatment for the frail. No bad faith is needed. The physician is using judgment on behalf of each patient, and that ruins the comparison. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

## Why it matters
A larger trial does not help. The standard error is about the same whether a doctor or a coin chooses, so more patients only make the wrong answer more convincing. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

Adjustment helps only for what was recorded. Stratifying on a recorded health score moves the estimate closer to the truth but not onto it, because patients within a band still differ. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients] The coin balances health as recorded, as sensed and as nobody has thought of, on average over randomizations; any one trial keeps a chance imbalance, which the standard error accounts for. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

## In the book
Each patient has a hidden health score. The new drug truly adds 10 percentage points to the probability of recovery. Each simulated trial has 400 patients, and 1,000 trials of each kind are run. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

When the doctor chooses, the estimates center on roughly three times the truth. When a coin chooses, they center on the truth. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients] The mean doctor-chosen estimate is 0.31 against a truth of 0.10, because the treated patients were 1.06 standard deviations healthier. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients] Stratifying on health in five bands lowers the estimate to about 0.12 (0.117). [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

## Pitfalls
These are failures of assignment, not of analysis. No adjustment applied afterward can repair an assignment mechanism that depended on unrecorded information. [sec-randomization-failures]

## Check yourself
- Q: In the doctor-chooses simulation, will a larger trial bring the estimate to the true 10 points? A: No. The bias stays, and the larger trial only makes the wrong answer more convincing. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]
- Q: Does adjusting for a recorded health score fully fix it? A: No. It brings the estimate closer, but patients within a band still differ and the choice depends on health itself. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

conjugate-prior.name: Conjugate prior
conjugate-prior.summary: A prior whose posterior belongs to the same family as the prior, so that updating reduces to simple arithmetic.
conjugate-prior.body:
## What it is
A prior is conjugate to the likelihood if the posterior belongs to the same family. For the Beta prior and a binomial likelihood the update is addition: add the responders to $a$ and the non-responders to $b$. [sec-beta]

$$
\theta \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b), \quad h \text{ heads}, \; t \text{ tails} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \theta \mid y \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a + h,\; b + t).
$$

## Why it matters
Multiplying the prior kernel $\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}$ by the likelihood kernel $\theta^{h}(1-\theta)^{t}$ gives $\theta^{a+h-1}(1-\theta)^{b+t-1}$, the kernel of Beta$(a+h, b+t)$. The normalizing constant is whatever makes it integrate to one, so nothing needs to be integrated by hand. [sec-beta]

For conjugate models, batch-wise updating is a running total of responders and non-responders. This makes interim analyses cheap: a handful of arithmetic operations. [sec-updating]

## In the book
In the two-group example, flat Beta(1,1) priors and 30 of 100 and 45 of 100 responders give Beta(31, 71) and Beta(46, 56). [6/the-bayesian-analysis]

For the log hazard ratio, a normal prior and a normal likelihood give a normal posterior with precision equal to the sum of the precisions. [sec-normal-normal]

## Pitfalls
Conjugacy is a convenience of form and says nothing about whether the prior is defensible. The protocol must still state and justify the prior. [sec-protocol-bayes]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the Beta posterior after 8 responders and 2 non-responders from Beta(1,1)? A: Beta(9, 3), by adding. [sec-beta]
- Q: What adds in the normal-normal model? A: The precisions. [sec-normal-normal]

consort-2025.name: CONSORT 2025
consort-2025.summary: The reporting guideline for the results of a randomized trial; the adaptive-designs extension (ACE) extends CONSORT 2010 and predates CONSORT 2025.
consort-2025.body:
## What it is
CONSORT 2025 is the reporting guideline for the results of a randomized trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The adaptive-designs extension, ACE, extends CONSORT 2010 and predates CONSORT 2025. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Why it matters
It is one of several guidelines around the protocol, and none is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
It is written for the generic randomized trial, so a Bayesian trial must add its own items. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## In the book
The items a Bayesian trial adds are the same ones the chapter has put in the protocol: the prior and its source, the success criterion with its threshold and calibration, the interim schedule and the simulation report, the software and seeds, and the sensitivity analyses to the prior. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
A report that gives each of them where the generic checklist asks for its traditional counterpart satisfies the intent of all of these lists. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
SPIRIT 2025 is the corresponding checklist for the protocol. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Pitfalls
Only a few guidelines are written for Bayesian analyses, and they are author guidelines. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which extension covers adaptive trials, and which CONSORT does it extend? A: ACE, which extends CONSORT 2010. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
- Q: What must a Bayesian report add to CONSORT items? A: The prior, success criterion with calibration, schedule and simulation report, software and seeds, and prior sensitivity. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

continual-reassessment-method.name: Continual reassessment method
continual-reassessment-method.summary: The first Bayesian phase 1 design: a one-parameter dose-toxicity curve through a skeleton is updated after each cohort to pick the next dose.
continual-reassessment-method.body:
## What it is
The continual reassessment method (CRM) of O'Quigley, Pepe and Fisher was the first Bayesian design in phase 1. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] It posits $p_d(a) = \pi_d^{\exp(a)}$ through $K$ doses, where $\pi_1 < \dots < \pi_K$ is a prespecified skeleton and $a$ has a prior, here $a \sim N(0, 1.34)$. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] After each cohort the next dose is the one whose posterior mean DLT probability is closest to the target. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] Two safety rules are standard: no skipping a dose and a stopping rule for an overly toxic lowest dose. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method]

## Why it matters
The protocol now names a skeleton and a prior, which the 3+3 never needed. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] The posterior is one-dimensional, so a grid works and no MCMC is needed. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method]

## In the book
The skeleton (0.05, 0.12, 0.25, 0.40, 0.55, 0.70) is close to the truth in scenario A and wrong in B and C. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] With 30 patients CRM selects the true MTD more often than the 3+3, but treats more patients at toxic doses. [17/comparing-the-designs] At 15 patients it is worse than the 3+3 in scenario B. [17/comparing-the-designs]

## Pitfalls
The skeleton is a shape, not the truth. A real simulation report should include scenarios in which it is badly wrong. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method] The one-parameter form is rigid. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does the CRM need in the protocol that the 3+3 does not? A: A skeleton and a prior on its parameter. [17/the-continual-reassessment-method]
- Q: Does CRM beat the 3+3 at every sample size? A: No. At n = 15 it is worse in scenario B, though at n = 30 it selects the true MTD more often. [17/comparing-the-designs]

functions.name: dose_crm
functions.title: One simulated one-parameter power-model CRM trial
functions.description: Dose-toxicity model p_d(a) = skeleton_d^exp(a) with a N(0, 1.34) prior on a. The posterior is computed on a grid of 401 equally spaced values of a on the interval from -4 to 4 (the prior and posterior are truncated to this range and renormalised on it). The trial starts at dose 1 and enrols N \%/\% cohort cohorts of size cohort (patients beyond cohort * (N \%/\% cohort) are not enrolled). After each cohort the posterior is updated and: (i) the trial stops with no dose selected (selected = 0) if the posterior probability that the lowest dose's toxicity exceeds target is more than 0.90 (this safety cutoff is checked after every cohort, including the first, with no minimum number of patients); otherwise (ii) the recommended dose is the one whose posterior mean toxicity is closest to target (either side of the target, so the recommended dose can exceed the target) and (iii) the next cohort is treated at that dose, except that escalation never skips: the next dose is at most one above the current one, while de-escalation can jump several levels. The selected dose is the recommendation computed after the last cohort. It is not restricted by the no-skipping rule and may be a dose that was never given. There is no early stopping for sample size or for a precisely estimated MTD.

cornfield-betting-odds.name: Cornfield and the betting odds of 1966
cornfield-betting-odds.summary: In 1966 Cornfield proposed relative betting odds as a sequential stopping criterion, an early form of the mixture e-value that lost to frequentist group sequential boundaries (later alpha spending).
cornfield-betting-odds.body:
## What it is

Cornfield proposed what he called relative betting odds as a sequential stopping criterion. The odds are the likelihood ratio of the alternative to the null, accumulated as the data arrive and averaged over a prior on the alternative. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966] His companion argument was that the stopping rule should not change the strength of the evidence. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966]

## Why it matters

For a simple null the betting odds are a [[test-martingale]], so [[villes-inequality|Ville's inequality]] bounds the probability that they ever cross a high level. That guarantee does not need his argument. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966]

## In the book

His proposal lost to frequentist group sequential boundaries, later alpha spending, for a reason that is not statistical. Betting odds require a declared prior on the alternative, and the reviewer has to accept it. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966] The [[mixture-method]] of the chapter makes the same trade. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966] The regulatory conversation about registering the prior is the modern version of that objection. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966]

Shafer and colleagues connect test martingales, Bayes factors and p-values, and Vovk and Wang develop calibration and combination rules for e-values. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why did Cornfield's betting odds lose to group sequential boundaries? A: They need a declared prior on the alternative that the reviewer must accept. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966]
- Q: What makes the odds valid at any stopping time for a simple null? A: They are a test martingale, so Ville's inequality applies. [12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-1966]

12/cornfield-and-the-betting-odds-of-196.t: Cornfield and the betting odds of 1966

counterfactual.name: Counterfactual
counterfactual.summary: For each patient we see only one outcome, never what would have happened under the other treatment, so a trial must compare groups instead.
counterfactual.body:
## What it is
For one patient we see one outcome. We never see what would have happened to the same patient under the other treatment. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

Write $Y(1)$ for the outcome if treated and $Y(0)$ for the outcome if not. The treatment effect for that patient is $Y(1) - Y(0)$, and we can never observe both terms. The book calls this the fundamental problem of causal inference in Rubin's potential outcomes language. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

What we can compare is groups. The difference in observed group means splits into the effect on those who were treated plus a selection bias term: [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

$$
\begin{aligned}
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid D=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid D=0]}_{\text{what the trial shows}}
\;=\;& \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid D=1]}_{\text{effect on those who were treated}}\\
&+\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid D=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid D=0]}_{\text{selection bias}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

## Why it matters
The selection term asks how different the two groups were before the drug did anything. If groups were chosen in a way that depends on prognosis, it is not zero, and the observed difference mixes the drug effect with the effect of the choice. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

If a coin that ignores everything about the patient makes the assignment, the term is zero on average and the difference in means estimates the average effect of the drug. The argument needs no assumption about which patient characteristics matter. [5/the-counterfactual-problem] This is the case for [[randomization]].

## In the book
The book uses the selection term again to read the Women's Health Initiative: women who chose hormone therapy differed from those who did not before any pill was taken. [5/the-womens-health-initiative-2002-randomization-against-observational-evidence] It also names the term as the reason the observational finding on [[confounding-by-indication]] fails. [5/confounding-by-indication-a-doctor-picks-the-patients]

## Pitfalls
The identity assumes complete adherence in the opening example. The intention-to-treat section separates assignment from receipt. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why can a trial never observe the individual treatment effect? A: Each patient has only one observed outcome, so $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ are never both seen. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]
- Q: When is the selection term zero? A: On average, when assignment is made by a coin that ignores the patient. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

covariate-adjustment.name: Covariate adjustment
covariate-adjustment.summary: Using prespecified prognostic baseline covariates in the analysis of a randomized trial to gain precision without bias, the cheapest precision a trial can buy.
covariate-adjustment.body:
## What it is
Randomization makes the unadjusted comparison unbiased, but not efficient. A baseline covariate that predicts the outcome explains part of the noise, so the analysis gives a narrower interval and more power from the same patients. It needs no prior, no interim look and no extra patients. [sec-randomization-covadj]

## Why it matters
FDA (May 2023, final, nonbinding) and EMA (adopted 26 February 2015) recommend prespecified adjustment, and neither requires it. [5/what-the-regulators-say] They differ on treatment-by-covariate interactions: FDA allows them if the primary estimate is the average effect, EMA says to leave them out. [5/what-the-regulators-say]

## In the book
For binary or time-to-event outcomes the odds ratio and hazard ratio are non-collapsible, so the conditional effect differs from the marginal one even without confounding. FDA's example has an odds ratio of 8.0 in each of two subgroups and 4.8 overall. [5/binary-and-time-to-event-outcomes-what-is-being-estimated] Standardization (g-computation) gives the marginal effect with the adjusted precision. [5/binary-and-time-to-event-outcomes-what-is-being-estimated]

In 500 simulated trials of 300 patients, the adjusted logistic coefficient centered on the conditional log odds ratio, while the standardized estimate shared the target of the unadjusted analysis with a smaller standard deviation. [5/binary-and-time-to-event-outcomes-what-is-being-estimated] Robust estimators remain valid when the working model is wrong. [5/estimators-that-do-not-depend-on-the-model-being-right]

The Bayesian version puts covariates in the outcome model and averages predictions over the trial sample. [5/the-bayesian-version] A fair benchmark for a Bayesian adaptive design is an adjusted traditional analysis. [5/the-bayesian-version]

## Pitfalls
- Do not test baseline balance: a baseline difference in a randomized trial is due to chance. [5/do-not-test-baseline-balance]
- Analyze as you randomized: include stratification factors. [5/analyze-as-you-randomized]
- Covariates measured after randomization should not be adjusted for. [5/what-the-regulators-say]

## Check yourself
- Q: Do the unadjusted and adjusted logistic odds ratios target the same quantity? A: Not necessarily: conditional and marginal effects differ without any confounding. [5/binary-and-time-to-event-outcomes-what-is-being-estimated]
- Q: Does either regulator require adjustment? A: No, both ask that whatever is done be prespecified. [5/what-the-regulators-say]

5/binary-and-time-to-event-outcomes-what.t: Binary and time-to-event outcomes: what is being estimated

5/estimators-that-do-not-depend-on-the-m.t: Estimators that do not depend on the model being right

functions.name: covadj_standardize
functions.title: Standardized (g-computation) marginal effects from a fitted logistic model
functions.description: Predicts every patient's risk under treatment and under control from the fitted model, averages over the trial sample, and reports the marginal risk difference, relative risk and odds ratio. The standard error uses the influence function of the plug-in estimator, which accounts for the sampling variation of the covariates as well as of the coefficients (model-based coefficient covariance).

functions.name: covadj_bayes_gcomp
functions.title: Bayesian g-computation for a binary outcome: posterior of the marginal effect
functions.usage:
covadj_bayes_gcomp(
  formula,
  data,
  trt,
  prior_sd = 2.5,
  ndraw = 4000,
  seed = NULL
)
functions.description: Fits a logistic model with independent normal priors on the coefficients (centered at zero, standard deviation prior_sd; a wide N(0, 10^2) prior on the intercept), approximates the posterior by a normal distribution at the mode (Laplace), and for each posterior draw averages the predicted risks under treatment and under control over the trial sample. The draws of the averages are draws from the posterior of the marginal risk difference and log odds ratio.

covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform.name: COVID anticoagulation multiplatform trials
covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform.summary: Three Bayesian platforms that harmonized protocols and combined patient-level data in a hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing across severity strata.
covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform.body:
## What it is

Three independently funded Bayesian platforms (REMAP-CAP, ATTACC, an international platform led from Canada, and ACTIV-4a in the United States) asked the same question early in the pandemic: therapeutic-dose against prophylactic-dose anticoagulation in COVID-19. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform]

## Why it matters

Separate reports would have invited conflicting results and a post hoc meta-analysis. The teams harmonized protocols and statistical analysis plans before the data were in, and combined patient-level data in a hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing across severity strata. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform] The shared object was a pre-agreed analysis, not a shared control group. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform]

## In the book

The stopping rule was superiority at posterior probability above 99% or futility at above 95% for an odds ratio below 1.2, applied separately by severity cohort. In critically ill patients enrollment stopped for futility (adjusted odds ratio 0.83, 95% CrI 0.67 to 1.03, futility probability 99.9%). In non-critically ill patients therapeutic dosing increased organ-support-free days (odds ratio 1.27, 95% CrI 1.03 to 1.58, probability of benefit 98.6%). [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform]

## Pitfalls

The finding was not a post hoc subgroup because the severity strata were specified in advance. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform] The approach works only when sponsors agree on the estimand beforehand. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform]

## Check yourself

- Q: What was shared across the three platforms? A: A pre-agreed analysis. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform]
- Q: What happened in critically ill patients? A: Enrollment stopped for futility. [20/the-covid-anticoagulation-multiplatform]

cox-model.name: Cox model
cox-model.summary: A regression model for the hazard with an unspecified baseline, whose treatment coefficient is the log hazard ratio.
cox-model.body:
## What it is
The Cox model writes $h(t \mid z) = h_0(t)e^{-\theta z}$ for a treatment indicator $z$, leaves $h_0(t)$ unspecified, and estimates $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$ from the partial likelihood. [sec-survival-traditional] Under 1:1 allocation the variance of $\hat\theta$ is approximately
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta) \approx \frac{4}{D},
$$
where $D$ is the total number of events (eq-sv-var). [sec-survival-traditional]

## Why it matters
The patients enter only through the events they produce. [sec-survival-traditional] Stratified randomization calls for a baseline hazard per stratum. Adding covariates changes the meaning of the hazard ratio, which is non-collapsible. [sec-survival-traditional]

## In the book
The events needed follow from the Cox variance, $4/D$: for a hazard ratio of 0.83 at 90% power the formula gives 1,211 events against the 1,225 planned for SELECT, and a hazard ratio of 0.90 needs 3,787. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Pitfalls
When the hazard ratio changes over time, the Cox estimate is a weighted average depending on censoring and follow-up, so the same drug can give different hazard ratios in different trials. [sec-survival-traditional] It then depends on how long the trial runs. [sec-survival-nph]

## Check yourself
- Q: How does the variance of the log hazard ratio estimate shrink as events D grow? A: It is about 4/D under 1:1 allocation. [sec-survival-traditional]
- Q: What does the book's sign convention make positive? A: $\theta$, positive when treatment reduces the hazard. [sec-survival-traditional]

cpim.name: Critical Path Innovation Meetings
cpim.summary: A nonbinding, informal FDA discussion of methods or technologies that are not tied to a single product or active application.
cpim.body:
## What it is
CPIM is a nonbinding, informal discussion of methods or technologies not tied to a single product or an active application. [3/critical-path-innovation-meetings-cpim] FDA's stated aim is to respond to a request within 14 days. [3/critical-path-innovation-meetings-cpim]

## Why it matters
For a group developing a general methodology, such as a class of Bayesian borrowing models, it is a low-cost way to get an informal view early. [3/critical-path-innovation-meetings-cpim]

## In the book
The meeting chooser lists CPIM for a general method that is not tied to a product, and marks it as not binding. [3/how-to-choose-the-meeting] The program is active and the discussions are product-independent. [sec-documents]

## Pitfalls
Because it is not tied to a product or application, it cannot give agreement on a specific design. [3/critical-path-innovation-meetings-cpim]

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a CPIM be about one sponsor's pending application? A: No, it covers methods not tied to a single product or active application. [3/critical-path-innovation-meetings-cpim]
- Q: Is it binding? A: No. [3/critical-path-innovation-meetings-cpim]

credible-interval.name: Credible interval
credible-interval.summary: A region that contains the parameter with stated posterior probability, such as 95%, given the data and the prior.
credible-interval.body:
## What it is
A credible interval is a statement about the parameter: given the data and the prior, the probability that $p_1 - p_0$ lies in the interval is 95%. [sec-intervals]

Two regions are common. The equal-tailed interval leaves 2.5% in each tail. The highest posterior density interval is the shortest region with 95% probability. For a skewed posterior they differ. [sec-intervals]

## Why it matters
A confidence interval is a procedure. If the trial were repeated many times, 95% of the intervals would contain the true value. For the one interval in the CSR, the true value is inside or not, and "95%" does not say how likely this interval covers the truth. [sec-intervals]

## In the book
For the running trial the 95% confidence interval for the difference is (0.017, 0.283) and the 95% credible interval is (0.015, 0.277). They are numerically close and mean different things. [sec-intervals]

The distinction matters with an informative prior, where the credible interval shifts and narrows. It also matters near boundaries, where a normal-approximation interval can stray outside $[0,1]$ while a Beta credible interval cannot. [sec-intervals]

Averaged over true rates drawn from the prior, a credible interval covers 95% by construction. [sec-intervals]

## Pitfalls
At a specific $p$ the frequentist coverage can differ from 95% (it is guaranteed only on average over the prior), which is why the FDA draft asks for operating characteristics under a range of scenarios. [sec-intervals] Many trialists read confidence intervals as credible intervals, and in large trials with weak priors they get away with it. [sec-intervals]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which interval supports the statement "the effect is in this range with 95% probability"? A: The credible interval. [sec-intervals]
- Q: Can a Beta credible interval leave $[0,1]$? A: No, by construction. [sec-intervals]

cumulative-meta-analysis.name: Cumulative meta-analysis
cumulative-meta-analysis.summary: A meta-analysis that adds trials one at a time in order of completion, showing when a pooled signal first became visible.
cumulative-meta-analysis.body:
## What it is

Jüni and colleagues published a cumulative meta-analysis of the randomized rofecoxib trials, adding one trial at a time in the order of completion. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]

## Why it matters

It shows how evidence built up over time. By the end of 2000 the pool had 52 myocardial infarctions among 20,742 patients and a pooled relative risk of 2.30 (95% CI 1.22 to 4.33, $p = 0.010$). A year later, with 64 events among 21,432 patients, it was 2.24 (1.24 to 4.02, $p = 0.007$). [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]

## In the book

The relative risk showed no heterogeneity by type of control group ($p = 0.41$) or by duration of treatment ($p = 0.82$). [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said] Observational studies put the cardioprotective effect of naproxen at 0.86 (0.75 to 0.99), far too small to explain VIGOR. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said] The authors concluded the drug should have been withdrawn several years earlier. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]

The traditional reading is a significance test on a pooled estimate: by the end of 2000 the interval excluded 1. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]

## Pitfalls

- A p-value of 0.010 does not say how large the harm probably was, how probable a clinically important harm was, or what to do while evidence was accumulating. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]

## Check yourself

- Q: What did the end-2000 interval for the pooled relative risk exclude? A: The value 1. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]
- Q: What does the cumulative p-value leave out? A: The size of the harm and what to do as evidence accumulates. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said]

cure-fraction.name: Cure fraction
cure-fraction.summary: The share of treated patients effectively cured, modeled by a mixture in which the rest follow the control hazard.
cure-fraction.body:
## What it is
In a mixture cure model a fraction $\pi$ of treated patients are effectively cured and the rest follow the control hazard: $S_1(t) = \pi + (1-\pi)S_0(t)$. [sec-survival-nph] In the Berkson-Gage model the uncured have a survival function of their own, and following the control hazard is a special case. [sec-survival-nph] A Bayesian promotion-time cure model is a non-mixture alternative. [sec-survival-nph]

## Why it matters
The posterior for $\pi$ is the quantity a patient cares about. [sec-survival-nph]

## In the book
One scenario cures 20 percent of patients over a control arm with hazard 0.15 per year (median survival 4.6 years). [sec-survival-nph] In the cure-model scenario the five-year RMST difference is 0.30 years and the cumulative hazard ratio at 5 years is 0.73, against 0.51 and 0.60 for proportional hazards. [sec-survival-nph]

## Pitfalls
$\pi$ is identifiable only if follow-up is long enough for the curve to plateau. With immature data the prior dominates, and it must be stated. [sec-survival-nph]

## Check yourself
- Q: When is the cure fraction identifiable? A: When follow-up is long enough for the curve to plateau. [sec-survival-nph]

functions.name: surv_nph_example
functions.title: Non-proportional hazards examples: delayed effect and cure model
functions.description: Control arm exponential with hazard h0. Delayed effect: treated hazard equals h0 before delay and hr * h0 afterwards. Cure model: a fraction cure of treated patients never fail, the rest follow the control hazard. Returns RMST by arm and its difference at the horizon, and the average hazard ratio log S1(tau)/log S0(tau) (the ratio of cumulative hazards, constant only under proportional hazards).

data-monitoring-committee.name: Data monitoring committee
data-monitoring-committee.summary: A small independent group that sees unblinded interim data and recommends to the sponsor whether to continue, modify or stop.
data-monitoring-committee.body:
## What it is

A DMC (older terms DSMB and IDMC) is a small independent group, typically three to seven members, with clinicians in the therapeutic area and at least one statistician. It reviews accumulating data and recommends to the sponsor whether to continue, modify or stop. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

FDA's 2006 guidance covers it, and a February 2024 draft revision is not final. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

## Why it matters

The DMC sees unblinded comparative data and the sponsor does not. An independent statistical group prepares the closed reports. Access by people who can influence the trial's conduct can make a confirmatory result uninterpretable. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

## In the book

The charter, fixed before the first patient, sets membership, meeting schedule, open and closed report content, stopping guidelines and the path to the sponsor. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

Boundaries are guidelines. A DMC may recommend stopping for harm without a boundary crossed. Discretion does not by itself inflate the efficacy error, as long as a claim of success stays restricted to crossings of the prespecified boundary. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

The sponsor learns only the recommendation. A recommendation to stop discloses much, and one to modify can disclose a great deal. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

The book's reporting template has the committee shown the posterior probabilities of benefit and harm and the predictive probability of success, each next to its boundary, and allows it to decline to stop at a crossed boundary and explain why. [11/a-reporting-template-for-the-dmc]

## Pitfalls

- What can damage the guarantee is a decision that uses comparative data outside the rule, and conduct that compromises integrity. [11/what-a-dmc-does]
- Early stops overestimate the effect. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

## Check yourself

- Q: Who sees unblinded interim comparisons? A: The DMC and an independent statistical group, not the sponsor or investigators. [11/what-a-dmc-does]
- Q: Can a DMC decline to stop at a crossed efficacy boundary? A: Yes, and the type I error stays at most alpha if success claims need a prespecified crossing. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

dawn-trial.name: DAWN
dawn-trial.summary: A stroke thrombectomy trial 6 to 24 hours after onset whose Bayesian adaptive enrichment plan used predictive probability stopping and a threshold that rises with enrichment.
dawn-trial.body:
## What it is

DAWN tested thrombectomy with the Trevo device in acute ischemic stroke 6 to 24 hours after onset, in patients with a mismatch between clinical deficit and infarct core [15/dawn-predictive-probability-for-expected-success-and-futility]. It used a Bayesian adaptive enrichment design [14/dawn-a-success-threshold-that-moves-with-the-enrichment].

## Why it matters

The statistical analysis plan makes predictive probability the stopping quantity, which is the [[goldilocks-design]] structure with a schedule of thresholds [15/dawn-predictive-probability-for-expected-success-and-futility].

## In the book

From 200 randomized patients, with at least 100 since the last enrichment, the trial stops for expected success if the predictive probability exceeds 95 percent at 200 and 250 patients, 90 percent at 300 and 350, 85 percent at 400, and 80 percent at 450 and 500 [15/dawn-predictive-probability-for-expected-success-and-futility]. It stops for futility if the predictive probability at the maximum sample size is under 10 percent [15/dawn-predictive-probability-for-expected-success-and-futility]. The thresholds fall as the sample grows, so an early stop needs more certainty than a late one [15/dawn-predictive-probability-for-expected-success-and-futility].

The baseline success threshold is 0.986 on the posterior probability of superiority, chosen by simulation, and it is raised if enrichment occurs [14/dawn-a-success-threshold-that-moves-with-the-enrichment]. The trial stopped at the first efficacy look with 206 patients and 49 percent against 13 percent functional independence [14/dawn-a-success-threshold-that-moves-with-the-enrichment].

## Pitfalls

Every branch of the design, enrich or not and stop or not, needs its threshold computed so that the error is controlled on all of them [14/dawn-a-success-threshold-that-moves-with-the-enrichment].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the stopping threshold for expected success rise or fall as the sample grows? A: It falls, from 95 percent to 80 percent [15/dawn-predictive-probability-for-expected-success-and-futility].
- Q: What happens to the success threshold if enrichment occurs? A: It is raised [14/dawn-a-success-threshold-that-moves-with-the-enrichment].

14/dawn-a-success-threshold-that-moves-w.t: DAWN: a success threshold that moves with the enrichment

ddt-qualification.name: Drug development tool qualification
ddt-qualification.summary: A formal FDA process that qualifies a tool, such as a biomarker or outcome assessment, for a stated context of use that any sponsor can then rely on.
ddt-qualification.body:
## What it is
DDT qualification is a formal process by which FDA qualifies a tool, such as a biomarker, a clinical outcome assessment or an animal model, for a stated context of use. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification] Once qualified, any sponsor can use the tool within that context without FDA re-reviewing its suitability in each application. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification]

## Why it matters
The context of use is the key idea: a tool is qualified for a purpose, not in the abstract. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification] For trial design the relevance is endpoints, since a qualified tool is the kind of "well-defined and reliable method of assessing response" that 21 CFR 314.126 asks for. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification] The 21st Century Cures Act put the process on a statutory footing. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification]

## In the book
The meeting chooser lists DDT qualification for a biomarker or outcome assessment that many sponsors will use. [3/how-to-choose-the-meeting] It is slow and typically pursued by consortia. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is a tool qualified for? A: A stated context of use. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification]
- Q: Who usually pursues it? A: Consortia. [3/drug-development-tool-ddt-qualification]

de-finetti-representation.name: de Finetti representation
de-finetti-representation.summary: An exchangeable sequence of binary outcomes is a mixture of independent coins, which produces both a parameter and a prior from one judgment.
de-finetti-representation.body:
## What it is
de Finetti's representation theorem says what an exchangeable sequence of binary outcomes looks like. If any number of further outcomes could be added and the sequence stays exchangeable, there is a probability distribution $\Pi$ on $[0,1]$ such that [sec-exchangeability]

$$
\mathbb{P}(y_1, \ldots, y_n) = \int_0^1 \prod_{i=1}^n \theta^{y_i} (1-\theta)^{1-y_i} \, d\Pi(\theta) .
$$

The mixing distribution $\Pi$ need not have a density. [sec-exchangeability]

## Why it matters
Read it as a mixture over the unknown response rate of independent-coin probabilities. The theorem does not assume a parameter and then a prior. It produces both from the single judgment of exchangeability. [sec-exchangeability]

The parameter $\theta$ is the limiting fraction of responders, and $\Pi$ is our uncertainty about it. [sec-exchangeability]

## In the book
The practical content is that "responses are Bernoulli($p$) given $p$" and the prior on $p$ come as a package. A protocol that specifies a likelihood without a prior has specified half of a Bayesian model. The traditional protocol specifies the likelihood half and handles the other half through the sampling distribution. [sec-exchangeability]

Gelman and colleagues and Lindley give the full treatment, including the proof and the link to subjective probability. [sec-exchangeability]

## Pitfalls
The theorem needs exchangeability, a judgment that can fail. [sec-exchangeability] The book uses it informally. [sec-exchangeability]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the theorem assume a prior? A: No. It produces the parameter and the prior from exchangeability. [sec-exchangeability]
- Q: What is $\theta$ in the theorem? A: The limiting fraction of responders. [sec-exchangeability]

decision-theory.name: Decision theory
decision-theory.summary: A framework in which a prior, a model for the data and a utility or loss together say when approving, stopping or continuing a trial beats waiting.
decision-theory.body:
## What it is
A hypothesis test asks whether the data are surprising if the drug does nothing, and leaves the rest to judgment outside the statistics. The decision framework puts that judgment inside the model. [sec-decision-decision] It needs three ingredients: a prior for the treatment effect, a model for the data (the same likelihood as the traditional analysis), and a utility or loss that says what the outcomes are worth. [sec-decision-decision]

At a terminal analysis, suppose approving a drug that does not work costs $L_{\mathrm{I}}$ and failing to approve a drug that does work costs $L_{\mathrm{II}}$. With posterior probability $p$ that the drug works, approving is better when [sec-decision-decision]

$$
p > \frac{L_{\mathrm{I}}}{L_{\mathrm{I}} + L_{\mathrm{II}}}.
$$

This is equation eq-ch01-rule. [sec-decision-decision]

## Why it matters
The threshold depends only on the ratio of the two costs. If a false approval is thirty-nine times as costly as a missed drug, the threshold is 39/40 = 0.975, so the one-sided $\alpha = 0.025$ is an implicit statement of that ratio. [sec-decision-decision] With a flat prior and a normal likelihood, approving above 0.975 is the same as rejecting when the one-sided p-value is below 0.025. [sec-decision-decision]

## In the book
Every protocol fixes what is known going in, what will count as success, and what the sponsor may do along the way. [1/the-three-things-a-protocol-fixes] The regulator can judge a design by what it does under pre-specified truths, without sharing the sponsor's prior or utility. [1/the-three-things-a-protocol-fixes]

## Pitfalls
The displayed threshold is not an interim stopping rule. An interim decision must also compare both terminal losses with the sampling cost and the expected value of continuing. [sec-decision-decision]

## Check yourself
- Q: What threshold on the posterior probability corresponds to a cost ratio of 39 to 1? A: 39/40 = 0.975. [sec-decision-decision]
- Q: When do the Bayesian rule and the one-sided test agree? A: With a flat prior, a normal likelihood and a single look. [sec-decision-decision]

delayed-treatment-effect.name: Delayed treatment effect
delayed-treatment-effect.summary: A benefit that appears only after a lag, typical of immunotherapy, which costs the log-rank test power.
delayed-treatment-effect.body:
## What it is
A delayed effect is one where treatment does nothing at first, then reduces the hazard. In the book's figure, treatment cuts the hazard by 40 percent only after a delay of one year. [sec-survival-nph] The power simulation below uses a different delayed scenario: no benefit for two years, then a hazard ratio of 0.583. [sec-survival-power-loss]

## Why it matters
The log-rank test loses power because early events carry weight but are uninformative about treatment. [sec-survival-nph]

## In the book
The simulation has 300 patients per arm, 5 years of follow-up and a control hazard of 0.15 per year. It compares a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 with no benefit for two years then a hazard ratio of 0.583. [sec-survival-power-loss] Treated survival at five years is 0.57 in both, and the number of events is similar. [sec-survival-power-loss] Power is 0.68 under the constant hazard ratio and 0.55 under the delayed path, with 287 events in both. [sec-survival-power-loss] Two responses: a weighted log-rank test, or a design that states the delayed-effect model with its simulation in the protocol. [sec-survival-power-loss]

## Pitfalls
Either choice must be made before the trial. [sec-survival-power-loss]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the Schoenfeld calculation warn about delay? A: No, it assumes a single hazard ratio. [sec-survival-power-loss]
- Q: Do both scenarios reach the same final benefit? A: Yes, 0.57 treated survival at five years. [sec-survival-power-loss]

functions.title: Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank statistics for two groups
functions.description: Computes the standardized weighted log-rank statistics with Fleming-Harrington weights \eqn{S(t)^\rho \{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma}, where S is the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate just before each event time, for the four pairs \eqn{(\rho, \gamma) \in \{(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\}}, together with the correlation matrix of the four statistics. The first statistic is the ordinary log-rank test. The maximum of the four, referred to the multivariate normal distribution with this correlation matrix, is the MaxCombo test.

design-alternative.name: Design alternative
design-alternative.summary: The effect size a trial is built to detect, the most consequential and least certain input to the sample size.
design-alternative.body:
## What it is

The design alternative $\theta_d$ is the effect the sample size is built to detect. ICH E9 section 3.5 names two ways to choose it: the smallest effect that would be clinically relevant, or the effect the sponsor anticipates [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative].

## Why it matters

Because $n$ scales as $1/\theta^2$, a halving of $\theta$ from 0.20 to 0.10 takes the information requirement from 263 to 1,051 [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative]. A design for the minimal clinically important difference is conservative, but it does not establish that the effect exceeds the minimum, since the null tested is still zero [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative]. A design for the anticipated effect is optimistic and, if wrong, produces a failed trial [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative]. The sponsor's pick is a prior elicitation the protocol never calls by that name [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative].

## In the book

Reviewers see common failures: the assumed effect is the observed effect of a small phase 2 trial, biased upward by selection; variability is taken from the same small trial; the control event rate comes from a historical cohort; no sensitivity analysis is given [9/what-the-regulator-sees-and-what-the-sponsor-can-do-wrong]. A sound protocol gives a table of power at 70%, 80%, 100% and 120% of the design alternative [9/what-the-regulator-sees-and-what-the-sponsor-can-do-wrong]. Only 28% of phase III trials repeating phase II regimens were positive [sec-power-zia].

## Pitfalls

A design alternative equal to the phase 2 estimate is biased upward, so a trial sized on it is underpowered at the true effect [sec-power-zia].

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to the information required when the design effect halves from 0.20 to 0.10? A: It rises from 263 to 1,051 [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative].
- Q: Does designing for the minimal clinically important difference show the effect exceeds it? A: No, the null tested is still zero [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative].

deviation-scale.name: Deviation scale
deviation-scale.summary: Three scales of evidence, central limit, moderate deviation and large deviation, that set the bar on the squared standardized statistic for a fixed test, a Bayes rule and an anytime-valid rule.
deviation-scale.body:
## What it is

The chapter puts monitoring on one scale and gets three prices of evidence. A single look asks for a constant $z_\alpha^2$. The Bayes rule asks for a slowly growing $\log n + C$. The normal-mixture rule valid at every stopping time asks for approximately $\log n + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)$. These are large-information approximations. [sec-sequential]

The Bayes bar follows the moderate deviation relation, and the anytime-valid mixture rule rests on the Bayes factor with its Ockham penalty [11/set-up]:

$$
n\theta^2 \asymp \log n,
$$

$$
L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2) \sim \log I_n
$$

$$
\mathrm{BF}_n = (1 + I_n\tau^2)^{-1/2} \exp\Bigl\{\frac{Z_n^2}{2}\cdot\frac{I_n\tau^2}{1+I_n\tau^2}\Bigr\}, \qquad
2\log \mathrm{BF}_n = Z_n^2 - L_n - \frac{Z_n^2}{1+q}, \qquad q = I_n\tau^2,
$$

The mean-path crossing approximation is

$$
n\,I\,\theta^2 = b_n^2,
$$

[11/the-sequential-power-calculation]

- Central limit, standard design: constant $z_\alpha^2$.
- Moderate deviation, Bayes: $\log n + C$, which grows slowly.
- Large deviation, anytime valid: $\log n + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)$.

[11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]

## Why it matters

The Bayes bar is governed by the moderate deviation relation $n\theta^2 \asymp \log n$. Under it the type I error induced by a Bayes rule at threshold one tends to zero polynomially at a single analysis, rather than being pinned at a constant. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]

## In the book

The mixture Bayes factor uses the Ockham penalty $L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2) \sim \log I_n$, the price for integrating the parameter out. Under the null $\mathrm{BF}_n$ is a nonnegative martingale, so Ville's inequality bounds the chance it ever reaches $1/\alpha$. [11/set-up]

Three logarithms are easily run together. The $\log\log n$ of the iterated logarithm is the envelope of a random walk, the $\log n$ is the price of integrating a parameter out, and $\log(1/\alpha)$ is a quantity of evidence fixed by an error level. [11/four-boundaries-compared]

The mean-path crossing approximation is $n\,I\,\theta^2 = b_n^2$, the fixed-sample requirement with the power margin removed. [11/the-sequential-power-calculation]

## Pitfalls

- These are properties of the normal-mixture construction, not universal costs of anytime validity. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]
- The mean-path approximation is not a median stopping time. [11/the-sequential-power-calculation]

## Check yourself

- Q: Which scale has a bar that grows like log n? A: The moderate deviation scale, the Bayes rule. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]
- Q: What extra term does the anytime-valid scale add? A: $2\log(1/\alpha)$. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]

functions.name: gs_tolls
functions.title: The three evidence tolls on the |Z| scale
functions.description: Fixed level bar z_\alpha, a Bayes bar with Ockham penalty L_n = \log(1 + q), q = I_n\tau^2, and an anytime-valid (e-value) bar at threshold 1/\alpha. Each of the last two is returned in two clearly labelled forms.

results.name: The three deviation scales (evidence tolls)
results.summary: A fixed level test, a Bayes rule and an anytime valid rule act at three different sizes of the squared standardized score; for the normal mixture the anytime valid bar exceeds the Bayes bar by a surcharge that is about 2 log(1/alpha) at large information.
results.statement: Let $Z_n$ be the standardized score at information $I_n$, $q = I_n\tau^2$ for a normal prior of scale $\tau$, and $L_n = \log(1+q)$ the Ockham penalty. The one sided fixed level test at level $\alpha$ acts when $Z_n \ge z_\alpha$. For the symmetric normal mixture, the exact Bayes factor rule with threshold $b$ acts when $Z_n^2 \ge (1 + 1/q)\{\log(1+q) + 2\log b\}$ with $Z_n > 0$ for a one sided claim, and the anytime valid rule at level $\alpha$ is the same with $b = 1/\alpha$. In the large information approximation these bars are $Z_n^2 \ge L_n + 2\log b$ and $Z_n^2 \ge L_n + 2\log(1/\alpha)$, so that the anytime valid rule requires about $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ more, in squared standardized units, than the Bayes rule at $b = 1$ (exactly $7.38(1 + 1/q)$). This is a property of the normal mixture construction and not a universal cost of anytime validity: other e processes, such as iterated logarithm confidence sequences, behave differently.

disproportionality-analysis.name: Disproportionality analysis
disproportionality-analysis.summary: Screening that flags drug and event pairs reported more often than their margins predict under independence.
disproportionality-analysis.body:
## What it is

For each drug and event pair the table has an observed count $n_{ij}$ and an expected count $E_{ij}$ computed from the margins under independence. Disproportionality asks which pairs are reported more than the margins predict. [sec-safety-gps]

## Why it matters

Spontaneous report tables have no exposure denominators, so they cannot give incidence. Disproportionality is what they can offer. [sec-safety-gps] The EMA guideline accepts the proportional reporting ratio, the reporting odds ratio and the Bayesian and empirical Bayes measures as screening tools, and says a statistical signal is only a hypothesis to be assessed clinically. [sec-safety]

## In the book

The simplest statistics are the relative reporting ratio $n_{ij}/E_{ij}$ and its cousins. [13/the-traditional-measure] Their weakness is at the sparse end: one report against an expected count of 0.05 gives a ratio of twenty, and a table with millions of cells holds many such pairs by chance. [13/the-traditional-measure] The [[gamma-poisson-shrinker]] fixes this by shrinkage. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Pitfalls

- A high score is a hypothesis for clinical assessment, not evidence of causation. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is a raw ratio of 20 on one report not a signal? A: For a rare pair the ratio is dominated by noise, and shrinkage pulls it toward one. [13/the-traditional-measure]
