fixed-allocation.name: Fixed allocation
fixed-allocation.summary: Setting the allocation ratio in the protocol, almost always 1:1, and keeping it for the whole study; the default that response-adaptive randomization must beat.
fixed-allocation.body:
## What it is

A traditional two-arm trial fixes the allocation ratio in the protocol and keeps it for the whole study [sec-rar-fixed]. Almost always the ratio is 1:1, implemented by permuted blocks, perhaps stratified [sec-rar-fixed].

## Why it matters

For equal variances the standard error of the difference is proportional to $\sqrt{1/n_1 + 1/n_0}$, smallest when $n_0 = n_1$ for a fixed total [16/why-11]. Permuted blocks also balance calendar time, so any change in patient mix hits both arms equally [16/why-11]. Allocation independent of outcomes keeps the randomization distribution exactly known [16/why-11].

## In the book

A 2:1 ratio costs 12.5 percent more patients, 3:1 costs a third more, and 9:1 costs almost three times as many [16/why-11]. For a control response of 0.30 and a treatment response of 0.45 the optimal share on treatment is only 52 percent [16/why-11]. Unequal ratios are justified when stated in advance, for example for safety exposure or a shared control [16/unequal-fixed-allocation-and-when-it-is-justified]. With $k$ experimental arms, Dunnett's result is that the control arm should be about $\sqrt{k}$ times as large as each treatment arm; with three arms equal allocation puts 25 percent on control and Dunnett's rule 36.6 percent [16/unequal-fixed-allocation-and-when-it-is-justified].

## Pitfalls

A fixed control share protects control accrual but does not establish acceptability of adaptive allocation among experimental arms [16/unequal-fixed-allocation-and-when-it-is-justified]. For a confirmatory two-arm trial, use fixed allocation [sec-rar-practice].

## Check yourself

- Q: What does 2:1 allocation cost in sample size for the same power? A: 12.5 percent more patients [16/why-11].
- Q: Why does blocking make time trends harmless? A: Each arm receives the same number of patients within a block, so changes in patient mix hit both arms equally [16/why-11].

16/unequal-fixed-allocation-and-when-it-.t: Unequal fixed allocation and when it is justified

fixed-sequence-testing.name: Fixed-sequence testing
fixed-sequence-testing.summary: Order hypotheses in advance and test each at the full alpha, stopping at the first failure.
fixed-sequence-testing.body:
## What it is

Order the hypotheses in advance by clinical importance: $H_1, H_2, \dots, H_k$. Test $H_1$ at the full $\alpha$. If it is rejected, test $H_2$ at the full $\alpha$, and so on. Stop at the first failure and do not test the rest. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]

## Why it matters

The familywise error rate is controlled at $\alpha$ with no division of the level, because at most one hypothesis can be the first true null, and it is tested at $\alpha$. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]

This is the most common strategy for a primary endpoint followed by key secondaries. It is what "primary/secondary hierarchy" means in a protocol. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]

## In the book

The price is that the order is final. A failure on the primary, or on an early secondary, makes all later results exploratory regardless of how impressive they look. This surprises clinical teams that have seen a large effect on endpoint 4. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]

Two consequences for writing the hierarchy: put first the endpoint with the best chance of success and the most important claim, since a failure ends the chain. And the sequence can be a tree and not a line, which is a graphical procedure. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]

## Pitfalls

- Testing four secondaries at alpha/4 regardless of the primary may be worse for the claims the sponsor cares about than a fixed-sequence or graphical procedure. [10/key-points]

## Check yourself

- Q: A primary endpoint fails. May the key secondaries be tested at full level? A: No, later results become exploratory. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]
- Q: Why is no division of alpha needed? A: At most one hypothesis can be the first true null, and it is tested at alpha. [10/fixed-sequence-hierarchical-testing]

forking-paths.name: Forking paths
forking-paths.summary: Multiplicity hidden in analyst choices: even one test is many if which test was run depended on the data.
forking-paths.body:
## What it is

The analyst who sees a promising subgroup usually chose how to cut: age above or below 65, 60 or 70, tertiles or a threshold. Gelman and Loken called this the garden of forking paths. Even if the analyst ran only one test, the choice of which test depended on the data. [sec-mult-subgroups]

The effective number of comparisons is the number of tests that would have been run had the data looked different. The multiplicity is hidden in decisions, not in the number of $p$-values. [sec-mult-subgroups]

## Why it matters

A Bayesian analysis conditions on the data it is shown. The regulator sees a message $M = \varsigma(X)$, where the reporting rule $\varsigma$ is chosen by the sponsor. [sec-mult-selected] The protocol is the specification of $\varsigma$. [sec-mult-selected]

## In the book

If the sponsor reports the largest of $K$ independent components, the likelihood of the reported value $m$ is given below. [sec-mult-selected]

$$
\mathcal{L}_\varsigma(\theta; m) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p(m \mid \theta_k) \prod_{j \ne k} F(m \mid \theta_j),
$$

with $F$ the distribution function of a component. For exchangeable components the ratio to the naive likelihood approaches $K$ in the upper tail. [sec-mult-selected]

With a common effect $\theta \sim N(0, 1)$ and only the maximum reported, the correct likelihood carries an extra factor $\Phi(m - \theta)^{K-1}$, which pulls the posterior down. [sec-mult-selected]

## Pitfalls

- The retort that optional stopping does not affect the posterior is correct only when the full sample path is reported. It is beside the point when the report is a summary chosen after the fact. [sec-mult-selected]
- The regulator cannot compute the correct posterior without knowing the reporting rule. [sec-mult-selected]

## Check yourself

- Q: Where does the multiplicity hide when only one test was run? A: In the choice of which test, which depended on the data. [sec-mult-subgroups]
- Q: What fixes the reporting rule for a regulator? A: The protocol. [sec-mult-selected]

sec-mult-selected.t: Why a Bayesian must also ask how the result was chosen

four-operation-ulcer-trial.name: Four-operation ulcer trial
four-operation-ulcer-trial.summary: A 1965 duodenal ulcer trial of four operations that Novick and Grizzle used to argue for Bayesian analysis, and the book's worked multiplicity example.
four-operation-ulcer-trial.body:
## What it is

Novick and Grizzle made one of the first cases for Bayesian analysis of trial data using an experiment then in progress that compared four operative treatments for duodenal ulcer. It has four arms, six pairwise contrasts, repeated analysis and a modest effect on a binary endpoint. [10/the-original]

The counts in the book are illustrative, set at the scale of that trial and not transcribed from the 1965 paper. They ship with the package as the dataset `ulcer`. [10/the-original]

## Why it matters

It is the structure on which the traditional apparatus does worst, so it shows both ways to pay for looking. [10/the-original]

## In the book

The best against worst contrast, drainage and vagotomy against 75 percent resection, is a difference of 12.4 percentage points in the recurrence rate, with $Z=2.45$. With six contrasts the Bonferroni-adjusted $p$ is 0.0855, not reportable, and Holm does not rescue it. [10/what-the-traditional-reading-does-with-it]

A group sequential design with four interim analyses at the corrected level would put the first boundary at 5.34. [10/what-the-traditional-reading-does-with-it]

The hierarchical model pays in the estimate instead. The best against worst contrast is shrunk from 1.053 to 0.464 on the log-odds scale, and the posterior probability that drainage and vagotomy is worse than 75 percent resection is 0.952, a number a clinician can use. It is not a claim of significance under strong familywise control. [10/what-the-hierarchical-reading-does-with-it]

The four operations are ordered by extent of resection, so a single prespecified linear trend contrast carries no multiplicity burden (trend $p = 0.0043$). [10/structure-that-the-correction-cannot-see]

## Pitfalls

- The companion lab's module 05 uses a different table for this trial, so its numbers differ from the chapter's. [10/the-original]
- The estimate of the between-arm spread rests on four arms and is the sensitive part. [10/what-the-hierarchical-reading-does-with-it]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does the best against worst contrast overstate the effect? A: It was chosen because it is the largest of six. [10/what-the-traditional-reading-does-with-it]
- Q: What single contrast avoids a multiplicity burden here? A: A prespecified linear trend over the ordered extent of resection. [10/structure-that-the-correction-cannot-see]

results.statement: In the four operation ulcer example (counts illustrative, at the scale of the 1965 trial of Novick and Grizzle), the Bonferroni adjusted $p$-value for best against worst is $0.0855$, while the hierarchical posterior probability that drainage and vagotomy is worse than 75 per cent resection is $0.952$, on a contrast shrunk from $1.053$ to $0.464$. futility-boundary.name: Futility boundary
futility-boundary.summary: The lower edge of the continuation region: stop if the interim statistic is below it. Binding rules enter the type I error, non-binding ones do not.
futility-boundary.body:
## What it is

An efficacy boundary is the upper edge of the continuation region. A futility boundary is the lower edge: if the interim statistic is below it, the trial stops because the treatment is unlikely to show benefit. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

- A binding boundary is part of the design. If crossed the trial stops, and the type I error assumes it does. The reduction can lower the efficacy boundaries a little. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]
- A non-binding boundary is a guideline. The type I error is computed as though it did not exist, so it is at most $\alpha$ whether the committee follows it or not. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

## Why it matters

Futility stops shorten trials of useless drugs and reduce false positives. The traditional position, encouraged by regulators, is the non-binding rule, because a DMC's decision to continue should never invalidate the type I error. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

## In the book

On a four-look O'Brien-Fleming design the book stops for futility at looks 1, 2, 3 if the standardized statistic is below zero. Under the null this stops the trial early about 69 percent of the time, and 50 percent at the first look alone. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

The rule costs some power under the alternative, because trials with a true benefit sometimes have a negative interim statistic by chance. A binding rule recovers a little of it, but if overridden the type I error is no longer controlled. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

EOLIA stopped for futility under a two-sided triangular test, with relative risk 0.76 (95% confidence interval 0.55 to 1.04). [11/a-futility-stop-and-its-reanalysis-eolia-2018]

## Pitfalls

- Power must be computed as if the futility rule were followed. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]
- A threshold of Z below 0 is crude. In practice the criterion is usually conditional power or predictive probability. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

## Check yourself

- Q: If a DMC overrides a binding futility rule, what happens to the type I error? A: It is no longer controlled. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]
- Q: Why is a non-binding rule safe for the type I error? A: Ignoring it can only increase the chance of crossing the efficacy boundary, and that is already at most alpha. [11/futility-boundaries-binding-and-non-binding]

gamma-poisson-shrinker.name: Gamma-Poisson shrinker
gamma-poisson-shrinker.summary: An empirical Bayes method that shrinks noisy reporting ratios with a two-component gamma mixture and ranks signals by their geometric mean and fifth percentile.
gamma-poisson-shrinker.body:
## What it is

Each pair has a true reporting ratio $\lambda_{ij}$, with $n_{ij} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_{ij} E_{ij})$. The ratios come from a mixture of two gamma distributions: [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

$$
\lambda \sim P\, \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_1, \beta_1) + (1 - P)\, \mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_2, \beta_2),
$$

eq-safety-gps, with five parameters estimated from the whole table by maximum marginal likelihood. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker] The posterior is again a two-component gamma mixture, with component $k$ becoming $\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_k + n, \beta_k + E)$. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

Signals are ranked by $\mathrm{EBGM} = \exp(\mathbb{E}[\log \lambda \mid n])$ and screened on its fifth percentile, EB05. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Why it matters

DuMouchel proposed it as the empirical Bayes method behind the FDA's data mining of its reports database. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker] It ranks signals by evidence as well as by size. [13/key-points]

## In the book

With illustrative hyperparameters, the single report with a raw ratio of twenty is shrunk and its lower bound is well below one, so it is not a signal. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker] Two pairs with the same raw ratio of four are treated differently: the pair with 40 reports has a high EB05 and is flagged, the pair with 12 less so. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker] A screening rule of EB05 above 2 flags the pairs with $n = 12$ and $n = 40$ and nothing else. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Pitfalls

- The illustrative values only show the mechanics. In a real analysis they are fitted to the whole table, because shrinkage is only as good as the estimated mixture. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]
- A high EB05 is a hypothesis, not evidence of causation. It does not correct for bias in the reporting mechanism. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Check yourself

- Q: Does a raw ratio of 20 on one report survive shrinkage? A: No, its EB05 is well below one. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]
- Q: Two pairs share a raw ratio of 4, with 12 and 40 reports. Which has the higher EB05? A: The one with 40 reports. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

gamma-posterior-hazard.name: Gamma posterior for a hazard
gamma-posterior-hazard.summary: For a constant hazard, a Gamma(a, b) prior and d events in exposure T give a Gamma(a + d, b + T) posterior.
gamma-posterior-hazard.body:
## What it is
For a single arm with constant hazard $\lambda$, $d$ events in total follow-up $T$ give likelihood $\lambda^d e^{-\lambda T}$ whatever the censoring pattern, if censoring is noninformative. [sec-survival-gamma] With a $\mathrm{Gamma}(a, b)$ prior the posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(a + d, b + T)$. The prior is worth $a$ events and $b$ years of exposure. [sec-survival-gamma]

## Why it matters
Dividing time into intervals with constant hazards gives independent gamma terms per interval. A random walk on $\log\lambda_k$ smooths the hazard and lets sparse late intervals borrow from earlier ones. [sec-survival-gamma] This piecewise exponential model underlies most Bayesian time-to-event analyses. [sec-survival-gamma]

## In the book
A control arm has 60 events in 400 patient-years, with a vague Gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior. [sec-survival-gamma] Median survival under the exponential model is $\log 2/\lambda$. Its posterior mean is not the plug-in $\log 2/0.15$, because the median is a reciprocal of the hazard, and its interval is asymmetric. [sec-survival-gamma] The posterior is transformed directly, with no delta method. [sec-survival-gamma] The posterior mean hazard is 0.150 (95% interval 0.114 to 0.190), and the posterior mean median is 4.7 years against the plug-in 4.62, with interval 3.6 to 6.1. [sec-survival-gamma]

## Pitfalls
A constant hazard is rarely realistic over years of follow-up. [sec-survival-gamma]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the posterior after d events in T years of exposure with a Gamma(a, b) prior? A: Gamma(a + d, b + T). [sec-survival-gamma]

sec-survival-gamma.t: The gamma posterior for a hazard

functions.description: Posterior Gamma(a + d, b + T) for d events in T patient-years, with the posterior mean and equal-tailed interval for the hazard and for the exponential median survival log 2 / lambda (exact, by the reciprocal transformation).

gbm-agile-trial.name: GBM AGILE
gbm-agile-trial.summary: A Bayesian response-adaptive glioblastoma platform designed for registration, with a seamless phase 2/3 structure and a shared control.
gbm-agile-trial.body:
## What it is

GBM AGILE (NCT03970447) is a Bayesian response-adaptive platform in glioblastoma designed with registration in mind, which I-SPY 2 was not. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform] It uses a seamless phase 2/3 structure. In stage 1 each arm is randomized adaptively against a shared control (temozolomide in newly diagnosed disease, lomustine in recurrent), with allocation proportional to the posterior probability of a hazard ratio below a benchmark and arms evaluated monthly. An arm that clears the bar graduates to stage 2 with fixed randomization to confirm the finding. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform]

## Why it matters

Patients are classified into signatures by newly diagnosed versus recurrent disease and MGMT methylation status, and 20% of each subtype's patients are assigned to control. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform] FDA's Bayesian draft names the platform as its example for the time machine, since the shared control must be used carefully when standard of care changes. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform]

## In the book

For regorafenib, efficacy required a Bayesian probability of benefit (hazard ratio below 1) of at least 98%, and enrollment stopped for limited efficacy when predictive power fell below 25% in all signatures. The report has since been corrected by an erratum. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform] The 98% is set by simulation so that the false positive rate is acceptable, not by a view about the prior. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform] The registry lists 17 arm entries, several running dose-finding and enhanced safety management phases first, which is a pattern worth copying. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform]

## Pitfalls

Thresholds like 98% are calibrated per design, so they cannot be carried over to another platform without a new simulation report. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a stage 1 graduate do next? A: Moves to stage 2 with fixed randomization. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform]
- Q: What share of each subtype is on control? A: 20%. [20/gbm-agile-a-registration-platform]

gittins-index.name: Gittins index
gittins-index.summary: The exact solution to the discounted infinite-horizon bandit problem: give each patient the arm with the highest index, which depends only on that arm's own history.
gittins-index.body:
## What it is

Each arm has a state, which for a binary outcome is its counts of successes and failures, and future rewards are discounted by a factor $\gamma < 1$ per patient [16/the-gittins-index]. The index of an arm in state $s$ is the highest achievable ratio of expected discounted reward to expected discounted time, over the stopping times $\tau$ at which one might abandon the arm:

$$
G(s) = \sup_{\tau > 0} \frac{\mathrm{E}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \gamma^t r_t \mid s\bigr]}{\mathrm{E}\bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \gamma^t \mid s\bigr]}.
$$

[16/the-gittins-index]

## Why it matters

Equivalently it is the constant payoff per patient at which a decision maker is indifferent between continuing with the arm and retiring to a sure thing [16/the-gittins-index]. The optimal policy gives each patient the arm with the highest index, and each arm's index depends only on its own history, so many arms are solved by tabulating one-arm indices [16/the-gittins-index].

## In the book

The index exceeds the posterior mean when the arm is uncertain, and the excess is the value of learning [16/the-gittins-index]. This premium makes an optimal policy try a new arm even when its estimate is mediocre, and a longer horizon raises it [16/the-gittins-index]. Gittins showed the result for geometric discounting [16/exploring-and-exploiting].

## Pitfalls

It is exact for an infinite, discounted horizon, whereas a trial has a fixed number of patients and a finite-horizon problem has no index solution [16/the-gittins-index]. The objective is the reward to patients in the trial, not that of a confirmatory comparison [16/the-gittins-index]. Practical designs use approximations, with [[thompson-sampling]] the most common [16/the-gittins-index].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does an untried arm's index sit above or at its posterior mean? A: Above, because uncertainty carries a premium for learning [16/the-gittins-index].
- Q: Why is the index not a design for a fixed-size trial? A: It solves the infinite discounted horizon; a finite horizon has no index solution [16/the-gittins-index].

goldilocks-design.name: Goldilocks design
goldilocks-design.summary: A trial that lets accrual run until two predictive probabilities say the sample is not too big and not too small, with thresholds calibrated by simulation.
goldilocks-design.body:
## What it is

The Goldilocks sample size design of Broglio, Connor and Berry does not fix its sample size [sec-sim-goldilocks]. At each look it computes $\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}$, success if enrollment stops now and pending outcomes complete, and $\mathrm{PP}_{\max}$, success at the maximum sample size [sec-sim-goldilocks]. It stops enrolling for expected success when the first is high and stops for futility when the second is low [sec-sim-goldilocks].

## Why it matters

The sample size is an output, bounded by $N_{\max}$, and the thresholds are calibrated by simulating type I error, not derived [sec-sim-goldilocks]. The design replaces an interim efficacy boundary, a futility boundary and sample size re-estimation with one pre-specified rule [sec-goldilocks]. Its price is a random sample size, so budgets must be planned for the maximum [sec-goldilocks].

## In the book

With immediate outcomes $\mathrm{PP}_{\text{stop}}$ collapses to an indicator and only the $\mathrm{PP}_{\max}$ futility rule remains [sec-sim-goldilocks]. In the chapter 14 sketch, futility at $F = 0.05$ cuts the expected sample size under the null by more than half, at a cost in power largest at the design alternative 0.15 [sec-sim-goldilocks]. In the chapter 15 example, 30 of 50 against 15 of 50 stops enrollment, and equal rates of 18 of 50 stop for futility [sec-goldilocks]. DAWN's plan is a trial-sized version [sec-sim-goldilocks].

## Pitfalls

Stopping enrollment when the predictive probability is high is an efficacy decision and spends type I error [sec-goldilocks]. The look frequency and the delay length change the calibration [sec-goldilocks].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which predictive probability triggers futility? A: $\mathrm{PP}_{\max}$, when it is low [sec-goldilocks].
- Q: Does the design fix the sample size? A: No, it is an output bounded by $N_{\max}$ [sec-sim-goldilocks].

Because the rule is pp > c, the empirical error is at most alpha, with equality up to Monte Carlo ties.

governance-firewall.name: Governance and firewalls
governance-firewall.summary: Who sees unblinded comparative data in an adaptive trial: an independent statistical center and a DMC see it, and the sponsor does not.
governance-firewall.body:
## What it is
Adaptive trials need someone to see unblinded comparative data during the trial in order to apply the adaptation rules, and the sponsor must not. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
The integrity concern is that knowledge of interim results, or even of what decision was made, can change the behavior of investigators, patients and sponsor staff. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]

## Why it matters
The FDA DMC guidance of 2006 remains the starting document, with a draft revision issued in February 2024. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
Nothing about the Bayesian rule changes the firewall; what changes is the number the committee reads. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept]

## In the book
A workable arrangement has four parties. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
The independent statistical center holds the randomization code, runs the interim analyses and computes posterior and predictive probabilities. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
The DMC applies or overrides the rules, and the charter states that the prespecified rules are guides so the committee keeps its judgment on safety. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
The sponsor's blinded team receives only what the charter allows, and regulators may see more than the sponsor. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
The DMC should receive the simulation report or a summary, so its members know what the rules were designed to do. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]

## Pitfalls
For response-adaptive randomization the allocation ratios themselves can reveal results. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what] The usual safeguard is a burn-in period of equal allocation before adaptation begins, with the statistical center and not the sponsor holding the algorithm. [20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitoring-board]
Firewalls in a platform trial are more complex since arms enter and leave, and a sponsor of one arm should not see data of competing arms. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
A DMC asked to apply a rule it does not understand will either follow it blindly or ignore it. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]

## Check yourself
- Q: Who computes the decision quantities? A: The independent statistical center. [23/the-data-monitoring-committee-firewalls-and-who-sees-what]
- Q: Does a Bayesian design change the firewall? A: No, it changes what the DMC reads. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept]

graphical-procedure.name: Graphical procedure
graphical-procedure.summary: A multiple testing framework where hypotheses are nodes with weights and edges pass a rejected hypothesis's level to others, so the graph is the protocol.
graphical-procedure.body:
## What it is

Bretz, Maurer, Brannath and Posch gave a framework that unifies Bonferroni, Holm, fixed sequence, fallback and gatekeeping procedures in one picture. Each hypothesis is a node with a weight $w_i$, its share of $\alpha$, with $\sum w_i \le 1$. Directed edges carry weights $g_{ij}$, the fraction of $H_i$'s level that passes to $H_j$ if $H_i$ is rejected. [10/graphical-procedures]

The algorithm rejects any $H_i$ with $p_i \le w_i\alpha$, removes it, passes its weight along the edges, updates the edge weights, and repeats. It controls the familywise error rate strongly because each step is a closed-test shortcut. [10/graphical-procedures]

## Why it matters

The graph is the protocol. A statistician can draw it for the clinical team, the team can see which results unlock which, and the same picture goes into the statistical analysis plan. [10/graphical-procedures]

## In the book

The example has two primary endpoints and two secondaries. Each primary gets half the level. A rejected primary passes its level to the secondary that clinically follows it, and a rejected secondary passes its level to the other primary. [10/graphical-procedures]

In the second scenario P1 at 0.020 fails alone, but P2 is rejected and passes to S2. S2 is rejected and returns its level to P1, which then clears 0.025, and S1 follows. A single common marginal $p$-value of 0.015 is not enough when each primary has only half of the level, 0.0125. [10/graphical-procedures]

For an outcomes trial with a group sequential design, the protocol needs three statements: the spending function for each hypothesis, the rule that a transferred weight is spent from the look at which the transfer happens, and the graph with its weights printed. [10/graphical-procedures]

## Pitfalls

- A design that says only "alpha is spent by O'Brien-Fleming" has left the key secondary undefined. [10/graphical-procedures]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does an edge weight g_ij mean? A: The fraction of H_i's level passed to H_j when H_i is rejected. [10/graphical-procedures]
- Q: Why can two primaries at p=0.015 each fail when alpha is 0.025? A: Each has only half of the level, 0.0125, and nothing unlocks. [10/graphical-procedures]

group-sequential-design.name: Group sequential design
group-sequential-design.summary: A design with planned interim looks at fractions of the information, where boundaries keep the total type I error at its nominal level.
group-sequential-design.body:
## What it is

A trial that looks at accumulating data needs a rule for stopping that keeps the type I error at its nominal level. In a group sequential trial the interim analyses are written at information fractions $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_K = 1$, and that is the whole of the design language the chapter needs. [11/the-traditional-starting-point-one-look-one-test]

ICH E9 calls group sequential designs the usual vehicle, because assessing grouped outcomes at periodic intervals is more practicable than continuous review. [sec-sequential]

## Why it matters

Every look is another chance for chance to produce a convincing-looking result. Every sequential method is a response to that inflation, and methods differ only in what they charge for the right to look. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

## In the book

Boundaries come from the Wang-Tsiatis family $b_k = c\, t_k^{\Delta - 1/2}$, with Pocock at $\Delta = 1/2$ and O'Brien-Fleming at $\Delta = 0$. The constant $c$ is found so that the crossing probabilities sum to 0.025 under the null. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them] The trade-off: Pocock inflates the sample size by about 18 percent and stops on average at 0.59 of the information, O'Brien-Fleming inflates it by about 2 percent and stops at 0.75. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

Other families include Armitage's plans, Whitehead's triangular test, futility boundaries added by Pampallona and Tsiatis, and the unified family of Kittelson and Emerson. A design is chosen by weighing maximum sample size, expected sample size and stopping probabilities, not by ranking families. [sec-ch10-families]

The final bar for four O'Brien-Fleming looks is 2.02 and the sample-size inflation is about 2 percent. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

## Pitfalls

- The number and timing of looks must be written down before the data are seen. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]
- Where only a few looks at fixed fractions are planned and no prior information is used, the traditional design is hard to improve on. [11/traditional-and-bayesian-monitoring-side-by-side]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a group sequential design fix in advance? A: The boundaries, or a spending function, at planned information fractions. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]
- Q: Why is a fixed 1.96 cutoff at every look not a test? A: Looks are correlated but not identical, so the chance of at least one crossing exceeds 0.025 and grows with the number of looks. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

gsdesign.name: gsDesign
gsdesign.summary: An R package for group sequential design, including spending functions, boundaries, power and sample size calculation.
gsdesign.body:
## What it is
gsDesign is an R package for group sequential design. [sec-software-tools] It includes spending functions and boundaries, and power and sample size calculation. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
A reader can use it to check the book's own boundary code. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
The book suggests comparing its boundaries with `gs_boundary` and `gs_spending_boundary`. [sec-software-tools] The build machine had gsDesign 3.11.0. [sec-software-tools] The book's own boundary code can be checked against it, which makes gsDesign an independent reference for a calculation the reader would otherwise have to trust. [sec-software-tools] Its listed alternative, rpact 4.4.0 on the build machine, covers confirmatory adaptive design: group sequential designs, sample size reassessment and combination tests, with simulation. [sec-software-tools]

## Pitfalls
The description covers only purpose, so check the documentation for current features. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which bayestrials functions does the book suggest comparing against gsDesign? A: gs_boundary and gs_spending_boundary. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Which version was installed? A: 3.11.0. [sec-software-tools]

gusto-trial.name: GUSTO
gusto-trial.summary: A myocardial infarction trial of accelerated tPA against streptokinase that the book reanalyzes with priors built from two earlier megatrials at several weights.
gusto-trial.body:
## What it is
GUSTO randomized 41,021 patients with acute myocardial infarction to four strategies, including accelerated tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) and two streptokinase arms. [22/the-trial-and-its-traditional-analysis]
Thirty-day mortality was 6.3 percent on accelerated tPA and 7.2 and 7.4 percent on the two streptokinase-only arms. [22/the-trial-and-its-traditional-analysis]
The prespecified comparison gave a 14 percent relative reduction in mortality (95 percent interval 5.9 to 21.3 percent), $p = 0.001$, an absolute benefit of one percentage point at a substantially higher drug cost. [22/the-trial-and-its-traditional-analysis]

## Why it matters
Brophy and Joseph asked what a cardiologist should have believed given the earlier megatrials GISSI-2 and ISIS-3. [22/the-bayesian-question]
They weighted the earlier trials at 100, 50 and 10 percent and concluded that the clinical superiority of tPA "remains uncertain". [22/the-bayesian-question]

## In the book
With GUSTO alone the probability that tPA lowers mortality was 0.9995, and 0.17, 0.44 and 0.98 at the three weights in Brophy and Joseph's arm model. [22/the-bayesian-question]
The book puts the prior on the risk difference, with the earlier trials at weight $w$, and `reanalysis_gusto()` reproduces both models. [22/the-bayesian-question]
In the book's difference model, that tPA lowers mortality at all is very probable under every weight (at least 0.968); the low probabilities in Brophy and Joseph's arm model come from pooling each arm's rate across trials. That it lowers mortality by a full percentage point is unlikely once the earlier trials count at half weight or more. [22/the-bayesian-question]
The models part company because pooling each arm's rate across trials absorbs the difference between trials into the difference between agents, the mechanism of Simpson's paradox. [22/the-bayesian-question]

## Pitfalls
Borrowing within-trial treatment contrasts avoids pooling dissimilar baseline mortality rates; an arm-level model needs trial-specific baseline risks and justified borrowing. [22/the-bayesian-question]
The decision to pay for tPA turns on whether the benefit is large enough to matter, and on the price of a life year. [22/the-bayesian-question]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the book's difference model agree with the arm model on GUSTO alone? A: Yes, they part company as the earlier trials gain weight. [22/the-bayesian-question]
- Q: What question does the one-point threshold address? A: Whether the benefit is large enough to justify the price. [22/the-bayesian-question]

functions.name: reanalysis_gusto

functions.description: Thirty-day mortality, accelerated tPA against streptokinase, from the GUSTO counts of Brophy and Joseph (1995, Table 1), with the earlier trials GISSI-2 and ISIS-3 entering at weight w (each earlier patient counts as w of a GUSTO patient). Two models are reported.

hazard-ratio.name: Hazard ratio
hazard-ratio.summary: The ratio of event hazards between arms, a clean summary only when hazards are proportional.
hazard-ratio.body:
## What it is
The hazard ratio compares the instantaneous event rates of two arms. The book's convention is benefit-positive: $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$ is positive when treatment reduces the hazard. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Why it matters
Sample size in event units depends on it. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 percent power and 1,225 events. [sec-survival-traditional] A hazard ratio of 0.90 needs far more events, so tens of thousands of patients followed for years. [sec-survival-traditional]

## In the book
Under non-proportional hazards one hazard ratio misdescribes both phases of an effect. [sec-survival-nph] In the book's scenarios the cumulative hazard ratio at five years is not constant, "which is the point". [sec-survival-nph] Across 54 oncology trials, the hazard ratio gave on average a larger effect than the ratio of restricted mean survival times (average ratio 1.11). [sec-survival-nph-tests] The label summary is still usually a hazard ratio. [sec-survival-regulation]

## Pitfalls
A hazard ratio is one summary measure among others, such as the RMST difference. The choice is made before the trial. [sec-survival]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is a hazard ratio of 0.8 a 20 percent hazard reduction? A: Yes, a 20 percent relative reduction in the hazard. It is not a 20 percent reduction in the risk of the event by a given time, and it says nothing about the absolute reduction. [sec-survival-info]

sec-survival-nph-tests.t: Tests built for a delayed effect

healey-als-platform.name: HEALEY ALS platform trial
healey-als-platform.summary: A platform trial the book uses as the contrast to EPAD, with a funding model that does not depend on the commercial pipeline it serves.
healey-als-platform.body:
## What it is

The Healey ALS Platform Trial is named in the book only as a contrast to EPAD. [20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-arm] It appears in the chapter on master protocols and platform trials, where platforms are described as machinery that keeps site contracts, database, randomization system, monitoring board and regulatory file standing. [sec-platform]

## Why it matters

The book lists three needs before a platform's first arm: a legal framework that arm sponsors will sign, a governance structure that answers who decides, and a funding model that does not depend on the commercial pipeline the platform is meant to serve. The Healey platform is the contrast on the funding point. [20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-arm]

## In the book

A platform survives its first arm only if governance is built for arms that are not yet known. Typically a single data monitoring committee oversees all arms, an independent statistical center runs the unblinded interim analyses, and a separate committee approves applications for new arms. [20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitoring-board] The book's discussion question asks the reader to list what EPAD lacked that Healey ALS had, and which of those a statistician could have fixed. [20/key-points]

## Pitfalls

The book gives no design numbers or results for the Healey platform, so nothing about its operating characteristics should be inferred from this entry. [20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-arm]

## Check yourself

- Q: What role does the Healey platform play in the book? A: It is the contrast to EPAD on funding. [20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-arm]
- Q: Which of the three pre-arm needs is organizational rather than statistical? A: All three, as EPAD's lesson is organizational. [20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-arm]

20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-.t: EPAD: a platform that never opened an arm

20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitori.t: Governance, firewalls and the monitoring board

hierarchical-model.name: Hierarchical model
hierarchical-model.summary: A model in which group parameters are draws from a common distribution with estimated spread, so that groups borrow strength from one another.
hierarchical-model.body:
## What it is

Two groups are exchangeable if nothing we know distinguishes the rate of one from that of the other. That does not make the rates equal. It makes their joint prior symmetric. [sec-borrowing-hier] The hierarchical model treats the group rates as conditionally independent draws from a common distribution with unknown parameters. For binary data from $K$ groups:

$$
y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b).
$$

This is eq-hier. [sec-borrowing-hier] The spread $\tau_b$ controls borrowing: near zero the groups are nearly identical, and large $\tau_b$ leaves them nearly independent. [sec-borrowing-hier]

## Why it matters

Because $\tau_b$ is estimated, borrowing falls when the groups disagree. [sec-borrowing-hier] For a normal outcome the posterior mean is approximately a weighted average (eq-shrink), $\mathbb{E}[\theta_k \mid y] \approx \lambda_k \bar\theta + (1-\lambda_k)\hat\theta_k$ with $\lambda_k = \sigma_k^2/(\sigma_k^2+\tau_b^2)$, so a small group with a large $\sigma_k^2$ is shrunk more. [sec-borrowing-hier]

## In the book

The model is used in multicenter trials, where the groups are centers. In the eight-center topical-cream trial, centers had 5 to 37 patients per arm. [sec-borrowing-hier] It is also the basket trial model, and REBYOTA used it with dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study. [sec-borrowing-basket] [sec-borrowing-rebyota]

## Pitfalls

Shrinkage lowers total error only under conditions, and an individual group can be estimated worse. [sec-borrowing-hier] With few groups $\tau_b$ is poorly estimated and the answer depends on its prior: with four historical trials, half-normal priors with scale 0.5 and 1.0 can give quite different borrowing. [sec-borrowing-hier]

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to borrowing if the groups disagree? A: The posterior for $\tau_b$ moves up and borrowing falls. [sec-borrowing-hier]
- Q: Which groups are shrunk more? A: Small groups, which have large sampling variance. [sec-borrowing-hier]

sec-borrowing-rebyota.t: REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study

functions.name: borrow_basket_posterior
functions.title: Hierarchical logit-normal basket model on a grid
functions.usage: borrow_basket_posterior(y, n, mu_grid = NULL, tau_grid = NULL, nq = 81)
functions.description: Half-normal(1) prior on tau, N(0, 2^2) on mu (logit scale), Gauss-type quadrature over basket effects. All likelihoods, quadrature sums and grid weights are computed on the log scale (log-sum-exp), so well-defined posteriors never produce NaN, even when some grid points have a vanishing integrated likelihood.

functions.name: borrow_map_prior
functions.title: Meta-analytic-predictive prior from historical controls (normal-normal, logit scale)
functions.usage:
borrow_map_prior(
  y,
  n,
  tau_scale = 0.5,
  nsamp = 2e+05,
  seed = NULL,
  tail_tol = 1e-06
)
functions.description: Model: empirical logits est_i = log((y_i + 0.5) / (n_i - y_i + 0.5)) with known variances se2_i, est_i ~ N(theta_i, se2_i), theta_i ~ N(mu, tau^2). The prior on the overall logit mean mu is flat (improper) and is integrated out analytically, which gives the factor sqrt(v) in the marginal posterior of tau; the prior on tau is half-normal with scale tau_scale. The posterior of tau is evaluated on a grid with step about 0.005 starting at min(0.001, tau_scale / 100) (log-spaced below 0.001 when that is smaller).

historical-control.name: Historical control
historical-control.summary: A control group taken from outside the current randomized comparison, such as an earlier trial or registry, whose use ICH E10 and regulators treat with caution.
historical-control.body:
## What it is

In a single-arm trial the effect is judged against what is expected without treatment, and that expectation comes from a published control arm, a registry, earlier trials or routine care. ICH E10 calls this the externally controlled trial and lists it among five kinds of control group. [sec-borrowing-external] Assignment is not randomized and the controls may be nonconcurrent, so the design is regarded as suitable only when the effect is large relative to the variability of the natural course. [sec-borrowing-external]

## Why it matters

In a small or pediatric rare-disease trial the number of eligible patients may not support a conventional-size randomized control arm at all. [sec-borrowing-traditional]

## In the book

Three mechanisms make an external control misleading: selection, time and measurement. Each gives a bias and not a variance, so a larger external sample does not help. [sec-borrowing-external] Pocock (1976) listed conditions for combining historical and randomized controls: same treatment, same protocol, same institutions where possible, same prognostic factors and no unexplained outcome differences. [sec-borrowing-external] FDA issued a draft guidance on externally controlled trials in February 2023, and the MHRA and EMA followed in 2025 with a draft guideline and a concept paper. Both stress pre-specification and fitness for purpose. [sec-borrowing-external] Propensity-score methods decide how much external data enters, but cannot repair covariates that were not measured. [sec-borrowing-external]

## Pitfalls

Matching on measured covariates removes only the measured bias, as the NSCLC case study shows. [sec-borrowing-nsclc] The FDA rare-diseases guidance reserves external controls for specific circumstances. [sec-borrowing-external]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does a larger external sample not fix an external control? A: The three mechanisms produce bias, not variance. [sec-borrowing-external]
- Q: Which source gave the classic list of conditions for historical controls? A: Pocock (1976). [sec-borrowing-external]

sec-borrowing-external.t: External and historical controls: the traditional objections

sec-borrowing-guide.t: Putting it together: a decision guide

sec-borrowing-nsclc.t: When borrowing failed: the NSCLC case study

sec-borrowing-traditional.t: What the traditional design does with prior data

history-of-bayesian-trials.name: History of Bayesian trials
history-of-bayesian-trials.summary: The decision-theoretic view of trials is as old as the randomized trial, running from Thompson in 1933 to the FDA draft guidance of January 2026.
history-of-bayesian-trials.body:
## What it is
The decision-theoretic view of trials is as old as the randomized trial. [sec-decision-history] The book gives a short chain of episodes.

## In the book
- Thompson asked in 1933 for the probability that one treatment is better than another and proposed allocating patients accordingly. [sec-decision-history]
- Wald's sequential analysis came from the wartime problem of sampling only as much as needed. [sec-decision-history]
- Grundy, Healy and Rees posed the economic choice of the amount of experimentation in 1956, and Raiffa and Schlaifer's 1961 decision theory supplied the preposterior analysis. [sec-decision-history]
- Anscombe and Colton observed in 1963 that a trial informs the treatment of a much larger population of future patients. [sec-decision-history]
- Novick and Grizzle gave a Bayesian analysis of a four-arm surgical trial in 1965. [sec-decision-history]
- Cornfield gave a Bayesian sequential test in 1966 and set out the Bayesian outlook in 1969. [sec-decision-history]
- Berry restated the case for Bayesian interim analysis in 1985, and Lewis and Berry evaluated Bayesian designs by their classical operating characteristics. [sec-decision-history]
- In January 2026 the FDA issued draft guidance on Bayesian methodology for drugs and biologics, and the EMA released a concept paper for consultation. [sec-decision-history]

## Pitfalls
The objections deserve their strongest form. The prior can decide the answer, the type I error rate of a Bayesian rule is not controlled by the Bayes calculation itself, interim peeking can bias a trial, and a Bayesian design is harder to review. [sec-decision-history] Whitehead's "case for frequentism" is the standard statement of the opposing view. [sec-decision-history]

## Check yourself
- Q: Who asked in 1933 for the probability that one treatment is better than another? A: Thompson. [sec-decision-history]
- Q: What did Lewis and Berry do? A: They evaluated Bayesian decision-theoretic designs by their classical operating characteristics. [sec-decision-history]

hochberg-procedure.name: Hochberg procedure
hochberg-procedure.summary: A step-up version of Holm that rejects at least as many hypotheses but needs independent or suitably positively dependent test statistics.
hochberg-procedure.body:
## What it is

Hochberg runs the order in the other direction from Holm. Start from the largest $p$-value and compare it with $\alpha$, the next largest with $\alpha/2$, and so on. At the first $p_{(j)} \le \alpha/(k-j+1)$, reject that hypothesis and all with smaller $p$-values. [10/hochberg]

It is a step-up version of Holm's step-down test and rejects at least as many hypotheses. [10/hochberg]

## Why it matters

It is more powerful than Holm, which matters when several endpoints are moderately significant. [10/hochberg]

## In the book

The price is an assumption. The guarantee holds when the statistics are independent or positively dependent, such as nonnegative correlation among one-sided normal statistics, which covers comparisons with a shared control. [10/hochberg]

Its step-up logic rests on the Simes inequality, and Hommel gave a more powerful procedure under the same conditions. [10/hochberg] The Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure is likewise controlled under positive dependence of this kind, which is why the book links the two. [sec-mult-fdr]

In Table 10.3 Bonferroni, Holm and Hochberg all reject only E1 ($p = 0.004 < 0.025/6 = 0.0042$); the procedures separate only when several $p$-values are small. [10/hochberg] The key points of the chapter state it plainly: Holm uniformly beats Bonferroni with the same dependence-free guarantee, and Hochberg is more powerful but needs positive dependence. [10/key-points]

## Pitfalls

- FDA's multiple endpoints guidance states the dependence conditions and does not treat Hochberg as assumption-free. [10/hochberg]

## Check yourself

- Q: Which direction does Hochberg order the p-values? A: From the largest, as a step-up procedure. [10/hochberg]
- Q: What does Hochberg assume that Holm does not? A: Independence or a specific positive dependence of the test statistics. [10/hochberg]

sec-mult-fdr.t: Where familywise control is not the target: false discovery rate and prior probabilities

functions.description: Hochberg step-up procedure

holm-procedure.name: Holm procedure
holm-procedure.summary: A step-down version of Bonferroni that rejects everything Bonferroni rejects and sometimes more, with the same dependence-free guarantee.
holm-procedure.body:
## What it is

Order the $p$-values $p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(k)}$. Compare $p_{(1)}$ to $\alpha/k$. If it is rejected, compare $p_{(2)}$ to $\alpha/(k-1)$, and continue until a $p$-value fails. Then stop and retain that hypothesis and all remaining ones. [10/holm]

Holm controls the familywise error rate in the strong sense with no assumption on dependence. It rejects everything Bonferroni rejects and sometimes more. [10/holm]

## Why it matters

Holm is a uniform improvement over Bonferroni at no extra assumption. [10/holm] It is the closed test that uses Bonferroni for each intersection hypothesis. [10/closed-testing]

## In the book

In the six-endpoint example all three adjusted procedures reject only E1, with $p=0.004$ just under $0.025/6 = 0.0042$. Holm's next threshold is $0.025/5 = 0.005$, which 0.011 misses, so it stops. [10/hochberg]

The procedures separate when several $p$-values are small, for example 0.004, 0.005, 0.006 and the rest large. [10/hochberg]

In the ulcer illustration Holm and Bonferroni agree on the smallest $p$-value, and none of the other contrasts is stronger, so Holm does not rescue the finding. [10/what-the-traditional-reading-does-with-it]

## Pitfalls

- Plain Bonferroni may still be written into a protocol because its simplicity helps when many people must read it. [10/holm]
- Holm does not use the ordering of arms, such as recurrence falling as more stomach is removed. [10/what-the-traditional-reading-does-with-it]

## Check yourself

- Q: With six hypotheses, what is Holm's second threshold if the smallest is rejected? A: alpha divided by 5. [10/holm]
- Q: Can Holm reject fewer hypotheses than Bonferroni? A: No, it rejects everything Bonferroni rejects. [10/holm]

10/what-the-traditional-reading-does-wit.t: What the traditional reading does with it

i-spy-2-trial.name: I-SPY 2
i-spy-2-trial.summary: A Bayesian platform for neoadjuvant breast cancer that graduates arms by predictive probability of success in a hypothetical phase 3 trial.
i-spy-2-trial.body:
## What it is

I-SPY 2 is a platform for neoadjuvant breast cancer that has enrolled since 2010 and was later reconfigured as I-SPY 2.2. The primary endpoint of each arm was pathologic complete response (pCR) at surgery, with MRI tumor volume used to predict pCR for patients still in follow-up. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability] Each therapy was evaluated in each of up to ten *signatures*, the subtype combinations that might become a regulatory indication. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability]

## Why it matters

An arm graduated in a signature when its Bayesian predictive probability of success in a hypothetical 300-patient, equally randomized phase 3 trial reached 85%. It was dropped if that probability fell below 10% in all ten signatures, and no arm took more than 120 patients. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability] This ties the decision to the confirmatory trial the platform feeds, which a posterior probability of benefit does not. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability]

## In the book

A simulation with 50 patients per arm and a phase 3 of 150 per arm tested at one-sided 0.025 compares predictive and posterior probability for four phase 2 results. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability] Randomization was response adaptive within a signature, with 20% held on control, and a time machine smoothed the control response over time. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability] The platform also tested combination regimens against the shared control. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability]

## Pitfalls

It is a phase 2 screening platform: a graduation is a decision to run a phase 3, not an approval, and its false positive rate was calibrated for a screening stage. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability] Because allocation adapts toward responsive subtypes, the raw difference should not be read as the treatment effect. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability]

## Check yourself

- Q: What predictive probability graduates an arm? A: 85%. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability]
- Q: Why use the predictive scale rather than posterior probability? A: It accounts for the size and power of the phase 3 that follows. [20/i-spy-2-graduation-by-predictive-probability]

ich-e11a.name: ICH E11A
ich-e11a.summary: ICH guideline on pediatric extrapolation, adopted at Step 4 in August 2024, requiring a plan that assesses similarity between adult and pediatric populations.
ich-e11a.body:
## What it is

ICH E11A is the guideline on pediatric extrapolation, adopted at Step 4 in August 2024. It is a framework for deciding how much pediatric efficacy can be inferred from adult or other source data, with a place for Bayesian methods in the quantitative part. [sec-borrowing]

## Why it matters

The guideline asks for a *pediatric extrapolation plan* with three parts. The first assesses how similar the disease, the drug's pharmacology and the response to treatment are in source (adult) and target (pediatric) populations. The second describes gaps and uncertainties. The third plans the data to be generated in children, from PK and safety only (full extrapolation of efficacy) to a reduced efficacy trial to a full one. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] The more similar the populations, the less pediatric data are needed. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]

## In the book

Bayesian borrowing is one of the quantitative tools for the middle case, in which adult data inform the pediatric efficacy analysis. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] The guideline emphasizes that the evidence-based judgment of similarity comes first and the statistics second. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] The book's decision guide says to begin with the E11A plan and write the similarity judgment as a number ($\omega$, $a_0$ or $w$). [sec-borrowing-guide]

## Pitfalls

The guideline does not make the statistics the starting point. The similarity judgment should be defended with the pharmacology and the case in which it is wrong should be simulated. [sec-borrowing-guide]

## Check yourself

- Q: What range of pediatric data does the plan allow? A: From PK and safety only to a reduced efficacy trial to a full one. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]
- Q: When was E11A adopted? A: At Step 4 in August 2024. [sec-borrowing]

sec-borrowing-guide.t: Putting it together: a decision guide

ich-e9-r1.name: ICH E9(R1)
ich-e9-r1.summary: The ICH addendum on estimands and sensitivity analysis, Step 4, 20 November 2019, which defines the estimand and five strategies for intercurrent events.
ich-e9-r1.body:
## What it is
E9(R1) is the Addendum on Estimands and Sensitivity Analysis, Step 4, 20 November 2019. [sec-regulatory-ich] FDA labels its own publication of the document May 2021. [sec-regulatory-ich] It defines an estimand as "a precise description of the treatment effect reflecting the clinical question posed by a given clinical trial objective". [sec-regulatory-ich]

## Why it matters
It requires that "the targets of estimation are to be defined in advance of a clinical trial". [sec-regulatory-ich] It introduces intercurrent events, events after treatment initiation that affect the interpretation or existence of the measurements. [sec-regulatory-ich] A posterior probability is only as interpretable as the estimand it is posterior about. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## In the book
The pivotal protocol fixes the primary endpoint, the estimand with a strategy for intercurrent events such as rescue medication or discontinuation, and the primary analysis. [sec-regulatory-traditional] The five strategies are treatment policy, hypothetical, composite variable, while on treatment and principal stratum. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## Check yourself
- Q: How many strategies does E9(R1) name for intercurrent events? A: Five. [sec-regulatory-ich]
- Q: When must estimation targets be defined? A: In advance of the trial. [sec-regulatory-ich]

sec-regulatory-traditional.t: What a traditional submission looks like

ich-e9.name: ICH E9
ich-e9.summary: The ICH guideline on statistical principles for clinical trials, Step 4, 5 February 1998, still the foundation for randomization, blinding, analysis populations and multiplicity.
ich-e9.body:
## What it is
E9, Statistical Principles for Clinical Trials, reached Step 4 on 5 February 1998. [sec-regulatory-ich] It describes randomization, blinding, the analysis populations, the primary variable, interim analysis and multiplicity. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## Why it matters
After more than 25 years E9 remains the foundation. [sec-regulatory-ich] It says that all interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol, and that group sequential designs are the usual way to look repeatedly. [sec-regulatory-ich] On multiplicity it says the usual frequentist approach may necessitate an adjustment to the type I error. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## In the book
E9 mentions Bayesian approaches only briefly, in Section 1.2 and the Glossary, and does not elaborate them, so it neither prohibits nor privileges them. [sec-regulatory-ich] The document list gives it as Final (Step 4), 5 February 1998, covering randomization, blinding, the intention-to-treat principle, multiplicity and interim analysis. [B/documents]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does E9 forbid Bayesian analysis? A: No, it neither prohibits nor privileges Bayesian approaches. [sec-regulatory-ich]

ich-m11.name: ICH M11
ich-m11.summary: The harmonized structured protocol template and technical specification (CeSHarP), Step 4 in November 2025, into which a Bayesian design must be mapped.
ich-m11.body:
## What it is
ICH M11, the Clinical Electronic Structured Harmonised Protocol (CeSHarP), reached Step 4 in November 2025. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
It comes with a harmonized template and a technical specification, so protocols present the same information in the same place and can be exchanged in a format acceptable to regulators. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Why it matters
Neither M11 nor SPIRIT 2025 is specific to Bayesian designs, so the practical consequence is a mapping problem. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The structured format is harmonized across regulators, which helps. [23/ema-and-other-regulators]

## In the book
M11 has sections where design and statistics go, and a Bayesian design has components the template does not name: the prior, simulation-based calibration and predictive probability rules. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The book places the prior with the statistical hypotheses and analysis methods, the decision rules with the interim analysis section, the operating characteristics with the sample size justification, and the detailed model and computation in the SAP. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The sponsor checklist asks that the protocol be mapped into the M11 template and SPIRIT items with the Bayesian components where a reviewer would look. [23/checklists]

## Pitfalls
The test of a good mapping is that a reviewer who has read only the protocol knows the design is Bayesian, what the success criterion is and where the simulation report is. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
A protocol that mentions Bayesian methods only in an appendix invites the first review question to be where the prior is. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Check yourself
- Q: Where does the book put the operating characteristics in an M11 protocol? A: With the sample size justification. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
- Q: Does M11 name the prior? A: No, the template does not name Bayesian components. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spir.t: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025

ich.name: ICH
ich.summary: The body that brings regulators and industry together to agree guidelines, such as E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E20 and M15, that member regulators then adopt.
ich.body:
## What it is
The International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use brings regulators and industry together to agree guidelines. [sec-regulatory-ich] A guideline reaches Step 4 when the ICH Assembly adopts the final text, and regional regulators then implement it. [sec-regulatory-ich] Step 2 is a draft out for consultation. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## Why it matters
FDA publishes an ICH guideline as guidance and EMA as a scientific guideline. [sec-regulatory-ich] Six documents shape the book: E8(R1), E9, E9(R1), E20, E11A and M15. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## In the book
- E8(R1), Step 4, 6 October 2021, brings in quality by design. [sec-regulatory-ich]
- E9, Step 4, 5 February 1998, is the foundation, and it neither prohibits nor privileges Bayesian approaches. [sec-regulatory-ich]
- E20 is a draft at Step 2, endorsed 25 June 2025, and the work plan targets sign-off in February 2027. [sec-regulatory-ich]
- E11A, Step 4, August 2024, covers pediatric extrapolation. [sec-regulatory-ich]
- M15, Step 4, January 2026, covers model-informed drug development. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## Pitfalls
Until E20 is final it binds no region. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does Step 4 mean? A: The ICH Assembly adopts the final text. [sec-regulatory-ich]
- Q: Does E9 elaborate Bayesian approaches? A: No, it mentions them only briefly. [sec-regulatory-ich]

ignorability.name: Ignorability of assignment
ignorability.summary: When assignment depends only on recorded data, the posterior for the effect can be computed from the outcome model alone, and randomization guarantees it.
ignorability.body:
## What it is
Let $d_i$ be the arm, $x_i$ the recorded covariates and $y_i$ the outcome. Rubin showed that the posterior for $\theta$ can be computed from the outcome model alone if the assignment depends only on recorded data. Strictly, $\theta$ and the assignment parameters $\phi$ must also be independent a priori. Then the likelihood factorizes: [5/ignorability-of-the-assignment-mechanism]

$$
p(d, y \mid x, \theta, \phi) \;=\; \underbrace{p(d \mid x, \phi)}_{\text{assignment}} \;\times\; p(y \mid d, x, \theta),
$$

and the first factor drops out of the posterior of $\theta$. [5/ignorability-of-the-assignment-mechanism]

## Why it matters
If assignment depends on something unrecorded, such as a doctor's impression, the factorization fails and the posterior can be badly biased whatever the prior. Randomization makes the first factor a known constant. [5/ignorability-of-the-assignment-mechanism]

The book gives three Bayesian arguments for randomizing: Rubin's ignorability, the robustness argument of Kadane and Seidenfeld, and Berry's practical position. The Bayesian randomizes for credibility and robustness. [5/the-bayesian-arguments-for-randomizing]

## In the book
Response-adaptive randomization needs one more step, since assignment depends on earlier outcomes. If the assignment probabilities are known and depend on $\theta$ only through the recorded history, they can be omitted from the posterior. [5/ignorability-of-the-assignment-mechanism]

## Pitfalls
The Bayesian does not use the permutation distribution. What randomization buys is the factorization with a known assignment factor. [sec-randomization-bayesian] Under confounding, more data concentrate the posterior around the wrong value. [sec-randomization-bayesian]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does randomization do to the assignment factor? A: It makes it a known constant, because the coin ignores everything. [5/ignorability-of-the-assignment-mechanism]
- Q: Why does the Kadane and Seidenfeld argument favor randomizing? A: It yields an analysis whose validity does not depend on one person's beliefs about unmeasured determinants. [5/the-bayesian-arguments-for-randomizing]

implied-loss.name: Implied loss
implied-loss.summary: Every fixed-level test is a Bayes rule for some prior odds and loss ratio, which a trialist who fixes alpha has chosen without saying so.
implied-loss.body:
## What it is

A test is a Bayes rule for an implied loss. The Bayesian ledger holds one number, the [[bayes-risk]], which weighs the two errors by how likely each state is and how much each mistake hurts [sec-evidence-implied-loss]. The optimal rule rejects when $\mathrm{BF}_{10} > b$ with $b = \frac{\pi_0}{1-\pi_0}\cdot\frac{\ell_1}{\ell_0}$ [sec-evidence-bayesrisk]. A Neyman-Pearson most powerful test is a Bayes rule for some prior odds and loss ratio [sec-evidence-bayesrisk].

The implied Bayes factor threshold shrinks as information grows:

$$
2\log b_n \;=\; z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\frac{q}{1+q} - \log(1+q), \qquad\text{so}\qquad b_n \approx \frac{e^{z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2/2}}{\sqrt{q}} \to 0 .
$$

This is equation eq-implied-c. [sec-evidence-implied]

## Why it matters

A fixed $\alpha$ hides the loss ratio. As trials grow, a fixed level behaves as if the prior odds on the null or the harm of declaring a useless drug effective were shrinking toward zero [sec-evidence-implied]. In normal model the implied threshold satisfies $2\log b_n = z_{\mathrm{crit}}^2\,\frac{q}{1+q} - \log(1+q)$ [sec-evidence-implied].

## In the book

A posterior threshold of 0.975, 0.99 or 0.995 says declaring a useless drug effective (a false positive) is 39, 99 or 199 times worse than withholding a useful one [7/key-points]. The ratio is not statistical. It depends on the disease, and Isakov, Lo and Montazerhodjat find the best threshold differs by disease [sec-evidence-lossratio].

## Pitfalls

This is the point-null, two-sided calculation. It is not the benefit probability of the FDA criterion, and the two 0.975 thresholds are not interchangeable [sec-evidence-lossratio]. The one-sided confirmatory rule is a different decision problem [sec-evidence-bayestype1].

## Check yourself

- Q: What loss ratio does a posterior threshold of 0.99 imply? A: Declaring a useless drug effective is about 99 times worse than a false rejection [7/key-points].
- Q: What does a regulator holding alpha fixed behave like as trials grow? A: As if the prior odds on the null were shrinking toward zero [sec-evidence-implied].

ind-safety-report.name: IND safety report
ind-safety-report.summary: The expedited report under 21 CFR 312.32 of a serious and unexpected suspected adverse reaction, due within 15 calendar days, or 7 for fatal or life-threatening cases.
ind-safety-report.body:
## What it is

Under 21 CFR 312.32 the sponsor must notify FDA and all participating investigators in an IND safety report of a suspected adverse reaction that is both serious and unexpected. The deadline is as soon as possible and no later than 15 calendar days after the sponsor determines the information qualifies. [sec-safety]

An unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reaction is due no later than 7 calendar days after the sponsor's initial receipt. [sec-safety]

## Why it matters

The regulation lists the evidence that suggests a causal relationship, among it an aggregate analysis of specific events that occur more frequently in the drug group than in a control group. It is a requirement and prescribes no statistical method for that analysis. [sec-safety]

## In the book

The FDA guidance of December 2025 recommends a safety surveillance plan, aggregate review, and keeping individual treatment assignments blinded to the sponsor's study team, with unblinded aggregate review by a group independent of that team. Guidance recommends and does not require. [sec-safety] ICH E2A supplies the definitions of serious, unexpected and related events. [sec-safety]

The 7-day limit runs from initial receipt for a single interpretable case, whereas the 15-day limit runs from the date the sponsor determines the information qualifies. [sec-safety-reg] For events needing an aggregate analysis, the sponsor makes the determination once the analysis meets the criterion and then reports as soon as possible. [sec-safety-reg]

## Pitfalls

- No monitoring rule shortens or lengthens these limits. [sec-safety-reg]

## Check yourself

- Q: Which clock is shorter, and for what? A: Seven days, for an unexpected fatal or life-threatening reaction, from initial receipt. [sec-safety]

indirect-comparison.name: Indirect comparison
indirect-comparison.summary: Estimating an effect against a common comparator by adding log effects from two trials, with a power-prior weight to discount the second.
indirect-comparison.body:
## What it is

No trial compared tirzepatide with placebo. SURPASS-CVOT compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide and REWIND compared dulaglutide with placebo [sec-borrowing-chain]. On the log scale the effects add:

$$
\log\mathrm{HR}_{T:P}=\log\mathrm{HR}_{T:D}+\log\mathrm{HR}_{D:P},
$$

with variances adding if the estimates are independent (eq-chain). [sec-borrowing-chain]

## Why it matters

A guideline committee asks how much tirzepatide lowers cardiovascular risk against no incretin therapy. The chain assembles an answer no trial gives. [sec-borrowing-chain]

## In the book

SURPASS-CVOT gave a hazard ratio of 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83 to 1.01) and REWIND 0.88 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.99). At $a_0=1$ the chain gives 0.81 with interval 0.70 to 0.94. Dividing the REWIND variance by $a_0$ widens the interval to 0.67 to 0.98 at $a_0=0.5$ and 0.63 to 1.04 at $a_0=0.25$, so the benefit survives halving the weight but not quartering it. [sec-borrowing-chain] A published analysis used propensity-score adjustment to select 2055 of 9901 REWIND participants and found a hazard ratio of 0.72 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.94). [sec-borrowing-chain]

## Pitfalls

The chain assumes the dulaglutide effect in REWIND holds in the SURPASS-CVOT population, and the populations differ. The discount widens the interval and leaves the center, so it is the wrong correction if the effect differs. [sec-borrowing-chain] Neither analysis is a randomized comparison with placebo, and it supports a label discussion, not a primary efficacy claim. [sec-borrowing-chain]

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict the chained hazard ratio from 0.92 and 0.88. A: About 0.81. [sec-borrowing-chain]
- Q: What does lowering $a_0$ do to the estimate? A: Nothing, it only widens the interval. [sec-borrowing-chain]

information-fraction.name: Information fraction
information-fraction.summary: The share of the planned total information that has accrued at an interim look, such as events observed over events planned.
information-fraction.body:
## What it is

The information fraction is $t = n I / (N_{\max} I)$, the share of the planned total information that has accrued. [11/the-traditional-starting-point-one-look-one-test]

For a time-to-event endpoint, $t$ is the number of events observed divided by the number planned. For a binary endpoint with equal arms it is the fraction of the planned patients with outcome data. The final analysis is at $t = 1$. [11/the-traditional-starting-point-one-look-one-test]

## Why it matters

Real trials do not look at exact multiples of one quarter. A DMC meeting scheduled for the first Tuesday of a quarter may find 47 percent of the planned events, not 50, and a boundary computed for a $t$ that did not occur is wrong. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## In the book

Lan-DeMets spending computes the boundary at each look from the realized information fraction. Four looks planned at $t = 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1$ have an O'Brien-Fleming-type boundary of 2.68 at the second look. If the second look takes place at $t = 0.55$, that boundary becomes 2.82 and the later ones move slightly. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Pitfalls

- The timing of looks must not depend on the observed treatment effect. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]
- A trial that stops short of its planned size must decide in the protocol whether the remaining alpha is spent at the last look held. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Check yourself

- Q: What is $t$ for an event-driven trial when half of the planned events have been observed? A: One half, events observed over events planned. [11/the-traditional-starting-point-one-look-one-test]
- Q: May the look be moved because the interim effect looks good? A: No, timing must not depend on the observed effect. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

intention-to-treat.name: Intention to treat
intention-to-treat.summary: Analyze every randomized patient in the arm they were assigned to, whatever happened afterward, so the groups remain the ones the coin created.
intention-to-treat.body:
## What it is
The intention-to-treat (ITT) principle says to analyze every patient in the arm they were randomized to, whatever happened afterward. [5/the-itt-principle] ICH E9 section 5.2.1 says the primary analysis should include all randomized subjects, and that preserving the initial randomization in analysis is important in preventing bias. [5/the-itt-principle]

A patient assigned to the drug who never took a pill is still analyzed as a drug patient. [5/the-itt-principle]

## Why it matters
After randomization, patients stop the drug, take rescue medication, move away or die of something else. Dropping or moving them means the arms are no longer the groups the coin created. [sec-randomization-itt]

## In the book
The drug adds 10 percentage points to recovery for anyone who takes it. About 15 percent of the drug arm stops early, more often the sicker patients. Three analyses were compared on 4,000 patients in each of 300 trials: ITT, per-protocol and as-treated. [5/the-itt-principle]

ITT is diluted: it estimates the effect of assigning the drug. The per-protocol and as-treated analyses remove or reshuffle exactly the patients who differ in prognosis, and exceed what the drug does. [5/the-itt-principle]

ITT corresponds in spirit to the treatment-policy strategy of the [[estimand]] framework. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

## Pitfalls
Neither bias can be seen in the data of a single trial. [5/the-itt-principle] A per-protocol analysis is not among the five ICH E9(R1) strategies, because it drops patients on a post-randomization event. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the ITT estimate smaller than the drug's effect in those who take it? A: About one in seven did not take it, so ITT estimates the effect of assignment. [5/the-itt-principle]
- Q: Does a per-protocol analysis err toward or away from the truth in the book's simulation? A: Above the truth, since the stoppers differ in prognosis. [5/the-itt-principle]
