intercurrent-event.name: Intercurrent event
intercurrent-event.summary: An event after treatment starts, such as stopping the drug, rescue medication, switching or death, that affects the interpretation or existence of the measurements.
intercurrent-event.body:
## What it is
Intercurrent events are events after treatment initiation that affect either the interpretation or the existence of the measurements. Examples are stopping the drug, taking rescue medication, switching treatment and death before the endpoint. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

## Why it matters
Each one needs an explicit strategy, written into the [[estimand]]. The addendum names five. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

- Treatment policy: effect of being assigned the drug, with whatever follows. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]
- Hypothetical: effect if the event had not happened. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]
- Composite variable: effect on a combined outcome. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]
- While on treatment: effect up to the event. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]
- Principal stratum: effect in patients who would not have the event. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

## In the book
The drug-discontinuation event of the ITT simulation illustrates the strategies. Treatment policy uses the outcome regardless of the event. The composite strategy counts stopping as failure. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

For a Bayesian analysis under treatment policy, the model is fit to all randomized patients by arm. This requires the outcome to remain defined after the event, and terminal events such as death may need another strategy. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

## Pitfalls
The hypothetical strategy needs a submodel for the unobserved outcome, with priors on the unidentifiable part, and this deserves a sensitivity analysis because the data cannot correct it. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which two strategies compare the groups the coin made? A: Treatment policy and composite variable. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]
- Q: Why does the hypothetical strategy need sensitivity analysis? A: It rests on a model for what would have happened, and the data cannot correct its prior. [5/estimands-and-intercurrent-events]

interim-analysis.name: Interim analysis
interim-analysis.summary: Any analysis comparing arms on efficacy or safety before formal completion, which inflates the type I error if each look uses a fixed level.
interim-analysis.body:
## What it is

ICH E9 defines an interim analysis as any analysis intended to compare arms on efficacy or safety before formal completion. Interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol. [sec-sequential]

## Why it matters

Suppose a committee reviews the data $K$ times and declares success each time $Z > 1.96$. The chance that at least one statistic exceeds 1.96 is larger than 0.025, and it increases with $K$. Armitage and colleagues quantified this. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

Two equally spaced looks take the false positive rate from 2.5% to about 4.2%. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails] Four unadjusted looks at 1.96 give a type I error of 0.0631, more than two and a half times the nominal 0.025. [11/the-armitage-recursion]

## In the book

The inflation does not come from a flaw in the data. "Was $Z$ large at any of the looks" is a different event from "was $Z$ large at the end", and the null distribution computed for the second is the wrong one for the first. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

A committee that reviewed the data continuously at a fixed level would eventually see $Z$ exceed 1.96 with probability one, by the law of the iterated logarithm. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails] The rule that turns the data into a decision is part of the experiment, and the error rate belongs to the rule. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

## Pitfalls

- Looking is free for the posterior but not for the error rate: a Bayesian rule perfectly calibrated under the prior can still reject a true null far above 2.5%. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]
- A DMC that reviews safety without an efficacy comparison does not touch alpha at all. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to the false positive rate with two equally spaced looks at 1.96? A: It rises from 2.5% to about 4.2%. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]
- Q: Does continuous monitoring at a fixed cutoff ever stop being a problem? A: No, the cutoff is eventually crossed with probability one. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

jeffreys-scale.name: Jeffreys scale
jeffreys-scale.summary: Jeffreys' criterion that the evidence bar for a normal mean grows with the sample size, restated in terms of the prior information q.
jeffreys-scale.body:
## What it is

Jeffreys derived the growth of the bar for a normal mean with the Cauchy prior he recommended on invariance grounds. To leading order in $n$ the Bayes factor in favor of the null is $K = \sqrt{\pi n/2}\,\exp(-t^2/2)$, which falls through one at $t_{\mathrm{crit}} = \sqrt{\log(\pi n/2)}$ [sec-evidence-jeffreys]. Kass and Raftery give the scale on which Bayes factors are usually read [sec-evidence-calibration].

## Why it matters

The table restates the criterion in terms of $q$ and sets it beside the exact bar of the normal-mixture rule, which the rest of the chapter uses [sec-evidence-jeffreys].

## In the book

This is a large-information approximation, not an identity. Evaluated exactly, the Cauchy Bayes factor at $t_{\mathrm{crit}}$ is not one at small $n$ [sec-evidence-jeffreys]. At $q = 10$ the two bars in the table are approximately 1.66 and 1.62 [sec-evidence-jeffreys].

## Pitfalls

Two cautions. The bar is a function of the prior scale through $q$, not of $n$ alone. With $\tau = 0.25$ the rows read at $q = n/16$ and the crossing with 1.96 arrives at the thousands of events [sec-evidence-jeffreys]. The statement that the fixed level is too lenient beyond a phase I cohort holds only for a unit-information prior [sec-evidence-jeffreys]. Second, the calculation prices a point null, and against an interval null the bar depends on the interval and priors chosen [sec-evidence-jeffreys].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the Jeffreys bar depend on n alone? A: No, it depends on the prior scale through $q$ [sec-evidence-jeffreys].
- Q: Is $t_{\mathrm{crit}} = \sqrt{\log(\pi n/2)}$ exact? A: No, it is a large-information approximation [sec-evidence-jeffreys].

kaplan-meier-estimator.name: Kaplan-Meier estimator
kaplan-meier-estimator.summary: A model-free estimate of the survival function that handles censoring, and the curve every report of a time-to-event trial draws.
kaplan-meier-estimator.body:
## What it is
The Kaplan-Meier estimate of $S(t)$ handles censoring without a model. [sec-survival-traditional] It is the curve every report of a time-to-event trial draws. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Why it matters
It displays the data before any treatment comparison. The comparison itself uses the log-rank test or the Cox model. [sec-survival-traditional]

## In the book
The Fleming-Harrington weights use the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate: each event time is weighted by $S(t)^\rho\{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma$. [sec-survival-nph-tests] Survival curves in the book's scenarios overlap or cross early and separate late under a delayed effect. [sec-survival-nph]

## Pitfalls
Censoring must be noninformative for the likelihood results the book gives. [sec-survival-gamma] A single curve difference may hide a changing hazard ratio. [sec-survival-nph]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the estimator need a parametric model? A: No. [sec-survival-traditional]
- Q: What happens to patients still event-free at cutoff? A: They are censored. [sec-survival-traditional]

keyboard-design.name: Keyboard design
keyboard-design.summary: A model-assisted phase 1 design that lays equal-width keys over the DLT-rate axis and moves toward the key with the highest posterior probability.
keyboard-design.body:
## What it is
The Keyboard design of Yan and colleagues lays equal-width keys, each as wide as the target interval, over the DLT-rate axis. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard] It recommends the move toward the key with the highest posterior probability. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## Why it matters
Like BOIN and mTPI, its decisions are printed as a table by number of DLTs and number treated, so the logic can be checked by hand. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## In the book
The book mentions Keyboard alongside mTPI and mTPI-2 and does not simulate it. Which design to choose is an empirical question, and the evidence is simulation. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard] Published comparisons looked at accuracy, safety and reliability of several newer phase 1 designs. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## Pitfalls
Those comparisons are in stated scenarios at stated sample sizes. The protocol should report the chosen design's own operating characteristics in scenarios that include a badly placed target. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## Check yourself
- Q: How wide is each key? A: As wide as the target interval. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

kolmogorov-complexity.name: Kolmogorov complexity
kolmogorov-complexity.summary: The length of the shortest program that outputs a string; a string is random if it cannot be described by anything much shorter than itself.
kolmogorov-complexity.body:
## What it is
Compare 0101010101... with a string from coin tosses. The first can be described in a few words, "repeat 01". The second cannot be described more briefly than by writing it out. Kolmogorov turned this into a definition: a string is random if it cannot be described by anything much shorter than itself. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

Formally, the complexity of a string is the length of the shortest computer program that outputs it. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

## Why it matters
Randomness in this sense belongs to a sequence, not a procedure, and no finite sequence can be certified random because Kolmogorov complexity cannot be computed. A trialist can only apply tests. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

A sequence from a pseudo-random generator and a seed has low complexity by definition. That is not a flaw: what matters is that nobody can predict it without the seed. This is why the seed belongs in the sealed randomization specification. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

## In the book
A compression experiment used an everyday compressor in place of the shortest program. The alternation compressed to about 1 percent. The coin sequence compressed to about 0.18 of its size, with a floor of 0.125. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

The bits of a one-line multiplicative generator, $x_{k+1} = 75\,x_k \bmod 65537$, were not compressed either. The compressor could not tell them from a physically random quantum source. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

## Pitfalls
Passing a compression test is not a proof of randomness. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility] The equivalence between randomness and incompressibility holds for infinite sequences whose prefixes all have high prefix-free complexity, not for the finite-string definition. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a trialist certify a given schedule as Kolmogorov-random? A: No, the complexity cannot be computed. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]
- Q: What does a clinical trial need from its generator instead? A: Documented statistical quality, a recorded seed, and a schedule the enrolling staff cannot see. [5/randomness-as-incompressibility]

label-revenue-brought-forward.name: Label revenue brought forward
label-revenue-brought-forward.summary: A modeled estimate of the sales an earlier cardiovascular label would add, because patent expiry is fixed; the book treats it as an upper bound on revenue, not profit.
label-revenue-brought-forward.body:
## What it is
Patent expiry is fixed, so a cardiovascular indication reached earlier adds the same number of years of protected, label-driven sales. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
The estimate multiplies sales by an assumed label share and by the years brought forward. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]

## Why it matters
It is the largest sum in the accounting and rests on the least. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]

## In the book
Novo Nordisk reported global Wegovy sales of DKK 58.2 billion for 2024. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
The label share is not public, so the book assumes 10 to 25 percent, and converts at an assumed 6.9 DKK per dollar. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
For REWIND, Trulicity revenue in 2019 and the FDA approval of its cardiovascular indication on 21 February 2020 anchor the analogue, with an assumed 10 to 20 percent label share. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
The REWIND analogue assumes 24 months of linear enrollment and 85 months between registered start and primary completion. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
In REWIND the all-trial median saving is zero, because fewer than half of the simulated trials cross, so the revenue figures hold only conditionally on the rule acting. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
For the SELECT reconstruction, 2024 sales of about $8.4 billion, brought forward by the all-trial median saving of 2.2 years, give $1.8 to $4.6 billion. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
For REWIND, conditional on the rule acting, the decision comes at 680 of 1,257 events (month 51, 2.8 years early), giving $1.2 to $2.3 billion. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
The key points call the SELECT figure of order a few billion dollars of Wegovy revenue, an upper bound and not profit. [21/key-points]

## Pitfalls
Approval, reimbursement and uptake would not all have moved forward by the full statistical acceleration. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
The sales level, the label share and the exchange rate are assumptions. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
Multiplying a crossing probability by a conditional median would not give an expected revenue. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is the figure profit? A: No, it is revenue, and an upper bound. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]
- Q: Why is the REWIND saving only conditional? A: The Bayesian rule acts in fewer than half the simulated trials. [21/label-revenue-brought-forward]

large-deviation.name: Large deviation scale
large-deviation.summary: The scale where ruling out a null at error alpha needs a fixed quantity of evidence, log(1/alpha), accruing at the Kullback-Leibler rate.
large-deviation.body:
## What it is

Wald's expected sample size formula has three features that the book calls the large deviation ledger. The numerator, such as $\log\{(1-\beta)/\alpha\}$, is a fixed quantity of evidence in nats, set by the error levels alone. The denominator is a Kullback-Leibler divergence, the rate at which evidence accrues, linearly in $n$. The governing relation is $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \log(1/\alpha)$, the Chernoff-Stein relation. [sec-ch10-wald]

$$
\mathbb{E}_1[T] \approx \frac{(1-\beta)\log\{(1-\beta)/\alpha\} + \beta \log\{\beta/(1-\alpha)\}}{\mathrm{KL}(P_1 \| P_0)}
$$

## Why it matters

To rule out a null with error probability $\alpha$ requires evidence $\log(1/\alpha)$, and evidence comes at rate KL. It is a statement at exponential speed. [sec-ch10-wald]

## In the book

Ville's inequality is Markov's inequality at a stopping time. For the exponential martingale, the first passage to $1/\alpha$ is the first time the cumulative log likelihood ratio reaches $\log(1/\alpha)$. Wald's identity then gives $\mathbb{E}[T_\alpha] = \{\log(1/\alpha)/\mathrm{KL}\}(1 + o(1))$. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]

The surcharge of the normal-mixture rule is this Chernoff toll: the bar $\log(1/\alpha)$ is fixed and evidence accrues at rate KL. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]

## Pitfalls

- The surcharge is a cost of this construction and comparison, not a lower bound for all anytime-valid procedures. Realizable boundaries with iterated-logarithm rates exist and behave differently. [11/where-the-surcharge-comes-from]

## Check yourself

- Q: What is the governing relation of the ledger? A: $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \log(1/\alpha)$. [sec-ch10-wald]
- Q: What unit measures the fixed quantity of evidence? A: Nats. [sec-ch10-wald]

sec-ch10-wald.t: Wald's test and the large deviation ledger

lecanemab-phase-2b.name: Lecanemab phase 2b dose finding
lecanemab-phase-2b.summary: A Bayesian phase 2b trial in early Alzheimer disease that missed its primary criterion yet identified the dose carried into phase 3.
lecanemab-phase-2b.body:
## What it is
Study 201 of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease was a Bayesian phase 2b trial with five dose regimens and placebo, response-adaptive allocation, and interim analyses starting after 196 patients and then every 50. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b]

## In the book
It identified 10 mg/kg biweekly as the estimated 90 percent effective dose, the dose achieving 90 percent of the modeled maximum effect. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b] The trial did not meet its prespecified 12-month primary criterion: the posterior probability of at least a 25 percent reduction in decline was 0.64, short of the required 0.80. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b] The selected regimen was carried into the phase 3 program. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b]

## Why it matters
A design can fail its primary criterion and still produce the right dose, so the protocol should say in advance how dose-selection evidence will be read in that event. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b] A prespecified Bayesian criterion that is not met is a result, to be reported as one. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b]

## Check yourself
- Q: What was the posterior probability against the required threshold? A: 0.64 against 0.80. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b]
- Q: What does ED90 mean? A: The dose achieving 90 percent of the modeled maximum effect. [17/lecanemab-bayesian-dose-finding-in-phase-2b]

likelihood-ratio.name: Likelihood ratio
likelihood-ratio.summary: The ratio of the density under an alternative to the density under the null, multiplied across observations, which is a test martingale when both are single distributions.
likelihood-ratio.body:
## What it is

When the null and the alternative are each a single distribution, the likelihood ratio $\prod_i q(Y_i)/p_0(Y_i)$ is a test martingale. Under $p_0$ the expected ratio of densities is $\int (q/p_0)p_0 = 1$. [12/likelihood-ratios]

## Why it matters

This is Wald's SPRT statistic. For a simple alternative it is the best possible bet in the sense of growth. [12/likelihood-ratios]

## In the book

The limitation is that it requires committing to one alternative. A bet on a hazard ratio of 0.70 pays badly if the truth is 0.90. [12/likelihood-ratios] The remedy is to average over alternatives, which gives the [[mixture-method]]. [12/mixtures]

## Pitfalls

- Committing to one alternative makes the bet fragile when the true effect differs. [12/likelihood-ratios]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is the likelihood ratio a test martingale under the null? A: Its expected value under the null density is the integral of $(q/p_0)p_0$, which is 1. [12/likelihood-ratios]
- Q: What is its main limitation? A: It commits to a single alternative. [12/likelihood-ratios]

likelihood.name: Likelihood
likelihood.summary: The probability of the observed data viewed as a function of the unknown parameter; the Bayesian and traditional analyses share it.
likelihood.body:
## What it is
The likelihood $p(y \mid \theta)$ is the probability of the observed result under each possible value of the unknown parameter. In the diagnostic example, $\mathbb{P}(+ \mid D)$ viewed as a function of the unknown state is the likelihood. [sec-bayes-rule]

The likelihood enters Bayes rule as the factor that multiplies the prior:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

This is equation eq-bayes. [sec-bayes-rule]

## Why it matters
The traditional analysis uses the same likelihood. The maximum likelihood estimate is the value of $\theta$ at which $p(y \mid \theta)$ peaks, and a z test is a calculation on its sampling distribution. The Bayesian adds only the prior and the multiplication. [sec-bayes-rule]

The likelihood principle says that, given the data, the evidence about $\theta$ depends on the data only through the likelihood function, not on the stopping rule or on results that might have been observed but were not. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]

## In the book
For a time-to-event trial with $d$ total events, the book uses the approximate likelihood $\hat\theta \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, 4/d)$ for $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$. It is an approximation to the Cox partial likelihood in large samples. [sec-normal-normal]

For a binary endpoint, the likelihood of $h$ heads and $t$ tails is $\theta^{h}(1-\theta)^{t}$, which has the algebraic form of a Beta density. [sec-beta]

A protocol that specifies a likelihood without a prior has specified half of a Bayesian model. [sec-exchangeability]

## Pitfalls
Because the posterior depends on the data only through the likelihood, it is unchanged by the decision to look. The type I error of a stopping rule is a different matter, since it is a property of the procedure over repeated trials. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]

## Check yourself
- Q: Where does the likelihood peak for the traditional estimate? A: At the maximum likelihood estimate. [sec-bayes-rule]
- Q: Does the likelihood depend on the stopping rule? A: No, provided the stopping rule depends only on the data already observed: the likelihood is then the same up to a constant, so the posterior is unchanged. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]

lindleys-paradox.name: Lindley's paradox
lindleys-paradox.summary: A fixed p-value does not mean a fixed amount of evidence: holding p constant while the trial grows turns a rejection of the null into evidence for it.
lindleys-paradox.body:
## What it is

Lindley, following Jeffreys, noticed that the Ockham penalty can turn a rejection of the null into evidence for the null [sec-evidence-lindley]. Take trials of increasing size that all end with a two-sided p-value of exactly 0.01, so $|Z_n| = 2.576$. The frequentist reading is the same each time. The Bayes factor is not, because the penalty keeps growing while $Z_n^2$ stays at 6.63 [sec-evidence-lindley].

## Why it matters

A fixed p-value threshold cannot mean a fixed amount of evidence as a trial grows [sec-evidence-lindley]. A related point is that very large trials can reach significance for clinically trivial effects. Lindley's paradox adds that the same p-value in a larger trial is weaker evidence against the null [sec-evidence-lindley]. The Bayesian remedy is to ask whether $\theta$ exceeds a clinically relevant $a$, not whether it is exactly zero [sec-evidence-lindley].

## In the book

With prior $N(0, 0.25^2)$ and prior probability 0.5 on the null, at $n = 100$ the Bayes factor is 6.5 and the posterior probability of the null is 13%. By $n = 10{,}000$ the Bayes factor is 1.1 and that probability is 48%. At $n = 10^6$ it is 90% [sec-evidence-lindley].

## Pitfalls

The paradox lives at sample sizes far larger than those of most confirmatory trials of a large effect, and with a vague prior on a point null. It also depends on the prior scale. Picking $\tau$ after seeing the data is the dishonest reaction [sec-evidence-lindley].

## Check yourself

- Q: Two trials both give p = 0.01, one with 100 patients and one with a million. Which has stronger evidence against the null? A: The smaller one. At $n = 10^6$ the posterior probability of the null is 90% [sec-evidence-lindley].
- Q: What does the Bayes factor do as n grows with p fixed? A: It first rises, then falls below one [sec-evidence-lindley].

log-hazard-ratio.name: Log hazard ratio
log-hazard-ratio.summary: The scale on which a hazard ratio is modeled, with estimate standard error about 2 over the square root of the total events under 1:1 randomization.
log-hazard-ratio.body:
## What it is
In trials with a time-to-event endpoint, the treatment effect is a hazard ratio and the Beta-binomial model does not apply. The normal-normal model works on the log scale. [sec-normal-normal]

For 1:1 randomization with $d$ total events, the log hazard ratio estimate has standard error about $2/\sqrt{d}$. Each arm contributes about $d/2$ events, and the variance is about $1/d_1 + 1/d_0 = 4/d$. [sec-normal-normal]

With $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$, so a positive $\theta$ means benefit: [sec-normal-normal]

$$
\hat\theta \mid \theta \;\sim\; N\!\left(\theta,\; \frac{4}{d}\right).
$$

## Why it matters
The logrank test is, to a good approximation, the z test $z = \hat\theta \sqrt{d} / 2$, and the number of events, not patients, is the sample size in both frameworks. [sec-normal-normal]

## In the book
With $d = 200$ events and $\widehat{\mathrm{HR}} = 0.74$, $\hat\theta = 0.30$ and the standard error is 0.141. [sec-normal-normal] The approximation is the standard route of Bayesian design in survival studies. [sec-normal-normal]

## Pitfalls
The Cox partial likelihood is only close to normal in large samples. The approximation is a modeling choice, and a final analysis that wants the exact likelihood can use a piecewise exponential model. [sec-normal-normal]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the standard error of the log hazard ratio with 200 events? A: $2/\sqrt{200} = 0.141$. [sec-normal-normal]
- Q: Why use $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$? A: So that a positive value means benefit. [sec-normal-normal]

log-rank-test.name: Log-rank test
log-rank-test.summary: The standard comparison of two survival curves: observed minus expected events in the treated arm, summed over event times.
log-rank-test.body:
## What it is
At each event time the log-rank test compares the observed number of events in the treated arm with the number expected if both arms shared one hazard, and sums the differences. [sec-survival-traditional] It is the score test of a proportional hazards model. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Why it matters
Most event-driven trials analyze with a log-rank test or a Cox model. [sec-survival] When randomization was stratified, the test should be stratified on the same factors. [sec-survival-traditional]

## In the book
Under a delayed effect the log-rank test loses power, because the early events it weights are uninformative about treatment. [sec-survival-nph] A simulation with 300 patients per arm and treated survival at 5 years of 0.57 in both scenarios compares a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 with a two-year delay then 0.583. [sec-survival-power-loss] Fleming-Harrington weights with $\rho = \gamma = 0$ give the ordinary log-rank test. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## Pitfalls
The Schoenfeld calculation assumes a single hazard ratio and would not warn about the loss of power. [sec-survival-power-loss]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does it lose power under a delayed effect? A: Early events carry weight but say nothing about the treatment. [sec-survival-nph]

functions.name: fh_z
functions.title: Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank statistics for two groups
functions.description: Computes the standardized weighted log-rank statistics with Fleming-Harrington weights \eqn{S(t)^\rho \{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma}, where S is the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate just before each event time, for the four pairs \eqn{(\rho, \gamma) \in \{(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\}}, together with the correlation matrix of the four statistics. The first statistic is the ordinary log-rank test. The maximum of the four, referred to the multivariate normal distribution with this correlation matrix, is the MaxCombo test.

margin-synthesis.name: Margin synthesis
margin-synthesis.summary: A noninferiority analysis that asks for the posterior probability that the new drug keeps a stated fraction of the control effect, carrying the full historical uncertainty.
margin-synthesis.body:
## What it is

Regulatory practice preserves a fraction $f$ of the control's effect against placebo, $\delta_{CP}$, estimated from historical trials as $N(d,s_{CP}^2)$. The fixed-margin approach multiplies the lower 95% limit of $\delta_{CP}$ by $1-f$ to get the margin [19/margin-synthesis]. The synthesis alternative asks for

$$
\Pr\bigl(\theta_{NC}<(1-f)\,\delta_{CP}\mid\text{data}\bigr),
$$

the posterior probability that the new drug retains at least the fraction $f$ (eq-ni-synth). [19/margin-synthesis]

## Why it matters

The fixed margin reduces the historical estimate to one conservative number, while the synthesis carries the full uncertainty. Both rest on the constancy assumption, and the synthesis makes it visible. [19/margin-synthesis]

## In the book

With a hypothetical 10-point historical event reduction with standard error 0.02 and half preserved, the trial with estimate 0.01 and standard error 0.015 (upper limit 0.039) does not meet the fixed margin. The two answers differ because the fixed margin stacks two conservative operations. [19/margin-synthesis] The synthesis is not automatically more lenient: for an estimate of 0.04 the retention probability is low. [19/margin-synthesis] In the simple margin case with margin 0.04, a skeptical prior centered at the margin is the natural regulatory prior. [sec-borrowing-ni]

## Pitfalls

If care has improved and the control effect shrank, a power prior with $a_0<1$ only widens $\delta_{CP}$ and leaves its center. A shrunken effect must be modeled directly with an attenuation parameter and checked over plausible downward shifts. [19/margin-synthesis]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the synthesis estimate? A: The posterior probability of keeping at least fraction $f$ of the control effect. [19/margin-synthesis]
- Q: Does discounting by $a_0$ fix a shrunken control effect? A: No, it leaves the center where it was. [19/margin-synthesis]

functions.name: ni_synthesis
functions.title: Noninferiority margin synthesis
functions.description: With \eqn{\delta_{CP}} the benefit of the control over placebo (positive, from historical trials, \eqn{N(d, s_{CP}^2)}) and \eqn{\theta_{NC}} the new-minus-control event difference (N(est, se^2), events bad), the new drug retains at least a fraction f of the control effect iff \eqn{\theta_{NC} < (1-f)\delta_{CP}}. Returns the synthesis probability and the fixed-margin comparison (f times the 95 percent lower limit of \eqn{\delta_{CP}}).

master-protocol.name: Master protocol
master-protocol.summary: One protocol with several substudies that keeps trial infrastructure standing and lets questions pass through it, as basket, umbrella or platform designs.
master-protocol.body:
## What it is

A conventional program builds a trial, answers one question and takes it down. A master protocol keeps the site contracts, database, randomization system, monitoring board and regulatory file standing and lets questions pass through. [sec-platform] FDA's June 2026 draft defines it as "a protocol designed with multiple substudies, which may have different objectives and involve coordinated efforts to evaluate one or more drugs". [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

## Why it matters

The idea is not Bayesian. The frequentist STAMPEDE opened in 2005 and shows that a shared control and a standing infrastructure pay for themselves. [sec-platform] The master protocol holds what is common: eligibility, endpoints, schedule of assessments, randomization system, statistical framework and governance. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

## In the book

The treatment-specific part sits in a module, called an intervention-specific appendix, sub-protocol, substudy appendix or, in REMAP-CAP, a domain-specific appendix. It holds the dose, safety monitoring, exclusions and decision thresholds. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] The terms and taxonomy were set out by Woodcock and LaVange (2017). [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] The three kinds are umbrella, basket and platform. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

## Pitfalls

A master protocol supports a marketing application for each drug on the evidence of that drug's comparison, and the legal standard of substantial evidence is not lowered. [20/what-changes-in-the-protocol] The FDA 2026 document is a draft that recommends and does not bind. [sec-platform]

## Check yourself

- Q: What belongs in the master document and what in the module? A: Common items in the master, drug-specific dose, safety and thresholds in the module. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]
- Q: Is a master protocol necessarily Bayesian? A: No. [sec-platform]

maximum-tolerated-dose.name: Maximum tolerated dose
maximum-tolerated-dose.summary: The highest dose whose probability of a dose-limiting toxicity is acceptable, the target of classical phase 1 oncology trials.
maximum-tolerated-dose.body:
## What it is
The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) is the highest dose whose probability of a dose-limiting toxicity (DLT) is acceptable. [17/what-a-phase-1-trial-in-oncology-is-for] The acceptable level is a target toxicity rate, commonly 0.20 to 0.33, and the chapter uses 0.25. [17/what-a-phase-1-trial-in-oncology-is-for] The true MTD in the book's scenarios is the highest dose with DLT probability at most 0.25. [17/operating-characteristics-by-simulation]

## Why it matters
For cytotoxic drugs, both efficacy and toxicity were expected to rise with dose, so the highest tolerable dose was expected to be the most active one. [17/what-a-phase-1-trial-in-oncology-is-for] The toxicity-only designs of the chapter all aim at this dose. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents]

## Pitfalls
The MTD paradigm assumes that more is better until it hurts. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents] That is a poor assumption for targeted therapies, immunotherapies and antibody-drug conjugates, where efficacy may plateau well below the MTD. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents] A drug may be taken for months or years, and chronic low-grade toxicity can cause dose reductions that a short DLT window cannot show. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents] A dose chosen as the MTD can then be both more toxic and no more effective than a lower one. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents] The FDA's stated concern is that patients may be left on doses with more toxicity and no more benefit. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which dose is the true MTD in the book's scenario A? A: Dose 3. [17/operating-characteristics-by-simulation]
- Q: Why can the MTD be the wrong target for an antibody-drug conjugate? A: Efficacy may plateau below it, and chronic toxicity may force dose reductions. [17/why-the-mtd-is-a-poor-target-for-modern-agents]

maxsprt.name: MaxSPRT
maxsprt.summary: A sequential Poisson test for drug and vaccine surveillance whose log likelihood ratio is maximized over relative risks above one.
maxsprt.body:
## What it is

Kulldorff and colleagues proposed a maximized sequential probability ratio test for drug and vaccine safety surveillance. [sec-safety-aggregate] With a Poisson count $c$ against an expected count $\mu_0$ under no excess risk, the statistic is the log likelihood ratio maximized over relative risks above one, $c\log(c/\mu_0) - (c-\mu_0)$ when $c > \mu_0$. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Why it matters

It is the likelihood-ratio machinery of the e-value chapter with a fixed alternative replaced by its maximum. [sec-safety-aggregate] A signal is declared when it crosses a critical value calibrated for the planned surveillance. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## In the book

Because the alternative is maximized, it needs a critical value from calibration rather than the $1/\alpha$ of an e-value. [sec-safety-aggregate] Surveillance of marketed products and vaccines is sequential in the Wald sense. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Pitfalls

- A signal is a trigger or a hypothesis for review depending on what the safety plan states. [sec-safety-aggregate]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does MaxSPRT not use the threshold $1/\alpha$? A: It maximizes over alternatives, so its critical value needs calibration. [sec-safety-aggregate]

mcp-mod.name: MCP-Mod
mcp-mod.summary: A two-step dose-response method: a multiple contrast test over prespecified shapes, then model fitting and target-dose estimation.
mcp-mod.body:
## What it is
MCP-Mod combines a multiple comparison step with a modeling step. [sec-dose-response] Before the data, the protocol names candidate shapes (linear, Emax, exponential, umbrella) with guessed parameters. Each gives an optimal contrast of dose means. [sec-dose-response] The test of no dose-response is the maximum contrast statistic, with its critical value from their joint distribution, holding familywise type I error at one-sided 0.025. [sec-dose-response] If a signal appears, the passing models are fitted and a target dose is estimated by selection or averaging. [sec-dose-response]

## Why it matters
It is on FDA's fit-for-purpose list with a determination of 26 May 2016, the frequentist dose-finding method there. [sec-dose-response]

## In the book
With five doses, 40 per dose and standard deviation 1, the critical value is below the Bonferroni value for four comparisons because the monotone contrasts are positively correlated. [sec-dose-response] When the top dose returns to the placebo mean, the top-dose test has only its type I error rate, while the contrast test with an umbrella candidate keeps power. [sec-dose-response]

## Pitfalls
The candidate set is prespecified, and a truth outside it loses power, the counterpart of the CRM skeleton choice. [sec-dose-response] The test detects a non-flat dose-response, not benefit at some dose. [sec-dose-response]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why use an umbrella among the candidates? A: A top-dose-only comparison fails when the top dose returns to placebo. [sec-dose-response]

functions.name: mcp_contrasts
functions.title: Optimal contrasts and critical value of the MCP-Mod multiple contrast test
functions.description: For each candidate dose-response shape (a column of shapes, evaluated at the doses) the optimal contrast with equal group sizes is the centered, unit-length shape. The critical value is the one-sided 1 - alpha quantile of the maximum of the contrast statistics, whose joint null distribution is multivariate normal with correlation crossprod(contrasts) (known standard deviation). Needs the mvtnorm package.

functions.name: mcp_power
functions.title: Rejection probabilities of the MCP-Mod contrast test and two traditional tests
functions.usage:
mcp_power(
  mu,
  contrasts,
  crit,
  n,
  B = 20000,
  sd = 1,
  alpha = 0.025,
  seed = NULL
)
functions.description: Simulates dose means with known standard deviation and reports the probability of a one-sided signal for the multiple contrast test, for the top dose against the first (placebo) at level alpha, and for the best of all pairwise comparisons with placebo with a Bonferroni correction.

meta-analytic-predictive-prior.name: Meta-analytic-predictive prior
meta-analytic-predictive-prior.summary: A prior for a new trial control parameter, taken as the predictive distribution from a random-effects meta-analysis of several historical control arms.
meta-analytic-predictive-prior.body:
## What it is

The meta-analytic-predictive (MAP) prior of Neuenschwander and colleagues (2010) runs a random-effects meta-analysis of the historical control rates, using the hierarchical model (eq-hier), and takes the predictive distribution of the control parameter in a new trial as the prior. [sec-borrowing-map] The predictive distribution is wider than the meta-analytic mean because it includes the between-trial variation $\tau_b$. [sec-borrowing-map] The hierarchical model for $K$ groups is:

$$
y_k \mid p_k \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n_k,p_k),\qquad \mathrm{logit}\,p_k \mid \mu,\tau_b \sim N(\mu,\tau_b^2),\qquad (\mu,\tau_b)\sim \pi(\mu,\tau_b).
$$

This is eq-hier. [sec-borrowing-map]


## Why it matters

A MAP prior does not become more informative than the heterogeneity warrants, however many historical patients there are. [sec-borrowing-map]

## In the book

Four illustrative historical control arms of 80, 100, 70 and 150 patients (400 in total) give a normal-normal model on the logit scale with a half-normal prior with scale 0.5 on $\tau_b$. The predictive distribution is converted to a Beta prior by matching mean and variance. [sec-borrowing-map] The pooled analysis that ignores between-trial variation would claim an effective sample size of 402, while the MAP prior is worth far fewer patients. That difference is the number a regulator can ask for. [sec-borrowing-map] The R package RBesT fits MAP priors by MCMC and approximates them by mixtures of conjugate distributions, while the chapter uses a simpler approximation from `bayestrials`. [sec-borrowing-map]

## Pitfalls

A MAP prior is still an exchangeability assumption. If standard of care changed or the population is different, it is confidently wrong. [sec-borrowing-map] The robust MAP prior adds a vague component for protection. [sec-borrowing-map]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is a MAP prior worth less than the pooled count of patients? A: It includes between-trial variation. [sec-borrowing-map]
- Q: When is a MAP prior confidently wrong? A: When the new trial differs systematically from the historical ones. [sec-borrowing-map]

sec-borrowing-ess.t: How much does the borrowed information weigh? Effective sample size and conflict

functions.name: borrow_map_prior
functions.title: Meta-analytic-predictive prior from historical controls (normal-normal, logit scale)
functions.usage:
borrow_map_prior(
  y,
  n,
  tau_scale = 0.5,
  nsamp = 2e+05,
  seed = NULL,
  tail_tol = 1e-06
)
functions.description: Model: empirical logits est_i = log((y_i + 0.5) / (n_i - y_i + 0.5)) with known variances se2_i, est_i ~ N(theta_i, se2_i), theta_i ~ N(mu, tau^2). The prior on the overall logit mean mu is flat (improper) and is integrated out analytically, which gives the factor sqrt(v) in the marginal posterior of tau; the prior on tau is half-normal with scale tau_scale. The posterior of tau is evaluated on a grid with step about 0.005 starting at min(0.001, tau_scale / 100) (log-spaced below 0.001 when that is smaller).

mhra.name: MHRA
aliases: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
mhra.summary: The UK regulator, which consulted in 2025 on a draft guideline for external control arms built from real-world data.
mhra.body:
## What it is
The MHRA is the UK medicines regulator. It applies the same statistical principles as EMA, since both adopt ICH guidelines. [sec-regulatory-eu] Its document in the book is the draft guideline on the use of external control arms based on real-world data to support regulatory decisions. [sec-regulatory-eu]

## Why it matters
External controls are a form of borrowing. [sec-regulatory-eu] The draft parallels FDA's February 2023 draft guidance on externally controlled trials. [sec-regulatory-eu] The three regulators share pre-specification, control of false positive conclusions, simulation and integrity. [sec-regulatory-eu]

## In the book
The MHRA consulted on the draft in 2025. [sec-regulatory-eu] The document table lists it as Draft, 2025, relied on in the borrowing chapter. [sec-regulatory-table]

## Pitfalls
It is a draft, so its status can change, and the book gives the status as of November 2026. [sec-regulatory-table]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which year did the MHRA consult on external control arms? A: 2025. [sec-regulatory-eu]
- Q: Which FDA document does it parallel? A: The February 2023 draft on externally controlled trials. [sec-regulatory-eu]

midd-program.name: MIDD paired meeting program
midd-program.summary: An FDA program of paired meetings on modeling and simulation approaches for a specific development program, the procedural counterpart of ICH M15.
midd-program.body:
## What it is
The model-informed drug development paired meeting program offers paired meetings with FDA on modeling and simulation in a specific development program. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program] Examples are dose selection, trial design simulation, and an exposure-response model supporting a labeling claim. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program]

## Why it matters
It is the procedural counterpart of ICH M15. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program] M15 sets principles for assessing model credibility, and the program is where a sponsor tests a particular modeling plan against FDA's reading. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program] M15 defines model-informed drug development as the use of computational modeling and simulation that can integrate nonclinical data, clinical data and prior information. [sec-regulatory-ich]

## In the book
A Bayesian adaptive design with a model-based dose-response component can fall under both the CID and MIDD programs. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program] The book's advice is to ask which fits the question. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program] A dose that depends on a model points to the MIDD program. [3/how-to-choose-the-meeting]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which program handles the models that feed a design's decision rules? A: The MIDD paired meeting program. [3/the-midd-paired-meeting-program]
- Q: Is the outcome binding? A: No. [3/how-to-choose-the-meeting]

minimization.name: Minimization
minimization.summary: Each new patient is assigned to the arm that makes the total imbalance across several factors smaller, usually with probability 0.8, for small trials.
minimization.body:
## What it is
Minimization is the method for small trials with many prognostic factors. Taves, and independently Pocock and Simon, proposed assigning each new patient in a way that depends on what has happened so far. Look at the patient's level of each factor, count earlier patients with those levels in each arm, and assign to the arm that makes the total imbalance smaller. [5/minimization]

## Why it matters
It balances the margins of each factor, for example the number of women in each arm, but not necessarily the combinations. [5/minimization] In the simulation it cut the imbalance in a known trait to a fraction of that under simple randomization. [5/seeing-the-difference]

## In the book
In its deterministic form it is not random at all, and anyone who knows the current counts can predict the next assignment. Pocock and Simon therefore assign to the preferred arm with probability $p$ above one half, 0.8 being common, and use a fair coin on ties. The function `assign_minimization` implements this. [5/minimization]

The analysis should include the minimization factors as covariates, because the assignment is not independent of them. [5/minimization] A Bayesian trial can use covariate-dependent assignments such as minimization without changing the likelihood. [5/ignorability-of-the-assignment-mechanism]

## Pitfalls
Minimization does nothing for a hidden trait. [5/seeing-the-difference] The deterministic version is predictable. [5/minimization]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does minimization use a probability such as 0.8? A: Deterministic assignment can be predicted from the current counts. [5/minimization]
- Q: Does it balance combinations of factors? A: Not necessarily. It balances the margin of each factor. [5/minimization]

functions.name: assign_minimization
functions.title: Pocock-Simon minimization
functions.description: Marginal minimization over the columns of X: assign to the arm with the smaller count of same-level patients summed over factors, with probability p_follow.

minimum-bayes-factor.name: Minimum Bayes factor
minimum-bayes-factor.summary: A bound on how strongly any prior in a stated class can make the data favor the alternative, used to calibrate a p-value.
minimum-bayes-factor.body:
## What it is

Sellke, Bayarri and Berger showed that for $p < 1/e$ and a stated class of alternatives, the Bayes factor in favor of the null is at least [sec-evidence-calibration]:

$$
\mathrm{BF}_{01} \;\ge\; -e\, p \log p.
$$

This is eq-sbb. The class has a non-increasing hazard for $-\log p$ under the alternative. The bound is not a statement about every prior [sec-evidence-calibration].

## Why it matters

It says something that does not depend on a particular prior, at the cost of being generous to the alternative. With even prior odds it gives a lower bound on the posterior probability of the null [sec-evidence-calibration].

## In the book

A two-sided p-value of 0.05 corresponds at best to a Bayes factor of about 2.5 and a posterior probability of the null of at least 29%. So the common misreading of p = 0.05 as "95% sure the effect is real" overstates: even the alternative most favorable in the class gives at most 71% [sec-evidence-calibration]. At p = 0.01 the Bayes factor is at most 8 and the null keeps at least 11%. Only at p = 0.001 does it reach 53 [sec-evidence-calibration]. In a worked trial with Z = 2.8 the bound allows at most 13.6 for $\mathrm{BF}_{10}$ [7/a-worked-comparison].

## Pitfalls

The bound does not replace a design-specific calculation, and it understates what a reasonable analysis would find [sec-evidence-calibration]. It should be quoted with its class [sec-evidence-calibration]. The proposal to tighten thresholds for discovery is controversial and does not apply to regulatory trials [sec-evidence-calibration].

## Check yourself

- Q: What posterior probability of the null does p = 0.05 allow at the very least, from even odds? A: About 29% [sec-evidence-calibration].
- Q: Why is the bound generous to the alternative? A: It asks which alternative in the class would make the data look best for $H_1$ [sec-evidence-calibration].

sec-evidence-calibration.t: How small can the Bayes factor be? Calibrating the p-value

functions.name: min_bf
functions.title: Lower bound on the Bayes factor for the null
functions.description: type = "pvalue": Sellke-Bayarri-Berger bound -e\,p\log p over symmetric unimodal alternatives for p < 1/e, extended by the value 1 for p \ge 1/e (where no evidence against the null is possible under the calibration); the limit 0 is returned at p = 0. type = "gaussian": bound exp(-z^2/2) over all point alternatives, with x a z statistic.

mixture-method.name: Mixture method
mixture-method.summary: Averaging likelihood-ratio martingales over a distribution of alternatives to get an e-value that does not commit to one effect size.
mixture-method.body:
## What it is

If $L_n(\theta)$ is a likelihood-ratio martingale for each $\theta$ in the alternative, then for any mixing distribution $H$, [12/mixtures]

$$
E_n = \int L_n(\theta)\,dH(\theta)
$$

is again a test martingale, because an average of martingales with unit start is a martingale with unit start. [12/mixtures]

For a Gaussian trial with $X_i \sim N(\theta, 1)$, $S_n = \sum_{i\le n} X_i$ and $H_0:\theta \le 0$, mixing over a half-normal distribution with scale $\rho$ gives, with $A_n = n + \rho^{-2}$, [12/mixtures]

$$
E_n^{+} = \frac{2}{\rho\sqrt{A_n}}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{S_n^2}{2A_n}\Bigr)\,\Phi\!\Bigl(\frac{S_n}{\sqrt{A_n}}\Bigr).
$$

This is eq-evalues-mix. [12/mixtures]

## Why it matters

Mixing removes the need to commit to one alternative. The scale $\rho$ plays the role of a prior standard deviation on the effect and is a design parameter. [12/mixtures] Ville's inequality holds for the whole composite null. [12/mixtures]

## In the book

The mixture e-value is a Bayes factor: the ratio of the marginal likelihood under a half-normal prior to the likelihood at the null value. [sec-evalues-bf] In the authors' sweep the integrated Bayes risk changes by only a few percent across $\rho$ from 0.10 to 0.32, so the threshold matters more than $\rho$. [12/mixtures]

An equal-weight mixture over $K$ prespecified subgroup analyses is a valid fixed-look e-value for the global null, but it loses to the Sidak maximum when the statistics are correlated. [sec-evalues-subsets]

## Pitfalls

- The fixed-look mixture has no time index, so applying its constant threshold repeatedly would eventually cross under the null with probability one. [sec-evalues-subsets]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is an average of test martingales a test martingale? A: An average of martingales with unit start is a martingale with unit start. [12/mixtures]
- Q: Which matters more for cost, $\rho$ or the threshold? A: The threshold. [12/mixtures]

sec-evalues-subsets.t: Many subgroups at once: a negative result for the mixture e-value

moderate-deviation-sample-size.name: Moderate deviation sample size
moderate-deviation-sample-size.summary: A sample size equation from the Bayes decision rule that replaces the fixed critical value by a boundary growing like the square root of log n, giving larger fixed designs.
moderate-deviation-sample-size.body:
## What it is

The Bayes-optimal boundary on the standardized scale is

$$
t_{\text{crit}} = \sqrt{\log n + C}\,\bigl(1 + o(1)\bigr), \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0/\pi_a}{\pi(\theta_0)\sqrt{2\pi/I(\theta_0)}},
$$

which is eq-md-boundary [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n]. Replacing $z_\alpha$ by it gives the sample size equation

$$
n\,I\,\theta^2 = \left(\sqrt{\log n + C} + z_\beta\right)^2 .
$$

This is eq-md-ss, solved by fixed-point iteration [9/the-power-function-and-the-sample-size-equation]. The matching power function (eq-md-power) is

$$
\text{Power}_n(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\sqrt{nI}\,\theta - \sqrt{\log n + C}\right) + o(1), \qquad \theta > 0 \text{ for the one-sided benefit rule}.
$$

[9/the-power-function-and-the-sample-size-equation] For a unit-information prior with equal prior odds $C = 0$ and the boundary is $\sqrt{\log n}$. [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n]

## Why it matters

With $C = 0$ the boundary exceeds 1.96 for every $n$ above 46. It is 2.63 at $n = 1000$ and 3.03 at $n = 10{,}000$ [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n]. The result runs against the book's thesis: the fixed design is larger, not smaller [sec-power].

## In the book

At $\theta = 0.20$ the ratio to the textbook size is 1.30, about 30% larger. It is 1.52 at $\theta = 0.10$ and 1.73 at $\theta = 0.05$ [9/the-surprising-result]. The extra patients buy a type I error that falls with $n$ [9/the-surprising-result]. For $d$ parameters the boundary is $\sqrt{d\log n}$, which is 2.63, 3.72 and 4.55 for one to three at $n = 1000$ [9/many-parameters-and-many-endpoints]. The saving comes from monitoring, not from the fixed design [9/where-the-saving-is-and-where-it-is-not].

## Pitfalls

Calibrated to 0.025, the fixed-sample Bayesian design needs the same sample size as the traditional one [sec-power-sidebyside]. Any stated $C$ must name its unit, events or information [9/the-power-function-and-the-sample-size-equation]. The expression is asymptotic [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the moderate deviation design need fewer patients than the textbook design? A: No, about 30% more at $\theta = 0.20$ [9/the-surprising-result].
- Q: Where does the Bayesian saving lie? A: In monitoring [9/where-the-saving-is-and-where-it-is-not].

results.name: Moderate deviation sample size equation
results.summary: A Bayes rule whose bar grows like the logarithm of the sample size has an implicit sample size equation, the textbook formula with the critical value replaced by the square root of log n plus a constant.
results.statement: For the moderate deviation rule, which acts when $Z_n^2 \ge \log n + C$ (with $Z_n > 0$ for a one sided claim), the power against an effect $\theta$ with information $I$ per unit of $n$ is $\Phi\big(\sqrt{nI}\,|\theta| - \sqrt{\log n + C}\big) + o(1)$. Setting this equal to $1-\beta$ gives the sample size equation $n I \theta^2 = \big(\sqrt{\log n + C} + z_\beta\big)^2$, which is the textbook equation with $z_\alpha$ replaced by $\sqrt{\log n + C}$. The formula is an asymptotic approximation; it is not claimed to predict the size of any particular trial, including SELECT, whose planned size (1,225 events for a design hazard ratio of 0.83; the textbook formula gives about 1,211) is close to the textbook calculation at its own design alternative.

results.name: Moderate deviation and textbook sizes at the SELECT hazard ratio of 0.80 (not a prediction of SELECT's size)
results.summary: At a hazard ratio of 0.80 and 90 per cent power the textbook formula gives 844 events and the moderate deviation formula more; SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83, where the textbook formula gives about 1,211 events against the planned 1,225, so the formula does not predict SELECT's size.
results.statement: For a hazard ratio of 0.80 ($|\log\mathrm{HR}| = 0.2231$, $Z = |\log\mathrm{HR}|\sqrt{d}/2$ in terms of $d$ events) and 90 per cent power, the textbook calculation at one sided 0.025 calls for 844 events, and the moderate deviation calculation calls for 1,067 events at equal prior odds and 1,255 at prior odds of two to one against. SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 per cent power, one sided 0.025 and 1,225 planned events, with one interim at two thirds of them (Ryan et al. 2020), and the observed hazard ratio was 0.80 on 1,270 events (Lincoff et al. 2023). The textbook calculation at the design hazard ratio gives about 1,211 events, close to the plan, so the comparison at 0.80 changes the design alternative and does not show that the moderate deviation formula predicts or explains SELECT\'s size.

monte-carlo-error.name: Monte Carlo error in calibration
monte-carlo-error.summary: The binomial sampling noise in a simulated rate, which also makes the calibrated threshold an estimate that needs enough trials and a fresh-seed check.
monte-carlo-error.body:
## What it is

The Monte Carlo standard error of a simulated rejection probability is $\sqrt{p(1-p)/B}$ for $B$ trials [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from]. The calibrated $c$ is itself a quantile of a simulated distribution, so it inherits this noise [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].

## Why it matters

A design calibrated on a small simulation can be miscalibrated on the fresh data that will decide the trial [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from]. A reported "0.0252 against a target of 0.025" with no standard error invites the question of whether it is a violation [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].

## In the book

At $p = 0.025$, $B = 10{,}000$ gives 0.0016, which is 6 percent of the target [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from]. With $B = 100{,}000$ it is 0.0005, and showing an error of 0.0250 within $\pm 0.0005$ needs about 380{,}000 trials [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from]. The experiment calibrates $c$ on $B$ trials with 30 seeds and evaluates each on 400,000 fresh null trials [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from]. In the null grid, an excess of a fraction of a point at the worst grid point was under two standard errors, so probably noise [14/type-i-error-across-the-null-space].

## Pitfalls

The validation estimate is unbiased, but the calibration estimate is not, because it was chosen to hit the target [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].

## Check yourself

- Q: How many calibration trials at minimum? A: At least $10^5$, and more near a boundary one must defend [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].
- Q: Why validate on a different seed? A: The calibration estimate was chosen to hit the target, so only fresh data give an unbiased error estimate [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].

oc_simulate(

mrc-streptomycin-trial.name: MRC streptomycin trial
mrc-streptomycin-trial.summary: The 1948 Medical Research Council trial in pulmonary tuberculosis whose contribution was concealed random allocation in sealed envelopes, not the coin itself.
mrc-streptomycin-trial.body:
## What it is
The 1948 Medical Research Council trial compared streptomycin with bed rest against bed rest alone in acute pulmonary tuberculosis. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed] It is the book's first example of the distinction between sequence generation and concealment. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]

## Why it matters
Hill, who designed the trial, used random allocation, as Fisher had in agricultural experiments. His chief aim was to prevent selection bias in the choice of patients for each arm. He paired it with concealment. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]

## In the book
- What was tested: streptomycin with bed rest against bed rest alone. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]
- Design feature: the allocation was determined from a series of random numbers and kept in sealed envelopes, so the admitting physician decided eligibility before knowing the treatment. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]
- Yoshioka documents how the random numbers and envelopes were actually used. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]

The lesson is that the contribution of the trial was not the coin but the concealment. A list the admitting doctor could see would have recreated the doctor-chosen arm of the confounding simulation. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed] See [[confounding-by-indication]].

The regulatory descendant is 21 CFR 314.126(b)(4), which requires a method of assignment that minimizes bias. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]

## Pitfalls
The book reports the design, not an outcome comparison, for this trial. The point it draws is about process, which is a property of assignment and not of the mathematics of randomness. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed] [sec-randomization-failures]

## Check yourself
- Q: What was the real contribution of the trial, the coin or the concealment? A: The concealment. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]
- Q: Why did the envelopes matter? A: The admitting physician decided eligibility before knowing which treatment the patient would get. [5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concealment-before-the-word-existed]

5/the-mrc-streptomycin-trial-1948-concea.t: The MRC streptomycin trial (1948): concealment before the word existed

mtpi-design.name: mTPI design
mtpi-design.summary: Toxicity probability interval designs that pick the next dose by the posterior mass of underdosing, equivalence and overdosing intervals.
mtpi-design.body:
## What it is
The toxicity probability interval designs divide the DLT-rate axis into an underdosing interval, an equivalence interval around the target and an overdosing interval. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard] The first version is Ji and colleagues (2007). [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard] The modified form, mTPI, computes the posterior mass of each interval divided by its width and moves toward the interval with the largest value. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard] The mTPI-2 design changes how the intervals are formed, in response to a weakness of mTPI that its authors frame as an Ockham's razor problem. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## Why it matters
As with BOIN, the protocol carries a table of decisions by DLTs and number treated, and the logic can be checked by hand. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## In the book
Which design to choose is an empirical question answered by simulation. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard] One study compared CRM, mTPI and BOIN on correct selection, allocation near the MTD and an accuracy index. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## Pitfalls
Such comparisons hold only in stated scenarios at stated sample sizes. The protocol should report the chosen design's own operating characteristics, including a badly placed target. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does mTPI divide by the interval width? A: The posterior probability mass of each interval. [17/the-other-interval-designs-mtpi-mtpi-2-and-keyboard]

multi-arm-multi-stage-design.name: Multi-arm multi-stage design
multi-arm-multi-stage-design.summary: A group sequential platform design in which every research arm is compared with a shared control at each interim look, and arms that fail a pre-specified bar are dropped.
multi-arm-multi-stage-design.body:
## What it is

The multi-arm multi-stage (MAMS) design follows the logic of a group sequential trial with one change: at each interim look every research arm is compared with the control, and arms that fail a pre-specified bar are dropped while the others continue. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] The MAMS design for time-to-event outcomes, with stopping for lack of benefit on an intermediate outcome, was introduced by Royston and colleagues in 2003. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## Why it matters

Three features carry over to every platform: an intermediate outcome first, concurrent controls only, and new arms by amendment. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] Early stages use a lenient hazard-ratio cutoff that tightens, so arms with no sign of benefit leave at a fraction of the cost. The intermediate outcome need not be a validated surrogate. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## In the book

General MAMS methods calibrate boundaries through the joint distribution of test statistics across stages and arms to control a chosen error rate such as the pairwise or familywise rate. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] The cutoffs were derived under proportional hazards, and non-proportional hazards need an appropriate summary measure and delayed-effect simulations. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] Online error-rate control methods exist for hypotheses that arrive over time. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] STAMPEDE is the standing example. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## Pitfalls

A MAMS error calculation for a fixed family assumes the family is known, so for added arms the family must be chosen and justified. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens at each interim look? A: Each arm is compared with control, and arms that fail the bar are dropped. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]
- Q: Is the Bayesian machinery required for a platform? A: No, STAMPEDE shows it is optional. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

multi-armed-bandit.name: Multi-armed bandit
multi-armed-bandit.summary: The problem of assigning patients one at a time among arms with unknown success rates, balancing treating the patient now against learning for later patients.
multi-armed-bandit.body:
## What it is

Suppose two treatments have unknown success probabilities $p_0$ and $p_1$ and patients arrive one at a time [16/exploring-and-exploiting]. Each assignment treats the patient, which is the reward, and teaches us about the arm [16/exploring-and-exploiting]. Assigning the arm that looks better exploits what is known, and assigning the other arm explores [16/exploring-and-exploiting]. The problem is named for a row of slot machines with unknown payout rates [16/exploring-and-exploiting].

## Why it matters

A trial that explores too little may lock onto the wrong arm, and one that explores too much wastes patients on the arm it already suspects is worse [16/exploring-and-exploiting].

## In the book

The best policy solves a Bellman equation on the posterior state with $m$ patients still to treat [16/the-bellman-equation]:

$$
V(\pi_t, m) = \max\Bigl\{ \underbrace{m \max_k \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k]}_{\text{stop and treat}},\; \max_k \Bigl( \mathrm{E}_{\pi_t}[p_k] + \mathrm{E}\bigl[ V(\pi_{t+1}, m-1) \mid \pi_t, \text{arm } k \bigr] \Bigr) \Bigr\}.
$$

It is solvable exactly only for small problems, so the book looks at two approximations: the [[gittins-index]] for the discounted infinite horizon and [[thompson-sampling]] [16/the-bellman-equation]. Robbins formulated the sequential allocation problem, and Gittins showed that with geometric discounting the optimal policy is an index policy [16/exploring-and-exploiting].

## Pitfalls

The bandit objective is the reward to patients in the trial, which is not the objective of a confirmatory comparison [16/the-gittins-index]. Villar, Bowden and Wason review these models in trial design and are frank about the obstacles [16/exploring-and-exploiting].

## Check yourself

- Q: What are the two things an assignment does? A: It treats the patient and teaches us about the arm [16/exploring-and-exploiting].
- Q: Why are approximations needed? A: The Bellman equation is solvable exactly only for small problems [16/the-bellman-equation].

multiplicity-across-arms.name: Multiplicity across arms
multiplicity-across-arms.summary: The question of which comparisons in a platform form one family for error control, with FDA not recommending adjustment across unrelated drugs.
multiplicity-across-arms.body:
## What it is

A traditional trial with several arms and one control usually controls the familywise error rate at 0.025 by Bonferroni, Holm or Dunnett's step-down procedure. A platform raises the question of what the family is. [20/multiplicity-across-arms] Five unrelated drugs sharing a control would never be put in a common family in separate trials. [20/multiplicity-across-arms]

## Why it matters

FDA "generally does not recommend the use of multiplicity adjustments to strongly control the probability of making at least one type I error across the multiple comparisons of different drugs". The expected total number of type I errors is the same in independent trials or one trial. [20/fda] The draft keeps the adjustment for several doses of one drug, combination components or several endpoints, with the family defined before the data. [20/fda]

## In the book

EMA notes that errors are correlated, that the chance of at least one false positive may fall while several rise, and that tightening each level would need thresholds stricter than Bonferroni, so it offers larger control groups. [20/ema] A Bayesian platform moves the question: each arm has a criterion $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$, calibrated by simulation. [20/bayesian-error-control-across-arms] With exchangeable arms, shrinkage multiplies information by $1/w$, as in the table where each posterior standard deviation falls from 0.30 to 0.20. [20/bayesian-error-control-across-arms] The multiple $1/w$ is an upper bound that treats the common mean as known, and an arm far from its neighbors is shrunk toward them. [20/bayesian-error-control-across-arms]

## Pitfalls

Shrinkage across arms is most defensible for one drug class, doses or related subgroups, and is not a substitute for the multiplicity decision across unrelated drugs. [20/bayesian-error-control-across-arms]

## Check yourself

- Q: Which comparisons does FDA still adjust? A: Doses, combination components and endpoints of one drug. [20/fda]
- Q: What does the shared control do to the error count? A: Same mean, but errors correlate. [20/fda] [20/ema]

multiplicity.name: Multiplicity
multiplicity.summary: Multiplicity is the problem that every extra question a trial asks is another chance for luck to look like a discovery.
multiplicity.body:
## What it is

Most trials have a primary endpoint, several secondary ones, a few doses, some prespecified subgroups and an interim analysis or two. Each added question is another chance for luck to produce a result that looks like a discovery. Multiplicity is the name for this problem; the procedures that control it are among the most settled parts of trial statistics. [sec-multiplicity]

The family is defined by the claims the sponsor may make, not by the number of tests the statistician runs. A statistician who runs forty tests but whose protocol rests the claim on one prespecified comparison has a family of one. [sec-mult-problem]

## Why it matters

A sponsor who reports the best of twenty results as though it were the only one asked has not told the reader how the result was found. A regulator who approves on it has accepted a risk that nobody measured. [sec-multiplicity]

## In the book

ICH E9 lists three sources: multiple primary variables, multiple treatment comparisons, and repeated evaluation over time or interim analyses. [10/what-counts-as-the-family] Keeping K analyses open and guaranteeing 0.025 for the best of them makes the trial grow by the factor $((z_K + z_\beta)/(z_1 + z_\beta))^2$. [sec-mult-cost]

With twenty independent tests of a useless drug the chance of at least one significant result is about 0.40. [sec-mult-problem]

Exploratory endpoints, safety endpoints and descriptive subgroup displays are outside the family because no claim is made on them, and the protocol should say so. [10/what-counts-as-the-family]

## Pitfalls

- Dividing alpha among co-primary endpoints is unnecessary and costs power, because success on all of them is tested at the full level. [10/what-counts-as-the-family]
- Reviewers will ask for the family, the procedure, the interim spending and the status of secondaries if the primary fails, all before unblinding. [sec-mult-review]

## Check yourself

- Q: A protocol says the claim rests on one prespecified comparison, but the analyst runs forty tests. How big is the family? A: One, because the family is defined by the claims. [sec-mult-problem]
- Q: Does keeping many analyses open cost patients? A: Yes, by the factor $((z_K + z_\beta)/(z_1 + z_\beta))^2$, about 1.48 for five analyses and 2.38 for a hundred, at 80 percent power and one-sided 0.025. [sec-mult-cost]

non-proportional-hazards.name: Non-proportional hazards
non-proportional-hazards.summary: A hazard ratio that changes over time, as with delayed or cure-type effects, which breaks the single hazard ratio summary.
non-proportional-hazards.body:
## What it is
Hazards are non-proportional when the hazard ratio changes over time, so no single hazard ratio summarizes the treatment effect. [sec-survival-nph] Immunotherapy trials have taught oncologists that hazards need not be proportional. A treatment may do nothing for months and then produce durable responses in a minority. Curves overlap or cross early and separate late. [sec-survival-nph] One response is to change the estimand to the restricted mean survival time up to a horizon $\tau$ (eq-sv-rmst): [sec-survival-nph]

$$
\mathrm{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^\tau S(t)\,dt.
$$

## Why it matters
The log-rank test loses power, and the Cox hazard ratio depends on how long the trial runs. [sec-survival-nph] No FDA or ICH document, to the authors' knowledge, sets a required method. [sec-survival-regulation] A cross-pharma straw-man guidance treats the choice of test and the plausible scenarios as a design-stage matter settled by simulation. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## In the book
Three Bayesian responses: a piecewise treatment effect with a hierarchical prior, a mixture cure model, and the RMST estimand. [sec-survival-nph] With 300 patients per arm, a control hazard of 0.15 per year and the same treated survival of 0.57 at five years, power is 0.68 under a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 and 0.55 under a two-year delay, with 287 events in both. [sec-survival-power-loss]
FDA practice is to accept prespecified alternatives to the log-rank test as sensitivity analyses and to scrutinize post hoc ones. [sec-survival-regulation]

## Pitfalls
Choosing weights or a horizon after seeing the curves invalidates the type I error. [sec-survival-power-loss] Agreement with the agency at a pre-submission meeting matters more than the method. [sec-survival-regulation]

## Check yourself
- Q: Name three Bayesian responses. A: Piecewise effect, mixture cure model, RMST. [sec-survival-nph]
