noninferiority-margin.name: Noninferiority margin
noninferiority-margin.summary: The largest loss to the active control that is acceptable, built from the control's historical effect over placebo and fixed before unblinding.
noninferiority-margin.body:
## What it is
A noninferiority trial with no placebo arm cannot show by itself that the new drug works. The comparison is informative only if the control's effect is known from earlier placebo-controlled trials and is assumed to hold now. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from] The FDA guidance builds the margin in two steps. $M_1$ is the whole effect of the active control over placebo that can be assumed in the present trial, conventionally the conservative limit of a meta-analytic interval. $M_2$ is the margin actually used, preserving a clinically meaningful fraction of that effect, so $M_2\le M_1$. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from]

## Why it matters
How much to preserve is a clinical judgment, and the margin should be justified for the setting and not read from a convention. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from] The margin must be fixed in the protocol and justified before unblinding. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from]

## In the book
Two ways to use the historical estimate are described. The fixed-margin approach sets the margin from the historical confidence limit and runs an ordinary test. The synthesis approach combines the historical and current estimates and carries both uncertainties into one test. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from] In SURPASS-CVOT the margin of 1.05 did the work, and a margin of 1.00 would have been a superiority trial. [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice]

## Pitfalls
The scheme rests on the constancy assumption: the control's historical effect is the effect it would have in this trial. It cannot be checked within the trial. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from] Assay sensitivity, the ability to tell an effective from an ineffective treatment, therefore matters, and poor adherence or crossover helps the sponsor. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which is larger, $M_1$ or $M_2$? A: $M_1$, since $M_2\le M_1$. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from]
- Q: Does sloppiness hurt or help a noninferiority sponsor? A: It helps, by pulling the arms together. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from]

4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-i.t: SURPASS-CVOT: a noninferiority margin in practice

sec-testing-ni.t: Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin

noninferiority-trial.name: Noninferiority trial
noninferiority-trial.summary: A trial against an active control with the null hypothesis moved: the claim is that the new drug is not worse than a margin allows.
noninferiority-trial.body:
## What it is
When an effective treatment exists, withholding it for placebo is often unethical, so the new drug is compared with an active control. [sec-testing-ni] Let $\gamma = \log \mathrm{HR}$. For margin $M>1$ on the hazard ratio scale the hypotheses are

$$
H_0:\ \gamma \ge \log M \qquad\text{against}\qquad H_1:\ \gamma < \log M.
$$

This is equation eq-ni-hyp. [sec-testing-ni] The test is one-sided at 0.025, equivalent to checking that the upper limit of the two-sided 95% interval is below $\log M$. [sec-testing-ni] Blackwelder put the burden of proof on the claim of similarity for noninferiority. [sec-testing-ni]

## Why it matters
The answer depends entirely on $M$, a number the data do not supply. [sec-testing-ni] A sloppy trial pulls the arms together and makes any drug look noninferior. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from]

## In the book
SURPASS-CVOT compared tirzepatide with dulaglutide 1.5 mg, with a pre-specified noninferiority margin of 1.05 for the upper limit of the 95.3% interval. [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice] The primary outcome occurred in 801 patients (12.2%) on tirzepatide and 862 (13.1%) on dulaglutide, hazard ratio 0.92 (95.3% CI 0.83 to 1.01). [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice] Noninferiority was established, since 1.01 is below 1.05, and superiority was not, since 1.01 is above 1.00. [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice]

## Pitfalls
A margin changed after the data are seen is not a margin. [4/where-the-margin-comes-from] The traditional report does not give the probability that the hazard ratio lies below a given value. [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice]

## Check yourself
- Q: Can a trial win noninferiority and lose superiority? A: Yes, the two nulls differ. [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice]
- Q: Why was dulaglutide a legitimate control? A: REWIND had shown it reduces cardiovascular events against placebo. [4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-in-practice]

4/surpass-cvot-a-noninferiority-margin-i.t: SURPASS-CVOT: a noninferiority margin in practice

sec-testing-ni.t: Noninferiority and equivalence: testing against a margin

noninformative-prior.name: Noninformative prior
noninformative-prior.summary: A prior with a very large variance that adds essentially no information on its own scale, but is vague only on one parameterization.
noninformative-prior.body:
## What it is

A noninformative or reference prior, such as a normal with a very large variance, adds essentially no information. For a normal likelihood the posterior is the likelihood, and the posterior probability that $\theta > 0$ equals one minus the one-sided p-value [sec-priors-three]. In the 508-event example, a very large variance gives 0.994, which is one minus the p-value of 0.006 [sec-priors-three].

## Why it matters

"Noninformative" is a statement about one parameterization. A prior vague on a parameter is generally informative about every nonlinear function of it [sec-priors-flat]. The FDA draft says no single approach is universally preferred, and that such priors are not invariant to transformation [sec-priors-fda].

## In the book

Independent Jeffreys Beta(1/2, 1/2) or uniform Beta(1, 1) priors on two arms put 49 to 56 percent prior probability on a risk difference larger than 30 points in either direction [8/key-points]. A prior that says "no opinion" about each rate says the drug is very likely dramatically effective or harmful [8/independent-beta-priors-imply-an-extreme-prior-on-the-risk-difference]. A vague $N(0, 10^2)$ on logistic coefficients pushes mass to the boundaries because the inverse logit saturates [8/flat-priors-on-logistic-coefficients]. A weakly informative default such as a half-normal on a between-trial standard deviation is common for nuisance parameters [sec-priors-three].

## Pitfalls

A flat prior is a choice with implicit commitments on every other scale. Compute what it implies about the estimand before calling it neutral [8/what-can-go-wrong]. In a large trial with a normal likelihood the issue disappears [8/what-can-go-wrong].

## Check yourself

- Q: Under a flat prior and a normal likelihood, what is the posterior probability of benefit? A: One minus the one-sided p-value [sec-priors-three].
- Q: Why can independent uniform priors on two response rates be a problem? A: They imply a prior on the risk difference that favors extreme differences [8/independent-beta-priors-imply-an-extreme-prior-on-the-risk-difference].

8/independent-beta-priors-imply-an-extre.t: Independent beta priors imply an extreme prior on the risk difference

sec-priors-flat.t: Why default flat priors fail on the scale that matters

normal-approximation-posterior.name: Normal approximation to the posterior
normal-approximation-posterior.summary: Turn a reported estimate and 95 percent interval into a normal likelihood on the log scale, combine it with a normal prior and read posterior probabilities at chosen thresholds.
normal-approximation-posterior.body:
## What it is
Let $\hat\theta$ be the estimate on the log scale and $s$ its standard error. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
A reported 95 percent interval $(\ell, u)$ gives
$$
s = \frac{\log u - \log \ell}{2 \times 1.96}.
$$
[sec-reanalyses-normal]
With a normal prior $\theta \sim N(m_0, s_0^2)$, the posterior is normal with precision equal to the sum of the precisions and mean equal to the precision-weighted average. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
$$
\frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{s^2} + \frac{1}{s_0^2},
\qquad
m_1 = s_1^2\left(\frac{\hat\theta}{s^2} + \frac{m_0}{s_0^2}\right).
$$

## Why it matters
Write $\theta = -\log RR$ so that positive means benefit; then for a threshold $\theta^\ast$, $\Pr(\theta > \theta^\ast \mid \text{data}) = \Phi((m_1 - \theta^\ast)/s_1)$. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
The prior is worth $s^2/s_0^2$ trials of the present size, so a prior with $s_0 = s$ counts as much as the trial itself. [sec-reanalyses-normal]

## In the book
A skeptical prior is centered at no effect with enough spread that a large benefit is unlikely a priori, an enthusiastic prior is centered at the effect the trial was designed to detect, and a reference prior is flat. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
The family follows Spiegelhalter and colleagues, and elicited skeptical priors have an earlier statement in Freedman and Spiegelhalter, with the CHART trials as the worked example. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
A positive trial is convincing when it persuades the skeptic, and a negative trial when it discourages the enthusiast. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
For ANDROMEDA-SHOCK the interval 0.55 to 1.02 gives the log hazard ratio and its standard error. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
The book reduces SURPASS-CVOT and REWIND the same way, from published intervals. [sec-cases-surpass]

## Pitfalls
The approximation is on the stated effect scale and the book's numbers are not replications of published odds-ratio analyses. [sec-reanalyses-andromeda]
Ratios are reported back on their natural scale. [sec-reanalyses-normal]

## Check yourself
- Q: A prior has $s_0 = s$. How much is it worth? A: As much as the trial itself. [sec-reanalyses-normal]
- Q: How do you get $s$ from a 95 percent interval? A: Divide the difference of the log limits by $2 \times 1.96$. [sec-reanalyses-normal]

normal-normal-model.name: Normal-normal model
normal-normal-model.summary: A normal prior and a normal likelihood on the log hazard ratio give a normal posterior whose precision is the sum of the two precisions.
normal-normal-model.body:
## What it is
With prior $\theta \sim N(m_0, \tau^2)$ and the likelihood $\hat\theta \mid \theta \sim N(\theta, 4/d)$, the posterior is normal: [sec-normal-normal]

$$
\theta \mid \hat\theta \;\sim\; N\!\left(m_1, s_1^2\right), \quad
\frac{1}{s_1^2} = \frac{1}{\tau^2} + \frac{d}{4}, \quad
m_1 = \frac{m_0/\tau^2 + \hat\theta\, d/4}{1/\tau^2 + d/4}.
$$

## Why it matters
This is the weighted average of the Beta-binomial case with weights given by precision. The data have precision $d/4$, a prior has $1/\tau^2$, and the prior's effective sample size in events is $4/\tau^2$. A $N(0, 0.2^2)$ prior is worth 100 events and $N(0, 0.35^2)$ about 33. [sec-normal-normal]

## In the book
A trial observes $d = 200$ events and $\widehat{\mathrm{HR}} = 0.74$, so $\hat\theta = 0.30$ with standard error $0.141$, $z = 2.12$ and one-sided p-value $0.017$. [sec-normal-normal]

With a flat prior, $\Pr(\theta > 0) = 0.983$, exactly one minus the p-value. With the skeptical prior of 33 events the posterior mean is 0.258 (HR 0.77) and the probability is 0.975. With the strong prior of 100 events it is 0.958. [sec-normal-normal]

## Pitfalls
The likelihood is an approximation, a modeling choice and not an exact result. It treats $\hat\theta$ as sufficient, which holds only approximately for a Cox model, and ignores the discreteness of event times. [sec-normal-normal]

At a threshold of 0.975 the first prior passes, the second only in the fourth decimal, and the third fails, so the prior must be specified before the data. [sec-normal-normal]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the ESS in events of a $N(0, 0.2^2)$ prior? A: $4/\tau^2 = 100$ events. [sec-normal-normal]
- Q: With a flat prior, how does $\Pr(\theta > 0)$ relate to the one-sided p-value? A: It equals one minus the p-value exactly. [sec-normal-normal]

sec-normal-normal.t: Normal-normal on the log hazard ratio

nsclc-borrowing-case.name: NSCLC borrowing failure
nsclc-borrowing-case.summary: A study in which a matched real-world control augmented with a fixed-weight power prior did not reproduce the randomized result in first-line lung cancer.
nsclc-borrowing-case.body:
## What it is

Struebing and colleagues (2024) built a matched real-world external control arm in first-line non-small cell lung cancer and augmented it with historical-trial data through a fixed-weight power prior. They compared the result with the survival result of the randomized trial whose control arm it replaced. The augmented external control did not reproduce the randomized result. [sec-borrowing-nsclc]

## Why it matters

A power prior with a fixed discount lowers the weight of the historical data but does not change their center. Discounting does not remove differences between sources. [sec-borrowing-nsclc]

## In the book

If real-world patients differ from trial patients in prognostic factors that matching did not capture, the augmented control stays biased. Matching on measured covariates removes only the measured bias. [sec-borrowing-nsclc] The book uses it as the example to show a team that proposes replacing a concurrent control with a matched external one. [sec-borrowing-nsclc] The decision guide says to expect the lesson to apply when the only sources are non-randomized. [sec-borrowing-guide]

## Pitfalls

It is one case and should not be generalized beyond what it shows. [sec-borrowing-nsclc]

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict: does a fixed discount repair prognostic differences? A: No, it changes weight and not center. [sec-borrowing-nsclc]
- Q: What bias does matching remove? A: Only the measured bias. [sec-borrowing-nsclc]

obrien-fleming-boundary.name: O'Brien-Fleming boundary
obrien-fleming-boundary.summary: An efficacy boundary proportional to one over the square root of the information fraction: early looks are almost impossible to cross and the final bar stays near 1.96.
obrien-fleming-boundary.body:
## What it is

O'Brien-Fleming uses a critical value proportional to $1/\sqrt{t_k}$, which is $\Delta = 0$ in the Wang-Tsiatis family $b_k = c\, t_k^{\Delta - 1/2}$. Early looks are nearly impossible to cross, and the final critical value is close to the single-test value. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them] As a spending function it is the first half of the book's equation (eq-spending, the second half is Pocock's):

$$
\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}, \qquad
\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}.
$$

[11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Why it matters

For a cardiovascular outcomes trial with an event-driven analysis and a durable commercial case, the final result should carry the weight of a fixed trial, so O'Brien-Fleming is almost universal. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

## In the book

For four equally spaced looks the boundaries are 4.05, 2.86, 2.34, 2.02 (exact solution of the recursion, $c = 2.024$). Polson and Sokolov print 4.05, 2.87, 2.34, 2.03 from the rounded constant 2.026, and the third decimal is not something a protocol should hinge on. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

The first look requires $Z > 4.05$, a one-sided $p$ of about $2.6 \times 10^{-5}$. The final look requires $Z > 2.02$, a $p$ of about 0.021. The unadjusted 0.025 at the end becomes 0.021. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

The cost is about 2 percent more patients for 90 percent power if the trial runs to the end. When the treatment works the design stops on average at about 75 percent of the planned information. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

As a spending function, $\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}$ spends about 0.0015 of the 0.025 by $t = 0.5$. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Pitfalls

- A boundary does not fix the point estimate at stopping, and a design with an O'Brien-Fleming boundary is not immune to early-stop bias. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

## Check yourself

- Q: What bar does the final look of a four-look O'Brien-Fleming design ask for? A: About 2.02. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]
- Q: What does it cost in sample size? A: About 2 percent. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

ocean-a-outcomes-trial.name: OCEAN(a)-Outcomes
ocean-a-outcomes-trial.summary: A running olpasiran outcomes trial used to show how a sibling trial, Lp(a)HORIZON, moves its probability of success, read as an implicit Bayes factor.
ocean-a-outcomes-trial.body:
## What it is
OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran, Amgen) is a randomized, double-masked phase 3 trial with 7,297 participants and a primary endpoint of time to coronary heart disease death, myocardial infarction or urgent coronary revascularization. [sec-cases-current]
Its primary completion is estimated for March 2028. [sec-cases-current]

## Why it matters
When an analyst moves the probability that a related trial succeeds from $p_0$ to $p_1$ after a sibling reads out, the analyst has implicitly applied a Bayes factor, the ratio of posterior odds to prior odds. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]
The formula is
$$B = \frac{p_1/(1 - p_1)}{p_0/(1 - p_0)}.$$ [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]

## In the book
Lp(a)HORIZON (pelacarsen, Novartis) enrolled 8,323 participants. [sec-cases-current]
Novartis announced on 4 September 2026 that its primary endpoint was not met, and full results followed on 7 November 2026. [sec-cases-current]
The full results reported a hazard ratio of 1.02 (95 percent interval 0.90 to 1.15) overall and 1.00 (0.87 to 1.15) among patients with Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]
On a flat-prior normal approximation, a 10 percent or larger benefit is largely ruled out for pelacarsen at its depth of lowering. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]
The book could not confirm a published analyst estimate, so it uses an illustrative move from 50 to 20 percent, which is not a finding about any analyst. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]

## Pitfalls
HORIZON informs OCEAN(a) only to the extent that olpasiran's benefit is expected to track pelacarsen's. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]
A hierarchical model with the depth of lowering as a covariate makes that assumption explicit, which one revised probability does not. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does a drop from 50 to 20 percent imply about the evidence? A: An implicit Bayes factor, here an illustration only. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]
- Q: Does the HORIZON result decide OCEAN(a)? A: No, it helps only if the two drugs share how benefit scales with Lp(a) lowering. [21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-oceana]

21/what-a-lpahorizon-result-does-to-ocea.t: What a Lp(a)HORIZON result does to OCEAN(a)

ockham-penalty.name: Ockham penalty
ockham-penalty.summary: The automatic charge a Bayes factor makes for a flexible alternative, growing like the logarithm of the information in the trial.
ockham-penalty.body:
## What it is

The Ockham penalty is the charge a Bayes factor makes for an alternative that is flexible. Take the alternative $\theta \sim N(0,\tau^2)$, centered at no effect. For large $k = I_n\tau^2$ the Bayes factor reads [sec-evidence-gaussian]:

$$
2 \log \mathrm{BF}_{10} \;\approx\; \underbrace{Z_n^2}_{\text{fit}} \;-\; \underbrace{\log(1+I_n\tau^2)}_{L_n,\ \text{Ockham penalty}}.
$$

This is eq-ockham. The first term is how well the best-fitting alternative explains the data. The second is a charge for flexibility [sec-evidence-gaussian].

## Why it matters

An alternative that spreads its prior over a wide range gives most of it to effects the data rule out, so it predicts the data worse than a sharp alternative. The more information, the larger the wasted share, and the penalty grows like $\log I_n$ [sec-evidence-gaussian].

## In the book

With $\tau = 0.25$ and $I_n = 400$ the penalty is $L_n = \log(26) = 3.26$ [sec-evidence-gaussian]. The Bayes factor reaches 1 only at $|Z_n| \approx 1.8$, a one-sided p-value of 0.036. [sec-evidence-gaussian] Lindley defined the information in an experiment as the mutual information between $\theta$ and the data. For a normal mean it is $\tfrac12\log(1 + q)$, half the penalty [sec-evidence-lindleyinfo]. Each quadrupling of the trial adds about one bit [sec-evidence-lindleyinfo].

## Pitfalls

The penalty belongs to a point null with a diffuse alternative. Against an interval null the penalties can cancel, and no general growth rate is claimed [sec-evidence-jeffreys].

## Check yourself

- Q: If the trial quadruples in size, what happens to the information it delivers about $\theta$? A: It grows by about one bit [sec-evidence-lindleyinfo].
- Q: What does the penalty do to the Bayes factor as $I_n$ grows? A: It lowers it, and the amount grows like $\log I_n$ [sec-evidence-gaussian].

one-sided-test.name: One-sided test
one-sided-test.summary: A test that counts only departures in the direction of benefit; regulators prefer a one-sided level of 0.025, half the conventional two-sided 0.05.
one-sided-test.body:
## What it is
A two-sided test counts departures from the null in either direction. A one-sided test counts only departures toward benefit. In the shuffle picture the one-sided p-value is the right tail and the two-sided is that tail plus its mirror image. [sec-testing-sided]

## Why it matters
ICH E9 section 5.5 asks the sponsor to "justify prospectively the use of one-sided tests" and prefers one-sided type I errors at half the two-sided level. With the conventional 0.05, half is 0.025. [sec-testing-sided] A one-sided 0.025 is the same bar as a two-sided 0.05, since both reject when the 95% interval excludes zero on the favorable side. [sec-testing-sided] The FDA draft Bayesian guidance of January 2026 uses this language. [sec-testing-sided]

## In the book
A paper reporting "p = 0.04, two-sided" for a helpful drug has a one-sided p-value of 0.02 and meets the bar; "one-sided p = 0.04" does not. [sec-testing-sided] The binary trial gives one-sided p-values of 0.014 (normal), 0.020 (Fisher) and 0.021 (randomization). [sec-testing-sided] The sample size formula uses $z_{0.025} = 1.96$ either way. [sec-testing-sided]

## Pitfalls
If the sponsor sees the drug ahead and then declares a one-sided test at 0.05, the type I error rate has doubled to 5%. [sec-testing-sided] A one-sided test gives no weight to harm, and a strongly negative difference can give a one-sided p-value near 1. Safety review handles harm. [sec-testing-sided]

## Check yourself
- Q: A two-sided p of 0.04 corresponds to what one-sided p? A: 0.02. [sec-testing-sided]
- Q: Where is harm handled? A: In the safety analyses and interim monitoring, not the efficacy test. [sec-testing-sided]

one-trial-with-confirmatory-evidence.name: One trial with confirmatory evidence
one-trial-with-confirmatory-evidence.summary: A 1997 amendment letting FDA treat one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence as substantial evidence, at its discretion.
one-trial-with-confirmatory-evidence.body:
## What it is
The Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997 added a sentence to section 505(d). [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence] If the Secretary determines, based on relevant science, that data from one adequate and well-controlled clinical investigation and confirmatory evidence are sufficient, those data may be treated as substantial evidence. [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence] The confirmatory evidence may come from before or after the trial. [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence]

## Why it matters
The power is discretionary: it is FDA's determination, not a right of the sponsor. [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence] It has been used more often over time, especially in oncology, rare diseases and pediatric settings where a second trial is impractical or unethical. [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence] The permission is of the form "if FDA agrees", so the route goes through a meeting. [sec-regulatory-force]

## In the book
Plans for one trial should be discussed with FDA before the trial starts. [3/the-2026-substantial-evidence-draft] REBYOTA was approved on one phase 3 trial plus a Bayesian model that borrowed from a phase 2b study. [3/rebyota-one-trial-standing-in-for-two] Its observed posterior probability of superiority was 0.991, which clears the 0.9750338 threshold for one adequate and well-controlled trial and misses the 0.9993275 bar for one trial standing in for two, so the evidence counts as one adequate and well-controlled trial, not two, and approval rested on the totality of evidence. [3/rebyota-one-trial-standing-in-for-two]

The arithmetic behind the standard: two independent trials each at one-sided 0.025 pass a useless drug with probability $0.025 \times 0.025 = 1/1600$, while a single trial at 0.025 passes it 1 time in 40. [3/what-the-standard-implies-for-the-numbers]

## Pitfalls
The thresholds in REBYOTA were case-specific evidentiary criteria agreed with FDA, not numerical standards set by the 1997 amendment. [3/rebyota-one-trial-standing-in-for-two] An informative Bayesian prior is a close cousin of "one trial plus confirmatory evidence", but FDA still evaluates its relevance, weight and contribution. [3/the-2026-substantial-evidence-draft]

## Check yourself
- Q: Who decides that one trial plus confirmatory evidence suffices? A: FDA, as a determination based on relevant science. [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence]
- Q: When should a sponsor raise the plan? A: Before initiating the single trial. [3/the-2026-substantial-evidence-draft]

operating-characteristics.name: Operating characteristics
operating-characteristics.summary: How often a trial design declares success or stops under assumed true effects: type I error, power, expected sample size, early stopping and bias.
operating-characteristics.body:
## What it is

A regulator who is asked to accept a design wants to know how often it will go wrong and how often it will go right [sec-simulation]. The answers are the design's operating characteristics. For a fixed-sample trial a formula gives them in a line, and for a group sequential trial a short numerical integration does [sec-simulation].

## Why it matters

For designs with response-adaptive allocation, arm dropping, borrowing or predictive stopping, a closed formula is usually unavailable [sec-simulation]. The operating characteristics then come from running the design many times against assumed truths, and the written result is the [[simulation-report]] [sec-simulation].

## In the book

For a two-arm binary trial with control rate 0.30 and treatment rate 0.45, the fixed design needs 160 per arm [14/the-fixed-sample-design]. Its exact type I error is 0.0252 and exact power is 0.794 [14/the-fixed-sample-design]. Adding looks at 40, 80 and 120 per arm with an O'Brien-Fleming boundary is still analytic, with no random numbers drawn [14/the-group-sequential-design].

For the four-look Bayesian design the book reports power, expected total sample size, probability of stopping early for success or futility, and the bias of the estimate at stopping [14/power-expected-sample-size-early-stopping-and-bias].

## Pitfalls

Reporting only the type I error at the design null reports the easy half [14/type-i-error-across-the-null-space]. The error must hold over the whole null space [14/type-i-error-across-the-null-space]. A bias table is needed because the final estimate is taken at a favorable moment when a trial stops on good data [14/power-expected-sample-size-early-stopping-and-bias].

## Check yourself

- Q: When can operating characteristics be computed without random numbers? A: For fixed and group sequential designs, where the answer is analytic [14/the-group-sequential-design].
- Q: Why does a Bayesian adaptive design usually need simulation? A: Because adaptations leave the standard normal setting and no closed formula exists [14/what-goes-in-the-traditional-sap].

optimizer-smart-trial.name: OPTIMIZER Smart
optimizer-smart-trial.summary: A heart failure device trial analyzed with a fixed 30% Bayesian borrowing weight from an earlier study, without which the success criterion was missed.
optimizer-smart-trial.body:
## What it is

The OPTIMIZER Smart System (cardiac contractility modulation, Impulse Dynamics, PMA P180036) was reviewed by an FDA device panel on 4 December 2018 and approved on 21 March 2019 for heart failure patients in NYHA class III with ejection fraction 25 to 45%. [sec-borrowing-optimizer]

## Why it matters

The pivotal trial FIX-HF-5C randomized 160 patients 1:1 and used a Bayesian model with 30% fixed borrowing from 229 patients with ejection fraction above 25% in the earlier FIX-HF-5 study. The endpoint was the change in peak VO2 at 24 weeks, with success at posterior probability above 0.975. [sec-borrowing-optimizer]

## In the book

With borrowing the posterior probability was between 0.977 and 0.989 under four ways of handling missing data. FIX-HF-5C alone gave 0.957 and 0.960 under two imputation models, 0.916 for the complete-case analysis and 0.911 with last observation carried forward, below 0.975 in each. [sec-borrowing-optimizer] The success of the device therefore depended on the borrowed 30%. [sec-borrowing-optimizer]

## Pitfalls

If the earlier study overstated the effect, the conclusion rests on that overstatement. The FDA device guidance expects simulated operating characteristics under such discrepancies. [sec-borrowing-optimizer] The fixed weight is the device analogue of a power prior with $a_0=0.3$. [sec-borrowing-optimizer]

## Check yourself

- Q: Would the trial have met 0.975 without borrowing? A: No, the posterior probabilities were 0.911 to 0.960. [sec-borrowing-optimizer]
- Q: What kind of borrowing is a fixed 30% weight? A: Static. [sec-borrowing-idea]

overdose-control.name: Escalation with overdose control
overdose-control.summary: A dose-escalation rule that picks the highest dose whose posterior probability of overdosing stays within a feasibility bound.
overdose-control.body:
## What it is
Escalation with overdose control (EWOC) changes the criterion for the next dose. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control] Instead of the dose whose estimated DLT rate is closest to the target, it chooses the highest dose for which the posterior probability of overdosing does not exceed a feasibility bound $\eta$. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control] The bound often starts at 0.25 and is raised as the trial proceeds. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control]

## Why it matters
A dose with some chance of being too toxic is not the one most likely to be chosen. This builds a patient-safety constraint into the decision and was an early attempt to give ethical control a formal expression. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control]

## In the book
The Bayesian logistic regression model applies the same idea to interval probabilities of the DLT rate. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control] In the worked example the admissible-dose bound is 0.25 on the probability of overdosing. [sec-dose-blrm]

## Pitfalls
With either design the decisions rest on a posterior that depends strongly on the prior. The FDA draft on Bayesian methodology says the prior should be justified and subjected to sensitivity analysis. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control]

## Check yourself
- Q: How does EWOC differ from CRM in choosing a dose? A: It bounds the posterior probability of overdose instead of picking the dose closest to target. [17/escalation-with-overdose-control]

p-value.name: P-value
p-value.summary: The probability, under the null and over repetitions of the trial, of a result at least as favorable to the drug as the one observed.
p-value.body:
## What it is
The ingredients are a null hypothesis $H_0$ (a zero average effect), a test statistic that is large when the data favor the drug, and the data. [sec-testing-pvalue] Then

$$
p \;=\; \mathbb{P}\bigl(\text{test statistic at least as favorable to the drug as the one observed} \;\bigm|\; H_0 \text{ true}\bigr) ,
$$

equation eq-testing-pvalue, with the probability taken over repetition of the trial. [sec-testing-pvalue] It answers: if nothing is going on, how often would luck look this good? [sec-testing-pvalue]

## Why it matters
Sloppy definitions drive misuse. A p-value of 0.014 does not mean a 1.4% chance that the drug does not work. [sec-testing-pvalue] It depends on the plan: the same 9 heads and 3 tails have different p-values under different stopping rules. [sec-testing-pvalue] It depends on how many questions were asked, and ICH E9 section 5.6 says multiplicity may necessitate an adjustment. [sec-testing-pvalue]

## In the book
In the simulated trial, in reruns with both arms known to be at 30%, about 1.0% reach a difference of 0.15 or larger; the p-values computed from the one trial's data range from 0.014 to 0.021 because a real trial does not know the common rate. [sec-testing-sampling] The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial gave P = .06 with a hazard ratio of 0.75 (95% CI 0.55 to 1.02), which is inconclusive, not evidence of no effect. [4/andromeda-shock-what-not-significant-does-and-does-not-mean]

## Pitfalls
It mixes the effect size with the trial size. A large p-value is not evidence of no effect. [sec-testing-pvalue] The ASA statement collects these points and Goodman lists twelve misreadings. [sec-testing-pvalue]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is a p-value the probability the null is true? A: No, it is about the data given the hypothesis. [sec-testing-pvalue]
- Q: Why must interim looks be pre-specified? A: The p-value depends on the stopping rule and the number of analyses. [sec-testing-pvalue]

panoramic-trial.name: PANORAMIC
panoramic-trial.summary: A pragmatic UK primary care COVID platform with a Bayesian logistic analysis whose molnupiravir comparison was a clear negative result.
panoramic-trial.body:
## What it is

PANORAMIC took the pragmatic platform approach into UK primary care. It analyzed its primary outcome with Bayesian logistic regression using weakly informative Cauchy priors. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic]

## Why it matters

Not every pandemic platform was an elaborate Bayesian adaptive design. RECOVERY was a large, pragmatic, open-label platform analyzed with frequentist methods, and PANORAMIC shows that simplicity and volume can do the work of a more elaborate adaptive design. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic]

## In the book

The molnupiravir comparison randomized 25,783 participants between December 2021 and April 2022 to molnupiravir plus usual care or usual care alone. The platform's total of 26,411 includes other comparisons. Hospitalization or death within 28 days was about 1% in each group (adjusted odds ratio 1.06), a clear negative result. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic] A platform that can enroll that many community patients in under five months shows that its value comes first from infrastructure and speed. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic] The book contrasts it with RECOVERY, whose first major result was a dexamethasone rate ratio of 0.83 for 28-day mortality. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic]

## Pitfalls

The book groups it with RECOVERY as evidence that a platform's value comes first from infrastructure and speed, not from adaptive machinery. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic]

## Check yourself

- Q: What prior did PANORAMIC use? A: Weakly informative Cauchy priors in Bayesian logistic regression. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic]
- Q: What did molnupiravir show? A: Hospitalization or death in about 1% of each group, adjusted odds ratio 1.06. [20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery-and-panoramic]

20/pragmatic-pandemic-platforms-recovery.t: Pragmatic pandemic platforms: RECOVERY and PANORAMIC

pdufa.name: PDUFA
pdufa.summary: The user fee law under which FDA commits to review goals and meeting timelines, and the August 2026 guidance defining six formal meeting types.
pdufa.body:
## What it is
PDUFA, the Prescription Drug User Fee Act, is the law, periodically reauthorized, under which sponsors pay fees and FDA commits to review goals and meeting timelines. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa] The current commitments are in the PDUFA VII goals letter for fiscal years 2023 through 2027. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa] The guidance *Formal Meetings Between the FDA and Sponsors or Applicants of PDUFA Products* (August 2026) withdraws the December 2017 guidance. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]

## Why it matters
It defines six meeting types: Type A, Type B, Type B (EOP), Type C, Type D and INTERACT. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa] Type C is the usual route for design questions between milestones, such as a Bayesian analysis plan. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]

## In the book
- FDA responds to a request within 14 calendar days for Type A, Type B (EOP) and Type D, and within 21 for Type B and Type C. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]
- The meeting is scheduled within 30 days for Type A, 60 for Type B, 70 for Type B (EOP), 75 for Type C and 50 for Type D. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]
- A Type C meeting on a novel design takes roughly three months from request to answer. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]

## Pitfalls
Minutes are not a binding contract, but an agreement documented in minutes is persuasive. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which meeting suits a stalled program? A: Type A. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]
- Q: How soon is a Type C meeting scheduled? A: Within 75 days of receipt. [3/formal-meetings-under-pdufa]

pediatric-extrapolation.name: Pediatric extrapolation
pediatric-extrapolation.summary: Inferring pediatric efficacy from adult or other source data, with Bayesian borrowing as one quantitative tool after a judgment of similarity.
pediatric-extrapolation.body:
## What it is

Pediatric extrapolation uses source data, usually from adults, to infer efficacy in children. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] ICH E11A (Step 4, August 2024) asks for a plan with three parts: a similarity assessment, the gaps and uncertainties, and a pediatric data plan that ranges from pharmacokinetics and safety only to a full efficacy trial. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]
Pediatric trials are where borrowing is most often justified, because enrollment is small and withholding treatment from children is ethically difficult. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] The FDA Bayesian draft names pediatric extrapolation as a core use of an informative prior, with empagliflozin and linagliptin in pediatric type 2 diabetes as examples where Bayesian analyses were supportive. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]

## Why it matters

Undiscounted adult data would often overwhelm a small pediatric sample, so a prior centered on the adult effect with inflated variance is often more reasonable than pooling. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] Adult and pediatric sources can be related as equally relevant, exchangeable, linked by a bias parameter, or linked by a pharmacometric model. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]

## In the book

In the bias-parameter form the pediatric effect is $\theta_p=\theta_a+b$ with $b\sim N(0,\omega^2)$, and the sponsor's similarity judgment is the number $\omega$. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] A worked example takes an adult log odds ratio of $-0.5$ with standard error 0.08 and a pediatric estimate of $-0.35$ with standard error 0.30, under the mixture

$$
\theta_P\sim w\,N(\hat\theta_A,\,0.08^2+\omega^2)+(1-w)\,N(0,1).
$$

This is eq-ped-mix. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] With $w=0.7$ and $\omega=0.15$ the posterior weight on the adult component rises to 0.87 and Pr(benefit) is 0.98, against 0.88 for the trial alone. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] If the pediatric estimate were $-0.05$, the weight falls only to 0.75 and Pr(benefit) is 0.89, against 0.57 alone. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]

## Pitfalls

The mixture is a weak safeguard in a trial this small: with a standard error of 0.30 the data cannot tell the components apart, so the answer is mostly the prior. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] Drift here means the pediatric effect is not the adult effect, and its range is a clinical judgment about physiology. [sec-borrowing-pediatric] Simulations should include scenarios where children respond less well. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]

## Check yourself

- Q: What is $\omega$? A: The allowed adult-pediatric difference, the sponsor's similarity judgment. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]
- Q: Which comes first in E11A, similarity or statistics? A: The evidence-based judgment of similarity. [sec-borrowing-pediatric]

permuted-block-randomization.name: Permuted block randomization
permuted-block-randomization.summary: Patients are grouped in blocks, and each block contains an equal number of each treatment in random order, which keeps arm sizes balanced.
permuted-block-randomization.body:
## What it is
Permuted block randomization fixes the arm sizes at intervals. Patients are grouped in consecutive blocks of, say, four. In each block two get the drug and two get control, in random order, and there are six possible orders. [5/permuted-block-randomization]

## Why it matters
After every block the arms are exactly balanced in size, and at any moment the imbalance cannot exceed half a block. Both arms also have patients from each period, which protects against a slow time trend. [5/permuted-block-randomization]

## In the book
Block length fixed at four is predictable. If the first three patients were drug, drug, control, the fourth must be control. A clinician who can see past assignments can use that to select patients. [5/permuted-block-randomization] The standard remedy is to vary block length at random, for example blocks of 4 and 6, and to keep block sizes out of the protocol text. [5/permuted-block-randomization]

Blocks do nothing for covariate imbalance: a block makes the number of patients per arm equal and says nothing about which patients. The "block" boxplots match the "simple" ones. [5/seeing-the-difference]

For [[randomization-test|permutation tests]], the shuffle should respect the blocks. Ignoring them made the test conservative under a time trend: the empirical type I error was 0.011 for the unrestricted shuffle and 0.022 within blocks, against a nominal 0.025. [sec-randomization-inference]

## Pitfalls
The price is predictability, especially in open-label trials or trials with unmasked packaging. [5/permuted-block-randomization] Blocks help with arm size and time trends. For covariates, stratification inside blocks or [[minimization]] is needed. [5/seeing-the-difference]

## Check yourself
- Q: With blocks of four, the first three assignments were drug, drug, control. What is the fourth? A: Control, which is why fixed block length is predictable. [5/permuted-block-randomization]
- Q: Do blocks reduce imbalance in a known covariate? A: No. The block boxplots match simple randomization. [5/seeing-the-difference]

phase-1-trial.name: Phase I trial
phase-1-trial.summary: The first exposure of humans to a drug, asking about tolerability, pharmacokinetics and, in oncology, the maximum tolerated dose.
phase-1-trial.body:
## What it is
Phase I is the first exposure of humans to the drug. In most therapeutic areas it enrolls 20 to 100 healthy volunteers; in oncology it enrolls patients for whom standard therapy has failed. [sec-lifecycle-p1] The questions are tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and, in oncology, the maximum tolerated dose. [sec-lifecycle-p1]

The traditional oncology design is the 3+3 rule: treat three patients at a dose, escalate if none has a dose-limiting toxicity, add three more if one does, and stop if two or more do. [sec-lifecycle-p1] It fits no dose-toxicity curve and so identifies a dose with little precision. [sec-lifecycle-p1] Model-based designs replace it, for example the Bayesian logistic regression model. After each cohort the posterior is updated and the next dose is chosen subject to a cap on the posterior probability of overdosing. [sec-lifecycle-p1]

## Why it matters
Phase I is a safety problem first. Phase I produces a posterior over the dose-toxicity curve that becomes the prior for dose selection in Phase II. [2/key-points] [sec-lifecycle-reading]

## In the book
In March 2006 six healthy volunteers in London received the first human doses of TGN1412 and two received placebo. Within hours all six who got the drug developed a cytokine storm with multiple organ failure. [sec-lifecycle-p1] The doses were given within minutes of one another, so the first reaction could not inform the others. Staggered dosing is now standard. [sec-lifecycle-p1]

## Pitfalls
A sequential design is a safety device before it is an efficiency device. [sec-lifecycle-p1]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does the 3+3 rule use? A: Only toxicity counts at the current dose. [2/key-points]
- Q: What did TGN1412 show? A: A design that cannot update between patients can be dangerous. [2/key-points]

sec-lifecycle-p1.t: Phase I: is it safe, and at what dose?

sec-lifecycle-reading.t: A Bayesian reading of the phases

functions.name: dose_three_plus_three
functions.title: One simulated 3+3 trial
functions.description: The rule implemented, step by step. Treat a cohort of 3 at dose 1. At the current dose: with 0 DLTs in 3, escalate; with 1 DLT in 3, treat 3 more at the same dose, escalate if the total is 1 DLT in 6 and otherwise stop; with 2 or 3 DLTs in the first 3, stop immediately (no expansion cohort). Escalation moves up exactly one dose, and a dose is never revisited: there is no de-escalation to a lower dose for further testing, no expansion of the dose below the stopping dose, and no confirmation of the selected dose. When the trial stops for excess toxicity at dose d the recommended dose is d - 1 (0, "none", if d = 1), which may have been given to only 3 patients. If the top dose passes (0 DLTs in 3, or 1 DLT in 6 after expansion) the top dose is selected, with no expansion cohort after 0 DLTs in 3. There is no sample size cap, so the trial length is random. This is the traditional "3+3" of the usual textbook form; Storer's (1989) designs, which expand and de-escalate after initial toxicity, are different rules.

phase-2-to-phase-3-optimism.name: Phase 2 to phase 3 optimism
phase-2-to-phase-3-optimism.summary: A phase 2 estimate that justified moving on is biased upward, so a phase 3 trial sized on it is underpowered and succeeds less often than its nominal power suggests.
phase-2-to-phase-3-optimism.body:
## What it is

A drug is taken into phase III because phase II looked good. A design alternative equal to the phase II estimate is therefore biased upward, a trial sized on it is underpowered at the true effect, and its probability of success is better estimated by the assurance (power averaged over a realistic, shrunk prior) than by the 90% in the protocol [sec-power-zia]. In a simulation the same selection inflates a prior centered on the phase 2 estimate [sec-priors-selection].

## Why it matters

Planning on a shrunk estimate reports the probability of success the program will face, and the time to learn it is before the trial is funded [sec-power-zia]. For a phase 2 estimate of 0.14 with standard deviation 0.10, a 90% power trial has assurance well below that [9/a-comparison].

## In the book

Zia and colleagues examined 181 phase III studies in advanced solid tumors. Of these, 43 used regimens identical to those in 49 preceding phase II studies. Twelve of the 43 (28%) were positive, 81% had lower response rates than phase II, and the mean difference was 12.9 percentage points [sec-power-zia]. In a synthetic example, a flat posterior $N(0.30, 0.141^2)$ and a skeptical one $N(0.20, 0.115^2)$ give different optimal pivotal sizes, with the expected net present value flat from 400 to 800 per arm [sec-power-zia]. The costs, US\$20 million fixed plus US\$0.1 million per patient, and a US\$1 billion value are invented [sec-power-zia].

## Pitfalls

The study concerns chemotherapy in solid tumors, and other areas differ [sec-power-zia]. The 28% does not identify the fraction of ineffective treatments [sec-evidence-practice].

## Check yourself

- Q: What fraction of phase III trials repeating phase II regimens were positive? A: 28% (12 of 43) [sec-power-zia].
- Q: Which direction is the bias in a phase 2 estimate that justified a phase 3? A: Upward [sec-power-zia].

phase-2-trial.name: Phase II trial
phase-2-trial.summary: The phase where most drugs fail, asking whether the drug moves an endpoint at all and which dose to carry into Phase III.
phase-2-trial.body:
## What it is
Phase II is where most drugs fail and where most of the value of a development program is created or destroyed. [sec-lifecycle-p2] Phase IIa is proof of concept, a small study asking whether the drug moves a clinical or biomarker endpoint. Phase IIb is dose ranging against placebo, to choose the dose for Phase III. [sec-lifecycle-p2]

## Why it matters
Bayesian methods have their strongest claim here, because the purpose is learning rather than confirming. [sec-lifecycle-p2] The natural output is a posterior over the dose-response curve and a predictive probability that Phase III will succeed, not a p-value. [sec-lifecycle-p2] The traditional design uses fixed-dose arms or a single-arm response test. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

## In the book
ASTIN tested a neutrophil inhibitory factor in acute ischemic stroke. Patients were allocated adaptively among many doses and placebo with a Bayesian dose-response model, and the design had rules to stop for futility or efficacy. [sec-lifecycle-p2] It found no effect and stopped early for futility at 966 patients according to the published report. [sec-lifecycle-p2] A conventional group sequential design with a futility rule could also have stopped early. [sec-lifecycle-p2]

## Pitfalls
A Phase III designed around the Phase II point estimate is usually underpowered. [sec-lifecycle-p2]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does Phase II ideally output? A: A posterior over the dose-response curve and a predictive probability of Phase III success. [sec-lifecycle-p2]
- Q: What was ASTIN's most valuable output? A: A fast, well-founded negative result. [sec-lifecycle-p2]

sec-lifecycle-p2.t: Phase II: does it work, and at what dose?

sec-lifecycle-reading.t: A Bayesian reading of the phases

phase-3-trial.name: Phase III trial
phase-3-trial.summary: Large randomized, usually blinded trials that confirm efficacy and characterize safety, on which the regulatory decision rests.
phase-3-trial.body:
## What it is
Phase III trials are large, randomized and usually blinded, designed to confirm efficacy and characterize safety in the population for which the drug will be licensed. They enroll hundreds to tens of thousands of patients and cost from tens to hundreds of millions of dollars. [sec-lifecycle-p3] The traditional FDA standard is two adequate and well-controlled trials, or one adequate and well-controlled trial with confirmatory evidence. [sec-lifecycle-p3]

## Why it matters
This is the stage at which the type I error rate is the contract with the regulator and at which interim analyses are governed by the strictest rules. [sec-lifecycle-p3] A Bayesian criterion here is judged by its operating characteristics under a pre-specified design. [2/key-points]

## In the book
In December 2006 Pfizer stopped ILLUMINATE, a Phase III outcomes trial of torcetrapib, after the data monitoring committee found an excess of deaths on the drug. [sec-lifecycle-p3] Torcetrapib had been associated with higher blood pressure in earlier studies. [sec-lifecycle-p3] The episode shows that off-target information from earlier phases belongs in the prior for Phase III, and that an interim analysis is as valuable for stopping for harm as for benefit. [sec-lifecycle-p3]

## Pitfalls
The type I error rate is the contract with the regulator, so a Bayesian Phase III design must keep it through calibration or borrowing rules. [sec-lifecycle-p3] The traditional design is fixed or group sequential at type I error 0.025. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the traditional FDA evidentiary standard? A: Two adequate and well-controlled trials, or one adequate and well-controlled trial with confirmatory evidence. [sec-lifecycle-p3]
- Q: What earlier information belonged in the Phase III prior for torcetrapib? A: Higher blood pressure seen in earlier studies. [sec-lifecycle-p3]

sec-lifecycle-p3.t: Phase III: confirming, and the regulatory decision

sec-lifecycle-reading.t: A Bayesian reading of the phases

phase-4-trial.name: Phase IV study
phase-4-trial.summary: Studies after approval: required postmarketing trials, surveillance of adverse events and confirmatory trials, where rare harms become visible.
phase-4-trial.body:
## What it is
Approval is not the end of learning. Phase IV comprises postmarketing studies required or agreed at approval, observational surveillance of adverse events, and confirmatory trials for drugs given accelerated approval on a surrogate endpoint. [sec-lifecycle-p4] Premarketing trials are often too small or too short to characterize rare harms. [sec-lifecycle-p4]

## Why it matters
Postmarketing surveillance is a sequential decision problem in which the action is to warn, restrict or withdraw, and the cost of waiting is counted in patients harmed. [sec-lifecycle-p4]

## In the book
Rofecoxib was approved in 1999 and withdrawn on 30 September 2004 after the APPROVe trial. In 2,586 patients with a history of colorectal adenoma it showed 46 confirmed thrombotic events on the drug against 26, rate ratio 1.92 (95% CI 1.19 to 3.11). [sec-lifecycle-p4] VIGOR had earlier shown fewer gastrointestinal events than naproxen but more myocardial infarctions. A cumulative meta-analysis found a clear excess of myocardial infarction at the end of 2000. [sec-lifecycle-p4]

Spontaneous reporting systems compare the observed count for a drug and event pair with the count expected under independence. The gamma-Poisson shrinker reports a posterior estimate, so an estimate from three reports is shrunk heavily toward the common distribution and one from three hundred is not. [sec-lifecycle-p4]

## Pitfalls
Evidence of harm can be in hand years before action. [2/key-points]

## Check yourself
- Q: How were the rofecoxib thrombotic events split in APPROVe? A: 46 on the drug against 26. [sec-lifecycle-p4]
- Q: Why shrink crude reporting ratios? A: They are unstable when counts are small. [sec-lifecycle-p4]

sec-lifecycle-reading.t: A Bayesian reading of the phases

phase-transition-probability.name: Phase transition probability
phase-transition-probability.summary: The probability that a program moves from one phase to the next, or from Phase III to approval, which drives the cost of each approved drug.
phase-transition-probability.body:
## What it is
The book writes $p_{12}$, $p_{23}$ and $p_{3A}$ for the probabilities of moving from Phase I to II, from II to III, and from III to approval. [sec-lifecycle-options]

## Why it matters
Each transition probability enters the cost per approved drug. Programs that use biomarkers to select patients have higher success probabilities. [sec-lifecycle-options] A Phase II predictive distribution gives the probability that Phase III will succeed. [sec-lifecycle-reading]

## In the book
Wong, Siah and Lo used over 400,000 trial records for more than 21,000 compounds and estimated that about 13.8 percent of programs entering Phase I eventually reach approval, and 3.4 percent in oncology. [sec-lifecycle-options] Over 2011 to 2020 the likelihood that a drug entering phase I was approved was 7.9 percent, and only 28.9 percent of candidates cleared phase II. [1/the-price-of-a-trial-of-being-wrong-and-of-waiting] Of 43 phase III studies that repeated the regimen of a preceding phase II study, only 12 (28 percent) were positive. [1/the-price-of-a-trial-of-being-wrong-and-of-waiting]

## Pitfalls
Raising a transition probability by advancing more compounds is not better selection. The case for predictive methods is that they advance the right ones. [sec-lifecycle-options]

## Check yourself
- Q: Do the published approval rates agree to the decimal? A: No. The book quotes 13.8 percent from one source and 7.9 percent from another, for different data and periods. [sec-lifecycle-options] [1/the-price-of-a-trial-of-being-wrong-and-of-waiting]
- Q: What did the 43 repeated Phase III studies show? A: Only 12 were positive. [1/the-price-of-a-trial-of-being-wrong-and-of-waiting]

1/the-price-of-a-trial-of-being-wrong-an.t: The price of a trial, of being wrong, and of waiting

sec-lifecycle-reading.t: A Bayesian reading of the phases

platform-trial.name: Platform trial
platform-trial.summary: A master protocol that fixes the disease and infrastructure and lets drugs enter and leave over time under pre-specified decision rules.
platform-trial.body:
## What it is

FDA's June 2026 draft describes a platform as a trial to "evaluate multiple drugs for one or more diseases, conditions, or disease subtypes in an ongoing manner, with drugs entering or leaving the platform". [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] A platform fixes the disease and the infrastructure and lets the drugs change. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] The EC, EMA and HMA question-and-answer document defines it as a shared framework in which investigational products enter and leave at different times under pre-specified decision rules. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

## Why it matters

A platform answers $k$ questions with one control group, enrolling $(k+1)m$ patients rather than $2km$. [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost] Saville and Berry simulated whole programs and found platforms found beneficial treatments with fewer patients and less time than a traditional strategy, under stated assumptions. [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost]

## In the book

Both frequentist and Bayesian platforms can accommodate new arms and share information, and both need a justified hypothesis family and demonstrated operating characteristics. [sec-platform] The Bayesian platforms use a decision rule per arm calibrated by simulation, with optional hierarchical sharing. [20/traditional-against-bayesian-platforms-what-differs] Governance typically has a single monitoring committee, an independent statistical center and an arm-approval committee. [20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitoring-board]

## Pitfalls

Arms added later create the non-concurrent control problem. [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost] A platform survives its first arm only if governance is built for arms not yet known, and EPAD never opened an arm. [20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitoring-board] [20/epad-a-platform-that-never-opened-an-arm]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a platform fix and what does it vary? A: It fixes disease and infrastructure and varies the drugs. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]
- Q: How many patients does a platform of five drugs at 80 per arm need? A: 480, against 800 for separate trials. [20/what-changes-in-the-protocol]

play-the-winner.name: Play the winner
play-the-winner.summary: An urn allocation rule that adds a ball for the treatment that succeeded, so allocation drifts toward the apparent winner; used in the ECMO trial.
play-the-winner.body:
## What it is

Zelen proposed the play-the-winner rule, and randomized versions followed [16/exploring-and-exploiting]. In its simplest urn form, start with one ball for each treatment and draw a ball to assign each patient [16/what-was-done]. After each outcome, add a ball for the treatment that succeeded, or for the other treatment after a failure [16/what-was-done].

## Why it matters

The ECMO trial of Bartlett and colleagues used a randomized play-the-winner rule [16/what-was-done]. As the urn drifted toward ECMO, one infant was assigned to conventional therapy and the other eleven to ECMO [16/what-was-done].

## In the book

The book simulates the urn with 12 infants and true survival 0.80 on ECMO and 0.20 on conventional therapy, against a fixed 6:6 trial analyzed by a one-sided Fisher exact test at level 0.025 [16/what-the-rule-did-to-the-information]. Play-the-winner puts few infants on the control arm, and in a sizable share of trials at most one, which makes a comparison essentially impossible [16/what-the-rule-did-to-the-information]. The rule gave more infants the treatment investigators believed in, at the cost of the information the trial was meant to produce [16/what-the-rule-did-to-the-information].

## Pitfalls

A rule that reacts to a few early outcomes can move allocation sharply on very little evidence, and an urn that has drifted toward a treatment that only looked best early takes a long time to correct [16/the-aftermath-and-what-it-means-for-design]. The pattern of every RAR design is in-trial reward against terminal information [16/what-the-rule-did-to-the-information].

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the urn do after a failure? A: It adds a ball for the other treatment [16/what-was-done].
- Q: What did play-the-winner cost the ECMO comparison? A: Information, because almost no infants were left on the control arm [16/what-the-rule-did-to-the-information].

pocock-boundary.name: Pocock boundary
pocock-boundary.summary: An efficacy boundary with the same critical value at every look, which stops early more easily but sets a final bar well above 1.96.
pocock-boundary.body:
## What it is

Pocock uses the same critical value at every look, which is $\Delta = 1/2$ in the Wang-Tsiatis family. Early stopping is easy, but the final critical value is well above 1.96. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them] As a spending function it is the second half of the book's equation (eq-spending, the first half is O'Brien-Fleming's):

$$
\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}, \qquad
\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}.
$$

[11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Why it matters

A trial in which an early answer is worth much more than a marginally larger sample, such as one in a serious acute illness, may choose a boundary closer to Pocock. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

## In the book

For four equally spaced looks the Pocock row has the same value, 2.36, at every look. A one-sided $p$ of 0.009 at the first look is enough to stop. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

To have 90 percent power the Pocock design needs about 18 percent more patients than the fixed design if the trial runs to the end, against about 2 percent for O'Brien-Fleming. When the treatment works it stops on average at about 59 percent of the planned information, against about 75 percent for O'Brien-Fleming. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

The spending-function form is $\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}$, which spends steadily. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

A third, informal rule uses a very small fixed nominal level at every interim look, for example two-sided $|Z| > 3$, and the unadjusted level at the end. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

## Pitfalls

- Under the null both designs run almost to the end when there is no futility rule, so Pocock's early-stop advantage appears only when the drug works. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does the Pocock design charge for earlier stops? A: A final bar of about 2.36 and about 18 percent more patients if it runs to the end. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]
- Q: When the treatment works, which stops earlier, Pocock or O'Brien-Fleming? A: Pocock, at about 59 percent against about 75 percent of the information. [11/obrien-fleming-pocock-and-the-family-between-them]

posterior-distribution.name: Posterior distribution
posterior-distribution.summary: The distribution of the unknown parameter after seeing the data, obtained by multiplying the prior by the likelihood and rescaling.
posterior-distribution.body:
## What it is
The posterior is what is believed about the parameter after the data, $\pi(\theta \mid y)$. It is the prior times the likelihood, rescaled to integrate to one. [sec-bayes-rule]

Bayes rule gives the posterior:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta)}{\int p(y \mid \theta')\, \pi(\theta')\, d\theta'} \;\propto\; p(y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

This is equation eq-bayes. [sec-bayes-rule]

## Why it matters
The traditional analysis asks how surprising a difference this large would be if the treatment had no effect. A trialist usually wants to know how likely it is that the new treatment is better and by how much. The posterior answers this directly. [sec-bayes]

Its statements are probabilities about the parameter given these data. A confidence interval is a statement about a procedure over repeated trials. [6/a-side-by-side]

## In the book
Put a flat Beta(1,1) prior on each arm of the running trial, 30 of 100 control and 45 of 100 treatment responders. The posteriors are Beta(31, 71) and Beta(46, 56). [6/the-bayesian-analysis]

There is no neat formula for the difference, so many samples are drawn from each posterior (Monte Carlo). The probability $\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid y)$ is 0.9855, against $1 - p = 0.9858$. [sec-bayes-summary]

The posterior also answers questions a p-value cannot: the probability that the effect exceeds a margin such as 5 or 10 percentage points. [6/the-bayesian-analysis]

## Pitfalls
With a flat prior and a nearly normal likelihood the posterior probability and one minus the one-sided p-value nearly coincide. The match is not a theorem of the model. It fails with an informative prior, a small sample or rates near 0 or 1. [sec-agree]

The same data under three normal priors gave 0.983, 0.975 and 0.958, so the prior must be specified before the data. [sec-normal-normal]

## Check yourself
- Q: After 45 of 100 responders and a flat prior, what is the posterior? A: Beta(46, 56). [6/the-bayesian-analysis]
- Q: Does a flat prior always make $1-p$ equal the posterior probability? A: No, only approximately, in nearly normal settings. [sec-agree]

posterior-predictive-distribution.name: Posterior predictive distribution
posterior-predictive-distribution.summary: The distribution of future data after averaging over the uncertainty about the parameter, wider than a plug-in prediction.
posterior-predictive-distribution.body:
## What it is
Decisions depend on what will happen next, such as how many of the next 50 patients will respond. The posterior predictive distribution averages the model for future data over the posterior: [sec-predictive-dist]

$$
p(\tilde y \mid y) = \int p(\tilde y \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta .
$$

## Why it matters
For a Beta$(a', b')$ posterior and $m$ future patients, the number of future responders follows a beta-binomial distribution with mean $m a' / (a' + b')$. [sec-predictive-dist]

The traditional analogue is a plug-in calculation: assume $p = \hat p$ and compute a binomial. It ignores the uncertainty in $\hat p$ and is too narrow. [sec-predictive-dist]

Futility rules and Goldilocks-type sample-size choices are built on it. [sec-predictive-dist] The same two-stage logic, draw the parameter from its posterior and then the future data from the model, gives the probability that a trial in progress will succeed at its final analysis. [sec-predictive-dist]

## In the book
After 45 of 100 and a flat prior, the treatment-arm posterior is Beta(46, 56). The next 50 patients are predicted with the beta-binomial function `dbetabinom`. [sec-predictive-dist] A prediction made as if $\hat p = 0.45$ were the truth would be overconfident by about 20 percent. [sec-predictive-dist] In Table 6.8 the predictive standard deviation is 4.27 against 3.52 for the plug-in binomial, and the 95% predictive interval is 14 to 31 responders. [sec-predictive-dist]

## Pitfalls
The predictive is for future data and the posterior is for the parameter. [sec-predictive-dist]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which is wider, the posterior predictive or the plug-in binomial? A: The posterior predictive, because it includes the uncertainty about $p$. [sec-predictive-dist]
- Q: What distribution gives the number of future responders from a Beta posterior? A: Beta-binomial. [sec-predictive-dist]

posterior-probability-of-benefit.name: Posterior probability of benefit
posterior-probability-of-benefit.summary: The posterior probability that the treatment effect exceeds a threshold a, the quantity in the FDA draft's Bayesian success criterion.
posterior-probability-of-benefit.body:
## What it is

The January 2026 FDA draft describes the standard Bayesian success criterion [sec-evidence-fdacriterion]:

$$
\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) \;>\; c,
$$

which is eq-fda. The threshold $a$ says how big an effect counts, and $c$ says how sure one must be [sec-evidence-fdacriterion].

## Why it matters

With a flat prior and $a = 0$, the posterior probability is one minus the one-sided p-value, so $c = 0.975$ succeeds exactly when $Z_n > 1.96$ [sec-evidence-flat]. With a flat prior the type I error at no effect is $\alpha(a, c) = 1 - \Phi(a/s + z_c)$ [sec-evidence-mapping]. A skeptical prior raises the bar on the estimate [sec-evidence-informativeprior].

## In the book

With s = 0.10 and $a = 0.10$, the rule $c = 0.975$ has type I error 0.0015, and the calibrating $c$ falls to 0.83 [sec-evidence-mapping]. With skeptical priors of 0.2 and 0.1, the type I error at $c = 0.975$ falls to 0.014 and 0.003 and power falls to 0.79 and 0.59 from 0.85 [sec-evidence-informativeprior]. In a worked trial with estimate 0.28 and s = 0.10, the probability of benefit is 0.9974. The probability the effect exceeds 0.10 is 0.964, which clears $c = 0.95$ but not 0.975 [7/a-worked-comparison].

## Pitfalls

The pair $(a, c)$ means nothing until attached to a sample size and a model [sec-evidence-mapping]. Calibrating at $\theta = 0$ establishes superiority over zero, not benefit exceeding $a$ [sec-evidence-mapping].

## Check yourself

- Q: With a flat prior and a = 0, what c matches one-sided alpha 0.025? A: c = 0.975 [sec-evidence-mapping].
- Q: Does a calibrated criterion with a skeptical prior beat the z test at a single look? A: No, it has the same type I error and about the same power [sec-evidence-informativeprior].

posterior-probability-success-criterion.name: Posterior probability success criterion
posterior-probability-success-criterion.summary: A rule that declares success when the posterior probability that the treatment effect exceeds a threshold a is larger than a level c.
posterior-probability-success-criterion.body:
## What it is

The FDA Bayesian draft guidance describes a success criterion of the form $\Pr(\delta > a \mid \text{data}) > c$ [sec-sim-rule]. The treatment effect $\delta$ must exceed a threshold $a$ with posterior probability larger than a level $c$ [sec-sim-rule]. For two response rates, $\delta = p_1 - p_0$ [sec-sim-rule].

With independent Beta(1,1) priors the posterior in each arm is Beta$(1 + x_j, 1 + n_j - x_j)$, and the probability is a one-dimensional integral [sec-sim-rule].

## Why it matters

The rule has no type I error until $a$, $c$, the prior and the schedule of looks are all fixed, because the error rate belongs to the whole procedure, not to the posterior [sec-sim-rule]. With one look and a flat prior, $c = 0.975$ is roughly the familiar one-sided 2.5 percent test [sec-sim-rule]. Add a second look and the same $c$ is no longer a 2.5 percent test [sec-sim-rule].

## In the book

The threshold $a$ is a clinical quantity, the smallest effect worth having, and $c$ is a statistical quantity set by [[calibration]] [14/choosing-a-and-c]. The pivotal BNT162b2 trial used 0.995 at the interim analyses and 0.986 at the final one to keep the overall type I error at 2.5 percent [sec-sim-rule].

## Pitfalls

Reusing 0.975 at every look inflates the error. In the book's example the rule applied at any of four looks needs $c = 0.991$ to be a 2.5 percent test [sec-sim-inflation]. Examples with $a > 0$ depart from the draft's $a = 0$ calibrated superiority form; they show mechanics and are not a form the draft prescribes [14/choosing-a-and-c].

## Check yourself

- Q: Is $c = 0.975$ a 2.5 percent test when the trial looks four times? A: No. The book finds $c = 0.991$ gives 2.5 percent at four looks [sec-sim-inflation].
- Q: Which two quantities does the rule depend on besides the data? A: The effect threshold $a$ and the level $c$, plus the prior and the looks, which together fix the error rate [sec-sim-rule].

functions.name: oc_post_table
functions.title: Posterior probability table for a two-arm binary trial
functions.usage: oc_post_table(n, a = 0, prior = c(1, 1), G = NULL)
functions.description: Returns the matrix T[x0 + 1, x1 + 1] = Pr(p1 - p0 > a | x0, x1) for x0, x1 successes out of n per arm with independent Beta(prior) priors on each arm. Each entry is the exact rank-scale integral of prob_superior() (relative tolerance 1e-10), so exchangeable states give exactly 0.5 and concentrated or U-shaped posteriors are not truncated. When a = 0 the table is exchangeable and only half of it is integrated. It is computed once per look, so that a simulated trial reads its posterior probability by table lookup. Tables are cached within the session under a key that records n, a and prior exactly (to full double precision), so distinct arguments never share a table.

power-curve.name: Power curve
power-curve.summary: The plot of power against the true effect for a fixed sample size, showing the threshold effect below which a trial is more likely to miss than find a benefit.
power-curve.body:
## What it is

The power curve plots $\text{Power}(\theta)$ for fixed $n$ and $\alpha$ over the whole range of effects. [9/the-power-curve]

$$
\text{Power}(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\theta\sqrt{nI} - z_\alpha\right).
$$

(eq-power-z) It equals $\alpha$ at $\theta = 0$, rises through 50% at $\theta = z_\alpha/\sqrt{nI}$, and passes the design value $\theta_d$ at $1-\beta$ [9/the-power-curve].

## Why it matters

A single power number hides the shape. The trial has a threshold effect at which power is 50%, and below it effects are more likely missed than found [9/the-power-curve]. For a design with 90% power, that threshold is 60.5% of the design effect [9/the-power-curve]. The curve is also flat near the design point: going from 90% to 95% power needs 24% more information [9/the-power-curve].

## In the book

If the trial is sized for $\theta_d$ and the truth is $\rho\,\theta_d$, power is $\Phi(\rho(z_\alpha+z_\beta) - z_\alpha)$, which depends only on $\rho$. A trial sized for 90% power has 83% power at 90% of the design effect, 62% at 70%, and 37% at half [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative]. A trial with 90% power at hazard ratio 0.80 is, for an effect smaller than about a 13% hazard reduction, more likely than not to fail [9/the-power-curve].

## Pitfalls

At the left end of the curve the probability of a positive result for a drug that does nothing is $\alpha$, independent of $n$ [9/the-power-curve]. If the drug is better than assumed, the trial is overpowered and ends later than needed [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative].

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict the power if the true effect is half the design effect at 90% design power. A: About 37% [9/sensitivity-to-the-design-alternative].
- Q: What fraction of the design effect has 50% power? A: 60.5% [9/the-power-curve].

power-prior.name: Power prior
power-prior.summary: A prior that raises the historical likelihood to a power a0 between 0 and 1, so that a0 sets the fraction of historical patients that count.
power-prior.body:
## What it is

The power prior of Ibrahim and Chen (2000) down-weights historical data $D_h$ with a single parameter $a_0$ [sec-borrowing-power]:

$$
\pi(\theta \mid D_h, a_0) \propto L(\theta \mid D_h)^{a_0}\,\pi_0(\theta),\qquad 0\le a_0\le 1.
$$

Setting $a_0=0$ discards the historical data and $a_0=1$ pools them fully (eq-power). [sec-borrowing-power] If $a_0$ is fixed in advance the method is static. [sec-borrowing-power] With a Beta$(1,1)$ initial prior the power prior is Beta$(1+a_0y_h,\,1+a_0(n_h-y_h))$, so its effective sample size is $a_0 n_h+2$. With $n_h=100$ and $a_0=0.3$ the historical arm counts as about 30 patients. [sec-borrowing-power]

## Why it matters

The regulator sees the borrowing in one number, the effective sample size, and FDA's distinction between static and dynamic borrowing is the distinction between a fixed and a learned $a_0$. [sec-borrowing-power]

## In the book

If $a_0$ is given its own prior, the data can choose it. The *normalized power prior* divides by the $a_0$-dependent constant (eq-npp), and the marginal posterior of $a_0$ rises when the current data resemble the historical data. [sec-borrowing-power] In the rare-disease example, 12 responders in 40 historical controls are borrowed for a trial with 6 of 15 on control, and the marginal likelihood of the current controls guides $a_0$ (eq-borrow-marg). [sec-borrowing-rare] Pr(pT>pC) is 0.83 without borrowing and 0.95 at $a_0=0.5$, and the marginal likelihood is maximized at $a_0=1$ with m(1)/m(0)=2.3. [sec-borrowing-rare] The tirzepatide chain divides the REWIND variance by $a_0$. [sec-borrowing-chain]

## Pitfalls

The power prior discounts the precision of the historical data but does not move their center. With $a_0=0.3$ the prior is Beta$(10,22)$, centered at 0.3125, and nothing in the method notices a conflict if the truth is 40%. [sec-borrowing-power] In the NSCLC case study a fixed-weight power prior did not reproduce the randomized result. [sec-borrowing-nsclc]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does $a_0=0.3$ mean for a historical arm of 100? A: It counts as about 30 patients. [sec-borrowing-power]
- Q: Does discounting fix a biased center? A: No, it only widens the prior. [sec-borrowing-power]
