power.name: Statistical power
power.summary: The probability that a trial declares success when the true effect equals a stated value, a conditional probability and not a chance of success.
power.body:
## What it is

A one-sided trial can declare a useless drug effective (type I error, fixed at $\alpha$, conventionally 0.025) or miss an effective drug (type II error, $\beta$). The complement $1-\beta$ is the power [9/two-errors-and-one-guess]. With $Z = \hat\theta\sqrt{nI}$ and a true effect $\theta$,

$$
\text{Power}(\theta) = \Phi\!\left(\theta\sqrt{nI} - z_\alpha\right).
$$

This is eq-power-z [9/two-errors-and-one-guess].

## Why it matters

Type I error control is a central regulatory design criterion. Type II error is a business and ethical quantity that the sponsor chooses, usually at 0.10 or 0.20 [9/two-errors-and-one-guess]. At 90% power $(z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2 = 10.51$, and at 80% it is 7.85, so 90% power needs a third more patients [9/two-errors-and-one-guess].

## In the book

Power is a conditional probability: the chance of a significant result given that the true effect equals $\theta_d$. A statement such as "90% power" is regularly heard as "90% chance of success", which would be true only if the sponsor were certain of the effect [9/power-is-conditional]. A conventional power calculation can be represented as [[assurance]] under a point-mass prior [sec-power-assurance]. The power curve shows how power changes with the effect [9/the-power-curve].

## Pitfalls

Raising the sample size buys power (and precision) but leaves the type I error at 0.025 [9/the-power-curve]. Power is not a condition of approval in the way that error control is [9/two-errors-and-one-guess].

## Check yourself

- Q: Why does 90% power need about a third more patients than 80%? A: 10.51 over 7.85 is 1.34, whatever the effect [9/two-errors-and-one-guess].
- Q: Is 90% power a 90% chance of success? A: No, it is conditional on one effect value [9/power-is-conditional].

predictive-probability-monitoring.name: Predictive probability monitoring
predictive-probability-monitoring.summary: A phase 2 design that stops for futility or efficacy when the predictive probability of final success crosses a lower or upper threshold, with a printed stopping table.
predictive-probability-monitoring.body:
## What it is

Lee and Liu turned the predictive probability of success into a two-threshold monitoring design for phase 2 with a printed stopping table [sec-leeliu]. After each cohort compute the predictive probability that the trial ends in success; stop for futility if it is below $\eta_L$, stop for efficacy if above $\eta_U$, otherwise continue [sec-leeliu]. At the maximum sample size success needs $\Pr(p > p_0 \mid \text{data}) > \eta$ [sec-leeliu]. The predictive probability is approximated by

$$
\mathrm{PP} \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(q_n) - \Phi^{-1}(\eta)\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{1-r}}\right),
$$

[sec-leeliu]

## Why it matters

The rule depends only on $(n, s)$, so the decision for every interim outcome can be tabulated before the trial and printed in the protocol [sec-leeliu]. It computes a boundary in a Bayesian way and judges it in a frequentist way [15/what-the-predictive-probability-design-is-and-is-not].

## In the book

With $N = 40$, $p_0 = 0.20$, thresholds 0.05 and 0.95 and looks after 10, 20 and 30 patients, futility stops are at 0 responders after 10, 3 or fewer after 20, and 7 or fewer after 30 [sec-leeliu]. Efficacy stops are at 6 or more after 10, 9 or more after 20, and twelve or more after 30 [sec-leeliu]. Operating characteristics follow from exact enumeration, power is essentially unchanged and the sample size falls by roughly a third [sec-leeliu].

## Pitfalls

Once efficacy stopping is allowed, the type I error is not guaranteed to stay at the fixed-design value, so thresholds need recalibration [sec-leeliu]. The thresholds 0.05 and 0.95 are conventions; an economic reading gives (eq-ppstar)

$$
\mathrm{PP}^* = \frac{m c_2}{\rho V - (1-\rho) c_3},
$$

[15/the-economic-threshold-pp]

## Check yourself

- Q: How many responders out of 10 stop the trial for futility in the example? A: None, that is zero responders [sec-leeliu].
- Q: Is the type I error guaranteed after adding efficacy looks? A: No, recalibrate by enumeration or simulation [sec-leeliu].

predictive-probability-of-success.name: Predictive probability of success
predictive-probability-of-success.summary: The chance that the trial will meet its final success criterion if it continues, averaging over what the remaining patients might show.
predictive-probability-of-success.body:
## What it is

Conditional power fixes the effect $\xi$. The Bayesian replaces it by the posterior distribution of $\xi$ and averages [15/from-conditional-power-to-predictive-probability]:

$$
\mathrm{PP} = \int \mathrm{CP}(\xi)\, \pi(\xi \mid y_{1:n})\, d\xi = \Pr(\text{final success criterion met} \mid y_{1:n}).
$$

[15/from-conditional-power-to-predictive-probability]

For a binary endpoint with $m$ future patients the future responders are beta-binomial (eq-betabinom) and the predictive probability is the exact sum (eq-pp-binary) [15/the-exact-beta-binomial-computation]:

$$
\Pr(X = x \mid s, n) = \binom{m}{x}\frac{B(a_0+s+x,\; b_0+n-s+m-x)}{B(a_0+s,\; b_0+n-s)}, \qquad x = 0,\dots,m,
$$

$$
\mathrm{PP}(s, n) = \sum_{x=0}^{m} \Pr(X=x \mid s,n)\; \mathbf{1}\{\Pr(p > p_0 \mid s+x,\, N) > \eta\}.
$$

Marion's approximation (eq-marion) is

$$
\mathrm{PP} \approx \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(q_n) - \Phi^{-1}(\eta)\sqrt{r}}{\sqrt{1-r}}\right),
$$

[15/what-the-predictive-probability-design-is-and-is-not]

## Why it matters

It accounts for uncertainty in the effect, which conditional power does not [15/from-conditional-power-to-predictive-probability]. The final success criterion must be named when the number is reported, because it can be a frequentist test or a Bayesian rule [15/from-conditional-power-to-predictive-probability].

## In the book

With a normal prior and the normal-drift model the integral has a closed form, computed by `pp_normal` [15/the-normal-case]. For a binary endpoint no approximation is needed: the future responders follow a beta-binomial distribution, and the predictive probability is an exact sum [15/the-exact-beta-binomial-computation]. In a single-arm example with $N = 40$ and $p_0 = 0.20$, twenty patients with six responders give 0.457, with 5 responders 0.219, and with 7 responders 0.713 [15/the-exact-beta-binomial-computation]. The approximation of Marion needs only the current posterior probability and the information fraction [15/what-the-predictive-probability-design-is-and-is-not].

## Pitfalls

Neither a flat-prior value nor a design-alternative-prior value is the right one; they answer under different priors, so the prior must be pre-specified [15/the-normal-case]. The approximation is a design component to validate, not an identity [15/what-the-predictive-probability-design-is-and-is-not].

## Check yourself

- Q: How does PP relate to conditional power? A: It is conditional power averaged over the posterior of the effect [15/from-conditional-power-to-predictive-probability].
- Q: Does the binary case need simulation? A: No, it is an exact beta-binomial sum [15/the-exact-beta-binomial-computation].

prespecification.name: Prespecification
prespecification.summary: Fixing the prior, thresholds, schedule and analysis before the data are seen, which separates a designed Bayesian trial from a post hoc reanalysis.
prespecification.body:
## What it is
A trial's prespecified analysis is the one the protocol and statistical analysis plan fixed before the data were seen. [22/prespecification]
For GUSTO, EOLIA and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK that analysis was frequentist and fixed in advance. [22/prespecification]

## Why it matters
A Bayesian reanalysis is done after the results are known, by people who know them, so it is exploratory in ICH E9's sense. [22/prespecification]
The same discipline applies to a prospective Bayesian design: the FDA draft asks that the prior be stated and justified and that sensitivity be shown across a range. [22/prior-choice]
E9 says interim analyses should be carefully planned in advance and described in the protocol. [23/interim-schedule-and-decision-rules]

## In the book
The honest report lists every prior tried, and the book's tables show each row, including the pessimistic prior that gives the weakest result. [22/prespecification]
The recommended practice is to state each prior's mean and standard deviation, show the posterior across a range of them and say which readers each represents. [22/prior-choice]
The success criterion, the schedule, the prior and the stopping rule all go into the protocol and the statistical analysis plan, prospectively. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept]
A Bayesian SAP that defers the prior or the success threshold to a later version has not prespecified the design. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
The success criterion's a and c are justified, with calibration evidence or the agreed alternative route, before the data are seen. [23/the-success-criterion-and-its-calibration]

## Pitfalls
A reanalysis that reports one prior, chosen after the data, does not meet the standard. [22/prior-choice]
A look added after an external publication is a deviation from the simulated design. [23/interim-schedule-and-decision-rules]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why can a Bayesian reanalysis not be prespecified? A: Priors, thresholds and scale are chosen in the light of the answer. [22/prespecification]
- Q: What does a deferred success threshold do to a SAP? A: It means the design was not prespecified. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]

prior-data-conflict.name: Prior-data conflict
prior-data-conflict.summary: The case where the data disagree with an informative prior, which a single normal prior handles badly and a robust mixture prior handles by shifting weight.
prior-data-conflict.body:
## What it is

A prior-data conflict is a disagreement between an informative prior and the observed data. The effect scale here is $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$, so benefit is positive. [sec-priors-conflict] Suppose the prior is informative and well justified, and the data disagree. A single normal prior compromises by precision however far apart they are [sec-priors-conflict]. The FDA draft recommends that sponsors examine prior-data conflict and not assume it away [sec-priors-conflict].

## Why it matters

The standard defense is a robust mixture prior, an informative component combined with a weakly informative one [sec-priors-conflict]. For example, $0.8\, N(0.29, 0.10^2) + 0.2\, N(0, 1)$ is an 80 percent chance that the effect looks like the phase 2 estimate and a 20 percent chance that nothing is known [sec-priors-conflict]. After the data the weights update, and the component that predicted better gains weight [sec-priors-conflict]. Schmidli and colleagues developed this construction for historical controls [sec-priors-conflict].

## In the book

When the observed effect is $\hat\theta = -0.20$ on the $-\log$ HR scale (a hazard ratio of 1.22, harm), the pure informative prior still reports a positive posterior mean, while the mixture moves weight to the vague component and follows the data [sec-priors-conflict]. The FDA applied the construction in the pediatric belimumab trial in lupus [sec-priors-belimumab].

## Pitfalls

The weight 0.2 on the vague component is itself a prior judgment. Type I error when the informative prior is wrong, and the extra patients needed, must be simulated [sec-priors-conflict]. The mixture's ESS depends on what the data do [sec-priors-ess].

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a mixture prior do when data contradict its informative part? A: Its posterior weight moves to the vague component and the posterior follows the data [sec-priors-conflict].
- Q: Does a single normal prior notice conflict? A: No, it compromises by precision however far apart they are [sec-priors-conflict].

prior-distribution.name: Prior distribution
prior-distribution.summary: The distribution a sponsor states for the treatment effect before the trial, which the traditional design hides inside its design alternative.
prior-distribution.body:
## What it is

A prior is something a sponsor can state, justify, quantify and defend [sec-priors]. The Bayesian analysis is distinguished mainly by writing one of its assumptions down [sec-priors]. The traditional design has a prior of its own that rarely gets the name. Its protocol states alpha, power and a design alternative, and the prior column reads "Not stated" [sec-priors-implicit].

For example, the traditional design fixes the number of events for a hazard ratio design alternative $\theta_a$: [sec-priors-implicit]

$$
d = \frac{4(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{\theta_a^2}
$$

This is equation eq-events. [sec-priors-implicit]

## Why it matters

For time-to-event data with 1:1 allocation the design needs $d = \frac{4(z_{\alpha} + z_{\beta})^2}{\theta_a^2}$ events (eq-events). A hazard ratio of 0.75 gives $\theta_a = 0.288$ and 508 events [sec-priors-implicit]. The design alternative is a planning assumption that treats one value as known, and nobody believes it [sec-priors-implicit]. Averaging power over a stated prior gives assurance [sec-priors-implicit].

## In the book

Four sources recur: phase 2 data from the same program, the published literature and earlier programs, expert elicitation, and mechanistic models [sec-priors-sources]. Phase 2 is the most natural and the most misleading, because programs advance when phase 2 looks good. In a simulation, about a third of drugs advance, and a prior centered on their phase 2 estimate would be centered on more than twice the true effect on the log scale [sec-priors-selection]. In the illustration, advanced programs had a phase 2 hazard ratio of 0.71 and a true one of 0.86 [8/key-points].

## Pitfalls

The traditional analysis is not a bad choice for this reason. When a single test is run in a trial large enough that any reasonable prior is overwhelmed, it is simple and sufficient [sec-priors-implicit]. The numbers of the simulation are illustrative and not from any program [sec-priors-selection].

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the traditional design assume anything about the effect? A: It assigns no prior probability to any effect, but the power calculation treats one value as if it were known [sec-priors-implicit].
- Q: Why is a phase 2 estimate a risky prior center? A: Programs advance when it looks good, so it is biased upward [sec-priors-selection].

prior-elicitation.name: Prior elicitation
prior-elicitation.summary: The provenance of a prior in a sponsor's program, from phase 2 data, literature, structured expert judgment and mechanistic models, with its documented weaknesses.
prior-elicitation.body:
## What it is

A prior has an identifiable provenance that the guidance asks the sponsor to document. Four sources recur: phase 2 data from the same program, the published literature and earlier programs, expert elicitation, and mechanistic or pharmacometric models [sec-priors-sources].

## Why it matters

Each source has a failure mode. Phase 2 programs advance when results look good [sec-priors-sources]. A literature search is a sampling mechanism, so the prior should come from a pre-specified search guarding against "preferential selection of favorable studies" [sec-priors-sources]. Experts are overconfident: intervals stated as 90 percent contain the truth far less often [sec-priors-sources].

## In the book

The Sheffield Elicitation Framework has experts give individual judgments, share evidence, and agree on one distribution [sec-priors-sources]. Three rules protect the clinician and the sponsor: elicit observables, not parameters; elicit tails as well as the middle; and document the dissenters [sec-priors-sources]. A simulator's mean $\hat\mu$ and variance $\hat v$ can be converted to a beta prior by matching moments, with $a + b = \hat\mu(1 - \hat\mu)/\hat v - 1$ [sec-priors-sources]. The remedies for selected phase 2 estimates are to discount them, to center on the distribution of true effects in the class, or to use them only through a skeptical prior [sec-priors-selection].

## Pitfalls

A single consensus can hide a bimodal opinion that a mixture prior would represent honestly [sec-priors-sources]. A prior is not a mood [sec-priors-sources].

## Check yourself

- Q: Why elicit a response rate and not a log odds ratio? A: Observables are what clinicians can judge [sec-priors-sources].
- Q: What are three ways to handle a selected phase 2 estimate? A: Discount it, center on the class distribution, or use it only through a skeptical prior [sec-priors-selection].

sec-priors-sources.t: Where priors come from in a sponsor's program

prior-odds-constant.name: Prior odds in the sample size constant
prior-odds-constant.summary: The constant C in the moderate deviation boundary, which makes the price of prior skepticism explicit in patients.
prior-odds-constant.body:
## What it is

The constant $C$ collects the prior odds and the prior density at the null. For a unit-information prior $C = 2\log(\pi_0/\pi_a)$, and with equal odds $C = 0$ [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n]. Moving from even odds to two-to-one and four-to-one against the alternative raises $C$ from 0 to 1.39 and 2.77 [9/the-prior-odds-in-the-constant].

The moderate-deviation boundary for the critical $t$ value is:

$$
t_{\text{crit}} = \sqrt{\log n + C}\,\bigl(1 + o(1)\bigr), \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0/\pi_a}{\pi(\theta_0)\sqrt{2\pi/I(\theta_0)}},
$$

This is equation eq-md-boundary. [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n]

## Why it matters

Skepticism is paid for in patients, at a rate the formula makes explicit. The sponsor who says the drug is a long shot is told how many more patients it takes, and the sponsor who claims equal odds is told what that claim is worth [9/the-prior-odds-in-the-constant]. The requirement rises and the induced one-sided error falls as the odds worsen [9/the-prior-odds-in-the-constant].

## In the book

The unit matters. The package function `events_md()` uses the information convention ($n = d/4$, $I = 1$), where $C = 0$ is the unit-information prior at equal odds. In the events convention, $C_{\text{info}} = C_{\text{events}} + \log 4$, so the same numerical $C = 0$ means $C_{\text{info}} = \log 4 = 1.39$ [9/the-power-function-and-the-sample-size-equation]. For a standard Cauchy prior on a unit-variance Gaussian mean, $C = \log(\pi/2) = 0.452$ [9/the-fixed-n-test-has-no-memory-of-n].

## Pitfalls

This is not a way out of a regulatory error-rate expectation. Where the sponsor calibrates to a one-sided 0.025 by simulation, that target stays [9/the-prior-odds-in-the-constant]. Keeping $C = 0$ while switching units changes the implied prior [9/the-power-function-and-the-sample-size-equation].

## Check yourself

- Q: What does C equal at 4:1 odds against the alternative? A: $2\log 4 = 2.77$ [9/the-prior-odds-in-the-constant].
- Q: Does the required sample size go up or down as odds against the alternative worsen? A: Up [9/the-prior-odds-in-the-constant].

prior-specification.name: Prior specification in the protocol
prior-specification.summary: What a protocol or analysis plan must state about the prior: its form, provenance, weight, comparison priors, sensitivity, robustness and success criterion.
prior-specification.body:
## What it is

A prior section of a protocol should contain seven items: the analysis prior with its implied distribution for the estimand, its provenance, its effective sample size, comparison priors, the sensitivity analysis with a tipping-point report, a robustness provision, and the success criterion with its calibration [sec-priors-protocol].

## Why it matters

The FDA draft says "It is always critical for Bayesian analyses to have a prespecified prior" [sec-priors-fda]. It distinguishes the analysis prior from design priors used only in simulation [sec-priors-fda]. It describes three routes for the success criterion: calibration, direct reading of the posterior, and benefit-risk criteria. Informative priors need greater justification [sec-priors-fda]. The draft leaves open how large an ESS is acceptable [sec-priors-fda].

## In the book

Four failures recur: a prior chosen after the data, a single published estimate treated as a prior, a flat prior mistaken for no prior, and a prior that matters presented as one that does not [8/what-can-go-wrong]. The 2010 device guidance is the final precedent: agree the prior with the Agency beforehand, and it allows type I error control at a less stringent level when prior information is used [sec-priors-device]. ICH E20 treats the prior in the same spirit in Section 5.3 [sec-priors-fda].

## Pitfalls

The draft is not binding, and a sponsor relying on it should say so in the briefing document [sec-priors-fda]. What stays the same is the standard of evidence: a calibrated confirmatory design uses the same one-sided 0.025 [sec-priors-sidebyside].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which prior enters the inference, the design prior or the analysis prior? A: The analysis prior [sec-priors-fda].
- Q: When may a sponsor read the posterior probability directly? A: Where the prior accurately reflects external data, by agreement with the Agency [sec-priors-fda].

prognostic-covariate-adjustment.name: Prognostic covariate adjustment
prognostic-covariate-adjustment.summary: A method that builds a prognostic score from external data and uses it as a baseline covariate in a randomized analysis, cutting variance without borrowing outcomes.
prognostic-covariate-adjustment.body:
## What it is

Prognostic covariate adjustment (PROCOVA) builds a prognostic model of the control-arm outcome from external data, such as historical trial data. Each participant's predicted outcome, the "digital twin" prediction under control, is then a baseline covariate in the randomized analysis. [sec-borrowing-procova]

## Why it matters

The treatment effect is still estimated by comparing randomized arms, so the analysis stays valid, and the covariate absorbs outcome variation, so variance falls. [sec-borrowing-procova] No assumption about the stability of the control arm over time is made. [sec-borrowing-procova] The method is often the first to propose to a regulator wary of external controls. [sec-borrowing-procova]

## In the book

The EMA's CHMP adopted a qualification opinion in September 2022 for phase 2 and 3 trials with continuous outcomes. The model is fixed before the trial, and with an independently developed, pre-specified score PROCOVA can preserve asymptotic type I error control despite poor prediction. [sec-borrowing-procova] The contrast is that PROCOVA uses external data to sharpen a randomized comparison, whereas borrowing uses them to replace part of it. [sec-borrowing-procova] It is a special case of covariate adjustment with a single prognostic score. [sec-borrowing-procova]

## Pitfalls

Precision gains depend on prognostic performance, and small trials need suitable finite-sample inference. [sec-borrowing-procova] It gives up less and so buys less than a full borrowing design. [sec-borrowing-procova]

## Check yourself

- Q: Does PROCOVA borrow control outcomes? A: No, it uses external data only to build a score. [sec-borrowing-procova]
- Q: What does the sponsor gain? A: Variance reduction, which can become a smaller sample size. [sec-borrowing-procova]

project-optimus.name: Project Optimus
project-optimus.summary: FDA initiative, launched in 2021, behind the August 2024 oncology dosage guidance that asks sponsors to compare dosages rather than default to the MTD.
project-optimus.body:
## What it is
The final guidance of August 2024 (docket FDA-2022-D-2827, Oncology Center of Excellence with CDER and CBER) was developed through Project Optimus, launched in 2021. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks] It recommends that oncology sponsors compare multiple dosages, using pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, safety and efficacy information, rather than default to the MTD. It is a guidance: it states current thinking and does not bind. [sec-dose]

## Why it matters
In paraphrase, it asks that doses taken to registrational trials be chosen on more than the MTD, including late and low-grade toxicities. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks] Dose-ranging should compare several dosages, where feasible with randomization, to characterize dose-response and dose-toxicity, not to prove superiority. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks] Model-based and Bayesian methods are expected to be useful, and the guidance neither requires a specific design nor excludes the 3+3. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks]

## Pitfalls
The guidance does not address first-in-human starting-dose selection. It does not specifically address radiopharmaceuticals, cellular and gene therapies, oncolytic viruses, microbiota, cancer vaccines or pediatric development. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks] ICH E4 had already set these principles in 1994. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks] Exposure-response models fall under ICH M15. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the guidance require a model-based design? A: No, and it does not exclude the 3+3. [17/what-the-fda-guidance-asks]
- Q: What would a reviewer ask about a dose that does not maximize efficacy? A: The probability of choosing a dose that is too low or too toxic under each scenario. [17/randomized-dose-comparison-and-what-a-regulator-will-ask]

17/randomized-dose-comparison-and-what-a.t: Randomized dose comparison, and what a regulator will ask

proportional-hazards.name: Proportional hazards
proportional-hazards.summary: The assumption that the hazard ratio is constant over time, which makes a single hazard ratio a clean summary.
proportional-hazards.body:
## What it is
Under proportional hazards the hazard ratio does not change over time, so a single hazard ratio is a clean summary. [sec-survival-traditional] The log-rank test is the score test of such a model. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Why it matters
Non-proportional hazards break the shortcut that information about a log hazard ratio is proportional to the number of events. [sec-survival] The Schoenfeld calculation assumes a single hazard ratio. [sec-survival-power-loss]

## In the book
The proportional scenario cuts a control hazard of 0.15 per year by 40 percent from the start. [sec-survival-nph] In a power simulation, a constant hazard ratio of 0.75 serves as the comparison for a delayed effect: the power is 0.68 under proportional hazards against 0.55 under the delayed effect, with the same number of events. [sec-survival-power-loss] Under proportional hazards the log-rank test beats the MaxCombo test, which beats the late-weighted test. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## Pitfalls
When the hazard ratio changes, the Cox estimate becomes a censoring-dependent weighted average. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Check yourself
- Q: What breaks when hazards are not proportional? A: A single hazard ratio misdescribes the effect and the events-as-information shortcut fails. [sec-survival-nph]

proportional-reporting-ratio.name: Proportional reporting ratio
proportional-reporting-ratio.summary: A simple disproportionality statistic that flags a drug and event pair with a ratio of at least 2, chi-square at least 4 and three or more reports.
proportional-reporting-ratio.body:
## What it is

The proportional reporting ratio, with the reporting odds ratio, is a cousin of the relative reporting ratio $n_{ij}/E_{ij}$, used with a confidence interval and a screening rule. [13/the-traditional-measure]

Evans and colleagues flagged a pair when the ratio is at least 2, the chi-square statistic at least 4 and there are at least three reports. A common variant asks for a lower confidence bound above 1 with at least three reports. [13/the-traditional-measure]

## Why it matters

The statistics are simple, transparent and still used, and the EMA guideline names them. [13/the-traditional-measure]

## In the book

The weakness is at the sparse end. For a rare pair the ratio is dominated by noise: one report against an expected count of 0.05 gives a ratio of twenty. [13/the-traditional-measure] A table with millions of cells will contain many such pairs by chance alone. [13/the-traditional-measure] The [[gamma-poisson-shrinker]] was built to handle this. [13/the-gamma-poisson-shrinker]

## Pitfalls

- A statistical signal is only a hypothesis to be assessed clinically, so a flag is not evidence of causation. [sec-safety]

## Check yourself

- Q: What three conditions did Evans and colleagues require for a flag? A: A ratio of at least 2, chi-square at least 4 and at least three reports. [13/the-traditional-measure]
- Q: Where does the ratio fail? A: For rare pairs, where it is dominated by noise. [13/the-traditional-measure]

randomization-test.name: Randomization test
randomization-test.summary: A test that shuffles treatment labels under the same procedure used to randomize, giving the exact distribution of the statistic over possible assignments.
randomization-test.body:
## What it is
Take the observed outcomes, shuffle the group labels many times, and ask how often a shuffled difference is as large as the observed one. The test is justified by the design. [sec-randomization-inference]

Under the sharp null, $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every patient, each outcome would be the same whatever the arm, and only the assignment varied. The permutation distribution is then the exact distribution of the statistic over possible assignments. [sec-randomization-inference]

## Why it matters
It requires no model for the outcome, and type I error is controlled by construction. Fisher put it forward in 1935, and the normal-theory z and t tests approximate it. [sec-randomization-inference]

It also needs no random sample: it asks only about the patients actually enrolled. Generalizing to future patients is a separate step resting on clinical judgment. [sec-randomization-inference]

## In the book
The shuffle must follow the design. A null trial of 40 patients with an upward drift of two standard deviations was analyzed with a one-sided permutation test at nominal level 0.025. With block assignment the unrestricted shuffle was conservative, and the shuffle within blocks was close to nominal. [sec-randomization-inference] In Table 5.1 the empirical type I error is 0.011 for the unrestricted shuffle with block assignment and 0.022 within blocks, against 0.025 under simple randomization. [sec-randomization-inference]

## Pitfalls
A test that ignores the blocks treats as possible many assignments the design excluded. It gives away power. [sec-randomization-inference] The analysis should mirror the randomization, and stratification factors belong in the model. [5/analyze-as-you-randomized]

## Check yourself
- Q: If assignment used permuted blocks of four, which shuffles are allowed? A: Only those with two drug and two control in each block. [sec-randomization-inference]
- Q: What population does the p-value refer to? A: The patients actually enrolled, not a sample from anything. [sec-randomization-inference]

sec-randomization-inference.t: Randomization inference: the test the design justifies

sec-randomization-protocol.t: What to put in the protocol and what the regulator will ask

randomization.name: Randomization
randomization.summary: Assigning each patient to a treatment by chance, so that the groups differ only by luck of the draw and by the treatment.
randomization.body:
## What it is
Randomization assigns a patient to a treatment by chance. The p-values, posteriors and interim looks of the book all assume that the two groups differ only because of the treatment and by luck of the draw. [sec-randomization]

ICH E9 says randomization introduces a deliberate element of chance into the assignment, and tends to make the distributions of prognostic factors, known and unknown, similar across groups. [sec-randomization]

## Why it matters
If a coin ignores everything about the patient, the selection term is zero on average and the difference in observed means estimates the average effect of the drug. [5/the-counterfactual-problem] R. A. Fisher made this argument central to experimental design. [5/the-counterfactual-problem]

The failures without it come in four forms: historical controls, predictable schemes such as alternation, unconcealed allocation and self-selection by patients. [sec-randomization-failures]

## In the book
Sacks, Chalmers and Smith reviewed six therapies studied with both randomized and historical controls. The historically controlled studies were much more likely to report the new therapy as better. [sec-randomization-failures] Schulz and colleagues examined 250 controlled trials and found that inadequately concealed allocation went with odds ratios exaggerated by about 41 percent. [sec-randomization-failures]

The book covers [[simple-randomization]], [[permuted-block-randomization]], [[stratified-randomization]] and [[minimization]]. [sec-randomization-methods] Stratified blocks and minimization cut the imbalance in a known trait. Nothing helps a hidden trait. [5/seeing-the-difference]

## Pitfalls
Randomization does not guarantee balance in any single trial. It guarantees that the imbalance is due to chance, with a known distribution that the confidence interval and p-value account for. [5/seeing-the-difference]

A random list the investigator can see is a way of choosing patients with extra steps, so randomization is only as good as its [[allocation-concealment]]. [sec-randomization-failures]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does randomization balance a hidden trait in one trial? A: No. For a trait unrelated to the factors balanced on, its imbalance is as large as under simple randomization under all four methods. [5/seeing-the-difference]
- Q: What did Schulz and colleagues find about weak concealment? A: Odds ratios exaggerated on average by about 41 percent, an association and not a randomized comparison. [sec-randomization-failures]

rar-critique.name: Critiques of response-adaptive randomization
rar-critique.summary: The published case that outcome-adaptive randomization offers little over equal allocation in two arms, with its costs in power and variability, and the replies.
rar-critique.body:
## What it is

By the 2010s experience with Bayesian adaptive randomization in oncology produced criticisms that practitioners now regard as a fair statement of its costs [16/the-case-against-in-two-arms]. Korn and Freidlin argued that in two-arm trials it offers little over equal allocation [16/the-case-against-in-two-arms]. Thall, Fox and Wathen collected objections including lower power, highly variable arm sizes, a chance of more patients on the inferior arm, and sensitivity to time trends [16/the-case-against-in-two-arms].

## Why it matters

The replies matter too. Berry analyzed adaptive assignment as a decision problem and found randomization satisfactory when the disease is at least moderately common [16/the-case-for-and-the-replies]. On the book's reading the case is weakest in a two-arm confirmatory trial with a large outside population and strongest with several arms and a small population, and this is not a point of agreement [16/the-case-for-and-the-replies].

## In the book

The book reproduces the critique with a 400-patient trial at 0.30 against 0.45 under equal, Thompson and capped Thompson rules [16/reproducing-the-critique]. Thompson adds responders but power falls, and the number on the better arm varies much more [16/reproducing-the-critique]. The claim that RAR often puts more patients on the inferior arm is weaker in this scenario, where the effect is large and the outcome immediate [16/reproducing-the-critique]. The balanced review of Robertson and coauthors advises a burn-in, restricted extreme allocation, modeled time trends and an explicit ethical justification [16/the-case-against-in-two-arms].

## Pitfalls

The summaries follow the papers' main arguments and are not exhaustive [16/the-case-against-in-two-arms]. The loss of power is not a trade a sponsor should accept in a confirmatory setting [16/reproducing-the-critique].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which costs does the critique name for two arms? A: Lower power, variable arm sizes, and sensitivity to time trends [16/the-case-against-in-two-arms].
- Q: Which setting does the book find strongest for RAR? A: Several arms and a small population [16/the-case-for-and-the-replies].

rbest.name: RBesT
rbest.summary: An R package for Bayesian evidence synthesis: meta-analytic-predictive priors, robustification and operating characteristics for designs with historical data.
rbest.body:
## What it is
RBesT is an R package of Bayesian evidence synthesis tools. [sec-software-tools] It builds meta-analytic-predictive priors, robustifies them, and gives operating characteristics for designs that use historical data. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
The book marks it as relevant to the borrowing chapter. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
Of the tools listed, only rpact, gsDesign, BOIN, brms and rstan were version-checked on the build machine, so RBesT was not checked. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does RBesT construct? A: Meta-analytic-predictive priors, with robustification. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Which chapter topic is it relevant to? A: Borrowing. [sec-software-tools]

real-options.name: Phases as a sequence of options
real-options.summary: Each phase is paid for only if all earlier ones succeed, so the cost per approved drug is driven by attrition.
real-options.body:
## What it is
Let $p_{12}$, $p_{23}$ and $p_{3A}$ be the probabilities of moving from Phase I to II, II to III and III to approval, and $c_1$, $c_2$, $c_3$ the phase costs. Phase $k$ is paid for only if all earlier phases succeed, so the long-run cost per approval is the ratio of expected cost per start to expected approvals per start. [sec-lifecycle-options]

$$
C_{\mathrm{approved}} = \frac{c_1 + p_{12}c_2 + p_{12}p_{23}c_3}{p_{12}\,p_{23}\,p_{3A}}.
$$

This is equation eq-lifecycle-cost. [sec-lifecycle-options]

## Why it matters
The formula explains why attrition dominates the economics. Wong, Siah and Lo estimated that about 13.8 percent of programs entering Phase I reach approval, and 3.4 percent in oncology. [sec-lifecycle-options] Cost per approval falls as each transition probability rises or each phase cost falls. [2/key-points]

## In the book
The stylized baseline has $p_{12} = 0.5$, $p_{23} = 0.3$, $p_{3A} = 0.6$ and phase costs of 25, 60 and 250 million dollars, illustrative values and not data. [sec-lifecycle-options] The rows change one input at a time, such as a Phase II success rise from 0.30 to 0.40 or a Phase III cost cut by a fifth. [sec-lifecycle-options] The baseline cost per approval is 1028 million dollars; the Phase II rise cuts it by 14.9 percent and the cheaper Phase III by 8.1 percent. [sec-lifecycle-options]

## Pitfalls
The ranking of two savings depends on the perturbations chosen, so it is not a general ranking of inputs. Advancing more compounds is not in itself better selection. [sec-lifecycle-options]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is Phase III cost multiplied by $p_{12}p_{23}$? A: It is paid only if Phases I and II both succeed. [sec-lifecycle-options]
- Q: Is the baseline in the table data? A: No, the values are illustrative. [sec-lifecycle-options]

sec-lifecycle-options.t: The phases as a sequence of options

reanalysis-critics.name: Critiques of Bayesian reanalysis
reanalysis-critics.summary: The literature for and against reanalyzing a trial after its result is known, including de Grooth and Cremer's argument that many priors do not build consensus.
reanalysis-critics.body:
## What it is
Reanalyzing a trial after the result is known has a literature of its own, with supporters and critics. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
An early instance is the debate over ECMO in newborns, in which Ware described the trials and Kass and Greenhouse commented from a Bayesian perspective. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
Wijeysundera and colleagues reanalyzed 88 randomized trials from four general medical journals and concluded that Bayesian and frequentist analyses complement each other. [sec-reanalyses-critics]

## Why it matters
The case for reanalysis is that it states probabilities at clinically meaningful thresholds and that the posterior under several priors makes dependence on the prior visible. [sec-reanalyses-critics]

## In the book
The criticism the book cites is de Grooth and Cremer's commentary that reanalyzing trials using many priors does not contribute to consensus. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
It recommends testing whether a result would persuade a reasonable adversary and assessing bias and generalizability separately, which connects to the skeptical prior standing in for the adversary. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
In the book's own words, a table of many priors invites each reader to pick the row that agrees with prior belief. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
Two further objections follow from the structure: priors are chosen after the result is known, and which trials are reanalyzed is itself an unprespecified choice. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
Brophy's EXCEL reanalysis shows both: adding three other trials found by a stated search lowered the probability of any excess mortality with stenting from 99 to 85 percent. [sec-reanalyses-critics]

## Pitfalls
The book's reading is that each side is right about something different: a reanalysis shows what the data can support, and is weak as evidence when priors and trials were chosen after the fact. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
The rule that follows is to write the reanalysis down before looking, with fixed priors and trials chosen by a stated rule, and to report every prior tried. [sec-reanalyses-critics]

## Check yourself
- Q: What makes the choice of trials in a reanalysis auditable? A: A stated search rule. [sec-reanalyses-critics]
- Q: What does the book treat the result of a reanalysis as? A: Input to the next trial, not a verdict on the last one. [sec-reanalyses-critics]

sec-reanalyses-limits.t: What a reanalysis can and cannot claim

rebyota-trial.name: REBYOTA
rebyota-trial.summary: A phase 3 trial of a fecal microbiota product that used a Bayesian hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study.
rebyota-trial.body:
## What it is

REBYOTA (RBX2660) prevents recurrence of *Clostridioides difficile* infection after antibiotics and was approved on 30 November 2022. The sponsor first planned two phase 3 trials of about 300 patients each. After FDA's July 2013 enforcement discretion on fecal microbiota transplantation made enrollment difficult, it proposed a single phase 3 trial (study 2017-01, PUNCH CD3) plus a Bayesian integration of phase 2b study 2014-01. [sec-borrowing-rebyota]

## Why it matters

FDA wrote that the studies are generally exchangeable but not identical, and accepted a hierarchical model with dynamic borrowing, in which the amount borrowed depends on how similar the treatment effect is in the two studies. The January 2026 FDA draft guidance cites it as its example of borrowing from a previous trial of the same drug. [sec-borrowing-rebyota]

## In the book

Two success thresholds on the posterior probability of superiority were set as analogues of one-sided type I error rates of 0.025 (the usual level for one trial) and 0.00125 (a very persuasive single trial that could stand in for two), and after adjustment they were 0.9750338 and 0.9993275. The result was a success rate of 0.71 on RBX2660 against 0.57 on placebo (95% credible interval 0.02 to 0.24 for the difference), with posterior probability of superiority 0.991, meeting the one-trial threshold and missing the two-trial threshold. [sec-borrowing-rebyota] FDA requested a refined analysis aligning the success definition, the assessment period (9 weeks against 8 weeks) and the analysis populations. Both analyses reached the same conclusion. [sec-borrowing-rebyota]

## Pitfalls

The briefing document gives no borrowing weight or effective sample size, so the amount borrowed cannot be read from it. [sec-borrowing-rebyota]

## Check yourself

- Q: Did 0.991 meet the one-trial or the two-trial threshold? A: The one-trial threshold only. [sec-borrowing-rebyota]
- Q: What was the lesson? A: Data alignment, not the model. [sec-borrowing-rebyota]

sec-borrowing-guide.t: Putting it together: a decision guide

sec-borrowing-rebyota.t: REBYOTA: dynamic borrowing from a phase 2b study

recovery-trial.name: RECOVERY
recovery-trial.summary: The dexamethasone comparison in RECOVERY, reanalyzed by respiratory-support subgroup with hierarchical shrinkage that leaves strongly supported effects nearly unchanged.
recovery-trial.body:
## What it is
The dexamethasone comparison randomized hospitalized patients with Covid-19 to dexamethasone 6 mg once daily for up to ten days or usual care. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
Twenty-eight-day mortality was 22.9 percent (482 of 2104) on dexamethasone and 25.7 percent (1110 of 4321) on usual care, an age-adjusted rate ratio of 0.83 with 95 percent interval 0.75 to 0.93. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
The subgroup results by respiratory support at randomization were as important as the overall result. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]

## Why it matters
Subgroup analyses are a familiar source of false findings, and the Bayesian instinct is to shrink them toward a common mean by an amount the data choose. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
Shrinkage is not a rule that every subgroup be pulled to the mean. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]

## In the book
With $\theta_j = -\log RR_j$ in stratum $j$ and $\theta_j \sim N(\mu, \tau_b^2)$, the marginal likelihood of $\tau_b$ is
$$
p(\tau_b \mid \hat\theta) \propto p(\tau_b)\, V_\mu(\tau_b)^{1/2} \prod_j (s_j^2 + \tau_b^2)^{-1/2} \exp\left\{-\frac{(\hat\theta_j - \hat\mu(\tau_b))^2}{2(s_j^2+\tau_b^2)}\right\},
$$
[sec-reanalyses-recovery]
The conditional posterior mean of each $\theta_j$ is $(1 - B_j)\hat\theta_j + B_j \hat\mu$ with $B_j = s_j^2/(s_j^2 + \tau_b^2)$. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
With only three strata the data say little about $\tau_b$, and the book uses a uniform prior over $(0, 1]$. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
The shrinkage factors are small, and the shrunk estimates barely move; the pattern of benefit rising with severity is large and biologically expected. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
The clinicians' conclusion was to treat patients on oxygen or ventilation and not those without oxygen. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]

## Pitfalls
The posterior of $\tau_b$ is sensitive to its prior, and moving the upper bound from 1 to 3 changes the median and mean, so the book reports the median. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
The probability of harm in the no-oxygen stratum comes from the book's model, not from RECOVERY. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
A trial so large that its prespecified analysis was decisive shows shrinkage changing the numbers but not the practice. [22/a-reanalysis-is-not-a-new-trial]

## Check yourself
- Q: Do the data decide how much to shrink? A: Yes, through the posterior of $\tau_b$, though with three strata it depends on its prior. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]
- Q: Which subgroup motivated the advice not to treat? A: Patients without oxygen. [sec-reanalyses-recovery]

22/a-reanalysis-is-not-a-new-trial.t: A reanalysis is not a new trial

Posterior means and probabilities of benefit are averaged over the posterior of tau (with mu integrated out, so the conditional variance includes the variance of mu). Estimates are on the benefit-positive scale.

recruitment-speed.name: Recruitment and the value of speed
recruitment-speed.summary: Trials are slow because of accrual, and a gamma-Poisson posterior turns an enrollment count into a rate, while a recruit is worth the evidence it adds.
recruitment-speed.body:
## What it is
Most trials are slow because of accrual, not analysis, and the recruitment rate is the quantity a sponsor can least control. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment] The book models enrollment of eligible families as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$ per week. With the reference prior $\mathrm{Gamma}(1/2, 0)$ and $n$ families seen in $t$ weeks, the posterior is $\mathrm{Gamma}(n + 1/2, t)$. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment]

## Why it matters
The same calculation, with a prior borrowed from earlier sites, turns a protocol's accrual assumption into a predictive distribution of the end date. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment] A rate is not the whole story, because a recruit is worth the evidence it contributes: count the information a patient contributes, not the patients. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment]

## In the book
In November 1995 Michael Milken asked on CNN's Larry King Live for families with several men affected by prostate cancer to volunteer. More than 3,000 people called. Within three weeks about 300 qualified families were in hand, where Johns Hopkins had recruited 90 families over ten years. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment] A LOD score is a log likelihood ratio, and log likelihood ratios add across independent families. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment]

## Pitfalls
The comparisons are conditional on assumed conventional rates, since the conventional pace is not known. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment] The value of the acceleration rests on labeled assumptions. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment] A maximized LOD of 3 does not automatically imply a Bayes factor of 1000. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment]

## Check yourself
- Q: What posterior follows $n$ families in $t$ weeks under the reference prior? A: $\mathrm{Gamma}(n + 1/2, t)$. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment]
- Q: Why can broader recruitment lower information per family? A: A broad appeal brings in phenocopies and families not linked to the locus, which dilute the expected LOD. [sec-lifecycle-recruitment]

sec-lifecycle-recruitment.t: Recruitment and the value of speed

regret.name: Regret
regret.summary: The loss against an oracle that knows the best arm; the Lai-Robbins bound says the best possible policy still puts a log-order number of patients on the inferior arm.
regret.body:
## What it is

Regret measures how much a policy loses against an oracle that knows the best arm [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound]. For two arms the regret after $T$ patients is the expected number of patients on the inferior arm times the gap in response probabilities [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound]. Equal randomization puts half the patients on the inferior arm, so its regret grows linearly in $T$ [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound].

## Why it matters

Lai and Robbins showed that for a uniformly good policy the expected number of patients on an inferior arm $i$ satisfies [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound]

$$
\liminf_{T\to\infty} \frac{\mathbb{E}[N_i(T)]}{\log T} \;\ge\; \frac{1}{\mathrm{KL}(p_i, p^\ast)},
$$

where KL is the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the two arms' response distributions [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound]. The regret of the best possible policy is logarithmic, not linear [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound].

## In the book

A simulation compares equal allocation, Thompson sampling and the UCB1 rule, which adds a bonus $\sqrt{2\log t / N_i(t)}$ to each arm's mean [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound]. Polson and Sokolov observe that this logarithm matches the scale of the Bayes sequential boundary: for small effects $\mathrm{KL} \approx \theta^2/2$ and $n\,\mathrm{KL} \asymp \tfrac12 \log n$ [16/the-same-logarithm]. The analogy is exact for the deviation scale and misleading for the objective [16/an-analogy-that-does-not-transfer-as-design-advice].

## Pitfalls

The bound is asymptotic, so finite-horizon counts can sit below the plotted slope [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound]. Regret is a loss in the trial, power is a property of the final decision, and optimizing the first damages the second [16/an-analogy-that-does-not-transfer-as-design-advice].

## Check yourself

- Q: How does regret of equal allocation grow? A: Linearly in $T$ [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound].
- Q: Can any good policy avoid putting patients on the inferior arm? A: No, the number grows like $\log T$ with constant $1/\mathrm{KL}$ [16/regret-and-the-lai-robbins-bound].

16/an-analogy-that-does-not-transfer-as-.t: An analogy that does not transfer as design advice

remap-cap-trial.name: REMAP-CAP
aliases: Randomized, Embedded, Multifactorial Adaptive Platform trial for Community-Acquired Pneumonia
remap-cap-trial.summary: A multifactorial, embedded Bayesian platform for pneumonia with response-adaptive randomization that declared IL-6 receptor antagonists beneficial in COVID-19.
remap-cap-trial.body:
## What it is

REMAP-CAP is a platform designed before the pandemic it became known for. After the 2009 H1N1 pandemic an EU-funded network built the infrastructure, which began enrolling in April 2016 (NCT02735707) with a dormant pandemic stratum later activated for COVID-19. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design]

## Why it matters

Its design has four features. It is *multifactorial*: domains are sets of alternative interventions for one aspect of care, and a patient is randomized in every domain for which he or she is eligible. It is *embedded* in routine care. Its pandemic primary endpoint was organ-support-free days to day 21, analyzed with a Bayesian proportional-odds model. And allocation within a domain is updated to favor arms with higher posterior probability of being best. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design]

## In the book

In the IL-6 domain the triggers were superiority at posterior probability of being best above 99%, efficacy at odds ratio above 1 with probability above 99%, futility if the probability of an odds ratio above 1.2 fell below 5%, and equivalence of non-control arms if the probability of an odds ratio between 0.83 and 1.2 exceeded 90%. The platform declared that tocilizumab and sarilumab improved outcomes, including survival, in critically ill COVID-19 patients. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design] A domain can be declared complete without waiting for the others. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design] The domains may be pooled in a hierarchical sense across strata, which is borrowing under the same conditions. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design]

## Pitfalls

For confirmatory platforms the October 2026 EMA draft does not support response-adaptive randomization, a point to settle with the regulator. [20/shared-control-arithmetic] [20/traditional-against-bayesian-platforms-what-differs]

## Check yourself

- Q: What is a domain? A: A set of alternative interventions for one aspect of care. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design]
- Q: Can a patient join several domains? A: Yes, in every domain for which eligible. [20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-randomization-and-an-embedded-design]

20/remap-cap-domains-response-adaptive-r.t: REMAP-CAP: domains, response-adaptive randomization, and an embedded design

20/traditional-against-bayesian-platform.t: Traditional against Bayesian platforms: what differs

reproducibility.name: Reproducibility
reproducibility.summary: The practice that every simulation shows its seed beside the result, that Monte Carlo error is reported, and that stored output is regenerated deliberately.
reproducibility.body:
## What it is
Every simulation either calls `set.seed()` in the chunk or passes `seed =` to the package function, so the seed is visible next to the result. [sec-software-repro] Functions draw from R's global generator after the seed is set. [sec-software-repro]

## Why it matters
A chunk is repeatable, but its results depend on the order of the random calls inside it. [sec-software-repro] Monte Carlo results are reported with their Monte Carlo error. [sec-software-repro] A different seed gives values that differ in the third decimal place. [sec-software-example]

## In the book
- Quarto's freeze mechanism (`freeze: auto` in `_quarto.yml`) stores each chapter's output, so a rebuild reuses it unless the chapter source changed. [sec-software-repro]
- Slow chunks are knitr-cached, keyed to a checksum of the installed package. [sec-software-repro]
- To regenerate after a package change, reinstall it, delete the chapter's directory under `_freeze/` and its knitr cache, and render again. [sec-software-repro]
- The authors recommend recording `sessionInfo()` for exact reproduction. [sec-software-repro]
- The worked example uses 20,000 simulated trials per run with seeds 1, 3 and 2. [sec-software-example]

## Pitfalls
The calibration run's rejection proportion is the calibration target, not an error assessment, so a fresh null run with another seed is needed. [sec-software-example]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why check the type I error on a fresh run with another seed? A: The calibration run's rejection rate is the target, not an assessment. [sec-software-example]
- Q: What does FDA's Bayesian draft say to report about computing? A: Software versions, code and MCMC seed numbers. [3/use-of-bayesian-methodology-in-clinical-trials-of-drug-and-biological-products-draft-january-2026]

3/use-of-bayesian-methodology-in-clinica.t: Use of Bayesian Methodology in Clinical Trials of Drug and Biological Products (draft, January 2026)

functions.name: oc_simulate
functions.title: Simulate a two-arm binary trial with interim looks
functions.usage:
oc_simulate(
  p0,
  p1,
  looks,
  a = 0,
  prior = c(1, 1),
  nsim = 20000,
  seed = NULL,
  fut = NULL,
  method = c("table", "normal")
)
functions.description: Equal allocation, looks at cumulative per-arm sample sizes looks. Success is declared when Pr(p1 - p0 > a | data) > c at any look; optionally the trial stops for futility at the first look where that probability falls below fut. Efficacy stopping is applied later by oc_summarize(), so one simulation serves every candidate c (common random numbers) and oc_calibrate() can find c from a null simulation.

functions.name: oc_calibrate
functions.title: Calibrate the success threshold c to a one-sided type I error
functions.description: Returns a threshold c at which the empirical type I error in the supplied null simulation (the fraction of simulated trials whose posterior probability exceeds c at any attended look) is at most alpha: the 1 - alpha quantile ("higher" rule) of oc_max_pp(). Because the rule is pp > c, the empirical error is at most alpha, with equality up to Monte Carlo ties.

requires-recommends-permits.name: Requires, recommends, permits
requires-recommends-permits.summary: A sorting of regulatory sources by force: statutes and regulations bind, guidances recommend, and permissions depend on FDA agreeing.
requires-recommends-permits.body:
## What it is
The force of a document varies, so the book sorts sources into categories. [sec-regulatory-force] A statute binds, a regulation binds, and a guidance "contains nonbinding recommendations". [sec-regulatory]

## Why it matters
A sponsor should never describe a draft as "FDA requirements" in a protocol or meeting package. [sec-regulatory-force] A permission is not an entitlement. [sec-regulatory-force] The permissions that matter most to Bayesian adaptive designs are all of the form "if FDA agrees". [sec-regulatory-force]

## In the book
- Requires: FD&C Act 505(d), the FDAMA 1997 single-trial provision, FDORA 2022, and 21 CFR 314.126. [sec-regulatory-force]
- Recommends: final guidances such as Adaptive Designs 2019, draft guidances such as Bayesian Methodology (January 2026), and ICH Step 2 and Step 4 documents. [sec-regulatory-force]
- Permits: one trial plus confirmatory evidence, non-calibrated Bayesian success criteria with FDA agreement, and nonconcurrent controls in rare circumstances. [sec-regulatory-force]
- Process: formal meetings and the CID and MIDD programs define how to ask, not the evidentiary standard. [sec-regulatory-force]

## Pitfalls
A guidance is nonbinding, but a departure without prior discussion is a risk to the program. [sec-regulatory-fda]

## Check yourself
- Q: "FDA requires a simulation report for any Bayesian design." Accurate? A: No, the Bayesian draft recommends it and is only a draft. [3/key-points]
- Q: Is a permission an entitlement? A: No, it is available only if the agency concurs. [sec-regulatory-force]

response-adaptive-randomization.name: Response-adaptive randomization
response-adaptive-randomization.summary: Allocation that shifts toward the arm that is looking better as outcomes accrue, trading some information for benefit to patients inside the trial.
response-adaptive-randomization.body:
## What it is

Response-adaptive randomization (RAR) lets the odds shift toward the treatment that is looking better [sec-rar]. Thompson's motive in 1933 was ethical: to spare patients from being "sacrificed" to the inferior treatment [sec-rar]. In operations research it is a multi-armed bandit problem [sec-rar].

## Why it matters

It asks a randomized trial to do two jobs. The comparison is cleanest when allocation is fixed and balanced, while a bandit maximizes benefit inside the study by abandoning the losing arm [sec-rar].

## In the book

In a two-arm trial of 400 patients (0.30 against 0.45), Thompson sampling put 87 percent on the better arm but cut power from 88 percent to 61 percent [16/reproducing-the-critique]. In a four-arm trial with a fixed control share of one quarter, a burn-in and a cap, the adaptive design put about half of 600 patients on the best arm and had higher power for the best arm against control than equal allocation [16/the-multi-arm-case]. The book's conditions for a case for RAR: several experimental arms, a fast endpoint, a trial large enough to converge but small in population, a fixed control share with concurrent controls, and an exploratory or seamless role [16/where-rar-fits].

## Pitfalls

For a confirmatory two-arm trial, use fixed allocation [sec-rar-practice]. The EMA draft of October 2026 concludes that RAR is not supported in confirmatory platform trials [sec-rar-reg]. A fixed control share alone does not establish regulatory acceptability [sec-rar-reg]. Drift in calendar time is the failure that matters most ([[time-trend-bias]]) [sec-rar].

## Check yourself

- Q: In which setting does the book find the best case for RAR? A: Several experimental arms with a shared control held at a fixed share [16/the-multi-arm-case].
- Q: What does a two-arm confirmatory trial call for? A: Fixed allocation [sec-rar-practice].

sec-rar-drift.t: Time trends: the failure that matters most

restricted-mean-survival-time.name: Restricted mean survival time
restricted-mean-survival-time.summary: The area under the survival curve up to a horizon, whose difference is the average event-free time gained and needs no proportional hazards.
restricted-mean-survival-time.body:
## What it is
$$
\mathrm{RMST}(\tau) = \int_0^\tau S(t)\,dt,
$$
the area under the survival curve up to horizon $\tau$ (eq-sv-rmst). Its posterior is computed from draws of the survival curve. [sec-survival-nph]

## Why it matters
The RMST difference is the average event-free time gained within $\tau$, in months or years, the unit patients and payers think in, and it does not require proportional hazards. [sec-survival-nph]

## In the book
The control arm, with hazard 0.15 per year, has RMST 3.52 years over five years. [sec-survival-nph] In 54 oncology trials with reconstructed patient data, the hazard ratio gave on average a larger effect than the RMST ratio (average ratio 1.11, with substantial variation), and the authors recommend routine RMST reporting. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## Pitfalls
It requires a horizon. The choice of $\tau$ is part of the estimand and must be fixed in the protocol. [sec-survival-nph] A supportive RMST analysis chosen after a blinded look at the pooled curve would draw a regulatory objection. [18/exercises]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does the RMST difference measure? A: Average event-free time gained within $\tau$. [sec-survival-nph]

sec-survival-nph-tests.t: Tests built for a delayed effect

functions.name: surv_rmst
functions.title: Restricted mean survival time for a piecewise-exponential arm
functions.description: Closed form: on each interval, S decays exponentially from its value at the left endpoint, so the integral is S(b_k)(1 - exp(-lambda_k w_k))/lambda_k. With a cure fraction pi, S(t) = pi + (1 - pi) S0(t).

functions.name: surv_nph_example
functions.title: Non-proportional hazards examples: delayed effect and cure model
functions.description: Control arm exponential with hazard h0. Delayed effect: treated hazard equals h0 before delay and hr * h0 afterwards. Cure model: a fraction cure of treated patients never fail, the rest follow the control hazard. Returns RMST by arm and its difference at the horizon, and the average hazard ratio log S1(tau)/log S0(tau) (the ratio of cumulative hazards, constant only under proportional hazards).

retatrutide-triumph-3.name: TRIUMPH-3
retatrutide-triumph-3.summary: A retatrutide trial in obesity with cardiovascular disease whose imprecise cardiovascular interval the book turns into posteriors under flat, discounted SELECT and skeptical priors.
retatrutide-triumph-3.body:
## What it is
TRIUMPH-3 is an 80-week randomized phase 3 trial in obesity with established cardiovascular disease, with 1,946 participants in the registry and a registered primary outcome of percent change in body weight. [sec-cases-current]
Lilly announced topline results on 23 July 2026. [sec-cases-current]

## Why it matters
A class prior turns an imprecise cardiovascular interval into a posterior. [sec-cases-current]

## In the book
The announcement reports 44 five-component events on pooled retatrutide against 52 on placebo, hazard ratio 0.82 with interval 0.55 to 1.22. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]
The three-component hazard ratio in the same announcement was 1.12 (0.64 to 1.96). [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]
The class prior is SELECT, hazard ratio 0.80 (0.72 to 0.90), discounted by inflating its variance: doubling for half weight, quadrupling for quarter weight. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]
For contrast the book uses a skeptical normal prior with standard deviation 0.15 and a flat prior. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]
The disagreement among the rows is the scientific question: whether a class effect measured with a three-component outcome in semaglutide carries over to a triple agonist and a five-component outcome. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]

## Pitfalls
With 96 events in all, none of the rows is a confirmatory result. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]
The three-component hazard ratio above 1 is a reason to give the class prior a low weight, not to hide it. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]

## Check yourself
- Q: How is half weight for the SELECT prior implemented? A: By doubling its variance. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]
- Q: Does the frequentist reading that benefit is not established conflict with the Bayesian one? A: No, it is a correct statement about the interval, and the Bayesian reading adds how much depends on the prior. [21/retatrutide-in-triumph-3]

functions.name: normal_update
functions.title: Conjugate normal update
functions.description: Combines a normal prior N(\mu_0, \sigma_0^2) with an estimate \hat\theta of standard error se (normal likelihood).

rewind-trial.name: REWIND
rewind-trial.summary: A dulaglutide cardiovascular outcomes trial with a marginal effect, used in the book as the case where the scheduled design beats continuous Bayesian monitoring.
rewind-trial.body:
## What it is
REWIND randomized 9,901 patients with type 2 diabetes to weekly dulaglutide or placebo, enrolling from August 2011 to August 2013, with a median follow-up of 5.4 years. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-1]
The primary composite occurred in 594 of 4,949 on dulaglutide and 663 of 4,952 on placebo: 1,257 events, hazard ratio 0.88, 95 percent interval 0.79 to 0.99, $p = 0.026$. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-1]
It was designed to show cardiovascular superiority with 90 percent power, not merely to exclude the 2008 margin. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-1]

## Why it matters
Information is almost identical to SELECT, but the effect is half the size on the log scale, 0.128 against 0.223, and the final standardized score is 2.27 rather than 3.98. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-1]
It is the unfavorable case, where the advantage of continuous monitoring should shrink. [sec-cases]

## In the book
The Bayesian rule declares efficacy in only part of the simulated trials, so its all-trial median is the maximum of 1,257 events. [21/the-bayesian-reconstruction]
The four-look design again has the highest power, and the e-value rule fails outright. [21/the-bayesian-reconstruction]
The book concludes that the scheduled design was the right choice if the expected effect was a hazard ratio near 0.88. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-1]
The final data are read with a normal approximation: log 0.88 with a standard error of about 0.058, under a flat prior and skeptical priors with standard deviations 0.2, 0.1 and 0.05. [sec-cases-rewind-prior]
The direction of the effect is robust to skepticism, and its size is not. [sec-cases-rewind-prior]

## Pitfalls
The reconstruction conditions on the observed hazard ratio, which barely cleared the bar. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-1]
Precision at the upper bound of the interval is a property of the full trial and cannot be got from half of it. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-1]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why does continuous monitoring help less here than in SELECT? A: The effect is half as large on the log scale, so the score only reaches 2.27. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-1]
- Q: What does the book still use Bayesian machinery for in REWIND? A: Reporting the final posterior for the hazard ratio under skeptical priors. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-1]

21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have.t: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept

sec-cases-rewind.t: REWIND: where the scheduled design wins

functions.name: select_simulate
functions.title: Monte Carlo of the calibrated SELECT rules
functions.usage:
select_simulate(
  d_tot = 1270,
  HR = 0.8,
  nsim = 40000,
  tau = 0.25,
  alpha = 0.025,
  seed = NULL,
  batch = 4000,
  design_events = min(1225L, d_tot),
  interim_fraction = 2/3
)
functions.description: Simulates Gaussian score paths on a grid of event counts (steps of two, plus the interim, planned and total event counts), calibrates the posterior bar p* to type I error alpha, and compares four rules: a hypothetical O'Brien-Fleming design with four equally spaced looks, an e-value mixture, the Bayes rule, and SELECT's actual design. The effect is benefit-positive, theta = -log(HR). Paths are processed in batches to bound memory.

functions.name: select_look_table
functions.title: Look table at the observed effect
functions.description: Benefit-positive convention: theta = -log(HR), score S = theta * I, and the signed statistic z = S / sqrt(I), which is positive for benefit (HR below one) and negative for harm.

functions.title: Normal-approximation posterior with thresholds

robust-mixture-prior.name: Robust mixture prior
robust-mixture-prior.summary: A mixture of an informative prior and a vague prior whose weights are updated by the data, so that borrowing fades when the current data conflict.
robust-mixture-prior.body:
## What it is

Schmidli and colleagues (2014) protect a MAP prior with a vague component:

$$
\pi_{\text{rob}}(\theta) = w\,\pi_{\text{MAP}}(\theta) + (1-w)\,\pi_{\text{vague}}(\theta).
$$

This is eq-robust. [sec-borrowing-map] The conjugate update of a mixture is a mixture of conjugate updates, with weights multiplied by the marginal likelihood of the current data under each component. [sec-borrowing-map]

## Why it matters

If the current control data look like the MAP prior, the weight stays on the informative component. If not, the weight moves to the vague component and the posterior reverts to the current data. [sec-borrowing-map] The posterior mixture weight says how much of the answer comes from outside the trial, so it is the quantity to report. [sec-borrowing-map]

## In the book

The weight $1-w$ on the vague component is a design choice, and 0.1 to 0.5 is the book's working range, not a figure from the literature. [sec-borrowing-map] In the drift example the prior is 0.8 Beta$(31,71)$ plus 0.2 Beta$(1,1)$ with a historical arm of 100 patients and 30 responders. [sec-borrowing-ess] Belimumab in pediatric lupus is the clearest regulatory example. [sec-borrowing-belimumab]

## Pitfalls

A robust prior learns agreement slowly. A control arm of 30 has a standard error of about 0.08, so a true rate 0.10 above the historical rate is within two standard errors and the weight barely moves. [sec-borrowing-map] At a ten point drift the robust prior still has a type I error above the power prior's. [sec-borrowing-drift]

## Check yourself

- Q: Where does the weight go if the current data conflict? A: To the vague component. [sec-borrowing-map]
- Q: Does it protect against a moderate drift in a control arm of 30? A: Very little. [sec-borrowing-ess]

sec-borrowing-belimumab.t: Belimumab in pediatric lupus: a robust mixture and a tipping point

sec-borrowing-drift.t: What borrowing costs: type I error and power under drift

sec-borrowing-ess.t: How much does the borrowed information weigh? Effective sample size and conflict

functions.title: Control priors compared in the borrowing chapter
functions.description: Control priors compared in the borrowing chapter

functions.name: borrow_ess_robust
functions.title: Dynamic effective sample size of a robust prior (mixture-weighted proxy)
functions.description: Convention: the effective sample size (ESS) of a Beta(a, b) component is a + b, so the informative component Beta(1 + yh, 1 + nh - yh) has ESS nh + 2 and the vague Beta(1, 1) component has ESS 2. The function returns the posterior-weight-averaged component ESS, w_post * (nh + 2) + (1 - w_post) * 2, where w_post is the posterior weight on the informative component after observing yc of nc current controls.

robust-reporting-guideline.name: ROBUST reporting guideline
robust-reporting-guideline.summary: A seven-item checklist for reporting a Bayesian analysis of a clinical study, written for authors and not a regulatory requirement.
robust-reporting-guideline.body:
## What it is
ROBUST is a seven-item checklist for reporting a Bayesian analysis of a clinical study. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
It is one of only a few guidelines written for Bayesian analyses, and they are author guidelines. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Why it matters
Generic checklists such as SPIRIT and CONSORT do not name the Bayesian components of a trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
A Bayesian trial adds the prior and its source, the success criterion with its threshold and calibration, the interim schedule and the simulation report, the software and seeds, and the sensitivity analyses to the prior. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## In the book
ROBUST sits with BARG and a consensus checklist for clinicians who read a trial analyzed by Bayesian methods. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The book's own sponsor and reviewer checklists carry the same content in operational form, from the estimand to the meeting plan. [23/checklists]

## Pitfalls
None of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Check yourself
- Q: How many items does ROBUST have? A: Seven. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
- Q: Who is ROBUST written for? A: Authors reporting a Bayesian analysis. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spir.t: Structured protocols: ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025

rofecoxib-case.name: Rofecoxib safety signal
rofecoxib-case.summary: Rofecoxib (Vioxx) was withdrawn in 2004 after trials showed more heart attacks, a case read here as a cumulative analysis of what could have been said earlier.
rofecoxib-case.body:
## What it is

Rofecoxib, sold as Vioxx, was a selective COX-2 inhibitor approved in 1999 for arthritis and pain. [sec-safety-rofecoxib] The VIGOR trial randomized 8076 patients and showed fewer upper gastrointestinal events on rofecoxib, but myocardial infarction in 0.4 percent against 0.1 percent on naproxen. [sec-safety-rofecoxib] The difference was attributed to a protective effect of naproxen. [sec-safety-rofecoxib]

## Why it matters

Merck withdrew the drug on 30 September 2004, after APPROVe showed confirmed thrombotic events in 46 of 1287 rofecoxib patients against 26 of 1299 on placebo, a rate ratio of 1.92 (95% CI 1.19 to 3.11). [sec-safety-rofecoxib]

## In the book

The cumulative meta-analysis by Jüni and colleagues had a pooled relative risk of 2.30 (95% CI 1.22 to 4.33) by the end of 2000. [13/what-the-traditional-analysis-said] See [[cumulative-meta-analysis]].

From that pool, $\log \widehat{RR} = 0.833$ with standard error $0.323$. A flat prior gives the published estimate, and skeptical priors with $s_0 = 0.3$ and $s_0 = 0.2$ were also used. [13/what-a-bayesian-reading-adds] The conclusion that harm was probable did not depend on the reviewer's prior. [13/what-a-bayesian-reading-adds]

The decision rule: rofecoxib is preferred for a patient when

$$
g\, d_G > r_0 (\mathbb{E}[RR] - 1)\, d_M.
$$

This is eq-safety-benefitrisk. [13/from-inference-to-decision] It is an illustration with stated inputs, not a regulatory benefit-risk analysis. [13/from-inference-to-decision]

The naproxen explanation and the harm explanation are competing models. The naproxen model predicts an elevated risk only against naproxen, and the harm model predicts it against every comparator. [13/the-naproxen-hypothesis-as-a-model-comparison]

## Pitfalls

- Explaining away an unwelcome signal with a plausible rival is how safety signals are most often lost. Writing the rival down as a model with its own predictions is the remedy. [13/the-naproxen-hypothesis-as-a-model-comparison]
- The book did not compute the Bayes factor between the two models. [13/the-naproxen-hypothesis-as-a-model-comparison]

## Check yourself

- Q: What did the 2004 APPROVe trial add to VIGOR? A: A placebo comparison, which showed a rate ratio of 1.92 for thrombotic events. [sec-safety-rofecoxib]
- Q: Why can a skeptic not dismiss the cumulative evidence? A: Under skeptical priors the direction of harm stays probable, even if the size is disputed. [13/what-a-bayesian-reading-adds]

13/the-naproxen-hypothesis-as-a-model-co.t: The naproxen hypothesis as a model comparison
