rpact.name: rpact
rpact.summary: An R package for confirmatory adaptive design: group sequential designs, sample size reassessment and combination tests, with simulation.
rpact.body:
## What it is
rpact is an R package for confirmatory adaptive design. [sec-software-tools] It covers group sequential designs, sample size reassessment and combination tests, with simulation. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
It is one of the established trial-design tools the book lists as in wide use. [sec-software-tools] The descriptions give only the purpose of each tool. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
On the machine where the book was built, rpact 4.4.0 was installed. [sec-software-tools] The R packages in the list are on CRAN, except bcrm. [sec-software-tools]

## Pitfalls
Consult the tool's documentation for current features and versions. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which version was installed when the book was built? A: rpact 4.4.0. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Is it a Bayesian-only tool? A: The book describes it as confirmatory adaptive design software with simulation. [sec-software-tools]

safety-signal.name: Safety signal
safety-signal.summary: Evidence that a harm may be present, which arrives by the thousand from data collected for another purpose and is useless if it waits for significance.
safety-signal.body:
## What it is

Efficacy questions arrive one at a time and are asked of a trial built to answer them. Safety questions arrive by the thousand, are asked of data collected for another purpose, and are answered too late if they wait for statistical significance. [sec-safety]

## Why it matters

A trial is sized for its efficacy endpoint, so the rare adverse event that matters most is usually the one the trial is least able to detect. [sec-safety] After approval the signal arrives as a trickle of spontaneous reports. [sec-safety] Safety is therefore where continuous, cumulative reasoning is most natural. [sec-safety]

## In the book

The chapter covers the rofecoxib cumulative signal, continuous monitoring with a posterior probability and an e-value, empirical Bayes screening of spontaneous reports, and toxicity monitoring inside a trial. [sec-safety]

Neither the DMC guidance nor the IND safety guidance prescribes a statistical rule. 21 CFR 312.32 is a requirement about what to report and when, while the guidances recommend how to monitor. [sec-safety-reg]

## Pitfalls

- A statistical signal is only a hypothesis to be assessed clinically. [sec-safety]
- A shrinkage screen is a hypothesis generator and is not a basis for a safety report by itself. [sec-safety-reg]

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is the most important adverse event often the hardest to see in a trial? A: The trial is sized for the efficacy endpoint, so it is least able to detect the rare event. [sec-safety]
- Q: Does any guidance prescribe a statistical stopping rule for safety? A: No, neither the DMC guidance nor the IND safety guidance does. [sec-safety-reg]

functions.name: safety_bf_monitor
functions.title: Bayes factor and posterior-probability monitoring for a safety signal
functions.usage:

functions.title: Bayesian toxicity stopping boundary

tox_bayes_boundary(
  looks = seq(5, 40, 5),
  qbar = 0.2,
  kappa = 0.75,
  a0 = 0.5,

)

functions.name: tox_oc
functions.title: Exact operating characteristics of a toxicity stopping boundary
functions.description: Dynamic programming over the toxicity count: probability of ever stopping and expected number of patients treated (stopping at a look counts that many patients).

functions.name: tox_pocock_boundary
functions.title: Pocock-type repeated binomial boundary for toxicity monitoring
functions.description: One-sided repeated exact binomial tests of H_0: q \le \bar q at the same looks, with a common nominal level a at every look: stop at look n if P(X_n \ge t \mid \bar q) \le a. The nominal a is the largest value on a fine grid whose overall stopping probability at qbar does not exceed alpha.

sample-size-re-estimation.name: Sample size re-estimation
sample-size-re-estimation.summary: Changing the planned sample size at an interim, either from blinded pooled variance or, riskier, from the unblinded interim effect, as in the promising zone design.
sample-size-re-estimation.body:
## What it is

When the planning value of the effect or variance is wrong, the trial is under- or over-powered, and there are two traditional responses [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone]. Blinded re-estimation updates the nuisance parameter from the pooled variance, needs no unblinding and has negligible effect on type I error [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone]. Unblinded re-estimation uses the interim effect [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone].

## Why it matters

Increasing $n$ from the interim effect makes the sample size depend on the data, and the type I error can exceed the nominal level, by more than a factor of two in extreme cases [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone]. Remedies are combination tests and the conditional error principle, both pre-specified [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone].

## In the book

The promising zone restricts the increase to intermediate conditional power. Below a futility limit the trial continues unchanged or stops, above a favorable limit it continues unchanged, and in between the sample size rises by a pre-specified rule up to a cap, for example twice the original size [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone]. A protocol that says the DMC may recommend an increase of up to 50 percent without a formula and a cap has not specified an adaptation [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone].

Regulators treat blinded re-estimation as low risk, while unblinded re-estimation needs type I error control by design and a prespecified algorithm. [sec-reg13]

## Pitfalls

A group sequential design with a futility boundary, planned for the larger sample from the start, can match or beat a promising zone design in power and average sample size [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone]. The adaptive design buys insurance against a misjudged effect, not free efficiency [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone]. Whether the unadjusted final test stays valid must be shown by theory or simulation [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which form of re-estimation is least risky? A: Blinded re-estimation from the pooled variance [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone].
- Q: Where does the promising zone increase the sample size? A: Where conditional power is intermediate, up to a pre-specified cap [15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-promising-zone].

15/sample-size-re-estimation-and-the-pro.t: Sample size re-estimation and the promising zone

sample-size.name: Sample size
sample-size.summary: The number of patients or events a trial needs, computed from two error rates and a guess about the treatment effect, and scaling as the inverse square of that effect.
sample-size.body:
## What it is

Setting power equal to $1-\beta$ and solving gives

$$
n = \frac{(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2}{I\,\theta^2}.
$$

This is eq-ss-standard. The numerator is the whole error specification, and the denominator is the science [9/two-errors-and-one-guess]. Halving the effect quadruples the sample size [9/two-errors-and-one-guess].

## Why it matters

The effect is the one input the trial has not informed, and the answer is most sensitive to it [9/two-errors-and-one-guess]. ICH E9 section 3.5 requires the protocol to give the calculation method and its assumptions [sec-power]. The sample size sentence in the protocol is a budget line [sec-power-cost].

## In the book

Endpoints differ only in what $I\theta^2$ means [9/the-same-formula-for-three-kinds-of-endpoint]. For events with 1:1 allocation, Schoenfeld gives

$$
d = \frac{4\,(z_\alpha+z_\beta)^2}{\log(\mathrm{HR})^2}.
$$

This is eq-ss-events. Moving from HR 0.50 to 0.80 multiplies the required events by 9.6, from 87 to 844, and HR 0.90 needs nearly 3,800 events at 90% power. The binary example, 30% against 45%, needs 214 per arm [9/the-same-formula-for-three-kinds-of-endpoint]. Moore and colleagues put the median cost of a pivotal trial at US\$19.0 million [sec-power-cost].

## Pitfalls

The binary formula is an approximation, and pooled-variance versions differ [9/the-same-formula-for-three-kinds-of-endpoint]. A time-to-event trial is complete when it has its events, and patient numbers need a second calculation [9/the-same-formula-for-three-kinds-of-endpoint].

## Check yourself

- Q: What happens to the required events if the hazard ratio moves from 0.50 to 0.80? A: They rise 9.6-fold, from 87 to 844 [9/the-same-formula-for-three-kinds-of-endpoint].
- Q: What are the two inputs besides the effect? A: The two error rates [9/two-errors-and-one-guess].

samplesizeproportions.name: SampleSizeProportions
samplesizeproportions.summary: R packages by Joseph and Belisle that compute Bayesian sample size criteria (ALC, ACC, WOC) for proportions and for means.
samplesizeproportions.body:
## What it is
SampleSizeProportions and SampleSizeMeans are R packages by Joseph and Bélisle. [sec-software-tools] They give Bayesian sample size criteria (ALC, ACC, WOC) for proportions and means. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
They are the book's reference for Bayesian sample size criteria. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
The lupus example in the power chapter uses SampleSizeProportions 1.1.3. [sec-software-tools]

## Pitfalls
The descriptions in the book cover only the purpose of each tool, so a reader should consult the documentation for current features and versions. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which three criteria do they implement? A: ALC, ACC and WOC. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Which version does the lupus example use? A: SampleSizeProportions 1.1.3. [sec-software-tools]

sampling-distribution.name: Sampling distribution of a trial result
sampling-distribution.summary: The pattern of observed differences if the same trial were rerun many times given a truth; its width is the standard error.
sampling-distribution.body:
## What it is
Rerun the binary trial ten thousand times, with 100 new patients per arm each time, and compute the observed difference in response rates each time. The histogram is the sampling distribution of the observed difference. [sec-testing-sampling] Its standard deviation is the standard error:

$$
\mathrm{SE}(\hat\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n} + \frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n}} ,
$$

which is equation eq-testing-se. For the book's numbers it is 0.0676. [sec-testing-sampling]

## Why it matters
Every test and interval in the chapter is a way of reading this distribution. [sec-testing] The standard error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{n}$, so halving it requires quadrupling the trial, and it grows with the variability of the outcome. [sec-testing-sampling]

## In the book
With a true effect of 0.15 the histogram is centered on the truth, so the observed difference is unbiased, but its standard deviation is about 0.067. In about 1.7% of reruns a drug that truly works shows no benefit or a harm. [sec-testing-sampling] With no effect, in roughly 1.0% of reruns the observed difference is 0.15 or larger. [sec-testing-sampling] That share is a p-value built from the picture. [sec-testing-sampling] For the continuous endpoint the standard error is $\sigma\sqrt{2/n} = 12\sqrt{2/100} = 1.70$ mmHg. [sec-testing-sampling]

## Pitfalls
A real trial does not know that both arms share one rate, so it cannot read the null histogram directly. The randomization test and the z test are two ways to learn it from one trial. [sec-testing-sampling]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the observed difference on average? A: The true effect, so it is unbiased, though wrong in any single trial. [sec-testing-sampling]
- Q: How much more data halves the standard error? A: Four times as many patients. [sec-testing-sampling]

scenario-grid.name: Scenario grid
scenario-grid.summary: The set of assumed truths a simulation study runs the frozen design against, including the null space, nuisance parameters, operations and misspecification.
scenario-grid.body:
## What it is

A simulation study is a set of scenarios, and the scenarios decide whether the report convinces [sec-sim-grid]. The book lists efficacy, nuisance, operational, misspecification and sampled-effect scenarios [sec-sim-grid]. The "worst case" type I error is the maximum over a set of models the sponsor decides to consider, and the report should state what set that is [sec-sim-grid].

## Why it matters

The error constraint covers the whole null space, not one point [14/type-i-error-across-the-null-space]. A reviewer can read "controlled at a given level" as "everywhere the null is true" [14/type-i-error-across-the-null-space].

## In the book

Efficacy scenarios include the global null, the design alternative, an intermediate alternative at half the design effect, and a large effect [sec-sim-grid]. For a binary endpoint the nuisance parameter is the control rate [sec-sim-grid]. If the maximum falls at the edge of the grid, the grid was too small [sec-sim-grid].

In the worked example the type I error was simulated across a grid of control rates with $p_1 = p_0$, and the worst-case threshold is the largest of the thresholds each rate needs [14/type-i-error-across-the-null-space]. The supremum over the composite null is attained on the boundary $p_1 = p_0$ for this monotone rule [14/the-null-boundary].

## Pitfalls

A nonmonotone rule, such as one that selects among arms or borrows an external control, has no such guarantee and needs a grid in every nuisance dimension [14/the-null-boundary]. Tuning a design to a scenario table is legitimate only if the final design is frozen and revalidated on fresh seeds [sec-sim-grid].

## Check yourself

- Q: Where is the supremum of the type I error over $p_1 \le p_0$ for the monotone rule? A: On the boundary $p_1 = p_0$ [14/the-null-boundary].
- Q: What does a maximum at the grid edge tell you? A: The grid was too small [sec-sim-grid].

functions.title: Simulate a two-arm binary trial with interim looks

oc_simulate(
  p0,
  p1,
  looks,
  a = 0,
  prior = c(1, 1),
  nsim = 20000,
  seed = NULL,
  fut = NULL,
  method = c("table", "normal")
)
functions.description: Equal allocation, looks at cumulative per-arm sample sizes looks. Success is declared when Pr(p1 - p0 > a | data) > c at any look; optionally the trial stops for futility at the first look where that probability falls below fut. Efficacy stopping is applied later by oc_summarize(), so one simulation serves every candidate c (common random numbers) and oc_calibrate() can find c from a null simulation.

functions.name: oc_summarize
functions.title: Operating characteristics of the rule "success if pp > c at any attended look"
functions.description: Operating characteristics of the rule "success if pp > c at any attended look"

functions.name: oc_calibrate
functions.title: Calibrate the success threshold c to a one-sided type I error
functions.description: Returns a threshold c at which the empirical type I error in the supplied null simulation (the fraction of simulated trials whose posterior probability exceeds c at any attended look) is at most alpha: the 1 - alpha quantile ("higher" rule) of oc_max_pp(). Because the rule is pp > c, the empirical error is at most alpha, with equality up to Monte Carlo ties.

seamless-phase-2-3-design.name: Seamless phase 2/3 design
seamless-phase-2-3-design.summary: One protocol that selects a dose or regimen at an interim and continues into confirmation under a prespecified rule.
seamless-phase-2-3-design.body:
## What it is
A conventional program has a phase 2 trial, a gap for analysis, a new protocol and new sites, then phase 3. A seamless phase 2/3 design merges them. A first stage compares several doses with a control and selects one or two on interim data. A second stage confirms under a prespecified rule. [17/phase-23]

## Why it matters
It removes the dead time between phases and uses the trial's own data to choose the dose. [17/phase-23] In an inferentially seamless design, first-stage data for the selected dose count in the final test, so the analysis must account for selection. In an operationally seamless design only second-stage data are used. [17/phase-23]

## In the book
FDA's 2019 guidance expects the selection rule, type I error control and the firewall for unblinded interim data to be written in advance. [17/phase-23] A simulation of the inferentially seamless case found that putting roughly 30 to 50 percent of patients in the first stage is close to optimal. [17/phase-23]

## Pitfalls
Power calculated for the eventually selected arm overstates design power, because the first stage sometimes advances the wrong arm. Simulate the selection. [17/phase-23] With a delayed first-stage endpoint, patients enrolled while it matures belong to the first-stage cost. [17/phase-23]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the price of a seamless design? A: Design complexity, a prespecified selection rule and inferential adjustment. [17/phase-23]

select-reconstruction.name: SELECT reconstruction
select-reconstruction.summary: A simulation that replays SELECT under four monitoring rules held to one error rate and reports when each would have decided, as medians among successes and over all trials.
select-reconstruction.body:
## What it is
The reconstruction holds SELECT's hazard ratio at 0.80 and compares four rules at the same one-sided type I error of 2.5 percent. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
The first is a four-look O'Brien-Fleming design at 25, 50, 75 and 100 percent of events, with boundaries 4.049, 2.863, 2.337 and 2.024. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
The second stops when a posterior probability of benefit under a normal prior with scale 0.25 passes a threshold calibrated by simulation on a fine event grid. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
The third stops when a mixture e-value reaches 40. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
The fourth is SELECT's own design, one interim at 817 events and a final analysis at 1,225. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]

## Why it matters
Speed means nothing unless the rules carry the same type I error under the monitoring each uses. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
A posterior rule at the conventional threshold of 0.975, monitored on the same grid, has a type I error well above 2.5 percent, so a claim of speed without the error is an artifact. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]

## In the book
Among simulated trials that declare efficacy, the Bayesian rule stops at a median of 464 events, the e-value rule at 612 and the four-look design at 952. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
Over all trials, counting a trial that never crosses as ending at its maximum, the Bayesian median is 486 events. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]

## Pitfalls
The calibration holds for a stated grid and horizon, not for literally continuous monitoring, and monitoring off the grid needs recalibration. [sec-cases-limits]
Nobody observed a SELECT that stopped early, and the conditional medians describe only the paths that crossed. [sec-cases-limits]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the Bayesian conditional median smaller than the mean-path crossing? A: A rule that can act at any moment stops early on paths where noise has helped. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
- Q: Which rule has less power, the calibrated Bayesian rule or the group sequential designs? A: The Bayesian rule has a little less power, the price of monitoring on a fine grid. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]

results.name: SELECT reconstruction, median events at decision with conditioning
results.summary: In our reconstruction of SELECT at hazard ratio 0.80, a calibrated Bayesian rule stops at a median of 464 events among trials that declare efficacy and 486 over all trials, against 817 for SELECT's planned design (one interim analysis with Lan-DeMets spending, then the final); the e value rule and a four look design are slower or less powerful.
results.statement: In the SELECT reconstruction (true hazard ratio 0.80, normal prior of scale 0.25 on the log hazard ratio, at most 1,270 events, rules evaluated at every second event, 40,000 simulated paths, SELECT designed for hazard ratio 0.83 with 90 per cent power, 1,225 planned events and one interim at two thirds, Ryan et al. 2020), the median number of events at decision among simulated trials that declare efficacy is 464 for the Bayesian rule calibrated to 2.5 per cent one sided, 612 for the e value rule and 952 for a hypothetical four look O\'Brien-Fleming design. Over all trials, counting a trial that never crosses at its maximum, the medians are 486, 714 and 952. Power is 0.947, 0.831 and 0.977, and the realized one sided type I errors are 0.025, 0.0058 and 0.0255 (the Bayesian rule is calibrated to 2.5 per cent, the e value rule is bounded by it). SELECT\'s planned design (interim at 817 of 1,225 events with Lan-DeMets O\'Brien-Fleming type spending, then final) has median 817 in both senses, power 0.974 and type I error 0.0254. A single unadjusted look would cross at 309 events on the mean path, a mean path approximation and not a stopping time. The reconstruction is ours and not the sponsor\'s, and it is a counterfactual, not a power calculation made before the trial.

select-trial.name: SELECT
select-trial.summary: A cardiovascular outcomes trial of semaglutide in adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes, used in the book as the favorable case for pricing Bayesian monitoring in events, time and money.
select-trial.body:
## What it is
SELECT randomized 17,604 adults with overweight or obesity and established cardiovascular disease, without diabetes, to weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo, at 804 sites in 41 countries. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke, analyzed as time to first event. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
It occurred in 569 of 8,803 patients on semaglutide and 701 of 8,801 on placebo: 1,270 events, hazard ratio 0.80 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.72 to 0.90. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
Mean follow-up was 39.8 months. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]

## Why it matters
The book picks SELECT as the favorable case: a large effect, cleanly estimated, in a trial big enough for the asymptotics to apply. [sec-cases]
The reconstruction asks what each monitoring scheme would have needed at the same one-sided error of 2.5 percent. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]

## In the book
SELECT was designed for a hazard ratio of 0.83 with 90 percent power at one-sided 0.025, which calls for 1,225 planned events. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
It planned one superiority interim analysis at two thirds of the planned events, which is 817, followed by the final analysis. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
At the actual interim, at 831 events, the efficacy boundary was crossed and the data monitoring committee recommended continuing. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]
Crossing a boundary is necessary but not sufficient for stopping. [21/what-the-monitoring-committee-would-have-seen]
The book carries SELECT's actual two-look design through every comparison as a fourth rule beside the four-look O'Brien-Fleming design, the Bayesian rule and the e-value rule. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
See [[select-reconstruction]] for the simulated medians.

## Pitfalls
Every number built on the reconstruction is a counterfactual, and nothing in the chapter claims that SELECT should have stopped early. [sec-cases]
A regulator may prefer the longer exposure for a drug intended for chronic use by people without diabetes. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept]

## Check yourself
- Q: How many events did SELECT report, and how many did it plan? A: 1,270 reported against 1,225 planned. [21/the-trial-as-conducted]
- Q: Did the committee stop SELECT at the interim, where the boundary was crossed? A: No, it recommended continuing. [21/three-monitoring-schemes-and-selects-own-design-one-error-rate]

sensitivity-analysis.name: Sensitivity analysis over the prior
sensitivity-analysis.summary: Re-reporting the result across a family of reasonable priors, usually by varying the prior scale, to show how far the conclusion depends on the prior.
sensitivity-analysis.body:
## What it is

The FDA draft asks that "sensitivity analyses should be planned that utilize a range of alternative reasonable choices for the prior distributions," for instance by varying the strength of borrowing [sec-priors-sensitivity]. For a normal prior the natural one-parameter family is the prior standard deviation $s_0$ at a fixed mean, because $s_0$ sets the ESS and spans a dogmatic prior ($s_0 \to 0$) to a noninformative one ($s_0 \to \infty$) [sec-priors-sensitivity].

## Why it matters

It turns "does the prior matter" into a curve. When the data are decisive the conclusion is robust to a wide family and breaks only for priors almost as informative as the trial [sec-priors-sensitivity].

## In the book

For the 508-event trial with observed HR 0.80, the curve is flat to the right. For prior standard deviations above about 0.15 (ESS up to about 180 events) the posterior probability of benefit stays above 0.98, and it falls below 0.975 only for a very tight skeptic worth about two thirds of the information in the trial [sec-priors-sensitivity]. The multiplatform heparin trials pre-specified an enthusiastic prior as such a check [sec-priors-sensitivity].

## Pitfalls

ESS is reported alongside a sensitivity analysis, not instead of one [sec-priors-ess]. The draft does not say how wide a family is enough [sec-priors-fda]. The family and success criterion go in the protocol, for example standard deviation from the ESS-zero reference to twice the proposed ESS, and mean over a stated range [sec-priors-protocol].

## Check yourself

- Q: What does a flat sensitivity curve say? A: The conclusion is robust and is driven by the data [sec-priors-sensitivity].
- Q: Why vary $s_0$ at fixed mean? A: It sets the prior's weight through the ESS [sec-priors-sensitivity].

sequential-updating.name: Sequential updating
aliases: posterior today is the prior tomorrow
sequential-updating.summary: Applying Bayes rule batch by batch gives the same posterior as using all the data at once, whatever path the data took.
sequential-updating.body:
## What it is
When data arrive in batches $y_1$ and then $y_2$, Bayes' rule can be applied twice. The first posterior becomes the prior for the second batch: [sec-updating]

$$
\pi(\theta \mid y_1, y_2) \;\propto\; p(y_2 \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta \mid y_1) \;\propto\; p(y_2 \mid \theta)\, p(y_1 \mid \theta)\, \pi(\theta),
$$

provided $y_1$ and $y_2$ are conditionally independent given $\theta$. [sec-updating] The last form is the posterior from all data at once. The path by which data arrived does not matter. [sec-updating]

## Why it matters
For conjugate models the update is a running total, so interim posteriors cost a handful of arithmetic operations and a Data Monitoring Committee can have them at any time. [sec-updating]

## In the book
With 100 patients in four batches of 25, starting from a flat prior, the four-step posterior is Beta(46, 56), the same as the one-step posterior. [sec-updating]

A simulation of five looks at 50 patients per arm shows two statements at once. The frequentist rejection rate across looks is above the nominal 0.025. The Bayesian posterior at stopping is right on average when truth is drawn from the analysis prior. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]

## Pitfalls
- A valid posterior at every look does not make looks free: a threshold right at one look must be raised, or looks limited, to hold type I error at 0.025. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]
- If true effects are not drawn from the analysis prior, the posterior at stopping is not calibrated to anything in the real world. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]
- The likelihood principle removes only the conceptual objection that Bayesian inference does not know about the looks. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does updating by patient, by batch or all at once change the posterior? A: No, the posterior is the same. [sec-updating]
- Q: Does looking change the posterior? A: No, but it changes the type I error of the stopping rule. [6/looking-does-not-change-the-posterior]

shared-control-arithmetic.name: Shared-control arithmetic
shared-control-arithmetic.summary: The sample-size, variance and correlation consequences of testing several experimental arms against one control group.
shared-control-arithmetic.body:
## What it is

With $k$ drugs and a control of $m$ patients, separate trials randomize $2km$ patients and a platform with one control randomizes $(k+1)m$ [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost]. The saving is

$$
1 - \frac{k+1}{2k} = \frac{k-1}{2k},
$$

which is 25% for two drugs, 37.5% for four and 40% for five (eq-shared-saving). [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost] With $n$ patients per arm and $n_0=rn$ on control, the variance of each contrast is $\frac{1}{n}\left(1 + \frac{1}{r}\right)$ (eq-contrast-variance). Dunnett's rule puts $r=\sqrt{k}$ on control. [20/shared-control-arithmetic]

## Why it matters

Two arms' test statistics have correlation $1/(1+r)$, which is 0.5 under equal allocation and 0.33 for four arms under the square-root rule. [20/shared-control-arithmetic] Five drugs at 80 per arm need 480 patients rather than 800. [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost]

## In the book

At 480 total patients the square-root rule lowers each contrast variance by 10% with four arms and 15% with six. [20/shared-control-arithmetic] If all four arms are null at one-sided 0.025, the expected number of false positives is $0.025k$ whatever the correlation, but the count distribution changes. With a shared control and equal allocation, at least one false positive falls from 9.6% to 7.8% and two or more rises from 0.4% to 1.7%. [20/the-number-of-false-positives] FDA's draft recommends a control allocation larger than any single arm, and EMA's draft points to larger control groups as the more efficient remedy. [20/shared-control-arithmetic]

## Pitfalls

The arithmetic assumes all $k$ arms run at the same time. Real platforms add arms later. [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost] The simulation report should show the distribution of the number of errors, not only the familywise rate. [20/the-number-of-false-positives]

## Check yourself

- Q: Predict the saving for five drugs. A: 40%. [20/separate-trials-and-what-they-cost]
- Q: Is the mean number of false positives changed by sharing the control? A: No, it stays at $k\alpha$. [20/the-number-of-false-positives]

shine-trial.name: SHINE
shine-trial.summary: A stroke trial of intensive against standard glucose control that combined group sequential stopping with limited adaptive allocation and was not a Bayesian trial.
shine-trial.body:
## What it is

SHINE (NCT01369069) compared intensive with standard glucose control for 72 hours in acute ischemic stroke with hyperglycemia [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis]. Its design combined group sequential stopping with response-adaptive randomization, and it was not a Bayesian trial [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis].

## Why it matters

It shows that a confirmatory-scale trial can combine a classical error-controlled stopping rule with limited adaptation of allocation, which is the conservative end of what the regulators describe [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis]. The book's practical guidance suggests a group sequential design with futility and efficacy boundaries to protect patients inside a two-arm trial [sec-rar-practice].

## In the book

The trial found no significant difference in favorable 90-day outcome, and severe hypoglycemia occurred in 15 of 581 patients (2.6 percent) on intensive treatment [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis]. A later paper compared the Bayesian adaptive design developed in the ADAPT-IT project with the frequentist design that was used, in a retrospective comparison [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis].

## Pitfalls

A Bayesian alternative is judged against the classical design by simulation and not by assertion [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis].

## Check yourself

- Q: Was SHINE a Bayesian trial? A: No; it combined group sequential stopping with response-adaptive randomization [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis].
- Q: What did the Bayesian re-analysis paper compare? A: The ADAPT-IT Bayesian adaptive design against the frequentist design that was used [16/shine-and-its-bayesian-re-analysis].

shrinkage.name: Shrinkage
shrinkage.summary: A hierarchical model pulls each group's estimate toward the common mean in proportion to how little information it carries, paying for multiplicity in the estimate.
shrinkage.body:
## What it is

A Bonferroni correction raises the evidence required for each result independently of what the others say. A hierarchical model treats the effects as draws from a common distribution. [10/the-idea]

$$
\hat\theta_j \mid \theta_j \sim N(\theta_j, s_j^2), \qquad \theta_j \mid \mu, \tau_g \sim N(\mu, \tau_g^2),
$$

For fixed $\mu$ and $\tau_g$ the posterior mean is a weighted average of the group's own estimate and the common mean. [10/the-idea]

$$
\mathbb{E}[\theta_j \mid y] = (1-B_j)\,\hat\theta_j + B_j\,\mu, \qquad B_j = \frac{s_j^2}{s_j^2 + \tau_g^2}.
$$

This is partial pooling. [10/the-idea]

## Why it matters

A group with a small standard error stays near its own estimate. A group with little information is pulled toward the mean. [10/the-idea] The correction for looking at many things is built into the estimate. [10/the-idea]

## In the book

In the ulcer illustration, $\tau_g$ is estimated by marginal likelihood with `shrink_eb_fit()`, and each arm is shrunk roughly half way to the common mean. [10/what-the-hierarchical-reading-does-with-it]

I-SPY 2 and REMAP-CAP handle multiplicity by modeling and a demanding threshold, not by familywise adjustment. [10/key-points]

## Pitfalls

- Shrinkage does not control the familywise error rate. A regulator who requires it needs the rule calibrated by simulation. [10/what-shrinkage-does-not-do]
- With one truly active group among many nulls, shrinkage works against it. A heavier-tailed or mixture distribution can help. [10/what-shrinkage-does-not-do]
- The amount of pooling depends on the exchangeability assumption, the form of the group effects and the hyperprior. [10/the-idea]
- Shrinking across unrelated drugs borrows from the wrong place. [sec-mult-platform]

## Check yourself

- Q: When $\tau_g$ is small, what does the model reproduce? A: The pooled analysis. [10/the-idea]
- Q: Where does shrinkage pay for looking at many groups, compared with Bonferroni? A: In the estimate, not the threshold. [10/key-points]

simon-two-stage-design.name: Simon two-stage design
simon-two-stage-design.summary: A single-arm phase 2 design that enrolls n1 patients, stops for futility if at most r1 respond, and otherwise continues to n, with exact binomial error rates.
simon-two-stage-design.body:
## What it is

A response rate $p$ is judged against an uninteresting rate $p_0$ and a target rate $p_1$ [sec-phase2-classic]. In the two-stage design of Simon, enroll $n_1$ patients and stop for futility if at most $r_1$ respond; otherwise enroll to a total of $n$ and declare the drug promising if more than $r$ respond [sec-phase2-classic].

## Why it matters

It is the design most protocols use for single-arm phase 2 trials, and it is older than the predictive probability designs [sec-phase2-classic]. Both error rates are exact binomial sums, so the design is computed, not simulated [sec-phase2-classic].

## In the book

Among the pairs of stages that meet the stated type I error and power, the optimal design has the smallest expected sample size under $p_0$ [sec-phase2-classic]. The book compares it, for $p_0 = 0.20$ and $p_1 = 0.40$, with the three-look [[predictive-probability-monitoring]] design [sec-phase2-classic]. The two are close under the null, and the main gain of the predictive design is the possibility of stopping for efficacy, plus a smaller maximum sample size [sec-phase2-classic]. Earlier work includes Gehan's first stage that stops when there are no responses [sec-phase2-classic].

## Pitfalls

Simon's design has a single look and stops for futility only [sec-phase2-classic]. Bayesian single-arm designs came after it: Herson proposed stopping on the predictive probability of a positive final result, and Thall and colleagues monitored on a posterior probability with thresholds chosen by frequentist operating characteristics [sec-phase2-classic].

## Check yourself

- Q: What defines the optimal Simon design? A: Among designs meeting the error rates, the smallest expected sample size under $p_0$ [sec-phase2-classic].
- Q: Does it allow stopping for efficacy at the first stage? A: No, it stops for futility only [sec-phase2-classic].

simple-randomization.name: Simple randomization
simple-randomization.summary: Each patient is assigned by a fair coin, independently of every other patient, which is unpredictable but can leave small trials unbalanced.
simple-randomization.body:
## What it is
The simplest method assigns each patient by a fair coin, independently of every other patient. [5/simple-randomization] The book assumes two arms and 1:1 allocation in this section. [sec-randomization-methods]

## Why it matters
Its strength is unpredictability: knowing all previous assignments tells you nothing about the next one. [5/simple-randomization] It is also the case in which the unrestricted permutation shuffle is the right test. [sec-randomization-inference]

## In the book
With $n = 40$ patients, the number in the treatment arm has standard deviation $\sqrt{40}/2 \approx 3.2$, so a split of 15 and 25 is not rare. [5/simple-randomization]

In the simulation with three binary traits, the gap in a known trait under simple randomization falls by a factor of $\sqrt{5}$ when the trial grows from 40 to 200 patients. [5/seeing-the-difference] The hidden trait is as imbalanced under simple randomization as under any other method. [5/seeing-the-difference]

## Pitfalls
In a small trial, chance may give unequal arm sizes and unequal covariate distributions. The loss in arm size is a little efficiency. The covariate imbalance is more serious. [5/simple-randomization] [[permuted-block-randomization]] fixes arm sizes. [[stratified-randomization]] and [[minimization]] fix known covariates.

## Check yourself
- Q: How does the gap in a known trait change under simple randomization when the trial grows from 40 to 200 patients? A: It falls by a factor of about $\sqrt{5}$. [5/seeing-the-difference]
- Q: Does simple randomization allow a clinician to predict the next assignment? A: No. Previous assignments say nothing about the next. [5/simple-randomization]

simulation-report.name: Simulation report
simulation-report.summary: The written and submitted account of a design's simulated operating characteristics: aims, rules, calibration, scenarios, Monte Carlo error, prior sensitivity and code.
simulation-report.body:
## What it is

The simulation report is the deliverable of a Bayesian adaptive design, in the way the sample size calculation is the deliverable of a traditional one [sec-simulation]. The book maps its contents to the ADEMP framework of aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures [sec-sim-report].

## Why it matters

The FDA 2019 guidance, the Bayesian draft and ICH E20 differ in detail and agree in substance [sec-sim-report]. They are drafts or guidance, not law, but a submission that omits what they list is unlikely to survive review without a good reason [sec-sim-report].

## In the book

The report states aims, the design as simulated, calibration, scenarios, estimand, performance measures, Monte Carlo error, prior, software and reproducibility, example trials and traceability [sec-sim-report]. In submitting, the FDA's Complex Innovative Trial Design paired meeting program expects a simulation report ahead of the meeting [sec-sim-software]. Reproducibility means fixing the generator and seed, recording versions, and archiving code and outputs [sec-sim-software].

## Pitfalls

Reports most often fall short on three items: enrolled versus completed patients, binding versus non-binding futility, and traceability between the simulated code and the protocol rules [sec-sim-report]. If the monitoring committee can ignore a futility recommendation, type I error must be calibrated with the futility rule ignored [sec-sim-report].

## Check yourself

- Q: What should be reported beside every simulated rate? A: Its Monte Carlo standard error [14/where-the-calibration-noise-comes-from].
- Q: What is the easiest way to keep code and protocol rules identical? A: Generate both from one specification [sec-sim-report].

skeptical-prior.name: Skeptical prior
skeptical-prior.summary: A prior centered at no effect whose spread makes the chance of reaching the design alternative small, standing for a colleague who thinks the drug does nothing.
skeptical-prior.body:
## What it is

Spiegelhalter, Freedman and Parmar proposed reporting a trial against reference priors, each standing for a recognizable audience [sec-priors-three]. For $\theta = -\log \mathrm{HR}$ the skeptical prior is $\theta \sim N(0, s^2)$ with $s = \theta_a / 1.645$, so that $\Pr(\theta > \theta_a) = 0.05$. It will concede only that the drug might work as hoped, with probability one in twenty [sec-priors-three].

## Why it matters

If a trial is positive even under the skeptical prior, the skeptic is convinced [sec-priors-three]. A skeptic requires a larger observed effect for the same posterior probability, which is how a Bayesian design can reproduce the early conservatism of an O'Brien-Fleming boundary [sec-priors-three]. The FDA draft says that "Skeptical priors express skepticism about the presence of very large treatment effects" [sec-priors-three].

## In the book

For 508 events and observed HR 0.80 ($\hat\theta = 0.223$, standard error 0.089, z = 2.51, one-sided p = 0.006), the skeptic with $N(0, 0.175^2)$ ends with a posterior probability of benefit of 0.988 and a posterior hazard ratio of 0.84 [sec-priors-three]. The prior is worth 131 events, a quarter of the trial [sec-priors-three]. In EOLIA, a strongly skeptical prior still put 88% on some benefit [sec-priors-eolia].

## Pitfalls

The spread is tied to the sponsor's own design alternative, so an optimistic sponsor has a correspondingly wide skeptic. The fair response to a reviewer who wants a different skeptic is sensitivity analysis, not an argument about whose skeptic is right [sec-priors-three]. A skeptical prior of ESS 131 in 508 events moves the estimate from 0.80 to 0.84, and the report should say so [8/what-can-go-wrong].

## Check yourself

- Q: What spread makes a skeptical prior skeptical? A: $s = \theta_a/1.645$, giving a 5% prior chance of reaching the design effect [sec-priors-three].
- Q: Does the skeptic's posterior move far in the 508-event example? A: Only from 0.80 to 0.84, and benefit stays above 0.975 [sec-priors-three].

sotorasib-dose-case.name: Sotorasib dose optimization case
sotorasib-dose-case.summary: The KRAS G12C inhibitor approved at 960 mg without a randomized dose comparison, the case most often cited for Project Optimus.
sotorasib-dose-case.body:
## What it is
Sotorasib is a KRAS G12C inhibitor for non-small-cell lung cancer. It is the case most often cited for Project Optimus. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized]

## Why it matters
This is the situation the August 2024 guidance was written for: a dose chosen without a randomized comparison of lower doses, with evidence for a lower dose collected only after approval. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized] The cost is then borne by patients and a postmarketing study, rather than by a randomized comparison in phase 1/2. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized]

## In the book
The pivotal single-arm trial used the 960 mg dose. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized] The accelerated approval of May 2021 came with a postmarketing requirement to compare that dose with a lower one. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized] The randomized comparison of 960 mg and 240 mg was run only after approval. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which two doses were compared after approval? A: 960 mg and 240 mg. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized]
- Q: What did the May 2021 approval require? A: A postmarketing comparison of that dose with a lower one. [17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-optimized]

17/sotorasib-and-the-dose-that-was-not-o.t: Sotorasib and the dose that was not optimized

special-protocol-assessment.name: Special Protocol Assessment
special-protocol-assessment.summary: An FDA procedure giving written agreement on the design, endpoints and statistical analysis of certain trials, useful for fixing a Bayesian prior and calibration before the data are seen.
special-protocol-assessment.body:
## What it is
An SPA is a request for FDA's written agreement on the design, endpoints and statistical analysis of certain trials, including trials intended to form the primary basis of an efficacy claim, whatever their phase. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
The current guidance is the April 2018 revision. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]

## Why it matters
If FDA agrees, the agreement is documented and FDA will not change its position on the agreed critical design elements unless a substantial scientific issue essential to determining safety or effectiveness is identified after the trial begins and the sponsor is notified. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
The statute also allows changes by agreement with the sponsor. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
It is worth considering for a Bayesian confirmatory trial because it gets the prior, the criterion and the calibration agreed in writing before the data are seen. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]

## In the book
The timeline lists an SPA request (a written submission with a 45-day review, optionally alongside a Type C meeting) at the phase 3 protocol stage, to agree on the design and analysis. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
A resubmission after FDA comments is reviewed on a 45-day goal. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]

## Pitfalls
FDA will not agree to what it has not seen, so the SAP and the simulation report must be complete. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
The process will expose any design that cannot be defended. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
An SPA does not guarantee approval, or even that FDA will file the application: the agreement is about the design and not the result. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does an SPA guarantee approval? A: No, it covers the design and not the result. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]
- Q: What can make FDA change an agreed design element? A: A substantial scientific issue essential to safety or effectiveness found after the trial begins, or agreement with the sponsor. [23/the-interaction-timeline-with-fda]

sec-protocol.t: Writing the Bayesian Protocol and Working With Regulators

spending-function.name: Lan-DeMets spending function
spending-function.summary: A prespecified nondecreasing function that says how much of the total type I error may be used by each information fraction, so looks need not be at planned times.
spending-function.body:
## What it is

Lan and DeMets fix a spending function $\alpha^*(t)$ instead of fixed boundaries. It is nondecreasing with $\alpha^*(0) = 0$ and $\alpha^*(1) = \alpha$, and says how much of the total type I error may have been used by information fraction $t$. At look $t_k$ the boundary $b_k$ is the one for which the cumulative crossing probability equals $\alpha^*(t_k)$. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

Two spending functions mimic the classical designs:

$$
\alpha^*_{\text{OBF}}(t) = 2\{1 - \Phi(z_{\alpha/2}/\sqrt{t})\}, \qquad
\alpha^*_{\text{Pocock}}(t) = \alpha \log\{1 + (e - 1)\,t\}.
$$

[11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Why it matters

The function is in the protocol, not the number or times of looks. The recursion needs only the past boundaries and the current $t$, so the calculation does not require knowing how many looks will occur. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## In the book

The first function spends about 0.0015 of the 0.025 by $t = 0.5$. The second spends steadily. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

Alpha is distributed, not consumed. A final critical value of 2.02 instead of 1.96 records where the rest went. A stop for superiority spends alpha, a stop for futility does not, and a DMC reviewing safety without an efficacy comparison does not touch alpha. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Pitfalls

- The sample size was chosen for a particular plan, so power assumed a particular boundary even though the final analysis stays valid. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]
- The timing of looks must not depend on the observed effect. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

## Check yourself

- Q: Does an interim look cost alpha in total? A: No, the trial still has 0.025 overall and the function says where it lives. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]
- Q: What happens if the second look comes at 0.55 instead of 0.6? A: The boundary at that look is recomputed from the realized fraction. [11/spending-functions-and-the-information-fraction]

11/spending-functions-and-the-informatio.t: Spending functions and the information fraction

functions.name: gs_spending_boundary
functions.title: Lan-DeMets alpha-spending boundaries
functions.usage:
gs_spending_boundary(
  t,
  alpha = 0.025,
  spending = c("ld_obf", "ld_pocock"),
  h = 0.005
)
functions.description: Boundaries are found look by look: the sub-density of the Brownian score below the earlier boundaries is carried forward with the same panelled Gauss-Legendre recursion as gs_crossing_two_sided(), and each boundary is the root of the incremental crossing probability. The spending increments and the root equation are evaluated on the log scale, so looks with negligible spending (for example t = 0.001 under O'Brien-Fleming spending) give large finite boundaries rather than overflow.

spirit-2025.name: SPIRIT 2025
spirit-2025.summary: A checklist of minimum items that the protocol of a randomized trial should address, the antecedent of which is SPIRIT 2013; it is not specific to Bayesian designs.
spirit-2025.body:
## What it is
SPIRIT 2025 is a checklist of minimum items a protocol of a randomized trial should address. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
SPIRIT 2013 is its antecedent. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Why it matters
Two standards shape the protocol document itself, ICH M11 and SPIRIT 2025, and neither is specific to Bayesian designs. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The chapter's regulatory anchor lists both under how to ask, when, and in what format. [sec-protocol]

## In the book
The ICH M11 template does not name the Bayesian components (prior, simulation-based calibration, predictive probability rules), so the sponsor places them where a reviewer would look for the traditional counterpart. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
The sponsor checklist asks that the protocol be mapped into the M11 template and the SPIRIT items. [23/checklists]
The items a Bayesian trial adds are the prior and its source, the success criterion with its threshold and calibration, the interim schedule and the simulation report, the software and seeds, and the sensitivity analyses to the prior. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Pitfalls
None of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement for a Bayesian trial. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is SPIRIT 2025 a regulatory requirement for Bayesian trials? A: No; the book says none of the reporting guidelines around the protocol is a regulatory requirement, and SPIRIT 2025 is not Bayesian-specific. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]
- Q: What does SPIRIT 2025 list? A: Minimum items a randomized-trial protocol should address. [23/structured-protocols-ich-m11-and-spirit-2025]

stampede-trial.name: STAMPEDE
stampede-trial.summary: A frequentist multi-arm multi-stage platform in prostate cancer that opened in 2005 with a shared control and added arms by amendment.
stampede-trial.body:
## What it is

STAMPEDE (Systemic Therapy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer: Evaluation of Drug Efficacy) was designed at the MRC Clinical Trials Unit at UCL as a multi-arm multi-stage trial. The first patient was randomized in October 2005 to one of six arms, a standard hormone therapy control and five research arms, with allocation 2:1:1:1:1:1. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## Why it matters

It is the standing reminder that Bayesian machinery is optional for a platform: a common control, pre-specified stopping rules, intermediate outcomes and standing infrastructure answered several questions in the time that separate trials would need. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## In the book

Early stages use failure-free survival as an intermediate outcome, ahead of the definitive outcome, overall survival. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] Its strategy was comparison-level testing, and its investigators report a familywise error rate of 6.75% for the three original comparisons reaching their targets. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] When the standard of care changed, the control regimen changed with it. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] The abiraterone comparison joined later and, in men starting long-term hormone therapy, reduced the hazard of death (hazard ratio 0.63). The correlation between its test statistic and those of the original arms was 0.12. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs] Each new arm was a substantial amendment needing ethics and regulatory review, and drug supply could set the pace. [20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitoring-board]

## Pitfalls

An arm opened after a change in standard of care would have a different control population from one opened before it. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

## Check yourself

- Q: How was control allocated at the start? A: 2:1:1:1:1:1, twice the share of each research arm. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]
- Q: How were new arms added? A: By substantial amendment. [20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-multi-stage-designs]

20/governance-firewalls-and-the-monitori.t: Governance, firewalls and the monitoring board

20/the-frequentist-platform-multi-arm-mu.t: The frequentist platform: multi-arm multi-stage designs

stan.name: Stan
stan.summary: A probabilistic programming language for Bayesian inference by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, used when conjugate formulas are not available.
stan.body:
## What it is
Stan is a probabilistic programming language for Bayesian inference by Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
Stan and brms are used to fit analysis models when conjugate formulas are not available. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
The build machine had rstan 2.32.7. [sec-software-tools] trialr fits its Bayesian clinical trial designs, including dose-finding and phase II designs, with Stan. [sec-software-tools] brms fits multilevel models through Stan with a formula interface, so a reader can use Stan without writing the model code. [sec-software-tools] The packages listed in the book are on CRAN, except bcrm. [sec-software-tools]

## Pitfalls
The descriptions in the book cover only the purpose of each tool, so a reader should consult the documentation for current features and versions. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: What algorithm does Stan use? A: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: When does the book reach for Stan or brms? A: When conjugate formulas are not available. [sec-software-tools]

statistical-analysis-plan.name: Statistical analysis plan
statistical-analysis-plan.summary: The document finalized before unblinding that carries the model, prior, computation and decision rules, with a separate simulation report as the central deliverable for a Bayesian design.
statistical-analysis-plan.body:
## What it is
The SAP is finalized before unblinding, and for a Bayesian design it carries the exact model, the likelihood, the parameterization of the prior, the computation, the handling of missing data and intercurrent events, the full set of success criteria and the sensitivity analyses. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
The computation covers software, sampler, chains, burn-in, convergence diagnostics and seeds. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]

## Why it matters
The Bayesian draft asks for all of this "as early as possible" and says FDA does not require any particular software. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
A Bayesian SAP that defers the prior or the success threshold to a later version has not prespecified the design. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]

## In the book
The simulation report is a separate document and for a complex adaptive design the central one; it replaces the closed-form power calculation for the reviewer. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
It contains the design as simulated, the scenarios, operating characteristics, Monte Carlo error, a comparison with a simpler design, sensitivity to the prior and the code, seeds and software environment. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
A type I error of 0.024 estimated from a thousand runs is not evidence that it is below 0.025. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
The worked chunk simulates a binary-endpoint trial with four looks at 50, 100, 150 and 200 under the null of 30 percent response in both arms, calibrates the threshold, and validates it on a fresh null run and on an alternative of 30 against 45 percent. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
The report is versioned and the protocol references a version by date, so the simulated design is demonstrably the design that was run. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]

## Pitfalls
The temptation in an adaptive design is to leave details to be fixed at an interim, and E20 says the opposite. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
The rejection proportion in the calibration run is the target, not an error assessment. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why validate the calibrated threshold on a fresh null run? A: The calibration run's rejection proportion is the target and not an error assessment. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]
- Q: Does FDA require particular software? A: No. [23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the-simulation-report]

23/the-statistical-analysis-plan-and-the.t: The statistical analysis plan and the simulation report

23/the-success-criterion-and-its-calibra.t: The success criterion and its calibration

functions.name: oc_simulate
functions.title: Simulate a two-arm binary trial with interim looks
functions.usage:
oc_simulate(
  p0,
  p1,
  looks,
  a = 0,
  prior = c(1, 1),
  nsim = 20000,
  seed = NULL,
  fut = NULL,
  method = c("table", "normal")
)
functions.description: Equal allocation, looks at cumulative per-arm sample sizes looks. Success is declared when Pr(p1 - p0 > a | data) > c at any look; optionally the trial stops for futility at the first look where that probability falls below fut. Efficacy stopping is applied later by oc_summarize(), so one simulation serves every candidate c (common random numbers) and oc_calibrate() can find c from a null simulation.

functions.name: oc_calibrate
functions.title: Calibrate the success threshold c to a one-sided type I error
functions.description: Returns a threshold c at which the empirical type I error in the supplied null simulation (the fraction of simulated trials whose posterior probability exceeds c at any attended look) is at most alpha: the 1 - alpha quantile ("higher" rule) of oc_max_pp(). Because the rule is pp > c, the empirical error is at most alpha, with equality up to Monte Carlo ties.

functions.name: oc_summarize
functions.title: Operating characteristics of the rule "success if pp > c at any attended look"

stein-estimator.name: Stein estimator
stein-estimator.summary: For three or more normal means the raw group averages are inadmissible under total squared error, and shrunken estimates beat them whatever the true means are.
stein-estimator.body:
## What it is

Stein showed that for three or more means in a multivariate normal model with known variances, the usual estimate (each group's own average) is inadmissible under total squared-error loss. Some estimator has smaller total squared error whatever the true means are. James and Stein gave one explicitly. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]

## Why it matters

It is the classical theorem behind shrinkage. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]

## In the book

Efron and Morris used early-season batting averages. Estimates shrunk toward the league mean predicted the rest of the season better than the raw averages did for most players, and the improvement came largely from the extreme players. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]

A player who hits 1 for 19 against one pitcher looks like evidence he cannot hit that pitcher. But there are many pitchers, and a hierarchical analysis across all of them gives an estimate lower than average but much nearer to it than 1/19. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]

## Pitfalls

- The theorem concerns that model and that loss. It does not show that the empirical-Bayes fit in the ulcer analysis improves every arm, the selected contrast, posterior coverage or a clinical decision. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]
- The key points repeat the limit: this is not a guarantee for any fitted procedure. [10/key-points]

## Check yourself

- Q: With how many means does the result start to hold? A: Three or more. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]
- Q: Where did the batting-average gain come from? A: Largely from the extreme players. [10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-batting-averages]

10/stein-efron-and-morris-and-the-battin.t: Stein, Efron and Morris, and the batting averages

stopping-rule-principle.name: Stopping rule principle
aliases: posterior does not depend on the stopping rule
stopping-rule-principle.summary: The posterior after stopping at a data-dependent time equals the posterior from a sample of that size fixed in advance, so a Bayesian may look as often as desired.
stopping-rule-principle.body:
## What it is

Let the trial stop at a random time $T$ determined by a rule that depends only on the data so far. The likelihood includes the probability that the rule would have continued until $T$ and stopped there. That factor depends only on the data, not on $\theta$, so it cancels in the posterior. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]

The posterior after stopping at $T$ is exactly the one computed had the sample size been fixed at $T$ in advance. This is the likelihood principle in sequential form. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]

## Why it matters

It is the foundation of the claim "you may look as often as you like". A frequentist $p$-value is a tail probability over other data sets that might have been seen, and which are possible depends on the stopping rule. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]

## In the book

A trial ends with 15 responders among 20 patients and null response probability one half. Under a flat prior the posterior is Beta(16, 6) whether 20 was planned or enrollment continued until the fifth non-responder, while the $p$-values differ. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]

In a simulation with prior $N(0, 0.5^2)$ and monitoring to $n = 400$ at a posterior probability of 0.975, the claim made at stopping matches the truth among trials that stop. Yet if the null is exactly true, the same rule declares benefit at about seven times the usual 2.5%. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]

## Pitfalls

- Calibration under the prior and a type I error answer different questions. The first averages over the prior, the second conditions on one $\theta$. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]
- The principle holds when the full sample path is reported. It does not remove the need to specify how a summary was chosen. [sec-mult-selected]

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the posterior change if the trial planned to stop at the fifth non-responder rather than at 20 patients? A: No, it is Beta(16, 6) in both cases. [11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-stopping-rule]
- Q: Does the frequentist error rate change with the stopping rule? A: Yes, the error rate belongs to the rule. [11/why-repeated-testing-at-a-fixed-level-fails]

11/the-posterior-does-not-depend-on-the-.t: The posterior does not depend on the stopping rule

stratified-randomization.name: Stratified randomization
stratified-randomization.summary: A separate permuted-block list is run inside each stratum, the combination of levels of a few prognostic factors, so each stratum is nearly balanced.
stratified-randomization.body:
## What it is
If a prognostic factor such as disease stage, prior treatment or study center is known to matter, we can balance it by design. A separate permuted-block list is run inside each stratum, the combination of factor levels. Every stratum then has near-equal arm sizes. [5/stratified-randomization]

## Why it matters
ICH E9 asks that the factors used to stratify be accounted for in the analysis. [5/stratified-randomization] Stratification removes variation between strata from the treatment comparison. An analysis that ignores the strata gives a standard error that is too large, a type I error below nominal and a loss of power. [5/analyze-as-you-randomized]

## In the book
Stratification has a ceiling. With $k$ binary factors there are $2^k$ strata, and each has its own incomplete block at the end of enrollment. With 20 patients per center and four factors, most blocks are unfinished. [5/stratified-randomization] The rule is to stratify on two or three strongly prognostic factors and to adjust for the same factors in the analysis. [5/stratified-randomization]

In an interactive response system, the schedule is a table of stratum, sequence number, treatment and kit number. The book generates one for three strata with block sizes of 4 and 6, using a recorded seed. [5/how-the-schedule-is-actually-made]

## Pitfalls
Too many strata leave unfinished blocks and buy little. [5/stratified-randomization] Stratified blocks cut imbalance in the known trait but do nothing for a hidden one. [5/seeing-the-difference]

## Check yourself
- Q: With four binary stratification factors, how many strata exist? A: $2^4 = 16$, and with small centers most blocks stay unfinished. [5/stratified-randomization]
- Q: What happens to the standard error if the analysis ignores the strata? A: It is too large, with wider intervals and lost power. [5/analyze-as-you-randomized]

subgroup-analysis.name: Subgroup analysis
subgroup-analysis.summary: Slicing trial results by age, sex, region or biomarker, the source of multiplicity that most often misleads.
subgroup-analysis.body:
## What it is

A trial that fails overall will be examined by age, sex, region, baseline severity, biomarker status and prior therapy. With twelve ways to slice the data, luck has twelve chances. [sec-mult-subgroups]

## Why it matters

Of all the sources of multiplicity, the subgroup analysis is the one that most often misleads. [sec-mult-subgroups]

## In the book

The classic warning is ISIS-2, which enrolled 17,187 patients with suspected myocardial infarction. Its authors showed that split by astrological birth sign, aspirin appeared to have no benefit for Gemini or Libra, although in the whole trial it reduced vascular mortality very strongly. Twelve signs gave twelve chances. [sec-mult-subgroups]

Wang and colleagues give a reporting standard: say how many subgroup analyses were done, state which were prespecified, and test for interaction rather than comparing $p$-values inside subgroups. [sec-mult-subgroups]

The traditional remedies are to prespecify few subgroups with a rationale, put the subgroup variable in the multiplicity graph when a claim is intended, test interaction first, and treat the rest as exploratory. They are all-or-nothing, and an estimate outside the family is reported at face value with all its noise. [sec-mult-subgroups]

A hierarchical model across subgroups moves the estimates toward the overall effect in proportion to how little information each carries. The book applies this to RECOVERY. [10/a-large-trial-with-many-subgroups-recovery]

## Pitfalls

- A significant effect in one subgroup and a non-significant effect in another is not evidence that the effects differ. [sec-mult-subgroups]
- The interaction test has little power at the usual sample size, so the honest result is usually "consistent with a common effect". [sec-mult-subgroups]

## Check yourself

- Q: What did ISIS-2 show with birth signs? A: Apparent no benefit of aspirin in two of twelve signs despite a strong overall effect. [sec-mult-subgroups]
- Q: What should a subgroup report test instead of within-subgroup p-values? A: The interaction between subgroup and treatment. [sec-mult-subgroups]

10/a-large-trial-with-many-subgroups-rec.t: A large trial with many subgroups: RECOVERY

substantial-evidence.name: Substantial evidence
substantial-evidence.summary: The legal standard for approving a drug: evidence from adequate and well-controlled investigations that qualified experts could fairly and responsibly read as showing the claimed effect.
substantial-evidence.body:
## What it is
Section 505(d) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act directs FDA to refuse approval if there is a lack of substantial evidence that the drug has the claimed effect under the labeled conditions of use. [3/what-the-statute-says] The Act defines substantial evidence as evidence consisting of adequate and well-controlled investigations. [3/what-the-statute-says]

## Why it matters
Everything in the book is aimed at this finding. [sec-regulatory] The standard is one of evidence and not of method: the statute names no test, level, sample size, prior or design. [3/what-the-statute-says] That gap is where Bayesian and adaptive design choices live. [sec-regulatory]

## In the book
The statute speaks of investigations in the plural, and for decades FDA read that as two independent positive trials. [3/what-the-statute-says] Since the 1997 FDAMA amendment, one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence can also meet the standard. [3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confirmatory-evidence] Two trials each tested at one-sided 0.025 pass a useless drug with probability $0.025 \times 0.025 = 1/1600$. [3/what-the-standard-implies-for-the-numbers] One trial at 0.025 passes a useless drug 1 time in 40. [3/what-the-standard-implies-for-the-numbers] So one very persuasive trial and two ordinary trials can give comparable protection against a false positive. [3/what-the-standard-implies-for-the-numbers]

## Pitfalls
- Frequentist testing at one-sided 0.025 became customary, but the law does not mention it. [3/what-the-statute-says]
- A statute binds, but a guidance only recommends, so a draft is never "FDA requirements". [sec-regulatory-force]

## Check yourself
- Q: Does the statute name a significance level? A: No, it names no test, level, sample size, prior or design. [3/what-the-statute-says]
- Q: What is the chance that a useless drug passes two independent trials at one-sided 0.025? A: 1/1600. [3/what-the-standard-implies-for-the-numbers]

3/the-1997-amendment-one-trial-and-confi.t: The 1997 amendment: one trial and confirmatory evidence

3/what-the-standard-implies-for-the-numb.t: What the standard implies for the numbers

superion-trial.name: Superion
superion-trial.summary: An interspinous spacer device trial whose Bayesian non-inferiority success threshold of 0.958 was set by simulation to control the type I error below 0.05.
superion-trial.body:
## What it is

The Superion interspinous spacer trial (PMA P140004) randomized against a comparator device [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958]. It used a Bayesian adaptive sample size of 250 to 350 evaluable patients, a non-inferiority margin of 10 percent and flat Beta(1,1) priors [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958].

## Why it matters

Success required a posterior probability of non-inferiority of at least 0.958, a value chosen to control the type I error below 0.05 [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958]. The stated power was 86.3 percent [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958].

## In the book

The final modified intention-to-treat sample was 190 against 201 patients [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958]. The posterior probability of non-inferiority was 0.9927, or 0.9944 per protocol, above the threshold, with approval on 20 May 2015 [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958]. The book's lesson is that 0.958 is not a conventional number: it is what a simulation of this margin, prior, error budget and adaptive sample size returned [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958].

## Pitfalls

The threshold makes sense only together with its margin, priors and adaptive sample size [14/choosing-a-and-c]. Calibrating a Bayesian threshold to a frequentist error rate by simulation is described in FDA's 2010 guidance on Bayesian statistics in medical device trials [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958].

## Check yourself

- Q: Why 0.958 and not a conventional number? A: It came from simulating this trial's margin, prior and adaptive sample size to control type I error below 0.05 [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958].
- Q: Did the trial clear the threshold? A: Yes, with a posterior probability of 0.9927 [14/superion-a-device-threshold-of-0958].

surcharge.name: Surcharge for anytime validity
surcharge.summary: The extra squared evidence, about 2 log(1/alpha), that the normal-mixture e-value rule needs over a Bayesian rule at posterior odds of one.
surcharge.body:
## What it is

For the normal-mixture e-value, at large information the anytime-valid rule needs approximately $2\log(1/\alpha)$ more units of squared evidence than a Bayesian rule at posterior odds of one. At $\alpha = 0.025$ that is 7.38. [sec-evalues]

Measured against that uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar it amounts to about seventy percent of a conventional trial. This compares boundary terms and is not an exact sample-size identity. [sec-evalues-surcharge]

## Why it matters

Whether a sponsor should pay depends on whether the trial needs validity at stopping times the protocol cannot anticipate. [sec-evalues-pay] The surcharge belongs in the sample size justification as an explicit line. [sec-evalues-pay]

## In the book

The e-process rule is the symmetric normal-mixture Bayes factor with $b = 1/\alpha$. [sec-evalues-surcharge] The half-normal mixture lowers the bar by about $2\log 2 = 1.39$. [sec-evalues-surcharge]

In the SELECT reconstruction the realized gap is smaller than seventy percent once the Bayesian rule is calibrated: the e-value rule needs 32 percent more events at the median than the calibrated Bayesian rule (612 against 464). [12/time-to-event-design-the-select-reconstruction] A sponsor should not read the figure as a 70 percent longer trial, because stopping early at a large effect is built into the e-value design. [sec-evalues-surcharge]

## Pitfalls

- It is a cost of one construction, not a universal cost of anytime validity. Iterated-logarithm boundaries behave differently. [sec-evalues-surcharge]
- Calibration narrows it. [sec-evalues-surcharge]

## Check yourself

- Q: At $\alpha = 0.025$, what is $2\log(1/\alpha)$ at large information? A: About 7.38. [sec-evalues]
- Q: Is seventy percent an exact sample-size identity? A: No. It compares boundary terms against the uncalibrated Bayes-factor bar. [sec-evalues-surcharge]
