results.name: The surcharge for validity at every stopping time is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement, as a comparison of boundary terms
results.summary: For the normal mixture e value rule, against the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar (posterior odds of one), the large information surcharge 7.38 is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial standardized requirement 10.51; this compares boundary terms and is not an exact sample size identity.
results.statement: With per observation standardized effect $\theta$, the information needed to act satisfies, in the large information approximation, $n_{\mathrm{MD}}\theta^2 = \log n_{\mathrm{MD}} + C$ for the Bayes rule and $n_{\mathrm{LD}}\theta^2 = \log n_{\mathrm{LD}} + C + 2\log(1/\alpha)$ for the anytime valid rule. Subtracting gives $(n_{\mathrm{LD}} - n_{\mathrm{MD}})\theta^2 = 2\log(1/\alpha) + \log(n_{\mathrm{LD}}/n_{\mathrm{MD}})$, and the last term is positive. On the standardized scale the surcharge $2\log(1/\alpha) = 7.38$ at $\alpha = 0.025$ is about 70 per cent of the fixed trial requirement $(z_\alpha + z_\beta)^2 = 10.51$ at 90 per cent power ($7.38/10.51 \approx 0.70$). This compares boundary terms asymptotically. It is not an exact sample size identity (at $\theta = 0.20$ and $C = 0$ the larger roots differ by about 80 per cent of the fixed requirement), and the exact surcharge is $7.38(1 + 1/q)$. The baseline is the uncalibrated Bayes factor bar; a calibrated Bayesian rule has already paid part of the surcharge, so calibration narrows the realized gap.

surpass-cvot.name: SURPASS-CVOT
surpass-cvot.summary: An active-comparator cardiovascular trial of tirzepatide against dulaglutide with a noninferiority margin, used to show what a Bayesian reading adds to a noninferiority result.
surpass-cvot.body:
## What it is
SURPASS-CVOT randomized 13,299 adults with type 2 diabetes and established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, double blind and 1:1, to weekly tirzepatide (up to 15 mg) or dulaglutide 1.5 mg. [sec-cases-surpass]
The modified intention-to-treat population was 13,165 (6,586 on tirzepatide and 6,579 on dulaglutide). [sec-cases-surpass]
The primary hypothesis was noninferiority: the upper limit of the 95.3 percent confidence interval for the hazard ratio had to lie below 1.05, with superiority if it lay below 1.00. [sec-cases-surpass]

## Why it matters
Two active drugs change the question: the lesson is what the margin and a transportability assumption allow a Bayesian reading to say. [sec-cases]

## In the book
The primary outcome occurred in 801 patients (12.2 percent) on tirzepatide and 862 (13.1 percent) on dulaglutide, hazard ratio 0.92, interval 0.83 to 1.01. [sec-cases-surpass]
Noninferiority was established ($p = 0.003$) and superiority was not ($p = 0.09$). [sec-cases-surpass]
The Bayesian reading gives posterior probabilities for noninferiority, for superiority and for a reduction of at least 10 percent, on a continuous scale. [sec-cases-surpass]
Superiority "failed" because the upper limit of 1.01 sat just above 1.00, yet the probability that the hazard ratio is below one is high; the two statements are not competing. [sec-cases-surpass]
Tirzepatide was never tested against placebo here, so an indirect chain through dulaglutide fills the gap, and the transportability assumption from REWIND is the whole of the argument. [sec-cases-surpass]

## Pitfalls
Under a skeptical prior the posterior would be pulled toward one, so the flat-prior numbers are the upper end of what the data support. [sec-cases-surpass]
The book omits secondary and component hazard ratios that it has not checked against the full report. [sec-cases-surpass]

## Check yourself
- Q: Was superiority shown, and why might a Bayesian still find the result useful? A: No ($p = 0.09$), but the posterior probability of a hazard ratio below one is a direct statement a prescriber can weigh. [sec-cases-surpass]
- Q: What assumption carries the indirect comparison with placebo? A: Transportability from REWIND. [sec-cases-surpass]

sec-cases.t: Case Studies: Cardiovascular, Alzheimer's and Vaccine Trials

sec-cases-surpass.t: SURPASS-CVOT: an active comparator and a noninferiority margin

test-martingale.name: Test martingale
test-martingale.summary: A nonnegative process that starts at one and whose expected next value equals its current value under the null, the wealth of a gambler who bets fairly.
test-martingale.body:
## What it is

Let $E_n$ be the gambler's wealth after $n$ observations, starting from $E_0 = 1$. If each bet is fair under the null, so that given the past the expected wealth after the next observation equals the wealth now, the process is a test martingale. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality] If the expected wealth can only fall, it is a test supermartingale, and everything below holds for it too. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

## Why it matters

[[villes-inequality|Ville's inequality]] bounds the probability that a test martingale ever crosses a high level, for the entire path. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality] That is what lets the analyst look after every patient and stop for any reason. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

## In the book

For a binary endpoint, patients enroll in matched pairs and $D_i = Y_{T,i} - Y_{C,i}$ is $+1$, $-1$ or $0$. [12/a-betting-martingale-for-a-binary-endpoint] With a betting fraction $\lambda$ the product $E_n = \prod (1 + \lambda D_i)$ is a test martingale for the composite null that the two arms have the same response probability. [12/a-betting-martingale-for-a-binary-endpoint] The common response probability never needs to be estimated. [12/a-betting-martingale-for-a-binary-endpoint]

A single-distribution [[likelihood-ratio]] is a test martingale, and so is any average of them, which gives the [[mixture-method]]. [sec-evalues-lr]

## Pitfalls

- Under the null the average wealth stays at one dollar, yet the typical path drifts down, because rare large excursions hold the average up. [12/a-betting-martingale-for-a-binary-endpoint]
- Not every sequential statistic is a martingale. The weaker notion is an [[e-process]]. [12/e-processes]

## Check yourself

- Q: A gambler's expected wealth after the next bet equals the wealth now under the null. What is the process called? A: A test martingale. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]
- Q: Under a true null, will most simulated wealth paths rise or fall? A: Most drift down, even though the average stays at one. [12/a-betting-martingale-for-a-binary-endpoint]

12/a-betting-martingale-for-a-binary-end.t: A betting martingale for a binary endpoint

thompson-sampling.name: Thompson sampling
thompson-sampling.summary: Allocation that draws one value from each arm's posterior and assigns the next patient to the arm with the largest draw.
thompson-sampling.body:
## What it is

With a uniform Beta(1, 1) prior on each success probability, the posterior after $s$ successes and $f$ failures is Beta$(1+s, 1+f)$ [16/thompson-sampling-in-four-lines]. Thompson sampling draws one value from each arm's posterior and assigns the patient to the arm with the largest draw [16/thompson-sampling-in-four-lines]. For two arms the probability that arm 1 is chosen is exactly $\Pr(p_1 > p_0 \mid \text{data})$ [16/thompson-sampling-in-four-lines].

## Why it matters

Early in a trial the allocation is close to one half, and as evidence accumulates it moves toward 0 or 1 [16/thompson-sampling-in-four-lines]. Nothing in the algorithm asks for a threshold, a boundary or a stopping rule [16/thompson-sampling-in-four-lines]. Kaufmann, Korda and Munos and Agrawal and Goyal showed that for Bernoulli arms it attains the Lai-Robbins bound asymptotically [16/the-same-logarithm].

## In the book

In the 400-patient two-arm simulation, Thompson sampling put a large share of patients on the better arm and added responders, but power fell below that of equal allocation and the number on the better arm varied much more between trials [16/reproducing-the-critique]. Its naive test had type I error of about 0.049, almost twice the nominal 0.025, even with no drift [16/reproducing-the-critique]. Amazon used it to choose web page layouts; the book calls the transfer to confirmatory trials limited [16/an-analogy-that-does-not-transfer-as-design-advice].

## Pitfalls

A recommendation of Thompson sampling for confirmatory trials on the strength of the regret analogy would be wrong [16/an-analogy-that-does-not-transfer-as-design-advice]. Burn-in and a cap on the allocation probability reduce but do not remove its problems [16/the-fixes].

## Check yourself

- Q: What is the chance arm 1 is chosen with two arms? A: The posterior probability that arm 1 is better [16/thompson-sampling-in-four-lines].
- Q: Does Thompson sampling need a stopping bar? A: No explicit bar; its exploration comes from the spread of the posterior [16/the-same-logarithm].

three-plus-three-design.name: 3+3 design
three-plus-three-design.summary: The rule-based phase 1 design that treats cohorts of three and escalates or stops by counting dose-limiting toxicities, with no model.
three-plus-three-design.body:
## What it is
The 3+3 is a rule-based method with no model, and it is still the most commonly used phase 1 design. [17/the-rule] Treat three patients. With no DLT, move up. With one DLT in three, treat three more: at most one DLT in six means move up, two or more means stop. Two or more DLTs in the first three also means stop. The MTD is the dose below the stopping dose. [17/the-rule]

## Why it matters
It is easy to explain to a team and an ethics committee, needs no software, and never escalates after two DLTs in a cohort. [17/the-rule]

## In the book
Across the three scenarios the 3+3 finds the true MTD in only about half or fewer of trials, and in roughly half it recommends a dose below the MTD (47 percent in scenario A, 53 percent in B). [17/operating-characteristics-by-simulation] Its mean sample size is between about 10 and 19 patients, and about three or fewer patients are treated at toxic doses on average. [17/operating-characteristics-by-simulation] One DLT in six with a Beta(0.25, 0.75) prior gives a Beta(1.25, 5.75) posterior. [17/what-six-patients-can-tell-you]

## Pitfalls
The rule states no target toxicity rate, and the 3+3 forgets all previous doses when it moves. [17/operating-characteristics-by-simulation][17/what-six-patients-can-tell-you] Little information is gathered at the recommended dose. [17/operating-characteristics-by-simulation] It may still be reasonable for a well-understood toxicity profile and few doses. [17/what-stays-the-same]

## Check yourself
- Q: What happens after one DLT among the first three patients? A: Three more are treated at the same dose. [17/the-rule]
- Q: Why is the 3+3 called safe? A: Few patients are exposed at toxic doses, at the price of a low chance of finding the MTD. [17/what-stays-the-same]

functions.name: dose_three_plus_three
functions.title: One simulated 3+3 trial
functions.description: The rule implemented, step by step. Treat a cohort of 3 at dose 1. At the current dose: with 0 DLTs in 3, escalate; with 1 DLT in 3, treat 3 more at the same dose, escalate if the total is 1 DLT in 6 and otherwise stop; with 2 or 3 DLTs in the first 3, stop immediately (no expansion cohort). Escalation moves up exactly one dose, and a dose is never revisited: there is no de-escalation to a lower dose for further testing, no expansion of the dose below the stopping dose, and no confirmation of the selected dose. When the trial stops for excess toxicity at dose d the recommended dose is d - 1 (0, "none", if d = 1), which may have been given to only 3 patients. If the top dose passes (0 DLTs in 3, or 1 DLT in 6 after expansion) the top dose is selected, with no expansion cohort after 0 DLTs in 3. There is no sample size cap, so the trial length is random. This is the traditional "3+3" of the usual textbook form; Storer's (1989) designs, which expand and de-escalate after initial toxicity, are different rules.

time-to-event-endpoint.name: Time-to-event endpoint
time-to-event-endpoint.summary: An endpoint measured as the time to death, progression or another event, with patients censored if the event has not happened by last contact.
time-to-event-endpoint.body:
## What it is
Let $T$ be the event time and $S(t) = \Pr(T > t)$ the survival function. The hazard is $h(t) = \lim_{\delta \to 0}\Pr(t \le T < t + \delta \mid T \ge t)/\delta$, the cumulative hazard is $H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,du$, and $S(t) = e^{-H(t)}$. [sec-survival-traditional] Patients event-free at the data cutoff, or lost to follow-up, are censored: their event time is only known to exceed the last contact. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Why it matters
Most confirmatory trials in cardiology and oncology are event driven. The endpoint is the time to death, progression or a major adverse cardiovascular event. [sec-survival] The estimand must name the population, the variable, the handling of intercurrent events and the summary measure, chosen before the trial. [sec-survival]

## In the book
SELECT planned 1,225 events and observed 1,270, and REWIND observed 1,257. A trial of 17,604 patients is, statistically, a trial of about 1,270 events. [sec-survival]

## Pitfalls
The information is the number of events of the primary endpoint as defined, so any change to the definition or its intercurrent-event handling changes the information. [sec-survival-traditional]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does a censored patient's record tell you? A: The event time exceeds the last contact. [sec-survival-traditional]
- Q: What does a time-to-event trial wait for? A: A target number of events, not a fixed sample size. [sec-survival]

time-trend-bias.name: Time trend bias
time-trend-bias.summary: Confounding of arm with calendar time when response drifts during enrollment, which inflates the type I error of response-adaptive randomization but not of blocked equal allocation.
time-trend-bias.body:
## What it is

Suppose the background response rate rises during enrollment because the standard of care improves or the site mix changes [16/the-mechanism]. An arm that benefited from early luck receives more of the later patients, who respond better on any treatment, and looks better still [16/the-mechanism]. Nothing about the treatment has changed, and the comparison is confounded with calendar time [16/the-mechanism].

## Why it matters

This is the central practical objection to RAR in confirmatory trials, and the property that fixed allocation with permuted blocks was designed to defeat [16/the-mechanism].

## In the book

In a null trial of 400 patients with response 0.30 in both arms, the response rises linearly across enrollment by a drift $d$ [16/simulation]. Under equal allocation, drift is harmless even for a 30-point drift [16/simulation]. Under Thompson sampling the naive test's type I error climbs with the drift, and capped Thompson reduces but does not remove the problem [16/simulation]. Three fixes should be pre-specified as a package: stratify the analysis by enrollment period, use burn-in and a cap, and keep control allocation fixed [16/the-fixes]. A fourth route models the trend, as in the Bayesian time machine [16/the-fixes].

## Pitfalls

Stratifying costs power [16/the-fixes]. Even with stratification, plain Thompson keeps a type I error near 0.05, twice the nominal one-sided 0.025, until the critical value is calibrated by simulation [16/the-fixes]. A Bayesian analysis does not by itself solve the confounding, because the model must contain the drift [sec-rar-reg].

## Check yourself

- Q: Why is equal allocation immune to drift? A: Allocation does not depend on the outcomes, so each period contributes equally to both arms [16/simulation].
- Q: What does stratifying by enrollment period require? A: Allocation fixed within each period and arms compared only within a period [16/the-fixes].

tipping-point-analysis.name: Tipping-point analysis
tipping-point-analysis.summary: Reporting the least extreme prior in a stated family for which the success criterion is no longer met, instead of the conclusion under one prior.
tipping-point-analysis.body:
## What it is

A tipping-point prior is the least extreme prior in a stated family for which the success criterion is no longer met. The idea is borrowed from the handling of missing data [sec-priors-tipping]. One family varies the prior standard deviation, another varies the prior mean at a fixed spread [sec-priors-tipping].

## Why it matters

It replaces a debate about the right prior with a statement about which priors the regulator would have to hold to disagree. A tipping point in an incredible region, such as a skeptic who thought the drug harmful or a prior worth two thirds of the trial, supports the claim that the data drive the conclusion [sec-priors-tipping]. One close to the sponsor's own prior is a warning that the prior drives the answer [sec-priors-tipping].

## In the book

For the 508-event trial, holding the skeptical spread of 0.175, benefit drops below 0.975 only if the prior mean expects harm on average [sec-priors-tipping] [sec-priors-sensitivity]. For pediatric belimumab in lupus, FDA requested a post hoc analysis borrowing from adult trials with weight $w$. The posterior probability of efficacy was at least 97.5 percent whenever $w$ was 0.55 or more [sec-priors-belimumab].

## Pitfalls

The family and criterion belong in the statistical analysis plan before unblinding. A family chosen after seeing the data would be a way of looking for a prior that works [sec-priors-tipping].

## Check yourself

- Q: What is a tipping-point prior? A: The least extreme prior in a family that reverses the success decision [sec-priors-tipping].
- Q: What did the belimumab analysis report? A: Efficacy of at least 97.5 percent once the borrowing weight was 0.55 or more [sec-priors-belimumab].

tite-boin.name: TITE-BOIN
tite-boin.summary: An interval design that assigns doses in real time while some enrolled patients still have pending toxicity data.
tite-boin.body:
## What it is
Late-onset toxicity means the outcome of each cohort is not known before the next is dosed. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs] The time-to-event CRM of Cheung and Chappell uses the fraction of the observation window completed for patients without a DLT, while observed DLTs contribute full information, so enrollment need not pause. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs] TITE-BOIN builds the same idea into the interval design. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs]

## Why it matters
TITE-BOIN allows real-time dose assignment while some toxicity data are pending. It addresses late-onset toxicity, which is common for targeted agents and immunotherapy, and rapid accrual. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs]

## In the book
BOIN12 is a related design for the efficacy-toxicity trade-off. It targets the optimal biologic dose and is simple enough that its decision rules can be tabulated in the protocol as BOIN's are. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs] A review covers design strategies for dose-optimization trials, including the randomized comparison the FDA guidance recommends. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs]

## Pitfalls
The reviewer will ask how late toxicities and dose reductions after cycle 1 are handled in the dose decision. [17/randomized-dose-comparison-and-what-a-regulator-will-ask]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why can enrollment continue under TITE-BOIN? A: Pending patients contribute partial information, so no pause is needed. [17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based-interval-designs]

17/late-onset-toxicity-and-utility-based.t: Late-onset toxicity and utility-based interval designs

17/randomized-dose-comparison-and-what-a.t: Randomized dose comparison, and what a regulator will ask

toxicity-monitoring.name: Toxicity monitoring
toxicity-monitoring.summary: A prespecified stopping table that pauses a single-arm study when the posterior probability of exceeding the acceptable toxicity rate is high, with exact operating characteristics.
toxicity-monitoring.body:
## What it is

Inside a trial the question is prospective: given a toxicity the protocol defines, when should enrollment pause? [sec-safety-tox]

The traditional counterpart is a repeated exact binomial test of $H_0: q \le \bar q$ after every five patients, up to 40, with $\bar q = 0.2$. A Pocock-type version uses the same nominal level at every look. [13/the-traditional-counterpart]

The Bayesian rule takes a Beta(0.5, 2.5) prior and, after every five patients, pauses if [13/the-bayesian-rule]

$$
\Pr(q > \bar q \mid x, n) > \kappa, \qquad \kappa = 0.75.
$$

This is eq-safety-toxrule. [13/the-bayesian-rule] It reduces to a table of counts, which is how it goes into a protocol and a DMC charter. [13/the-bayesian-rule]

## Why it matters

The type I error of a safety boundary is a design choice stated with its consequences, set by the asymmetric loss between exposing patients and delaying a good drug. [13/operating-characteristics]

## In the book

The Bayesian rule stops at 3 of the first 5 patients and 11 of 40. The Pocock-type rule at overall level 0.05 requires 4 of the first 5, and 14 of 40. [13/the-bayesian-rule] The Bayesian rule is a constant-nominal-level repeated test at these looks. It does not escape repeated-testing arithmetic and chooses a point on it. [13/the-bayesian-rule]

Operating characteristics are exact, from a dynamic program with no simulation. At the acceptable rate 0.2 the Bayesian rule pauses with probability 0.384. At a true rate of 0.3 expected enrollment is 19.7 of 40. [13/key-points]

## Pitfalls

- A DMC would not follow either table mechanically. The boundary is a flag that triggers a review. [13/operating-characteristics]
- The false alarm probability is guaranteed only for the stated schedule, not for looks off it. [sec-safety-link]

## Check yourself

- Q: Is the Bayesian toxicity rule outside the family of repeated tests? A: No. It matches a Pocock-type test with a constant nominal level. [13/the-bayesian-rule]

tox_bayes_boundary(
  looks = seq(5, 40, 5),
  qbar = 0.2,
  kappa = 0.75,
  a0 = 0.5,

)
functions.description: Stop at look n when the number of toxicities t satisfies \Pr(q > \bar q \mid t, n) > \kappa with a Beta(a0, b0) prior.

functions.name: tox_pocock_boundary
functions.title: Pocock-type repeated binomial boundary for toxicity monitoring
functions.description: One-sided repeated exact binomial tests of H_0: q \le \bar q at the same looks, with a common nominal level a at every look: stop at look n if P(X_n \ge t \mid \bar q) \le a. The nominal a is the largest value on a fine grid whose overall stopping probability at qbar does not exceed alpha.

trailblazer-alz-2.name: TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2
trailblazer-alz-2.summary: A donanemab trial in early Alzheimer's disease with a biomarker-guided treatment duration and baseline tau strata, used to show how a Bayesian analysis could handle prespecified features.
trailblazer-alz-2.body:
## What it is
TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 randomized 1,736 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease to donanemab or placebo, with efficacy measured at 18 months (76 weeks). [21/the-trial-as-conducted-2]
It reported a 35 percent slowing of decline on the integrated Alzheimer's Disease Rating Scale in the prespecified low and medium tau population of 1,182 participants, and 22 percent in the combined population of 1,736. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-2]

## Why it matters
It is a different kind of case from SELECT: the traditional apparatus handled two prespecified features, and regulators accept them when specified in advance. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-2]

## In the book
The first feature is treatment duration guided by a biomarker: participants completed donanemab once they reached a prespecified level of amyloid plaque clearance, and 52 percent of the low and medium tau participants had reached it by one year. [21/two-prespecified-design-features]
The trial therefore estimates the effect of the strategy "stop when cleared" against placebo, and the estimand has to say so. [21/two-prespecified-design-features]
The second is baseline tau stratification, which does not change with accumulating results and is not an adaptive feature. [21/two-prespecified-design-features]
A prespecified hierarchical model could estimate effects in both strata, 1,182 in the low and medium tau stratum and 552 in the high tau stratum, with borrowing. [21/two-prespecified-design-features]
The weight on a stratum's own estimate is $\tau_b^2/(\tau_b^2 + s^2)$, so smaller strata and smaller between-stratum variance mean more shrinkage; the table in the book is illustrative, not the trial's estimates. [21/two-prespecified-design-features]

## Pitfalls
A hierarchical model that shrinks a null stratum toward a positive pooled effect raises the false-positive rate for that stratum. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-2]
Such a model needs a prespecified model, a rationale for exchangeability and a simulation of type I error where the effect is in one stratum only. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-2]

## Check yourself
- Q: Is the tau stratification an adaptation? A: No, tau is measured at baseline and the strata do not change with results. [21/two-prespecified-design-features]
- Q: What does a regulator worry about for the biomarker-guided duration? A: The estimand and the integrity of blinding. [21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have-had-to-accept-2]

21/what-a-dmc-and-a-regulator-would-have.t: What a DMC and a regulator would have had to accept

trial-cost.name: Trial cost
trial-cost.summary: The money a trial spends, split in the book into variable cost that scales with person-time and fixed cost that does not, so that early stopping saves only part of the budget.
trial-cost.body:
## What it is
Moore and colleagues reviewed the pivotal trials of 59 novel agents approved by the FDA in 2015 and 2016. [21/trial-cost]
The median estimated cost of a pivotal trial was 19.0 million dollars, the costliest single trial was about 347 million, and the mean for the five cardiovascular pivotal trials was 157.2 million. [21/trial-cost]

## Why it matters
Cost is one of the currencies in which the book prices the SELECT saving. [sec-cases-worth]
The saving is not proportional to the whole budget: variable costs such as site payments, visits, monitoring, laboratory work and drug supply scale with person-time, while fixed costs such as protocol development, startup, regulatory work and the final analysis do not. [21/trial-cost]

## In the book
The book has no published cost for SELECT, which is far larger than the typical trial in that review. [21/trial-cost]
It takes the cardiovascular mean of 157 million dollars as the base case and 350 million and 600 million as scenarios for a larger trial, not as estimates for any particular trial. [21/trial-cost]
The modeled saving is the avoided share of person-time times the variable share, and the variable share is an assumption because the split is proprietary. [21/trial-cost]
For a trial of SELECT's size the modeled saving is of the order of tens to a couple of hundred million dollars. [21/trial-cost]

## Pitfalls
The figure leaves out the cost of longer exposure that a regulator might require to build the safety database, which would reduce the saving. [21/trial-cost]
The book ranks the cost row as an order of magnitude, a weaker basis than the events and patient-years rows. [21/summary-of-the-accounting]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the saving smaller than the avoided share of the budget? A: Only variable cost scales with person-time, and fixed cost does not. [21/trial-cost]
- Q: Is 157 million dollars the cost of SELECT? A: No, it is the cardiovascular mean from the review, used as a base case. [21/trial-cost]

trialr.name: trialr
trialr.summary: An R package for Bayesian clinical trial designs fitted with Stan, including dose finding and phase II designs.
trialr.body:
## What it is
trialr is an R package for Bayesian clinical trial designs fitted with Stan. [sec-software-tools] It includes dose-finding and phase II designs. [sec-software-tools]

## Why it matters
It is one of the established tools listed for readers who want existing implementations. [sec-software-tools]

## In the book
The book lists it among the R packages on CRAN, and did not check its version. [sec-software-tools]

## Pitfalls
The descriptions in the book cover only the purpose of each tool, so a reader should consult the documentation for current features and versions. [sec-software-tools]

## Check yourself
- Q: Which engine does trialr use to fit designs? A: Stan. [sec-software-tools]
- Q: Which kinds of designs does it include? A: Dose-finding and phase II designs. [sec-software-tools]

truncated-trial-bias.name: Truncated trial bias
truncated-trial-bias.summary: A trial stopped early because the observed effect was large overstates the true effect, and a boundary does nothing for the estimate at stopping.
truncated-trial-bias.body:
## What it is

A trial that stops at an early look because it crossed a boundary stopped because the observed effect was large, and a large observed effect is more likely to be a positive deviation from the truth. The estimate is biased away from the null. The bias is bigger the smaller the trial and the earlier the stop. [11/what-a-dmc-does]

## Why it matters

A boundary controls the type I error but does nothing for the point estimate at stopping. Even an O'Brien-Fleming design is not immune. A trial stopped early should report its estimate with the information fraction and the interval in view. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

## In the book

Bassler and colleagues matched 91 randomized trials stopped early for benefit, asking 63 distinct questions, to 424 nontruncated trials. The pooled ratio of relative risks was 0.71 (95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.77), so truncated trials gave on average a 29 percent lower relative risk. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

The difference was independent of whether a statistical stopping rule was present and of methodological quality, and it was greatest in smaller studies. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

The frequentist remedy is a bias-adjusted estimator, and a shrinkage prior is the Bayesian answer. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

## Pitfalls

- The size of the problem is debated. Freidlin and Korn argue the bias is smaller when boundaries are conservative. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]
- Bayesian shrinkage can reduce upward selection bias, but its bias and coverage depend on the prior and should be evaluated under the stopping rule. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

## Check yourself

- Q: What ratio of relative risks did Bassler and colleagues find? A: 0.71, truncated over nontruncated. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]
- Q: Does a conservative boundary remove the bias? A: No, it controls type I error but not the estimate at stopping. [11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler-and-colleagues-2010]

11/truncated-trials-overestimate-bassler.t: Truncated trials overestimate: Bassler and colleagues (2010)

two-bars.name: The two bars
two-bars.summary: A fixed-level test passes a constant bar on Z squared, while a Bayes rule passes a bar that grows with the logarithm of the information, and the two cross.
two-bars.body:
## What it is

A fixed-level one-sided test acts when $Z_n^2$ passes a constant bar, 3.84 at one-sided alpha 0.025, whatever the sample size. A Bayes rule that acts when the alternative is at least as probable as the null passes a bar that grows with the log of the information [sec-evidence-twobars]:

$$
Z_n^2 \;\ge\; L_n + C, \qquad L_n \sim \log n, \qquad C = 2\log\frac{\pi_0}{\pi_a}.
$$

This is eq-bayes-toll. The constant $C$ is zero at equal prior odds and positive when the null is favored [sec-evidence-twobars].

## Why it matters

At small samples the Bayes bar is lower, at large samples higher [sec-evidence-twobars]. They cross where, with $C = 0$,

$$
n^\ast \;=\; e^{z_\alpha^2} \;=\; e^{3.84} \;\approx\; 46.
$$

This is eq-crossing. The exact Gaussian expression puts the crossing at $I_n\tau^2 = 41.6$ [sec-evidence-twobars]. So the claim that Bayesian trials need less evidence fails against a single unadjusted look [sec-evidence-twobars].

## In the book

For $\tau = 0.25$ on the log hazard ratio, the crossing corresponds to $I_n > 730$ and about 2,900 events (exactly 666 and about 2,660), the size of a large cardiovascular outcome trial [sec-evidence-twobars]. A third toll for monitoring raises the bar by about 7.38 at alpha 0.025 [sec-evidence-tolls].

## Pitfalls

The comparison is for the uncalibrated point-null rule with a symmetric normal alternative. A Bayesian bar calibrated to the same type I error is never lower at a single look without an informative prior [sec-evidence-twobars].

## Check yourself

- Q: Which bar is higher for a very large trial, the fixed-level test or the uncalibrated Bayes rule? A: The Bayes rule [sec-evidence-twobars].
- Q: Where do the bars cross for a unit-information prior? A: At about 46 observations, exactly 41.6 [sec-evidence-twobars].

functions.name: crossing_n
functions.title: Information ratio at which the Bayes bar equals the fixed-level bar
functions.description: Solves (1+k)/k\,(\log(1+k) + 2\log c) = z_\alpha^2 for the information ratio k. For c = 1 (and c < 1) the Bayes bar increases through the fixed bar once (the Lindley regime), so there is one root. For c > 1 the bar is large at small k, dips, and rises again: there can be two roots, or none if the dip stays above the fixed bar. The scalar value is the upper crossover, the k beyond which the Bayes bar stays above the fixed bar; all = TRUE returns every root.

results.name: The Bayes factor bar exceeds the fixed level bar once information times prior variance passes about 46
results.summary: Against a single unadjusted look, the Bayes rule with a point null asks for more evidence than the fixed level test once the data carry about 46 times the information in the prior.
results.statement: At one sided $\alpha = 0.025$ the fixed level test acts when $Z_n \ge z_\alpha = 1.96$ (that is, $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge 3.84$), and the Bayes rule with equal prior odds acts, asymptotically, when $Z_n > 0$ and $Z_n^2 \ge L_n$ with $L_n = \log(1 + I_n\tau^2) \approx \log n$. They cross at $n^\ast = e^{3.84} \approx 46$, that is at $I_n\tau^2 \approx 46$ (the exact Gaussian expression gives 41.6), which is $n > 46$ for a unit information prior. At $\tau = 0.25$ on the log hazard ratio scale this needs $I_n > 730$, about 2,900 events (exact crossing 41.6: 666 and about 2,660 events). Beyond the crossing the Bayesian bar against a single unadjusted look is the higher one.

two-group-comparison.name: Two-group comparison
two-group-comparison.summary: The basic trial question of whether two arms differ, built in the book from one simulated trial with a binary and a continuous endpoint.
two-group-comparison.body:
## What it is
A trial ends with two rows of numbers, one per arm, and the question: are they different? [sec-testing] The book uses one trial with 100 patients per arm, allocated by a fair coin. [sec-testing-example] The binary version has a control response rate of 30% and a true drug rate of 45%. The continuous version has a true extra fall of 4 mmHg in systolic blood pressure and a patient standard deviation of 12 mmHg. [sec-testing-example]

## Why it matters
Patients differ, so a difference in averages comes with a question attached: would a gap like this appear anyway, from the luck of which patients landed where? [sec-testing-example] A test is a procedure for answering it honestly. [sec-testing-example] Notation: $p_j$ is the response probability in arm $j$, with $j = 0$ for control, and $\theta$ is the treatment effect, $p_1 - p_0$ or $\mu_1 - \mu_0$. [sec-testing-example]

## In the book
In the simulated binary trial 30 of 100 respond on control and 45 of 100 on the drug. [sec-testing-example] RECOVERY's dexamethasone comparison is statistically the same kind of trial: 482 of 2104 (22.9%) died on dexamethasone against 1110 of 4321 (25.7%) on usual care, an age-adjusted rate ratio of 0.83 (95% CI 0.75 to 0.93). [4/recovery-a-two-group-comparison-a-rate-ratio-and-an-interval] The analysis is frequentist: only a p-value and an interval. The same 2.8 point gap in a trial of 100 per arm would be buried in a standard error of about 0.06. [4/recovery-a-two-group-comparison-a-rate-ratio-and-an-interval]

## Pitfalls
Each patient has two potential outcomes and only one is seen. Randomization makes the observed gap an unbiased estimate of the unobservable average difference, with chance error measured by the standard error. [sec-testing-example]

## Check yourself
- Q: What is the true effect in the binary version? A: 15 percentage points, 45% against 30%. [sec-testing-example]
- Q: Why did the 2.8 point RECOVERY gap decide the question? A: The trial had thousands of patients, not 100 per arm. [4/recovery-a-two-group-comparison-a-rate-ratio-and-an-interval]

4/recovery-a-two-group-comparison-a-rate.t: RECOVERY: a two-group comparison, a rate ratio and an interval

sec-testing.t: Are They Different? Testing From the Ground Up

two-one-sided-tests.name: Two one-sided tests
two-one-sided-tests.summary: A test of equivalence that rejects two one-sided nulls, one at each end of the equivalence interval, and declares equivalence only if both reject.
two-one-sided-tests.body:
## What it is
TOST runs one one-sided test against each end of the equivalence margin, and equivalence is declared only if both reject. This is the same as the confidence interval lying entirely inside the margin. [4/equivalence] For bioequivalence it is applied to $\eta = \log\rho$ and is equivalent to checking that the 90 percent confidence interval lies inside $(\log 0.80, \log 1.25)$. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## Why it matters
Schuirmann's procedure gives the confidence-interval criterion a test form. Westlake had proposed a symmetric confidence interval for the same purpose. [sec-lifecycle-be] TOST is the standard in FDA's final guidance of May 2026. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## In the book
Under a reference prior each one-sided posterior tail probability equals the corresponding one-sided TOST p-value. If both p-values are below 0.05, the posterior probability of equivalence exceeds 0.90. [sec-lifecycle-be] The TOST p-value is the larger of the two one-sided p-values. [sec-lifecycle-be]

## Pitfalls
Most clinical efficacy trials that say equivalence mean noninferiority, and the one-sided test is the more common. Framing a trial as equivalence adds a lower-bound requirement that a noninferiority question does not need. [4/equivalence]

## Check yourself
- Q: When is equivalence declared by TOST? A: Only when both one-sided tests reject. [4/equivalence]
- Q: What is the TOST p-value reported for a data set? A: The larger of the two one-sided p-values. [sec-lifecycle-be]

sec-lifecycle-be.t: Bioequivalence: TOST and a posterior summary

type-i-error.name: Type I error
type-i-error.summary: Rejecting the null when the drug has no effect, a false-positive trial result; its probability is the level alpha of the test.
type-i-error.body:
## What it is
A type I error is rejecting $H_0$ when the drug has no effect: a false-positive trial, which could lead to approval of an ineffective drug if nothing else catches it. Its probability is the level of the test, $\alpha$. [sec-testing-errors] The language of type I and type II errors comes from Neyman and Pearson. [sec-testing-errors] It is a probability computed under the null world. [sec-testing-errors]

## Why it matters
The rate is a promise about the procedure, made before any data exist: if the drug does nothing, at most a fraction $\alpha$ of trials run this way will declare success. [sec-decision-traditional] It is the reason regulators trust the design. [sec-decision-traditional] Regulators fix $\alpha$ by convention and leave $\beta$ to the sponsor. [sec-testing-errors]

## In the book
Run the binary trial many times with no effect and apply the rule "reject if $Z > 1.96$": the rejection rate is the type I error rate, close to the nominal 2.5%. [sec-testing-errors] If a false-positive trial leads to approval, the cost falls mostly on future patients, who receive a drug that does not work. [sec-testing-errors]

## Pitfalls
The promise survives repeated use only if the analysis plan is fixed in advance. [sec-decision-traditional] At fixed information, lowering $\alpha$ generally increases $\beta$ and reduces power. [4/key-points] If a sponsor sees the drug ahead and then declares a one-sided test at 0.05, the type I error doubles to 5%. [sec-testing-sided]

## Check yourself
- Q: In which world is $\alpha$ computed? A: The null world, where the drug does nothing. [sec-testing-errors]
- Q: What happens to the error rate if you test naively at 1.96 at each of four looks? A: The overall one-sided error is about 0.063, more than twice 0.025. [1/what-the-apparatus-costs]

sec-testing-errors.t: Two kinds of error, and power

type-ii-error.name: Type II error
type-ii-error.summary: Failing to reject the null when the drug does work, which means abandoning something useful; its probability is beta and power is one minus beta.
type-ii-error.body:
## What it is
A type II error is failing to reject $H_0$ when the drug does work. Its probability is $\beta$, and the probability of avoiding it, $1 - \beta$, is the [[power]]. [sec-testing-errors] Unlike $\alpha$, $\beta$ is computed under a specific alternative. Power is a function of the true effect, so "90% power" invites the question: for what effect? [sec-testing-errors]

## Why it matters
A type II error falls on future patients, who will not receive a drug that would have helped, and on the sponsor who abandoned it. [sec-testing-errors] Sponsors pay for it, which is why they ask for more efficient designs. [sec-testing-errors]

## In the book
In the simulated trial with 100 patients per arm and a true rise from 30% to 45%, the power is 60%, so a drug that works would be missed four times in ten. [sec-testing-errors] Power is roughly 35% at 50 per arm, 78% at 150 and 97% at 300, and the customary 80% or 90% needs roughly 160 to 215 patients per arm. [sec-testing-errors] The continuous trial, with a 4 mmHg effect and standard deviation 12 mmHg, has power of about 65% at 100 per arm. [sec-testing-errors]

## Pitfalls
The two errors trade against each other. The only way to improve both at once is a smaller standard error, through more patients, a less noisy endpoint or better use of information. [sec-testing-errors] Success in one observed trial is not evidence that a 60% power design was good. [sec-testing-errors]

## Check yourself
- Q: What does the book call the sample size proportional to at one-sided 0.025 and 90% power? A: $(z_{0.025} + z_{0.10})^2 = 10.51$ divided by the squared standardized effect. [sec-testing-errors]
- Q: Does a large p-value show no effect? A: No. In a trial of 50 per arm the 30% versus 45% drug has power near one in three. [sec-testing-pvalue]

umbrella-trial.name: Umbrella trial
umbrella-trial.summary: A trial that evaluates multiple drugs concurrently for a single disease, often assigning patients to arms by biomarker.
umbrella-trial.body:
## What it is

FDA's June 2026 draft defines an umbrella trial as "a trial designed to evaluate multiple drugs concurrently for a single disease or condition". [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] An umbrella fixes the disease and varies the drug, often assigning patients to arms by biomarker. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

## Why it matters

The three master protocol kinds differ in what is held fixed. A basket fixes the drug and varies the population, as in tissue-agnostic approvals built on a molecular marker. A platform fixes the disease and the infrastructure and lets the drugs change over time. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

## In the book

In practice the terms overlap. I-SPY 2 is a platform with biomarker-defined signatures, and many baskets are platforms for one drug family. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] The taxonomy was set out by Woodcock and LaVange (2017), and early reviews of how often the three designs are used are cited. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] The FDA 2022 final guidance on oncology master protocols recommends a common standard-of-care control for multiple drugs in one disease. [sec-platform]

## Pitfalls

The umbrella is not the same as a platform: an umbrella evaluates drugs concurrently, while a platform lets drugs enter and leave in an ongoing manner. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform] The 2026 FDA text is a draft. [sec-platform]

## Check yourself

- Q: What does an umbrella trial hold fixed? A: The disease. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]
- Q: Which master protocol fixes the drug instead? A: The basket trial. [20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-umbrella-platform]

20/definitions-master-protocol-basket-um.t: Definitions: master protocol, basket, umbrella, platform

utility-function.name: Utility function
utility-function.summary: An elicited value for each joint efficacy and toxicity outcome, averaged under the posterior to score a dose.
utility-function.body:
## What it is
Let $\pi_E(x)$ be the probability of a favorable efficacy outcome at dose $x$ and $\pi_T(x)$ the probability of toxicity. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility] Elicit a utility for each of the four joint outcomes: efficacy without toxicity is best, no efficacy with toxicity worst. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility] The expected utility of a dose is the posterior average. A design picks the dose that maximizes it among acceptable doses, meeting a minimum efficacy and maximum toxicity bound at a stated posterior probability. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility]

## Why it matters
It states the benefit-risk trade-off directly, so the chosen dose can sit below the MTD. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility]

## In the book
In the illustrative curves, toxicity reaches 0.25 at dose 5, so the MTD is dose 5, but expected utility is highest at dose 4. The efficacy gain from 4 to 5 is small and the toxicity cost is not. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility] The numbers 100, 40, 0 and -60 are illustrative, not clinical. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility]

## Pitfalls
Utilities are elicited and subjective, and the winning dose depends on them. The protocol should record who elicited them, from whom, on what basis, and how the result changes if they change. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility]

## Check yourself
- Q: In the book's example, which dose maximizes expected utility? A: Dose 4, one below the MTD. [17/a-bayesian-formulation-utility]

vaccine-efficacy-trial.name: Vaccine efficacy trial
vaccine-efficacy-trial.summary: A trial that estimates vaccine efficacy from case counts in two arms; in the book BNT162b2 is a confirmatory trial whose prespecified Bayesian primary analysis met its success criterion before the emergency use authorization.
vaccine-efficacy-trial.body:
## What it is
A vaccine efficacy trial splits cases between the vaccine and placebo arms, models the vaccine share of cases with a beta-binomial model, and transforms that share into vaccine efficacy (VE); VE of 30% corresponds to a vaccine share of 0.7/1.7. [21/the-bayesian-element] The success bar is set on VE above a clinical margin, not on zero. [21/the-lesson-for-this-chapter]
As the example, the BNT162b2 phase 2/3 trial (Protocol C4591001, Pfizer and BioNTech) began in July 2020, and its statistical analysis plan makes the primary analysis Bayesian. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-3]
Unlike the SELECT and REWIND reconstructions, the Bayesian rule was the trial's own decision rule. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-3]

## Why it matters
It shows a regulatory path already traveled: a minimally informative prior, a margin, calibration to 0.025 one-sided, and thresholds fixed before the first case. [21/the-lesson-for-this-chapter]

## In the book
The model is conjugate beta-binomial with prior Beta(0.700102, 1) on the vaccine share of cases. [21/the-bayesian-element]
The success criterion is $\Pr(\mathrm{VE} \ge 30\% \mid \text{data})$ above 0.995 at an interim analysis and 0.986 at the final analysis, calibrated so the overall one-sided type I error is 2.5 percent. [21/the-bayesian-element]
The final analysis was planned at 164 first primary cases, with a nonbinding futility rule at a predictive probability of success of 5 percent or less. [21/the-bayesian-element]
The bar is on vaccine efficacy of 30 percent and not on zero, so the criterion has $a$ different from zero. [21/the-bayesian-element]
The trial counted 8 cases in the vaccine group and 162 in the placebo group, an efficacy of 95.0 percent with a 95 percent credible interval of 90.3 to 97.6 percent. [21/what-happened-and-what-the-regulator-did]
FDA issued an emergency use authorization on 11 December 2020 for ages 16 and older and approved the biologics license application on 23 August 2021. [21/what-happened-and-what-the-regulator-did]

## Pitfalls
The plan on ClinicalTrials.gov is a sponsor document with several amendments. [21/the-lesson-for-this-chapter]
FDA's announcements contain no statement on the Bayesian criterion, so the lesson concerns the sponsor's side. [23/bnt162b2-thresholds-calibrated-to-25]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why are there two thresholds, 0.995 and 0.986? A: One applies at the interim analyses and one at the final, calibrated for 2.5 percent overall. [21/the-bayesian-element]
- Q: How does this case differ from SELECT? A: The Bayesian analysis was the actual analysis, not a counterfactual. [21/the-trial-as-conducted-3]

21/what-happened-and-what-the-regulator-.t: What happened and what the regulator did

sec-cases-bnt.t: BNT162b2: a Bayesian confirmatory trial that led to an authorization

villes-inequality.name: Ville's inequality
villes-inequality.summary: For a test martingale, the probability that it ever reaches 1/alpha under the null is at most alpha, whatever the looks or the reason for stopping.
villes-inequality.body:
## What it is

For a test martingale $E_n$ with $E_0 = 1$, the bound holds for the whole path: [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

$$
\mathbb{P}_{H_0}\Bigl(\sup_{n} E_n \ge 1/\alpha\Bigr) \le \alpha .
$$

[12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality] Markov's inequality gives the bound at one fixed time. Ville's inequality gives it for the supremum over all times, the probability that the wealth is ever above $1/\alpha$. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

## Why it matters

The gambler may look after every patient, pause, resume, or stop for a reason the protocol never considered. The probability of ever declaring success under the null is still at most $\alpha$. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality] This is what "anytime-valid" means. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

## In the book

For likelihood ratios the bound is the one Wald used for the error rates of his sequential probability ratio test, and Ville's version covers any nonnegative martingale. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

The proof takes the first time $T$ at which $E_n \ge 1/\alpha$. The stopped process is again a nonnegative martingale, so its expectation is one, and Markov's inequality at the stopping time gives $\mathbb{P}(T \le n) \le \alpha$. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality] The argument does not use the distribution of the data, the number of looks, or the reason for stopping. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

In safety monitoring the same bound applies to a Bayes factor computed with a fixed prior under the alternative. [sec-safety-monitor]

## Pitfalls

- The bound is not tight. The wealth overshoots the boundary when it crosses, so the realized type I error is often below nominal. [12/two-arm-binary-design]

## Check yourself

- Q: What changes between Markov's and Ville's inequality? A: Markov bounds the wealth at one fixed time. Ville bounds the supremum over all times. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]
- Q: Does Ville's inequality need the stopping rule to be prespecified? A: No. The proof does not use the number of looks or the reason for stopping. [12/test-martingales-and-villes-inequality]

wald-sprt.name: Wald's sequential test
wald-sprt.summary: Accumulate the log likelihood ratio and stop when it leaves an interval, giving the smallest expected sample size at fixed error rates but no maximum size.
wald-sprt.body:
## What it is

For simple hypotheses $H_0$ and $H_1$, accumulate the log likelihood ratio $\Lambda_n = \sum_{i\le n} \log\{p_1(X_i)/p_0(X_i)\}$. Stop when it leaves $(\log B, \log A)$ with $A = (1-\beta)/\alpha$ and $B = \beta/(1-\alpha)$, accepting $H_1$ at the upper edge and $H_0$ at the lower. [sec-ch10-wald]

This is the posterior odds rule of a Bayesian with a two-point prior. Wald and Wolfowitz proved it has the smallest expected sample size under both hypotheses among tests with the same error probabilities. [sec-ch10-wald]

## Why it matters

It is the reference point for everything in sequential monitoring. [sec-ch10-wald]

## In the book

For a unit-variance normal mean, $H_0: \theta = 0$ against $H_1: \theta = 0.2$ with $\alpha = 0.025$ and $\beta = 0.10$, a fixed-sample test needs 263 patients. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is $\theta^2/2 = 0.02$ per patient, and Wald's approximation to the expected sample size under $H_1$ follows. [sec-ch10-wald]
$$
\mathbb{E}_1[T] \approx \frac{(1-\beta)\log\{(1-\beta)/\alpha\} + \beta \log\{\beta/(1-\alpha)\}}{\mathrm{KL}(P_1 \| P_0)}.
$$
[sec-ch10-wald]

Whitehead's triangular test is a closed alternative whose boundaries converge at the maximum information, so the trial always ends with a decision. [sec-ch10-families]

## Pitfalls

- The sample size has no upper bound. The 95th percentile under $H_1$ is above the fixed-sample size, and a few trials run several times longer. [sec-ch10-wald]
- It tests two simple hypotheses, whereas a trial's alternative is composite. The remedy is a prior on the effect and the mixture likelihood ratio. [sec-ch10-wald]

## Check yourself

- Q: Which hypotheses does the SPRT assume? A: Two simple hypotheses. [sec-ch10-wald]
- Q: Why do trials use group sequential designs instead? A: They have a hard end, a maximum sample size. [sec-ch10-wald]

weighted-log-rank-test.name: Weighted log-rank test
weighted-log-rank-test.summary: A log-rank variant, with Fleming-Harrington weights or the MaxCombo maximum, that favors late events when an effect is delayed.
weighted-log-rank-test.body:
## What it is
The Fleming-Harrington test multiplies each event time's contribution by $S(t)^\rho\{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma$, with $S$ the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate. [sec-survival-nph-tests] $\rho = \gamma = 0$ is the ordinary log-rank test. $(0, 1)$ weights late events. [sec-survival-nph-tests] The MaxCombo test takes the largest of usually four standardized statistics with $\rho, \gamma \in \{0, 1\}$ and refers it to their multivariate normal distribution. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## Why it matters
Under a delayed effect the weighted and MaxCombo tests have more power than the log-rank test. Under proportional hazards the order reverses: MaxCombo gives up a little, the late-weighted test more. [sec-survival-nph-tests] All three hold the level under identical curves. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## In the book
Under a 2-year delay followed by hazard ratio 0.583, the log-rank test has power 0.55, against 0.80 for FH(0,1) and 0.74 for MaxCombo. [sec-survival-nph-tests] Under proportional hazards (HR 0.75) the figures are 0.67, 0.55 and 0.65 (a fresh simulation; the 0.68 on the non-proportional-hazards page differs by Monte Carlo error). [sec-survival-nph-tests] Under the null the levels are 0.024, 0.022 and 0.021. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## Pitfalls
These test identical curves, and can reject when early harm and late benefit cancel, so significance need not mean patients did better. Modestly weighted tests were proposed to control that risk. [sec-survival-nph-tests] The primary test, weights and simulation go in the protocol before the curves are seen. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

## Check yourself
- Q: What weights does FH(0,1) favor? A: Late events. [sec-survival-nph-tests]
- Q: What does MaxCombo trade? A: A small power premium under proportional hazards for not knowing the shape. [sec-survival-nph-tests]

functions.title: Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank statistics for two groups
functions.description: Computes the standardized weighted log-rank statistics with Fleming-Harrington weights \eqn{S(t)^\rho \{1 - S(t)\}^\gamma}, where S is the pooled Kaplan-Meier estimate just before each event time, for the four pairs \eqn{(\rho, \gamma) \in \{(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)\}}, together with the correlation matrix of the four statistics. The first statistic is the ordinary log-rank test. The maximum of the four, referred to the multivariate normal distribution with this correlation matrix, is the MaxCombo test.

winners-curse.name: Winner's curse
winners-curse.summary: The largest of several observed effects is on average too large because it was selected as the largest, and shrinkage corrects it.
winners-curse.body:
## What it is

The largest of $k$ observed effects is on average too large, because it was selected as the largest. A hierarchical estimate pulls it back toward the mean by about the right amount. [10/the-idea]

## Why it matters

The correction for selection is an estimate that is smaller and more honest, not a harder test applied to an estimate that is still biased. [10/a-numerical-illustration-the-winners-curse]

## In the book

Six arms have true effects drawn from $N(0, 0.2^2)$ on the log odds scale, each estimated with standard error 0.28. The trial reports the arm with the largest observed effect. [10/a-numerical-illustration-the-winners-curse]

The raw estimate of the selected arm is too high on average, while the shrunken estimate has no average bias and a smaller root mean squared error. [10/a-numerical-illustration-the-winners-curse]

The same logic applies to the RECOVERY subgroups: estimates move toward the overall effect in proportion to how little information each carries. [10/a-large-trial-with-many-subgroups-recovery]

## Pitfalls

- In the simulation the true between-arm spread was known. In a real trial it is estimated, which adds uncertainty, and the model is only as good as its exchangeability assumption. [10/a-numerical-illustration-the-winners-curse]
- A related effect appears at early stops: the estimate after an early stop is biased away from the null. [10/the-idea]

## Check yourself

- Q: Does the raw estimate of the best-looking arm tend to be too high or too low? A: Too high. [10/a-numerical-illustration-the-winners-curse]
- Q: What does the book say fixes it? A: A smaller, shrunken estimate, not a harder test. [10/a-numerical-illustration-the-winners-curse]

womens-health-initiative.name: Women's Health Initiative
womens-health-initiative.summary: The estrogen plus progestin trial in healthy postmenopausal women, stopped early for harm on the monitoring board's recommendation in 2002.
womens-health-initiative.body:
## What it is

The estrogen plus progestin trial of the Women's Health Initiative, in healthy postmenopausal women, was stopped early for harm on the recommendation of its data monitoring committee. The principal results were published in JAMA in July 2002. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]

## Why it matters

It shows a stop for harm as a decision under uncertainty, made with discretion by people who see unblinded data and are independent of the sponsor. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]

## In the book

At the board's recommendation on 31 May 2002, after a mean of 5.2 years of follow-up, the test statistic for invasive breast cancer had exceeded the stopping boundary for that adverse effect and the global index statistic supported risks exceeding benefits. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]

Hazard ratios with nominal 95% confidence intervals: 1.26 (1.00 to 1.59) for invasive breast cancer (290 cases), 1.29 (1.02 to 1.63) for coronary heart disease (286 cases), 1.41 (1.07 to 1.85) for stroke, and 1.15 (1.03 to 1.28) for the global index. Total mortality was not affected, at 0.98 (0.82 to 1.18). [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]

## Pitfalls

- The nominal interval for breast cancer reaches 1.00. The stop rested on the crossing of a sequential boundary, not on that interval. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]
- Safety monitoring in such a trial is not a formal alpha-controlled test of a single endpoint. The committee weighs a pattern of outcomes. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]

## Check yourself

- Q: What triggered the stop? A: The statistic for invasive breast cancer exceeded its boundary, and the global index supported risks over benefits. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]
- Q: Was total mortality affected? A: No, the hazard ratio was 0.98. [11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-initiative-2002]

11/a-stop-for-harm-the-womens-health-ini.t: A stop for harm: the Women's Health Initiative (2002)

z-test.name: z test
z-test.summary: The randomization test with a bell curve in place of shuffling: the difference divided by its standard error, read against a standard normal.
z-test.body:
## What it is
Under the null, the difference in response rates is approximately normal with mean zero. The statistic uses the pooled rate $\bar p = (x_0 + x_1)/(2n)$: [sec-testing-z]

$$
Z = \frac{\hat p_1 - \hat p_0}{\sqrt{2\bar p(1-\bar p)/n}} .
$$

This is equation eq-testing-z. [sec-testing-z] The reason is the central limit theorem: the observed difference is an average of many small independent contributions. [sec-testing-z] $Z$ counts standard errors from zero, and $z_{0.025} = 1.96$. [sec-testing-z]

## Why it matters
It replaces heavy shuffling with a formula. [sec-testing-z] The z test is an approximation that is least reliable for binary outcomes at moderate $n$ close to the threshold. [4/key-points]

## In the book
For the binary trial $\bar p = 0.375$, the standard error is 0.0685 and $Z = 2.19$. The one-sided p-value is 0.014 and the two-sided one is 0.029. For the continuous trial $Z = 4.69/1.83 = 2.56$. [sec-testing-z] The randomization test gives one-sided 0.021 for the binary trial, because its tail includes the whole step at 0.15. A continuity correction moves the cutoff to 0.14, giving $Z = 2.04$ and a one-sided p-value near 0.021. [sec-testing-z]

## Pitfalls
With a binary endpoint, moderate $n$ and a p-value near the threshold, the choice of statistic can change the verdict, so the analysis plan names the test exactly. [sec-testing-z] The approximation fails when responses are rare, $n$ is small or extreme values dominate the mean. [sec-testing-z]

## Check yourself
- Q: Why is the pooled rate used? A: The null says both arms have the same $p$. [sec-testing-z]
- Q: Why do shuffling and the z test differ for the binary trial? A: Shuffled differences move in steps and the normal curve effectively counts only half of the step at 0.15. [sec-testing-z]

sec-testing-z.t: The normal approximation and the z test
